varieties.name: Abbondanza

origin.place: San Pietro Capofiume, Molinella, province of Bologna, Emilia-Romagna

varieties.history: A chance seedling found at San Pietro Capofiume near Molinella in 1896, widely planted in Emilia-Romagna and the Veneto from the 1930s to the 1970s and exported. A fully red mutant, Abbondanza Rossa, was found in Ferrara province in 1962. It is now grown mainly by amateurs and listed in the regional register of local varieties.

look.description: Medium, broad round-conical greenish-yellow apple streaked with orange-red (red over the whole skin in the Rossa sport).

taste.summary: Compact, firm cream-white flesh, moderately sweet and fairly juicy with a clear acidity and a strong, wine-like and fairly perfumed flavour. Excellent for cooking and drying as well as eating.
taste.peak: Winter maturity (November on); keeps several months even without refrigeration (Emilia-Romagna register sheet).

tree.notes: Medium vigour, branching tree bearing on spurs and mixed shoots. Flowers and crops abundantly, so thin to keep fruit size; little prone to biennial bearing or pre-harvest drop.

pollination.notes: Mid-late flowering in Italy; Brogdale records full bloom around 12 May (group 3).

climate.best_climates: The Po plain and the Apennine foothills of Emilia-Romagna; noted as adapting to colder hill districts, where it was planted in hedgerows and at woodland edges.
climate.poor_climates: Wet sites with heavy scab pressure.

health.other: Susceptible to scab; tolerates powdery mildew fairly well.

varieties.grow_notes: A robust, heavy-cropping keeper that stores for months even without refrigeration. Thin the crop for size and spray or choose an airy site against scab.

varieties.name: Adams Pearmain
varieties.history: Brought to the attention of the Horticultural Society in London in 1826 by Robert Adams, who sent it in under the name Norfolk Pippin; its birthplace is argued between Norfolk and Herefordshire, where it was grown as Hanging Pearmain. Marketed as Adams's Pearmain, it became a fixture of Victorian and Edwardian gardens and dessert tables.

look.description: Classic tapering pearmain shape; greenish-yellow skin turning golden, with a streaky orange-red flush on the sunny side and patches of russet.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained cream flesh that seems dry at first bite yet holds a fair amount of juice, with a rich, nutty, aromatic flavour in the Egremont Russet mould. Sweet overall, though some tasters find a tart, wine-like acidity (one compared it to a Mosel); it improves in store and is richest in midwinter.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Mar; flavour builds after several weeks in store
taste.peak: a winter apple; Orange Pippin says it keeps 3 months or more

tree.notes: A rather weak-growing partial tip-bearer, so prune lightly and avoid cutting away all the shoot tips. Inclined to crop more heavily in alternate years. There are reports that it may be partly triploid, which would fit its reputation as a poor pollen donor.

pollination.notes: Usually listed in group 3 (some older lists say 2; it flowers a little ahead of Cox at Brogdale). Reported to be a poor pollinator of other varieties. Blossom has a reputation for frost tolerance.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist lowland Britain and comparable mild maritime regions, where it has been grown for two centuries.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to leave the fruit dull and soft; no record of it doing well in warm regions.

health.other: Generally regarded as a healthy variety with good scab resistance; other disease ratings not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A good keeper for a garden orchard in southern or eastern England. Choose a reasonably vigorous rootstock to compensate for its modest growth, prune with tip-bearing in mind, and plant a group 2-4 diploid nearby for pollination.

varieties.name: Aia Ilu

origin.parentage: Open-pollinated seedling of Antonovka

varieties.history: Raised in 1946 by Aleksander Siimon at the Polli fruit-breeding station in Estonia from an open-pollinated Antonovka seedling. The name means 'garden beauty'; it is propagated by nurseries but not widely grown.

look.description: Very large, round to slightly conical apple, fully yellow when ripe with a faint red cheek on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Juicy, yellowish-white flesh of medium firmness with a sweet-sour flavour and only a weak aroma.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Nov; keeps a couple of months
taste.peak: Ripens in September and keeps a couple of months (et.wikipedia).

tree.notes: Medium-vigour tree with a rounded crown; bears young, regularly and heavily. Large white flowers with pink-edged petals.

pollination.notes: Flowers relatively early according to Estonian sources; no UK group recorded.

climate.best_climates: Cold Baltic and Nordic climates, where it is regarded as fully winter-hardy.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers and mild winters; untested outside northern Europe.

health.other: Sources disagree on scab: one rates its resistance low, another calls the variety disease-resistant. Resistant to powdery mildew.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy, productive autumn apple for very cold gardens. Harvest in September; the large fruit suits drying and stewing as well as eating.

varieties.name: Akane

origin.parentage: Jonathan x Worcester Pearmain

varieties.history: Bred in Morioka in the late 1930s (sources give 1937 or 1939) by crossing Jonathan with the English Worcester Pearmain, and only named and released around 1970. Its good disease resistance has made it a favourite of low-spray growers in North America.

look.description: Glossy, almost entirely cherry-red skin over a yellow-green ground; fruit can be small unless thinned.

taste.summary: Firm rather than crunchy, with plenty of juice and an unusually well-judged sweet-sharp balance in the Jonathan style, lifted by a strong apple perfume. Cut flesh is slow to brown, but picked fruit turns grainy within a few days, so eat it promptly; it hangs well on the tree for weeks and cooks to a pinkish sauce.
taste.best_eaten: late Aug-Sep, straight from the tree
taste.peak: Early season (NFC picks mid August); Orange Pippin says it does not keep well, best eaten fresh

tree.notes: Comes into bearing early and crops well. Thin the fruitlets for better size; ripe apples tend to drop.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 4; needs a compatible partner flowering at the same time.

climate.best_climates: Does well in warm-summer temperate climates (Japan, the US mid-Atlantic and Pacific Northwest) yet tolerates cold winters; colours readily.
climate.poor_climates: In cool, dull maritime summers fruit can stay small; its short keeping life limits its value where a long season is wanted.

health.other: Generally healthy; some resistance to scab, mildew, fire blight and cedar-apple rust. Pre-harvest drop and small fruit are the usual complaints.

varieties.grow_notes: A good early red apple for low-spray gardens. Thin hard in June for decent size and pick promptly as the fruit colours, since it drops and does not keep.

varieties.name: Åkerö

origin.place: Probably Åkerö manor, near Bettna, Södermanland, Sweden
origin.parentage: Unknown; one Wikipedia account suggests Grågylling x Vitgylling, and the Swedish pomologist C. G. Dahl thought it might be the German Schmidts Junkerapfel. Neither is proven.

varieties.history: An old Swedish dessert apple named in the 1850s by the pomologist Olof Eneroth after the manor where the oldest known tree grows; it may have been there since the mid-1700s. Long regarded in Sweden as one of the finest home-grown apples, it is the provincial apple of Södermanland and was once widely planted in Scandinavia and northern Germany.

look.description: Tall, egg-shaped fruit with a pale primrose to whitish-yellow skin, streaked and flushed pinkish red on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Firm, even hard, very juicy pale flesh with a sweet-sharp balance and an unusual aromatic, slightly spicy character that some describe as raspberry-like. Rather hard when first picked and better after some weeks in store.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Dec in Scandinavia; English records suggest it is ready earlier and keeps less well
taste.peak: Wikipedia cultivar list: best in November, keeps until February (Swedish conditions).

tree.notes: Strong, upright, almost pear-like branch habit. Swedish advice is to prune moderately and go easy on nitrogen but be generous with potash. Fruit may drop if left on the tree after it ripens.

pollination.notes: Early flowering; needs an early-blooming partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool northern European summers; in Sweden it is recommended from the south up to about the middle of the country (Swedish zones II-IV).
climate.poor_climates: Not recorded in hot climates; a Scandinavian apple unlikely to colour or keep well where summers are hot.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well documented in English sources; fruit tends to drop once ripe.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a partner that flowers early, and allow room for its tall upright growth. Feed lightly with nitrogen. Sources disagree on timing: the National Fruit Collection in Kent picks it as early as late August, while Swedish and Orange Pippin records place it in September-October and say it keeps into winter.

varieties.name: Alfriston
varieties.history: Raised in the late 1700s by a Mr Shepherd at Uckfield in Sussex and first known as Shepherd's Pippin; it took the name Alfriston in 1819. A respected Victorian cooker, it received an RHS Award of Merit in 1920.

look.description: Big, broad, slightly ribbed green to greenish-yellow cooker, with at most an orange tinge on the sunny side.

taste.summary: A sharp cooking apple with a brisk, fairly sugary acidity and coarse, yellowish flesh that is not especially juicy. It cooks down to a soft purée.
taste.peak: Wikipedia: use November to April.

tree.notes: Vigorous; fairly upright when young, spreading with age. A partial tip-bearer with some tendency to crop biennially, so prune lightly and renew rather than spur back hard.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering; needs a group 2-4 partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist British conditions; reported to cope even with exposed upland sites.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot or low-chill climates; an English late cooker is likely to struggle there.

health.other: Generally healthy, with some resistance to scab and canker; mildew resistance is variously reported as good or only average.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy, vigorous cooker suited to organic growing in most of Britain. Store the fruit cool for use through winter; it needs a mid-season pollinator.

varieties.name: Alkmene

origin.place: Kaiser Wilhelm Institute, Müncheberg, Brandenburg, Germany
origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Geheimrat Dr. Oldenburg
origin.raised_by: Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Breeding Research

varieties.history: Bred at Müncheberg in eastern Germany around 1930 from Cox's Orange Pippin and the German apple Geheimrat Dr. Oldenburg, and sold in Britain as Early Windsor. It holds an RHS Award of Garden Merit and has given the red sports Red Alkmene (Red Windsor) and Ceeval.

look.description: Medium, rounded apple with an orange-red flush and bold red stripes over greenish-yellow skin.

taste.summary: A Cox-style apple that is crisper, juicier and a little sharper than Cox, with honeyed sweetness when fully ripe. Firm, dense cream to yellow flesh; flavour is strong but fades within a few weeks of picking.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct, straight from the tree or within 2-3 weeks
taste.peak: Orange Pippin: picked mid-September, keeps only 2-3 weeks.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous spur-bearer that crops heavily; an easy, healthy choice for gardens in cooler parts of Britain.

pollination.notes: Early flowering and reported self-fertile; also a good pollen donor. Blossom is vulnerable to spring frost.

climate.best_climates: Cool to mild temperate climates such as Britain, including the north and Scotland, and northern Europe.
climate.poor_climates: Frost pockets threaten its early blossom; hot summers are outside its documented range.

health.other: Notably resistant to scab; early blossom is frost-tender.

varieties.grow_notes: A good Cox substitute for colder or wetter gardens where Cox struggles. Avoid frost hollows because it blooms early. Pick when fully coloured and eat soon, as it is a short keeper.

varieties.name: Allington Pippin

origin.parentage: King of the Pippins x Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: Raised by Thomas Laxton in Lincolnshire and first shown as 'Brown's South Lincoln Beauty', winning an RHS First Class Certificate in 1894. The Maidstone nursery Bunyard renamed it after the village of Allington in Kent and introduced it in 1896; it was once grown commercially as a dessert apple.

look.description: Neat, flat-ended conical apple, yellow with a modest red flush broken into stripes and a little russet.

taste.summary: Crisp and quite sharp at picking, when it doubles as a baking apple that keeps its shape. After a month or two in store it mellows into an intense, aromatic fruit-drop or pineapple flavour with a bittersweet edge while keeping a fresh acidity; it also makes excellent juice.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Dec, once mellowed in store; usable for cooking from picking
taste.storage_change: Firm enough to bake at picking; after a few months in store it mellows to an intense fruit-drop or pineapple flavour.
taste.peak: After a few months in store

tree.notes: Average vigour, spur-bearing and generally a good cropper, though crops can swing from year to year; thin heavy sets.

pollination.notes: Flowers in group 3 (some lists say 4); partly self-fertile but crops better with a mid-season partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool, temperate maritime climates such as lowland England, including the cooler east and north.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would likely soften the fruit and dull the flush; no record of success in warm regions.

health.other: Average overall disease resistance with some tolerance of scab; fruit reported to be prone to brown rot.

varieties.grow_notes: A dual-purpose garden apple that copes with ordinary English conditions. Thin in heavy years to even out cropping, and store the fruit a few weeks before eating fresh to let the flavour develop.

varieties.name: Amanda

origin.place: Long Ashton Research Station, near Bristol, England
origin.parentage: From Long Ashton's cider-apple crosses using Michelin, Dabinett, James Grieve Red and Worcester Pearmain; its own cross is not stated in the sources found
origin.raised_by: Liz Copas and Ray Williams, Long Ashton Research Station

varieties.history: One of 'The Girls', a set of cider apples mostly named after women, bred at Long Ashton between 1985 and 2003 and released by 2008. The aim was earlier-ripening bittersweets for England's commercial cider makers.

look.description: Medium to large greenish-yellow fruit with a variable red flush.

taste.summary: A medium bittersweet: low acid with over 0.2% tannin. It is used in early pressings rather than eaten.
taste.best_eaten: Not a dessert apple; press soon after harvest

tree.notes: Heavy-cropping and a partial tip-bearer, so avoid hard pruning of all the shoot tips.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group C (= 3) by one database; the RHS calls it early-flowering.

climate.best_climates: Southern and western English cider country; RHS hardiness H6 means it copes with cold winters throughout the UK and northern Europe.
climate.poor_climates: No records outside the UK.

health.other: No variety-specific disease data published; the RHS lists only the general apple problems.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant it in full sun on moist, well-drained soil, ideally facing south or west with shelter. It is a modern bittersweet for cider makers who want an early pressing before Dabinett and Michelin.

varieties.name: Ambassy

origin.parentage: A more highly coloured sport (clone) of Delcorf / Delbarestivale, which is itself Golden Delicious x Stark Jonagrimes

varieties.history: A French colour sport of Delcorf (sold in Britain as Delbard Estivale), selected for a redder skin and marketed by the French nursery Dalival under the names Ambassy and Dalili. The National Fruit Collection received it in 1994. Some fruit guides simply treat it as another trade name for Estivale.

look.description: Yellow apple heavily washed and streaked with orange-red, more brightly coloured than ordinary Delcorf.

taste.summary: Sweet, crisp and juicy, with enough acidity to taste fresher than its Golden Delicious parent. Tasters of the Delcorf family pick out light strawberry and pear hints; the cream flesh bruises easily but stays crisp for a couple of weeks.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, within two to three weeks of picking

tree.notes: Grows like Delcorf: a productive spur-bearer that holds its fruit well, but crops need thinning or the apples stay small and the tree may slip into alternate bearing.

pollination.notes: Group taken from the parent clone Delcorf/Estivale (group 3). Needs a diploid partner flowering at the same time. One NFC record shows Ambassy in bloom unusually early, so a group 2-3 partner is a safe choice.

climate.best_climates: Temperate western Europe with warm but not baking summers, such as France, the Low Countries and southern England, where the Delcorf family is grown commercially.
climate.poor_climates: In very hot summers early apples like this soften quickly and the red colour, which is the whole point of the sport, develops poorly; cold short-season areas are also marginal.

health.other: Average susceptibility to scab and mildew reported by the nursery. The fruit bruises easily, so handle gently at picking.

varieties.grow_notes: A good early red apple for a sunny site on fertile, well-drained soil. Thin the fruitlets in June to keep size up and help prevent biennial cropping, and plant a group 2-3 diploid nearby for pollination.

varieties.name: Ambrosia

origin.parentage: Chance seedling found among Jonagold trees; parents unknown, probably Golden Delicious with Starking (Red) Delicious or Jonagold

varieties.history: A chance seedling that came up in the Mennell family's orchard at Cawston in British Columbia's Similkameen Valley in the late 1980s, growing in a block of Jonagold. Its looks and sweetness led to commercial propagation in the 1990s, and it is now grown in Canada, Washington, New York, Chile, New Zealand and Europe.

look.description: Large, slightly conical fruit with a bright pinkish-red flush over a cream to pale yellow background.

taste.summary: Very sweet with almost no acidity, giving a pleasant but one-dimensional flavour with a pear-like note and, to some tasters, a light floral scent. Crisp and juicy though not as hard as Braeburn; left at room temperature it softens and turns more pear-like, and the cream flesh is slow to brown.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Jan; keep refrigerated, softens at room temperature
taste.storage_change: Crispness fades quickly at room temperature, when it can turn slightly pear-like; best kept chilled (Orange Pippin).

climate_flavour.note: Wikipedia: colours differently in warmer climates (colour, not flavour).

tree.notes: Comes into bearing young and crops regularly. Fruit ripens unevenly, so commercial orchards usually pick it in two passes.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 4; needs a compatible diploid pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Sunny interior valleys with hot days and cold nights, like its home in southern British Columbia, central Washington and Ontario.
climate.poor_climates: Areas with heavy cedar-apple rust pressure in eastern North America unless sprayed; irrigation stress in hot dry orchards leads to soft scald and poor keeping.

health.other: Very susceptible to cedar-apple rust; some resistance to powdery mildew. Soft scald in store has been linked to water stress in the orchard.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow in full sun with steady irrigation in dry regions. Where junipers are nearby in North America, plan to control cedar-apple rust. Pick over two passes as fruit colours and ripens.

varieties.name: American Golden Pippin
varieties.history: An early 19th-century apple of the lower Hudson Valley, associated with Westchester County and described in Thacher's American Orchardist of 1822. It was still in existence in 1905 but is not held in the UK National Fruit Collection.

look.description: Medium to large, flattish-conical yellow apple, sometimes flushed brownish red, with some russet.

taste.summary: Coarse yellowish flesh with a subacid, aromatic flavour; little else is recorded.

tree.notes: No reliable tree information found.

pollination.notes: Unknown.

climate.best_climates: Known only from the lower Hudson Valley of New York.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: Rare; identity should be checked against old descriptions because 'Golden Pippin' was applied to several different apples, including the unrelated English Golden Pippin.

varieties.name: American Mother

origin.place: Bolton, Massachusetts, USA (farm of General Stephen P. Gardner)

varieties.history: A chance seedling from General Stephen Gardner's farm at Bolton, Massachusetts, recorded in the 1840s. It became popular in Britain and Europe; in Austria's Lavant valley it was introduced around 1882 and is grown as the 'Lavanttaler Bananenapfel' because of its banana-like aroma.

look.description: Medium, slightly tall fruit with thin, smooth golden skin largely covered with red flush and stripes, becoming almost fully red in sun.

taste.summary: Tender, juicy, fine-grained yellow flesh, firm rather than crunchy, that is very sweet with little acid and an intense, unusual perfume that many liken to banana. It needs about a month in store to reach its best, and quality swings widely between seasons and sites: outstanding in a good year, mild and ordinary in a cool one.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Dec, after a few weeks in store
taste.peak: de Wikipedia: ready to eat December-January; Scott Farm: not long keeping

climate_flavour.note: Salt Spring: quality swings from year to year - aromatic and sweet in good years, 'flat and musty' in lesser ones.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous, rather upright tree that is weaker on poor soils; crops regularly with good care.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not verified; plant with another diploid apple of similar season.

climate.best_climates: Cool-temperate climates with cold winters: New England, Britain and central European uplands, where it is reported as undemanding and tolerant of harsh, frosty sites.
climate.poor_climates: Very hot, short-winter regions; though one southern nursery reports it doing well in the North Carolina piedmont, so it is more adaptable than its origin suggests.

health.other: Reported to have little scab and relatively low mildew susceptibility; tolerant of exposed, frost-prone sites.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for a cold or exposed garden. Feed it on poorer soils to keep growth going, and keep the fruit a few weeks before eating to let the aroma develop.

varieties.name: American Summer Pearmain
varieties.history: An old American summer apple of unrecorded origin, first described in 1817 and long valued in eastern US home orchards. It is a parent of Meku.

look.description: Medium, oblong-conical yellow-green apple flushed and streaked with red to purplish red.

taste.summary: Very tender, almost melting, juicy yellow flesh with a sweet, mildly subacid and pleasantly aromatic flavour. Picked early it is crisper and sweeter; left longer it softens and becomes better for pies.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-Sep, straight from the tree; keeps about a week
taste.peak: Aug-Sep (Apples of New York via Bard AppleDB); keeps about a week (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Smallish upright tree, easy for beginners. Fruit ripens over a period, so pick in several passes.

pollination.notes: Group 2 (Orange Pippin; Brogdale full bloom around 5-6 May).

climate.best_climates: Orange Pippin lists it as cold-hardy and suited to cool, warm and cold summers in temperate regions.
climate.poor_climates: No specific reports; very hot summers ripen it early and soften it.

health.other: Average general disease resistance, with some susceptibility to powdery mildew and fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: A good early dessert apple for small gardens; plant with an early-flowering partner. Eat or cook promptly, as the fruit does not keep.

varieties.name: Ananas Reinette
varieties.history: Believed to have arisen in the Netherlands and recorded in 1821, after which it spread through the Rhineland and much of northern Europe. It has been a useful breeding parent: Freiherr von Berlepsch and Zuccalmaglios Renette both descend from it.

look.description: Small, slightly barrel-shaped apple of clear golden yellow, freckled with conspicuous russet dots.

taste.summary: A small, crisp, juicy apple whose high-acid tang is balanced by plenty of sugar and a distinctive pineapple-like scent; some tasters find it almost sweet-shop in character. It grows sweeter as the skin deepens to gold but never loses its tang, and it makes a sharp, aromatic juice. The aroma is fullest after a warm summer.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Jan; keeps into February in a good store
taste.peak: Mid/late October to February (de.wikipedia, 'genussreif').

climate_flavour.note: de.wikipedia: the pineapple scent develops in warm conditions; in dry weather the fruit stays very small with little aroma.

tree.notes: Weak-growing and demanding about soil: it needs a fertile, moisture-retentive site, and on poor or droughty ground the tree and fruit both stay small. Spur-bearing and fairly regular.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering diploid; plant with another group 2-4 variety.

climate.best_climates: Warm, sheltered sites in temperate north-west and central Europe (Netherlands, Rhineland, southern England) with fertile soil and steady summer moisture.
climate.poor_climates: Dry or hot summers give small, less aromatic fruit; cold wet sites aggravate canker and mildew.

health.other: Known to be susceptible to powdery mildew and to fruit-tree canker, especially on heavy or wet soils.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it the best soil you have and a sunny, sheltered spot; a semi-vigorous rootstock helps offset its weak growth. Watch for mildew in spring and cut out canker promptly.

varieties.name: Anis

origin.place: Middle and lower Volga region, Russia
origin.parentage: Folk selection; a family of related clones (Anis Polosatyi, Anis Alyi, Anis Rozovo-polosatyi and others)

varieties.history: 'Anis' is a group of old Volga folk varieties that held the same place in the orchards of Saratov, Samara and neighbouring provinces that Antonovka held further west; surveyors have counted dozens of local forms. This record follows the main striped form, Anis Polosatyi (Anis Seryi). Do not confuse it with the French Fenouillet Gris, which is also sold as 'Anis' and is the apple the National Fruit Collection files under that name.

look.description: Small to medium, distinctly flattened apple, light green with a mottled and striped pinkish-red blush over half or more of the skin, dulled by a heavy bluish bloom.

taste.summary: Fine-grained, juicy white flesh with a sweet-sour balance and a distinctive anise-like fragrance that gives the group its name; ripe fruit is strongly scented.
taste.storage_change: fruit keeps 45-60 days (ru Wikipedia)
taste.peak: eaten from summer to early winter (ru Wikipedia)

tree.notes: Tall, strong tree with a dense crown and tough branches that can carry very large crops. As trees age, fruit size falls and alternate bearing creeps in, so thin and prune to keep it renewing.

pollination.notes: Flowering time under UK conditions not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Hard continental climates of the Volga basin, with very cold winters and hot, dry summers.
climate.poor_climates: Little information from mild maritime or humid climates.

health.other: Described as scab-resistant to moderately resistant. Small fruit is its main commercial drawback.

varieties.grow_notes: A very hardy heirloom for severe climates. Thin heavy crops to keep fruit size up and limit alternate bearing; several distinct Anis clones circulate under the name, so check which one you are buying.

varieties.name: Anna

origin.parentage: Red Hadassiya x Golden Delicious

varieties.history: Bred by Abba Stein at Kibbutz Ein Shemer on Israel's coastal plain by crossing the local low-chill apple Red Hadassiya with Golden Delicious; selected in 1959 and released in the early 1960s. It became the standard apple for subtropical gardens in Florida, the Gulf states, southern California and beyond.

look.description: Golden Delicious-shaped fruit, greenish-yellow with a red flush over about half the skin.

taste.summary: Light, mildly crisp and juicy, with a moderately fruity sweet-sharp balance and, for some tasters, a fresh, grassy finish. Picked early it is tart; left to ripen it turns more floral and sweet but goes soft. Keeps only about a week at room temperature (a few weeks chilled), and slices hold up well in pies and sauce.
taste.best_eaten: Within two weeks of picking (Jun-Jul in subtropical climates)
taste.peak: Very early (June); keeps about a week (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: Vigorous and very precocious. In warm climates it often produces a second, smaller late bloom and crop.

pollination.notes: Flowers very early (group 1). Partly self-fertile but sets much better with Dorsett Golden or Ein Shemer, which bloom at the same time; standard apples flower too late to help.

climate.best_climates: Mild-winter subtropical and warm-temperate places with about 150-350 chill hours: Florida, the Gulf Coast, southern California, Israel, coastal Australia and tropical highlands.
climate.poor_climates: Cold-winter regions: its small chill need is met by midwinter, so it blooms at the first warm spell and loses its flowers to frost. In the UK it would flower very early and crop erratically; the SE England harvest date is extrapolated.

health.other: Average disease resistance; in the humid subtropics watch for fire blight and summer fruit rots. Fruit bruises easily and keeps only briefly.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant with Dorsett Golden or Ein Shemer for a reliable set. In hot climates thin fruit early, summer-prune to keep the tree manageable, and water regularly through dry spells.

varieties.name: Annie Elizabeth

origin.parentage: Believed to be a seedling of Blenheim Orange; pollen parent unknown

varieties.history: Grown from seed by Samuel Greatorex at Knighton on the edge of Leicester around 1857 and named in memory of his infant daughter. The Leicester nursery Harrison & Sons distributed it, and the RHS awarded it a First Class Certificate in 1868; it has remained a favourite late cooker in the Midlands and the north.

look.description: Big, broad-based fruit with noticeable ribs, pale yellow on the shaded side and splashed and streaked bright crimson where the sun reaches it.

taste.summary: White, firm yet tender flesh with a brisk, lively acidity that softens over the winter into a pleasant sweet-sharp balance. Slices keep their shape when cooked, which makes it a good baking and tart apple, and by late winter it is mild enough to eat raw.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Apr; cooks well from picking, better raw after Christmas

tree.notes: Strong, upright grower that can take a few years to settle into cropping, after which it bears regularly. Blossom is fairly tolerant of late frost, which helps in colder districts.

pollination.notes: Flowers mid-late (group 4; at Brogdale a few days after Cox). Pair with a diploid in groups 3-5.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist temperate areas; long valued in the English Midlands and northern Britain for its hardiness, late frost-resistant blossom and long keeping.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer regions are untested and likely to give soft fruit that keeps poorly and loses its acidity.

health.other: Generally reported as a healthy tree with some resistance to scab, canker and mildew; few specific weaknesses recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for a colder or wetter garden where a late-keeping cooker is wanted. Give it room or a semi-dwarfing stock since it grows tall, be patient for the first crops, and store the fruit somewhere cool and frost-free.

varieties.name: Annurca

origin.place: Campania, southern Italy (traditionally the Pozzuoli / Phlegraean Fields area; now mainly the Caserta-Benevento border)

varieties.history: Campania's emblematic apple. Local tradition links it with apples mentioned by Pliny, painted at Herculaneum and described around Pozzuoli in the 16th century, while the modern name turns up in Neapolitan farming literature from the 1840s onwards. It now carries EU protected status as PGI 'Melannurca Campana' and is listed on Slow Food's Ark of Taste.

look.description: Small-to-medium, broad conical apple on a very short stalk; picked greenish-yellow with only a little striped colour, it turns a rich red after being sunned on straw beds.

taste.summary: Firm, very crunchy white flesh with a lively balance of sugar and acidity and a pleasant fragrance. The traditional post-harvest sunning deepens the colour and rounds off the sharpness, and the fruit stays crisp for months in store.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Mar, after the fruit has been reddened
taste.storage_change: Picked before it is ripe and laid out in the sun after picking until it turns red; the pectin changes during this sunning, which shapes the final eating quality.

tree.notes: The short stalk lets fruit fall before it is fully ripe, so in Campania it is picked unripe (from mid-September there) and finished on the ground in the sun. Two selected clones exist, the standard form and 'Rossa del Sud'. Little growing data from outside Italy.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records it flowering late, about with Golden Delicious (roughly group 4). Self-fertility not documented in English sources; assume it needs a partner.

climate.best_climates: Warm Mediterranean valleys and hills of Campania, where long sunny autumns allow the picked fruit to redden outdoors.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, short-season climates: at Brogdale it is not ready until late October and colours little on the tree. Performance in hard-winter regions is untested.

health.other: Prone to pre-harvest drop because of its short stalk. Disease susceptibility is not well documented outside Italy.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity for a warm, sunny garden. It flowers late, so pair it with a group 3-5 diploid; pick before the fruit starts dropping and, to copy the Campanian method, spread the apples in full sun for a couple of weeks, turning them now and then until they redden.

varieties.name: Antonovka

origin.parentage: Unknown folk selection; possibly carries wild Malus sylvestris in its ancestry

varieties.history: Russia's 'people's apple': a folk variety that spread out of Kursk province in the 1800s and became the mainstay of orchards across central Russia, Belarus and Poland. It is really a family of closely related clones, and its uniform, very hardy seedlings are widely used as rootstocks.

look.description: Medium to large, variable and often strongly ribbed apple, green-yellow ripening to straw yellow in store, usually without any colour, with russet in the stalk cavity and large pale dots.

taste.summary: Juicy, slightly coarse flesh with a brisk, acid-led taste and an exceptionally strong, sweet perfume when ripe. Sharp off the tree, it softens and mellows in store; famous for pies, purée and traditional Russian soaked (fermented) apples.

tree.notes: Large, vigorous, long-lived tree whose high, rounded crown spreads with age. Slow to start (often six years or more on seedling stock) but productive thereafter, though crops can be irregular.

pollination.notes: Orange Pippin lists group 3 and treats it as needing a partner; Russian sources call it partly self-fertile. Plant a pollinator for reliable crops.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates of central Russia, Belarus, Poland and the Baltic, and the northern prairies; the trees survive around -40 C.
climate.poor_climates: Warm southern regions, where it ripens early and loses its keeping quality; Russian pomologists noted it turns from a winter into a short-lived autumn apple as you go south.

health.other: Scab reports range from fairly resistant to susceptible; some resistance to fire blight and collar rot is reported. Codling moth is a pest in Russia.

varieties.grow_notes: An excellent choice for very cold gardens or for a classic cooking and fermenting apple. Give it room, be patient for the first crops, and plant a group 2-4 partner nearby.

varieties.name: Api

origin.place: Brittany, France (traditionally the Forest of Api)

varieties.history: A very old French apple, on record since 1628 and traditionally said to have been found in the Forest of Api in Brittany; the claim that it is the 'Appian' apple of Roman writers is unproven. Long prized as a decorative fruit for Christmas displays, it is still sold in North America as Lady Apple.

look.description: Tiny, flattened, slightly ribbed fruit with glossy skin: pale yellow with a bright, clean red cheek.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy white flesh with a sweet, gently aromatic flavour; much of the scent sits in the skin. Small enough to eat in a few bites, and some tasters notice an almond-like note after storage.

tree.notes: A small, upright, spur-bearing tree that is slow to come into bearing and may alternate heavy and light years. The persistent fruit hangs well on the branch.

pollination.notes: Generally listed in group 3, though it was among the earlier varieties to flower at Brogdale; pair with a group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Temperate Europe and the cooler fruit regions of North America (New England, New York, the Pacific Northwest), where it has long been grown for the holiday trade.
climate.poor_climates: No specific record of failure, but as an old northern French variety it is unlikely to suit low-chill or very hot climates.

health.other: Some susceptibility to scab reported; other disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Worth growing as much for its jewel-like fruit as for eating. Be patient while the tree establishes, thin heavy crops to help it bear every year, and plant a mid-season pollinator nearby.

varieties.name: Api Etoile

origin.parentage: Unknown; a member of the Api (Lady apple) group

varieties.history: A very old curiosity of the Api family, first described by the Swiss botanist Jean Bauhin (d. 1613) as a 'pentagonal apple'. It later spread to Italy and to Paris, and was rediscovered in Switzerland in 1981; it survives mainly in specialist collections.

look.description: Small, flattened fruit with five pronounced bumps that make a star outline seen from the end; pale green skin with a pink cheek and a waxy coating.

taste.summary: Firm, yellowish-white flesh. One grower source rates the flavour highly, aromatic with a sweet fruitiness and enough acid, while a German source says it looks better than it tastes; it is grown mainly for its novel shape.
taste.best_eaten: Winter, after some weeks in store

tree.notes: Described as having long, slender branches. Little reliable growing data is published.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded; plant with a mid-season diploid to be safe.

climate.best_climates: Central European conditions like its Swiss home; a very late variety that needs a long season to finish.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; as a late Alpine-region apple it is unlikely to suit low-chill or short-season areas.

health.other: No disease data found. The waxy skin is said to help the fruit keep.

varieties.grow_notes: A collector's apple grown for its star shape. Give it a warm, sheltered position so the late fruit ripens, and plant a mid-season pollinator nearby.

varieties.name: Aport

origin.place: Probably Ukraine or southern Russia; the celebrated strain was established at Verny (Almaty), Kazakhstan, from 1865

varieties.history: An old eastern European apple group that western collections such as Brogdale file under Emperor Alexander. Its fame comes from Kazakhstan: a settler from Voronezh province is said to have brought trees to Verny (now Almaty) in 1865, and in the Trans-Ili Alatau foothills the fruit grew huge and richly scented, winning prizes in Paris in 1900 and becoming the symbol of Almaty. Plantings collapsed after the 1990s and are now the target of state revival programmes.

look.description: Very large, broadly round to slightly heart-shaped apple with thick, waxy skin, yellow to greenish-yellow under bright red stripes and blush; single fruits can top 500 g.

taste.summary: Grown in the Almaty foothills, the fine-grained flesh is crisp and sweet-tart at harvest with a strong honeyed scent, turning softer and crumbly in store. In Britain the same apple (as Emperor Alexander) is coarser, drier and much less flavoured, so climate makes a big difference.
taste.storage_change: Fine-grained and crisp at harvest, becoming softer and crumblier in store (Wikipedia).
taste.peak: Picked second half of September in Almaty; keeps in cool store to mid-January/early February (Wikipedia).

climate_flavour.note: Wikipedia: Almaty growers credit the soil and altitude of the foothills for its strong honey aroma and sweet-tart taste.

tree.notes: Slow to come into bearing (often 7-10 years in Kazakhstan) and strongly biennial; Kazakh growers use drip irrigation to keep soil moisture steady. The heavy fruit bruises easily and can be blown down.

pollination.notes: Flowers with Emperor Alexander (group 3); plant a mid-season diploid partner.

climate.best_climates: Irrigated continental mountain foothills around 900-1,200 m, as near Almaty: hot days, cool nights and cold but fairly short winters.
climate.poor_climates: Low, hot plains (Kazakh specialists report poor fruit below about 850 m) and cool maritime climates, where the fruit is big but bland.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well documented; the main problems are late bearing, alternate cropping and bruising of the very large fruit.

varieties.grow_notes: Only worth growing for flavour where summers are hot and nights cool; elsewhere expect a large, mild cooking apple. Be patient for the first crops, thin to limit biennial bearing, and keep the soil evenly moist.

varieties.name: Arbroath Pippin
varieties.history: A very old Scottish dessert apple, catalogued by the National Fruit Collection under the name Oslin. It was on record by 1815 and is probably much older. Tradition credits the monks of Arbroath Abbey with bringing it from France, an idea Hogg favoured. Its branches form burr knots that root when planted, so it was easily propagated from cuttings; this explains names such as Burr Knot and Original Pippin.

look.description: Medium, regular, flattened-round fruit with thick pale-yellow skin densely freckled with brown dots; the skin often cracks.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, juicy yellowish flesh, sweet and rich, with a strong aromatic flavour Hogg considered unique to this apple. It is short-lived, so eat it within a few weeks of ripening.
taste.storage_change: does not keep well (about 2 weeks; Pomiferous)
taste.peak: picked late August (NFC, listed as Oslin)

climate_flavour.note: Pomiferous: prefers temperate, marine conditions (growth preference, not stated for flavour)

tree.notes: A free-growing, upright tree and a good bearer. The branches carry burr knots, which allow propagation from hardwood cuttings on its own roots. Old trees are prone to canker.

pollination.notes: No published group found. Estimated as group 2 from National Fruit Collection records, which show it among the earliest to bloom. Plant a group 1-3 partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool, short-summer climates such as eastern Scotland. An old writer noted it ripens in poorer climates and aspects than the finest dessert apples.
climate.poor_climates: Early flowering exposes the blossom to late frosts. Hot climates are untested.

health.other: Prone to canker as the tree ages, and the fruit skin often cracks. Other diseases are not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A historic choice for Scottish and northern gardens. It can be grown on its own roots from burr-knot cuttings; avoid frost pockets because of its early blossom, and eat the fruit fresh in late summer.

varieties.name: Ard Cairn Russet
varieties.history: Found around 1890 by the Cork nurseryman Baylor Hartland and named after his Ard Cairn nursery. It won an RHS Award of Merit in 1910 and is one of the better-known Irish heritage apples.

look.description: Medium, flat-topped conical fruit, heavily coated in russet over a yellow ground, with some red streaks showing through.

taste.summary: Dense, firm flesh that is sweet but low in acid and rather dry; the aroma is slight. Orange Pippin likens the flavour to banana. It is said to be at its best after a few months in store.
taste.peak: Orange Pippin says it is meant to be stored and is at its best in January.

tree.notes: Fairly vigorous; branches tend to form very narrow crotch angles, so train them out early. One grower reports light crops on a vigorous rootstock.

pollination.notes: National Fruit Collection flowering dates put it mid-season (group 3); Orange Pippin lists group 4. Plant with a group 3-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp maritime climates like southern Ireland and western Britain; reported to tolerate most temperate regions.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; very hot or very cold continental climates are untested.

health.other: Described as having fairly good all-round disease resistance.

varieties.grow_notes: A useful russet for wetter western sites. Train young branches to wider angles, and store the fruit for a while before eating; it also makes a good juice.

varieties.name: Ariane

origin.parentage: (Florina x Prima) x Golden Delicious

varieties.history: A scab-resistant apple from INRA's breeding programme at Angers, built over several generations from lines carrying the Vf resistance gene (originally from Malus floribunda) and selected from a (Florina x Prima) x Golden Delicious cross. It was introduced around 2000, with the first commercial orchards in 2002, and is grown in France for low-spray production.

look.description: Smallish fruit with a bright crimson flush over golden-green and a noticeably indented base.

taste.summary: Very crisp, dense, firm cream flesh that is moist rather than truly juicy, with a balanced sweet-sharp taste, a hint of pear-drop and a delicate fragrance; best eaten slightly chilled. Orange Pippin advises eating it within about a week rather than keeping it, which sits oddly with its reputation as a late keeper.
taste.peak: Best served slightly chilled (Orange Pippin); Wikipedia says it keeps three months or more and is good refrigerated for winter eating

tree.notes: Vigorous, spur-bearing tree prone to alternate cropping; needs careful pruning in the first years so light reaches the fruit for colour.

pollination.notes: Early-to-mid flowering over a long period (listed in group 2). Santana, Gala and GoldRush have been suggested as partners.

climate.best_climates: Temperate western Europe, especially the Loire and other French fruit regions; useful anywhere scab pressure is high.
climate.poor_climates: Shady or dull sites where the crimson colour fails to develop; very hot regions are untested.

health.other: Carries Vf (and reportedly Vg) scab resistance, effective against common scab races though Vf-breaking strains exist; reported to cope reasonably with other diseases.

varieties.grow_notes: A good low-spray choice for wet climates. Thin firmly to curb biennial bearing and keep the canopy open so fruit colours; pair with a group 2-3 diploid.

varieties.name: Arkansas Black

origin.parentage: Chance seedling, thought to be from Winesap

varieties.history: Appeared as a chance seedling in Benton County, north-west Arkansas, around 1870, and is usually taken to be a Winesap offspring. Valued in the Ozarks for its near-black colour and long keeping; it is a different apple from 'Arkansas' (Mammoth Black Twig).

look.description: Glossy, waxy fruit so deep a red-purple on the sunny side that it looks almost black, with small pale lenticels.

taste.summary: Very hard and tart at picking, it mellows enormously after one to two months in store into a firm, crisp apple with a dark, wine-like richness. Tasters pick out a hint of vanilla near the skin, almond towards the core and a spicy, honeyed sweetness over the remaining tartness; the waxy skin turns greasy in store.
taste.storage_change: Hard and fairly tart when picked; mellows and improves in storage, and the skin darkens almost to black.
taste.peak: After some months in store; keeps all winter

climate_flavour.note: Trees of Antiquity calls it one of the best apples for hot interior sites and says hot autumn weather lets the fruit ripen.

tree.notes: Vigorous and slow to start cropping. Ploidy is uncertain (listed as triploid by one source); it is in any case a poor pollen donor.

pollination.notes: Poor pollen; needs a good diploid pollinator such as Golden Delicious, and cannot be relied on to pollinate others.

climate.best_climates: Long, hot southern US summers (Ozarks, upper South, California) where its dark colour and late ripening are fully achieved.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, short seasons may not ripen it; in England it is likely to stay hard and sour.

health.other: Generally regarded as fairly disease-resistant, including to cedar-apple rust; few specific weaknesses recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Suited to warm regions with a long autumn. Leave the fruit on the tree as long as frost allows, then store it for several weeks before eating. Plant a reliable diploid pollinator nearby.

varieties.name: Arlet

origin.place: Swiss Federal Research Station, Wädenswil, Switzerland
origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Idared
origin.raised_by: Swiss Federal Research Station Wädenswil (Bernhard Krapf)

varieties.history: Crossed in 1958 at the Swiss federal fruit research station at Wädenswil and released in 1984; it was patented in 1989 and sold in North America as Swiss Gourmet. It is now grown more by gardeners than by commercial orchards.

look.description: Rounded to slightly tall fruit, yellow largely covered with a bright pinkish-red flush and stripes, with russet in the stalk cavity.

taste.summary: Crisp, very juicy, fine-grained cream flesh; sweet with a light, fresh acidity and a faint perfume. Pleasant and balanced but fairly mild overall, and it keeps its crunch well in store.
taste.storage_change: de.wikipedia: stays firm for a long time at room temperature without going soft.
taste.peak: de.wikipedia: November to February.

tree.notes: Precocious and regular-bearing spur type; one source rates growth as strong, another as average.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering; an average pollinator for other varieties.

climate.best_climates: Temperate to warm climates; grown in Switzerland and found in North American gardens from zone 5 to 8.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, scab-prone sites without spraying; areas with heavy cedar-apple rust.

health.other: Strongly scab-susceptible according to Swiss sources; very susceptible to cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it an open, airy site and a scab programme in wet areas. Pick in early October and store; it keeps well, even at room temperature, without going soft.

varieties.name: Aroma

origin.place: Balsgård Fruit Breeding Institute, Fjälkestad, Skåne, Sweden
origin.parentage: Ingrid Marie x Filippa

varieties.history: Crossed at Balsgård in southern Sweden in the late 1940s and released in 1973; it is now a leading apple in Sweden and Norway and the provincial apple of Skåne. Several redder sports exist, including Amorosa and Norwegian 'red Aroma' strains.

look.description: Large, broadly conical yellow apple with a striped and mottled orange-red to red cheek.

taste.summary: Very juicy, rather tender yellowish-white flesh with a sweet, well-balanced, fruity and aromatic flavour.
taste.peak: Store norske leksikon: usable October to January.

tree.notes: Spreading to drooping habit at the National Fruit Collection; widely grown commercially in Scandinavia.

pollination.notes: Mid-late flowering; needs a partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool Scandinavian climates; recommended for southern Sweden (zones 1-3) and a main commercial variety in Norway.
climate.poor_climates: Not recorded in warm climates; a Scandinavian apple likely to be soft and poorly coloured in hot summers.

health.other: Reported to have reasonable field resistance to scab and fruit rots.

varieties.grow_notes: A good dessert apple for cool northern gardens. Plant with another mid-season flowering variety and pick from late September.

varieties.name: Aromatic Russet
varieties.history: An English russet thought to date from around 1850. The National Apple Register records it with the synonyms Rook's Nest and Spice Apple; the National Fruit Collection holds an accession received from Scott's nursery under the name Aromatic Russet (Scott). Little else of its history is documented.

look.description: Small, somewhat irregular conical fruit almost entirely covered in brown russet, with at most a faint red flush.

taste.summary: Firm, greenish-white flesh with a rich, high-quality russet flavour that is noticeably sharper than Egremont Russet and sometimes carries a hint of lemon.

tree.notes: No reliable growing data found; treat as a typical English russet and prune as a spur-bearer until it shows otherwise.

pollination.notes: Listed as a group 3 diploid; any mid-season diploid will pollinate it.

climate.best_climates: Inferred from its English origin: cool, moist maritime climates like southern and central England.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; hot, dry summers are generally unkind to English russets.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity for russet enthusiasts. Grow it like Egremont Russet: open sunny site, reasonable loam, and a group 2-4 diploid partner nearby.

varieties.name: Arthur Turner
varieties.history: Raised at the Charles Turner nursery in Slough (the firm that introduced Cox's Orange Pippin) and shown to the RHS in 1912 as 'Turner's Prolific', winning an Award of Merit. Renamed the following year and released in 1915, it later received an RHS Award of Garden Merit in 1945 for its unusually showy blossom.

look.description: Large, broad, slightly ribbed fruit, greenish-yellow with a soft orange-brown flush on the sunny side and a rather tough skin.

taste.summary: A medium-sharp cooker with a touch of sweetness, so it needs little sugar. The white flesh cooks to a pale, creamy purée and is a classic for baking whole; cut flesh browns quickly.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-Oct; can be picked for cooking from August before full size
taste.peak: Aug-Oct (Chris Bowers nursery: 'for eating August to October').

tree.notes: Vigorous, upright tree that crops regularly and well. The large deep-pink blossom is ornamental in its own right.

pollination.notes: Flowers early in group 3 (several days before Cox at Brogdale). Needs a diploid partner in groups 2-4.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate gardens, including northern England and Scotland, where it is a dependable early cooker.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, dry summers are likely to shorten its already brief keeping life and soften the fruit; little evidence from warm regions.

health.other: Usually described as disease-resistant, notably to scab; no major weakness widely reported.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the easier cookers for a beginner or a colder site. Thin heavy crops for bigger fruit, use the apples within a few weeks of picking, and plant where the spring blossom can be enjoyed.

varieties.name: Ashmead's Kernel
varieties.history: Grown from seed around 1700 by a Dr Ashmead in Gloucester and long treasured in the Gloucestershire orchards. It earned an RHS First Class Certificate as late as 1981 and is now one of the most widely planted English heritage russets, including in North America.

look.description: Broad, slightly lopsided fruit, greenish-gold under a heavy coat of fawn russet, sometimes with a dull bronze cheek.

taste.summary: Dense, firm, crisp and fairly juicy flesh with an intense balance of strong sugar and strong acid, a nutty depth and an earthy undertone; the note tasters most often name is pear-drop, though few agree exactly. Tart if picked early, it grows sweeter and more aromatic over several weeks in store.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Feb, after at least a month in store
taste.storage_change: Lemony and sharp when first picked; mellows and sweetens as sugars develop in store; flavours develop over time in storage.
taste.peak: Pick late (mid Oct to late Nov); improves in store, keeping 3 months or more

tree.notes: Fairly upright, average vigour; a spur-bearer that is often a shy and slightly erratic cropper, so it rewards a sunny, sheltered spot and a reliable pollinator. One online database lists it as triploid but most UK sources treat it as diploid.

pollination.notes: Group 4 and self-sterile; fruit set can be patchy, so plant a dependable group 3-5 diploid partner close by.

climate.best_climates: Cool to warm temperate regions with enough summer sun to build sugar; does well in southern England and in many parts of North America, from New England to the Pacific Northwest and Virginia.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, wet, sunless sites give light crops of very sharp fruit; very hot, humid lowlands are less suitable.

health.other: Generally a fairly healthy tree; main drawback is light, irregular cropping. Some susceptibility to bitter pit reported.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it the warmest, sunniest position available and good soil so the fruit sweetens properly. Expect a few years before decent crops; plant with a reliable mid-season pollinator and store the fruit before eating.

varieties.name: Ashton Bitter

origin.place: Long Ashton Research Station, Bristol, England
origin.parentage: Dabinett x Stoke Red (as recorded by the National Fruit Collection)
origin.raised_by: G.T. Spinks, Long Ashton Research Station

varieties.history: Raised in 1947 by G.T. Spinks at the Long Ashton Research Station near Bristol, the UK's former cider research centre, as part of work to breed improved cider apples. It is an early-ripening bittersweet that comes into bearing quickly.

look.description: Small to medium, conical fruit, pale yellow largely covered with a red striped and washed flush; cream flesh.

taste.summary: A bittersweet with low acid and medium tannin, giving soft, mildly astringent juice. The flesh is fairly dry.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill in Oct

tree.notes: Noted as precocious (early to start cropping). Other growth details are poorly documented.

pollination.notes: Described as mid-season flowering.

climate.best_climates: Cool maritime cider country like Somerset and the West Midlands; early ripening suits areas with short autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Performance in hot or very cold climates is not recorded.

health.other: Disease record not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A useful early bittersweet that lets a cider maker start pressing before the main late varieties. Plant with other mid-season flowering cider apples.

varieties.name: Atlas

origin.place: Central Experimental Farm, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada
origin.parentage: Open-pollinated seedling of Manks Codlin

varieties.history: Grown at the Central Experimental Farm in Ottawa from seed sown in 1898, selected in 1912 and introduced around 1924 as a hardy apple for Canadian conditions. Its seed parent was the old Manx cooking apple Manks Codlin.

look.description: Truncate-conical, somewhat ribbed pale yellow apple striped with orange-red.

taste.summary: White, juicy flesh with a mild, sub-acid flavour; little else is recorded about its eating quality.

pollination.notes: Early-mid flowering at Brogdale (full bloom around 8 May).

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates such as eastern Ontario, for which it was selected.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; a hardy Canadian early-autumn apple is unlikely to suit hot or low-chill regions.

health.other: No disease ratings found.

varieties.grow_notes: Of interest mainly to collectors and cold-climate growers. Pick in early September and use within a few months.

varieties.name: Aurora Golden Gala

origin.place: Pacific Agri-Food Research Centre, Summerland, British Columbia, Canada
origin.parentage: Splendour x Gala
origin.raised_by: Pacific Agri-Food Research Centre (Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada)

varieties.history: A yellow dessert apple from the Summerland breeding programme in British Columbia, tested as 8S6923 and named in 2003. It is marketed mainly in Canada and the US, where it has done well in taste panels.

look.description: Medium, slightly tall fruit with thin, glossy, clear yellow skin.

taste.summary: Very crisp, breaking, juicy flesh with a sweet, well-balanced flavour and some aroma. It keeps its firmness for months in store.
taste.storage_change: Keeps its firmness through about six months of storage.

tree.notes: Little published tree data outside commercial trials.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not found; Gala and Splendour are both mid-season, so a mid-season partner is a reasonable choice.

climate.best_climates: Sunny inland fruit valleys with warm days and cold winters, like the Okanagan where it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in cool, wet maritime climates or very hot lowlands.

health.other: No disease ratings found.

varieties.grow_notes: A modern commercial yellow apple best suited to sunny, dry fruit regions. It can be picked quite ripe and still stores well.

varieties.name: Autumn Bough
varieties.history: An old American sweet apple recorded by 1851 and described in The Apples of New York (1905); the Southern name 'White Sugar' also belongs to it. Its many 'Bough' names overlap with the summer-ripening Sweet Bough, and registers mix the two, but it is treated as a later, separate variety. The UK National Apple Register lists it as the seed parent of Lodi and Carlton.

look.description: Medium to large, tall and somewhat ribbed fruit with plain yellow skin and scattered russet dots.

taste.summary: A sweet apple with little acidity and soft white flesh. Registers give only the basic sweet-to-subacid rating, and no fuller tasting notes were found.
taste.best_eaten: Fresh from the tree; soft-fleshed sweet apples do not keep long

tree.notes: No reliable modern growing notes found.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded; plant with any compatible diploid of similar season.

climate.best_climates: Grown historically in the north-eastern and southern United States, so it copes with continental summers.
climate.poor_climates: No documented weak spots; as a soft early-autumn apple it is unlikely to give much in cool, wet seasons.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage curiosity for collectors of old American sweet apples. Make sure the wood comes from a reliable source, because its names are easily confused with Sweet Bough. Pick as soon as the fruit colours to yellow and use it quickly.

varieties.name: Autumn Glory

origin.parentage: Fuji x Golden Delicious

varieties.history: A Washington State cross of Fuji and Golden Delicious made in 1976; Domex Superfresh Growers bought the rights in 2011 and market it exclusively under the Autumn Glory trademark. Not to be confused with an older English exhibition apple of the same name.

look.description: Medium to large apple in mixed red and gold.

taste.summary: Dense, crisp, juicy flesh that is high in sugar and low in acid, with warm notes that its marketers and reviewers liken to caramel and cinnamon.
taste.peak: Marketed October to June from storage.

tree.notes: A managed (club) variety grown only by licensed growers; tree details not published.

pollination.notes: No flowering data published.

climate.best_climates: Sunny, irrigated, hot-summer fruit districts like central Washington, where its Fuji and Golden Delicious parents excel.
climate.poor_climates: Short cool summers such as northern Britain, where a late-October apple may not ripen fully.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: Not generally available to home growers because it is a trademarked managed variety. Climate needs are inferred from its parents and growing region.

varieties.name: Autumn Glow
varieties.history: No published record of an apple called Autumn Glow was found in the UK National Fruit Collection database, Orange Pippin or other pomological sources consulted; it is offered by Keepers Nursery as a late-season dessert apple. It should not be confused with Autumn Glory, a name used both for an old Norfolk exhibition apple and for a modern American variety.

look.description: Appearance not documented in the sources checked.

taste.summary: Flavour and texture are not documented in the sources checked.
taste.peak: pick as late as possible for full flavour (Pomiferous)

tree.notes: No growing information found.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not recorded.

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: No independent growing advice available; follow the supplying nursery's guidance on pollination partners and rootstock.

varieties.name: Autumn Pearmain
varieties.history: One of the oldest English apples still in collections: the National Fruit Collection dates it to at least the late 1500s, and it appears in early 17th-century English fruit lists. The trees held at Brogdale cannot be told apart from Herefordshire Pearmain, so the two names may cover the same apple.

look.description: Truncated-conical, slightly ribbed fruit, dull green ripening to yellow, streaked and flushed red with a fine net of russet.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained cream flesh that is only moderately juicy, with a gentle sweetness and a quietly aromatic, nutty character typical of the old pearmains. A connoisseur's apple rather than a crunchy, juicy one.
taste.peak: Mid-September in Salt Spring's orchard; picked late September at NFC

tree.notes: Little modern growing data; treat as a typical old English dessert apple and prune as a spur-bearer until it shows otherwise.

pollination.notes: Listed by the RHS in flowering group 4; plant with another group 3-5 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist lowland England and similar cool maritime climates where it has been grown for centuries.
climate.poor_climates: Hot continental summers are likely to give soft, poorly coloured fruit; no evidence of use in warm regions.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded for this variety.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage choice for a mixed orchard in southern Britain. Give it a sunny, sheltered spot on reasonable loam and pair it with a mid-to-late flowering partner such as Ellison's Orange or Golden Delicious.

varieties.name: Bailey

origin.place: Perry, Wyoming County, New York, USA

varieties.history: A nineteenth-century 'sweet' apple from Perry in western New York, grown from about 1840. It was valued as a sweet table apple but was never a strong keeper.

look.description: Medium to large, roundish or slightly conical fruit, bright yellow mostly covered by deep red, with pale flecks.

taste.summary: Firm, yellow-tinged, moderately juicy flesh that is distinctly sweet with very little acid. Growers say the sweetness is fullest after the first frosts.
taste.storage_change: Not a good keeper.
taste.peak: Orange Pippin notes full sweetness develops after the first autumn frost.

tree.notes: Productive, but unsprayed trees give much poor-grade, scabby or knotty fruit.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter north-eastern US conditions like western New York.
climate.poor_climates: Humid areas where scab pressure is high produce blemished, misshapen fruit.

health.other: Prone to apple scab; fruit can be scabby and knotty without spraying.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow it for its old-fashioned sweet flavour in a cold-winter area, in an open, airy spot to limit scab. Eat the fruit within a couple of months.

varieties.name: Bakers Delicious

origin.place: Wales (found); introduced by Bakers nursery, Codsall, near Wolverhampton

varieties.history: A Welsh find, brought into commerce in 1932 by the Bakers nursery at Codsall near Wolverhampton. It has nothing to do with the American Delicious; the name refers to the nursery. Specimens are kept in the National Fruit Collection and in the Marcher Apple Network collections.

look.description: Medium, slightly conical yellow apple with a light orange to orange-red flush broken into streaks.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained cream flesh that is crisp and juicy, with a pleasantly aromatic flavour that has more depth than many early apples. Best eaten soon after picking as it does not keep long.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, fresh from the tree

tree.notes: Little published growing data. Treat as an ordinary early dessert apple and prune as a spur-bearer until it shows otherwise.

pollination.notes: Usually listed in an early flowering group (2), consistent with National Fruit Collection blossom dates. Not independently confirmed; assume it needs a pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist western Britain and similar maritime climates, where it was found and is still kept in collections.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot or continental climates; like most early English apples it would probably ripen soft and poorly coloured in a hot summer.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage early apple suited to gardens in the west and Midlands. Give it a sunny spot on reasonably drained soil and pick over two or three visits as the fruit colours, eating it straight away.

varieties.name: Baldwin

origin.raised_by: Found on the farm of John Ball; popularised by Col. Loammi Baldwin

varieties.history: A chance seedling from Wilmington, near Boston, first known locally as Woodpecker or Butters; Colonel Loammi Baldwin spread it in the late 18th century and it took his name. It was New England's leading apple for over a century until the severe winter of 1933-34 killed huge numbers of trees.

look.description: Large, roundish fruit flushed and striped bright red over yellow, with prominent pale russet dots.

taste.summary: Very hard, crisp, juicy flesh with a straightforward sweet flavour backed by a mild tartness; growers prize its firm texture more than any complexity. It holds its shape in pies, keeps three months or more and was long the classic New England cider apple.

tree.notes: Large, long-lived tree that is slow to bear and strongly biennial; thin fruit in the 'on' year.

pollination.notes: Triploid with poor pollen: needs two diploid partners flowering in groups 3-5.

climate.best_climates: New England, New York and similar humid continental climates with warm summers and cool autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Areas with severe winters (it was devastated by the 1934 freeze) and hot southern lowlands.

health.other: Bitter pit was once called 'Baldwin spot' after this variety; also biennial bearing and limited winter hardiness.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant where winters are not extreme and supply two pollinators. Thin crops hard in heavy years and keep calcium up to reduce bitter pit in storage.

varieties.name: Ballyfatten
varieties.history: A cooking apple from Northern Ireland, first recorded in 1802; it shares its name with a townland in County Tyrone. It is kept in the National Fruit Collection, but little has been written about it.

look.description: Tall, ribbed, conical fruit, pale greenish-yellow, with a mottled pinkish to red-brown flush and a little russet.

taste.summary: Firm, white, fairly dry flesh with a plainly acid flavour, suited to cooking rather than eating fresh.
taste.best_eaten: Cooking apple; keeping season not recorded
taste.storage_change: Tart straight from the tree; sweetens (quickly, per Wikipedia) in store and can then be eaten raw.
taste.peak: Oct-Dec from store (Future Forests: pick late Sept, keeps Oct-Dec).

tree.notes: Recorded as a tip-bearer, so prune lightly and avoid shortening every shoot; better as a standard or bush than a spur-trained form.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom in mid to late May, later than most varieties, so group 5 is inferred. Pair it with another late-flowering apple.

climate.best_climates: Cool, wet maritime climates like Ulster where it originated; its late bloom helps it avoid spring frosts.
climate.poor_climates: No record of performance in hot or continental climates; values are inferred from its Irish origin.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage cooker for Irish or northern British gardens, worth planting where late frosts are common. Because it fruits at the shoot tips, prune by renewal rather than hard spur pruning.

varieties.name: Bancroft

origin.place: Central Experimental Farm, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada
origin.parentage: Forest x McIntosh
origin.raised_by: Division of Horticulture, Central Experimental Farm, Ottawa

varieties.history: Selected at Ottawa in 1930 and released around 1935 as a late-keeping McIntosh-type apple for Canadian growers. It was once grown commercially in Ontario but is now mostly a heritage variety.

look.description: Medium, slightly flattened fruit almost covered in dark red flush and stripes over greenish yellow, with some dotted russet.

taste.summary: Fine-grained, juicy, greenish-white flesh with a mild subacid, refreshingly fruity flavour, finer in texture than McIntosh. It holds flavour and texture well into spring, though it softens in long storage.
taste.storage_change: Holds flavour and texture unusually well in store; best after Christmas and keeps to spring.
taste.peak: After Christmas, through to spring.

tree.notes: A tough, dependable tree that starts bearing young; spreading to drooping habit.

pollination.notes: Flowers early at Brogdale (about group 2); needs a pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates like eastern Ontario, where it was bred for hardiness and long keeping.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to give soft, poorly coloured fruit, as with other McIntosh types.

health.other: No disease ratings found.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy keeper for cold areas. Plant with an early-flowering pollinator, pick in mid-October and store cool for eating after Christmas.

varieties.name: Bardsey
varieties.history: A single old tree was found in 1998 growing in a sheltered recess against the wall of Plas Bach, a house built in the 1870s on Bardsey Island off the Llyn peninsula. Ian Sturrock had the fruit checked at Brogdale, where it matched no known variety, and he then propagated it; salt winds had trained the mother tree flat against the wall.

look.description: Medium-sized apple with a pink to orange-red flush over a pale skin.

taste.summary: Sweet and juicy with a light lemon scent and a fair amount of acidity. Best eaten within a few days of picking in late September and October; it keeps only two to three weeks and cooks to a puree.
taste.best_eaten: late Sep-Nov, fresh off the tree
taste.peak: Orange Pippin: keeps 2-3 weeks

tree.notes: Tough, healthy tree that crops early and regularly; it is a partial tip-bearer, so avoid shortening every shoot when pruning.

pollination.notes: Early-flowering (group 2); needs a group 1-3 partner.

climate.best_climates: Wet, windy maritime sites in western Britain and Ireland; it survived for decades in salt-laden Atlantic gales without spraying.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot or very dry summers; likely to lose colour and keeping quality there.

health.other: Reported as very resistant to scab and canker, and grown without sprays.

varieties.grow_notes: A good organic or low-input apple for exposed, wet western gardens where many varieties canker. Prune lightly because of its partial tip-bearing habit, and pair with an early-flowering partner.

varieties.name: Barnack Beauty

origin.place: Barnack, near Stamford, Northamptonshire (now Cambridgeshire), England

varieties.history: Arose in the village of Barnack, near Stamford, around 1840 and was put on the market about 1870 by Brown's nursery of Stamford. It won an RHS Award of Merit in 1899 and a First Class Certificate in 1909, and is a parent of Barnack Orange.

look.description: Handsome golden-yellow apple, about half covered in an orange-red flush with darker stripes.

taste.summary: Firm, very crisp, juicy creamy-white flesh with a sharp, tangy flavour tempered by some sweetness; not a sweet apple, and as useful for cooking as for eating. A sound late keeper rather than a perfumed one.

tree.notes: Upright tree of average vigour that crops well and regularly; largely tip-bearing, so prune lightly and renew rather than spur back hard.

pollination.notes: Group 4, needs a partner flowering in groups 3-5.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate lowland Britain; notably tolerant of thin chalky and limestone soils.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot or continental climates; short, cool seasons may not ripen this late apple fully.

health.other: Reported to be very resistant to scab with some mildew resistance.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for alkaline, chalky ground where many apples struggle. Prune as a tip-bearer and pick in October for winter eating.

varieties.name: Barnack Orange

origin.parentage: Barnack Beauty x Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: Raised in 1904 by W. H. Divers at Belvoir Castle by crossing the long-keeping Barnack Beauty with Cox's Orange Pippin. It never became widely grown but is kept in the National Fruit Collection.

look.description: Flattish, somewhat ribbed fruit with a yellow ground striped and flushed red; skin slightly greasy.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse flesh with only a little juice, carrying a good aromatic flavour that shows its Cox parentage.
taste.peak: picked early October (NFC)

tree.notes: No reliable growing data found. Its parent Barnack Beauty is a tip-bearer, so check the fruiting habit before pruning hard.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from Brogdale flowering dates (a few days ahead of Cox); plant with a group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Inferred from its English origin and Cox parentage: cool, moist temperate climates such as lowland England.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; hot summers would likely spoil colour and texture as with other English late dessert apples.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A collector's variety for English gardens. Grow on a semi-vigorous rootstock in a sunny spot with a mid-season pollinator, and observe how it fruits before settling on a pruning regime.

varieties.name: Barry

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: McIntosh x Cox's Orange Pippin
origin.raised_by: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva

varieties.history: A McIntosh x Cox's Orange Pippin seedling selected at the Geneva, New York station in 1936 and released commercially in 1957. It never became widely planted.
