look.description: Flattish, medium to large fruit with a dark, solid red to brownish-red flush over greenish-yellow.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse greenish flesh with a sweet, aromatic flavour.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering at Brogdale (full bloom around 13 May).

climate.best_climates: Cool-summer, cold-winter climates like upstate New York where it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; McIntosh-type apples generally soften and colour poorly in hot summers.

health.other: Rated resistant to cedar-apple rust; other ratings not found.

varieties.grow_notes: A collection variety; keeps about three months in a cool store. Plant with a mid-season pollinator.

varieties.name: Battleford
varieties.history: A Saskatchewan apple named after the town of Battleford, introduced in the mid-20th century for prairie gardens and valued above all for its winter hardiness. Details of its breeding, date and raiser could not be verified for this record.

look.description: A medium-sized prairie apple; its appearance could not be verified from reliable sources.

taste.summary: Grown on the prairies as an all-purpose apple for cooking and fresh eating; reliable tasting notes were not found.
taste.peak: Late Aug-early Sep; stores about 4 weeks (USask compilation)

tree.notes: Grown for its very hardy wood; other tree characteristics are not documented in sources available here.

pollination.notes: Assume it needs a pollinator; plant with another hardy apple or a crab.

climate.best_climates: Developed for the Canadian prairies, where winters regularly fall below -35 C and summers are short.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in warm or mild-winter climates; prairie apples generally ripen soft and poorly coloured in hot summers and may not get enough chill in mild ones.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: Worth considering only where winters are too severe for better-known apples. Give it a sheltered, sunny spot and a hardy pollinator such as a crab.

varieties.name: Baumann's Reinette

origin.parentage: Unknown seedling

varieties.history: Thought to come from the Belgian pomologist Van Mons and dedicated to the Baumann brothers' nursery at Bollwiller in Alsace; it was recorded in 1811. It became a classic Christmas apple in Germany and gained an RHS First Class Certificate in 1878.

look.description: Medium, flattish fruit almost covered in brilliant crimson flush and stripes; several colour forms exist.

taste.summary: Rather coarse, fairly juicy, slightly chewy flesh with a sweet-sharp but plain flavour and only a faint aroma. It looks better than it tastes and cannot match the aromatic reinettes.
taste.peak: Mid-December to March (German Wikipedia).

tree.notes: Fairly small tree that crops early, heavily and regularly. Wood is vulnerable to hard frost.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering; regarded as a good pollinator. Blossom fairly frost-hardy but can be caught by late frosts.

climate.best_climates: Sunny, moderately elevated central European sites with even moisture and rich soil.
climate.poor_climates: Frost hollows and wet, scab-prone sites.

health.other: Susceptible to scab, canker, aphids, wood frost, lenticel spotting, skin russeting and storage rots; resists shrivelling in store.

varieties.grow_notes: A reliable, decorative cropper for a sunny site with good soil. Avoid frost pockets and damp, scab-prone spots; store the fruit cool for winter use.

varieties.name: Baxter's Pearmain
varieties.history: A Norfolk apple introduced by George Lindley in 1821 and grown as a dual-purpose orchard variety in East Anglia.

look.description: Medium, oblong pearmain-shaped fruit; colour details not confirmed.

taste.summary: Pale, somewhat coarse and rather dry flesh with a slightly acid flavour that the National Fruit Collection compares to Blenheim Orange.

tree.notes: No reliable tree data found.

pollination.notes: Flowers fairly late-mid season at Brogdale (about group 4).

climate.best_climates: Drier eastern English conditions like its Norfolk home.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No disease data found.

varieties.grow_notes: A local East Anglian apple for heritage collections. Pick in mid-October and store for winter use, fresh or cooked.

varieties.name: Beacon

origin.place: University of Minnesota Fruit Breeding Farm, Excelsior, Minnesota
origin.parentage: Uncertain: given as Malinda x Wealthy by the National Fruit Collection and Wikipedia, but as (Malinda x Duchess of Oldenburg) x (Malinda x Tetofsky) by Orange Pippin

varieties.history: Raised in 1908 at the University of Minnesota breeding farm at Excelsior and released in 1936 as a cold-hardy early red apple for the northern prairies. It descends from Malinda, the Vermont apple behind many Minnesota introductions.

look.description: Medium, conical fruit striped and washed with deep red over yellow.

taste.summary: A soft, rather pulpy early apple with a mild, sweet flavour; some find it lively and juicy, others call it ordinary. Better for baking or sauce than for keeping.
taste.best_eaten: Sep, within a week or two of picking
taste.peak: Orange Pippin: early September, keeps about a week.

tree.notes: Average vigour with a drooping, spreading habit; a regular spur-bearer. Valued mainly for hardiness rather than quality.

pollination.notes: Orange Pippin gives group 4; National Fruit Collection records show it opening only a day or so before Bramley, so group 3-4 is realistic.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates of the upper Midwest and Canada where few early apples survive the winter.
climate.poor_climates: Warm regions, where its soft early fruit would go over quickly; susceptible to fire blight where that is common.

health.other: Susceptible to fire blight and somewhat to cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: Worth planting mainly where winters are too hard for standard varieties. Use the crop promptly for eating fresh, sauce or baking, as the fruit softens within days.

varieties.name: Beauty of Bath
varieties.history: Found at Bailbrook near Bath and put on the market by the Bath nursery of George Cooling around 1864; it gained an RHS First Class Certificate in 1887. For decades it was Britain's main commercial early apple, and growers spread straw under the trees to cushion the fruit as it dropped. It is a likely parent of Discovery.

look.description: Flattish, rather small-to-medium apple, pale greenish-yellow flushed and streaked bright red; the white flesh is often stained pink under the skin.

taste.summary: Soft, very juicy flesh with a sharp, refreshing bite that turns sweeter if eaten the moment it ripens. It has a distinctive early-summer tang but goes mealy within a day or two of picking.
taste.best_eaten: Early-mid Aug, straight off the tree; does not keep
taste.storage_change: Sharp at first and sweeter if caught fully ripe; does not keep more than a day or so.
taste.peak: Straight from the tree in early August, before it goes over-ripe

tree.notes: Makes a large, broad, flat-topped tree. Ripe fruit falls readily, so pick in several passes as the apples colour, or grass the ground beneath to soften the drop.

pollination.notes: Usually placed in RHS flowering group 2 (one source lists 3). Needs a diploid partner flowering early to mid season.

climate.best_climates: Cool and mild, damp climates such as western and southern Britain, where it ripens in early August with good colour; it was also widely planted in northern and eastern Europe.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers make the already short-lived fruit soften and drop even faster and dull the colour.

health.other: Generally healthy and scab-resistant. Main faults are heavy fruit drop at ripening, very short shelf life, and some bitter pit.

varieties.grow_notes: Best on a vigorous-to-medium rootstock in a garden where someone can pick and eat the apples daily during early August. It needs room to spread, and an early-flowering pollinator such as another group 2 or 3 diploid.

varieties.name: Beauty of Hants

origin.parentage: Said to be an open-pollinated seedling of Blenheim Orange
origin.raised_by: Mrs Eyre Crabbe (in whose garden it arose)

varieties.history: Arose before 1850 in the garden of Mrs Eyre Crabbe at Bassett near Southampton. It is reputed to be a seedling of Blenheim Orange and resembles that variety in flavour.

look.description: Large, roundish fruit with a greenish-yellow ground and a dull brownish-red flush.

taste.summary: Soft, juicy, yellowish flesh with a pleasant flavour that recalls Blenheim Orange, though juicier and less dry.

tree.notes: No reliable growing data found. Ploidy is unknown; its supposed parent Blenheim Orange is triploid.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from Brogdale flowering dates, which are close to Cox's. Until its ploidy is known, plant two diploid pollinators to be safe.

climate.best_climates: Inferred from its Hampshire origin: mild, moist southern English conditions.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; likely to give soft, poorly coloured fruit in hot summers.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A regional heritage apple for southern England. Allow room in case it inherits Blenheim's vigour, and provide mid-season pollinators.

varieties.name: Beauty of Kent
varieties.history: An English cooker thought to have arisen in Kent and in circulation by about 1820. Victorian pomologist Robert Hogg rated it among the most magnificent apples of its day for its size and colour, and it received an RHS Award of Merit in 1901.

look.description: Very large, broad-based, strongly ribbed fruit, deep yellow heavily washed and streaked red on the sunny side, with russet lining the stalk cavity.

taste.summary: Tender, rather coarse-grained flesh that is very juicy, with a gentle sub-acid flavour that is pleasant but not strong. Cooks readily into a soft, juicy fill.

tree.notes: Strong grower that makes a large tree and bears well. Historically noted as prone to canker on dwarfing stocks and on damp, heavy soils.

pollination.notes: Flowers with Bramley and slightly ahead of Cox at Brogdale; treat as group 3.

climate.best_climates: Southern English conditions on free-draining soil, where its size and colour develop fully.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, heavy ground encourages canker; hot climates are untested and likely to give soft fruit.

health.other: Canker is the recorded weakness, worst on dwarfing rootstocks and wet, heavy soils.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant on a vigorous rootstock in well-drained ground rather than a dwarfing stock on clay. Allow space for a large tree and cut out cankered wood promptly.

varieties.name: Beeley Pippin
varieties.history: Raised around 1880 by the Reverend C. Sculthorpe at Beeley in Derbyshire and taken into the National Fruit Collection in 1916. It remains little known outside collections.

look.description: Medium to large, broadly conical fruit, greenish yellow with an orange-red flush over a quarter to half of the skin.

taste.summary: Firm, fine, slightly tough flesh, juicy and sweet with a pleasant aromatic flavour and moderate acidity. An early apple best eaten soon after picking.

tree.notes: Average vigour with a spreading habit.

pollination.notes: Early flowering: Brogdale dates suggest group 2 and Orange Pippin lists group 1. Pair with another early-flowering diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cool English conditions, including the Derbyshire uplands where it arose.
climate.poor_climates: Early blossom is exposed to spring frosts in cold hollows.

health.other: No disease data found.

varieties.grow_notes: An early dessert apple for northern or upland English gardens. Because it blossoms early, avoid frost pockets and plant an early-flowering partner.

varieties.name: Belle de Boskoop

origin.parentage: Chance seedling of unknown parentage

varieties.history: Found in 1856 at the Ottolander nursery in the Dutch nursery town of Boskoop and put on the market in the 1860s. It became one of the standard winter apples of the Netherlands, Germany, Belgium and northern France, and red-skinned sports such as Rote Boskoop are now widely planted.

look.description: Big, broad, somewhat lopsided fruit with a rough greenish to golden skin, heavily netted with russet and washed with a dull brownish-red cheek.

taste.summary: Very sharp from the tree, with dense, very firm greenish-white flesh and plenty of juice; after some weeks in store the sugar shows through and tasters find a complex flavour with mellow honey undertones that varies with season and site. Unlike Bramley it keeps its shape when cooked, making it a fine pie apple.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Mar after storage; for cooking from picking
taste.storage_change: Sharp at picking; sweetens in storage or if left hanging late on the tree (Trees of Antiquity); tastes better after some time in storage, keeping six months chilled (Salt Spring).

tree.notes: Makes a large, wide-spreading, long-lived tree; best on a dwarfing or semi-dwarfing stock in gardens. Prefers heavy, moist, lime-rich soil.

pollination.notes: Triploid with poor pollen: plant two different early-flowering diploids (e.g. Discovery, James Grieve) so the partners can also pollinate each other. Early blossom is exposed to spring frost.

climate.best_climates: Cool to mild temperate lowlands of north-west Europe (Netherlands, Germany, Normandy, Belgium) with reliable rainfall and deep moist soils.
climate.poor_climates: Frost hollows and late-frost areas, because it flowers early; dry, light soils give small fruit and more storage disorders.

health.other: Prone to bitter pit and to flesh/core browning in store; early blossom vulnerable to frost. Generally robust against fire blight and only lightly troubled by scab.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it room or a restricting rootstock, and a site away from frost pockets. Feed and water to keep cropping even, which also reduces bitter pit, and provide two diploid pollinators because it cannot return the favour.

varieties.name: Belle de Pontoise

origin.parentage: Seedling of Emperor Alexander (Grand Alexandre)

varieties.history: Raised in 1869 at Pontoise, north-west of Paris, by the elder M. Rémy from a seed of the Russian-origin Emperor Alexander. It was valued in the late 19th century as a very large, productive winter apple for both gardens and market orchards.

look.description: Very large, rounded to slightly conical and often angular fruit; whitish-yellow skin washed and speckled with carmine and striped cherry-red, with grey dots.

taste.summary: Whitish, juicy flesh that is sweet with a clear tang; a late dessert apple that ripens in store around January and keeps for about five months.
taste.peak: Ripe for eating in January; keeps about 5 months (fr.wikipedia).

tree.notes: Vigorous and hardy, with long, strong, slightly arching branches; very fertile.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering (French group C). S-alleles S4S43.

climate.best_climates: Temperate northern France and similar climates.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Disease resistance not recorded. Harvest date inferred from its winter eating season.

varieties.grow_notes: A vigorous, heavy-cropping tree for a large garden or orchard; support heavy crops of big fruit. Plant with a mid-season diploid pollinator.

varieties.name: Belle Fleur de France
varieties.history: An old dual-purpose apple of the Low Countries and northern France, held in the UK National Fruit Collection since 1948. Its exact origin and date were not found.

look.description: Large, broadly conical, ribbed fruit, green to yellow with a solid red flush; cream flesh.

taste.summary: Firm, fairly juicy flesh with a good sweet-sharp balance leaning to sweet and moderate aroma; used both fresh and in the kitchen.

tree.notes: Vigorous, regular-bearing triploid spur-bearer with good crops.

pollination.notes: Triploid, so a poor pollen donor; needs two diploid partners. Brogdale dates put it late (about group 5); Orange Pippin lists group 4.

climate.best_climates: Temperate north-west European conditions like Belgium, northern France and southern England.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Average disease resistance overall: some scab resistance, some susceptibility to canker and powdery mildew.

varieties.grow_notes: A big, vigorous triploid for orchards or large gardens; give it room and two diploid pollinators. Suited to low-input or organic growing.

varieties.name: Bellefleur Krasnyi
varieties.history: A Russian variety dated to 1914 in the National Fruit Collection records; the name means 'red Bellefleur'. Its raiser and parentage were not found in the sources checked. It is distinct from the German Roter Bellefleur.

look.description: Rounded, medium-to-large fruit almost covered by a mottled red flush over pale cream-yellow; the flesh is tinged pink.

taste.summary: Sweet, crisp and firm but rather dry, with pinkish flesh.
taste.peak: picked mid October (NFC)

tree.notes: No reliable growing data found.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from Brogdale records, where it flowers early (about a week ahead of Cox); pair with a group 1-3 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Inferred from its Russian origin: cool continental climates with cold winters and moderate summers.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; mild, low-chill or hot-summer regions are unlikely to suit it.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A rarity from the Russian apple tradition. Its early blossom calls for an early-flowering partner and a site that is not a frost pocket.

varieties.name: Ben Davis

origin.place: Southern United States, probably Kentucky (Tennessee and Virginia also claimed)

varieties.history: Of disputed southern origin, it spread through the Ohio and Mississippi valleys in the 19th century and became the leading commercial winter apple around 1880-1910 because it shipped and kept so well, earning the nickname 'mortgage lifter'. Its poor eating quality later made it a byword for blandness; it is a parent of Cortland.

look.description: Handsome, uniform, thick-skinned fruit, yellow mottled and striped bright red.

taste.summary: Firm, coarse, rather dry white flesh with a mild, plain sweet-sharp flavour; often described as cottony. It softens and loses what little flavour it has late in storage.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Mar; better cooked or dried than fresh
taste.peak: Winter keeper (Orange Pippin); about 5 months refrigerated (Salt Spring)

tree.notes: Tough, adaptable and an early, heavy cropper, which explains its former commercial dominance.

pollination.notes: Plant with another diploid flowering in groups 3-5.

climate.best_climates: Hot continental summers of the US Midwest, Ozarks and upper South, where it was planted widely and coped with heat and drought.
climate.poor_climates: Cool maritime climates ripen it poorly and make an already plain apple worse.

health.other: Susceptible to cedar-apple rust; otherwise regarded as a robust, hardy tree.

varieties.grow_notes: Grown today mainly as a historical curiosity or for drying and cooking. Hardy and undemanding; give it a warm, sunny site and a pollinator in groups 3-5.

varieties.name: Benenden Early

origin.parentage: Saint Edmund's Pippin x Lady Sudeley

varieties.history: Raised around 1945 in Southampton by J. J. Gibbons and introduced in 1952 by the Stuart Low nursery at Benenden in Kent, which gave it its name. A rare variety today, held in the National Fruit Collection.

look.description: Large, broadly round-conical, sometimes irregular fruit; greenish-yellow skin largely covered with orange-red streaks.

taste.summary: Soft, rather coarse yellowish flesh with a mild, gently acidic flavour. An early apple to eat straight from the tree rather than store.
taste.best_eaten: Mid-late Aug, straight from the tree

tree.notes: Few growing records. Prune as a normal spur-bearing dessert apple.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not published. National Fruit Collection blossom dates put it close to Discovery and James Grieve, so a mid-season (group 3) diploid partner is likely to overlap.

climate.best_climates: Southern English conditions, where it was raised and ripens in mid August.
climate.poor_climates: No records from hot or very cold regions; its soft early fruit would probably deteriorate fast in hot summers.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity for collectors of Kent and southern English apples. Plant in full sun on fertile, free-draining soil and pick over a couple of weeks in August, eating the fruit fresh.

varieties.name: Benoni

origin.place: Farm of Mason Richards, Dedham, Massachusetts

varieties.history: An early-season dessert apple that appeared on the Dedham, Massachusetts farm of Mason Richards around 1830 and was later introduced to England by Rivers of Sawbridgeworth. Hogg rated it a delicious dessert apple; a redder sport, Red Benoni, also exists.

look.description: Small to medium, somewhat lopsided orange-yellow apple flushed light red and striped crimson, with a smooth, slightly greasy skin.

taste.summary: Tender, fine-grained, juicy yellow flesh with a sweet, gentle, moderately aromatic flavour. A short-season apple to eat from the tree.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, straight from the tree
taste.peak: Orange Pippin: late August, keeps about a week.

tree.notes: Upright tree that comes into bearing early and tends to over-crop, which drives a biennial cycle; thin fruit in heavy years.

pollination.notes: Needs a mid-season partner.

climate.best_climates: Temperate climates such as New England and southern England.
climate.poor_climates: Not recorded.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented; main problem is biennial bearing.

varieties.grow_notes: Thin heavily in a big year to keep it cropping annually. Pick in late August and eat within a week or two.

varieties.name: Ben's Red

origin.parentage: Given by the National Fruit Collection as Devonshire Quarrenden x Farleigh Pippin

varieties.history: Raised around 1830 by Benjamin Roberts at Trannack in west Cornwall and given an RHS Award of Merit in 1899. It remains a favourite Cornish garden apple; it is a dessert apple rather than a recognised cider variety.

look.description: Medium to large, flattish apple almost covered in dark red stripes; yellowish flesh.

taste.summary: Sweet and pleasant, with firm, crisp, rather dry flesh that can be slightly coarse. An early eating apple best enjoyed fresh from the tree.

tree.notes: Growth habit not well documented.

pollination.notes: Approximate group from NFC flowering records (around Egremont Russet's time).

climate.best_climates: Mild, wet maritime climates like Cornwall and south-west Britain, where it has long been grown.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot or strongly continental climates.

health.other: Disease record not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for south-west gardens wanting a local early dessert apple. Plant with another mid-season flowering variety for pollination.

varieties.name: Berner Rosen

origin.parentage: Chance seedling; German sources name Roter Winterkalvill x Sauergrauech as its parents
origin.raised_by: Found on the Baumann property; propagated by nurseryman Daepp of Oppligen

varieties.history: A Swiss seedling spotted around 1870 at Oppligen near Bern and spread by the local nurseryman Daepp, with first fruit recorded in 1888. It became a staple table and juice apple in Switzerland and travelled widely in central and eastern Europe, as its many Czech, Polish and Russian synonyms show.

look.description: Medium, roundish to slightly tall and irregularly ribbed apple, almost entirely washed dark red with faint stripes, a lilac-blue bloom and conspicuous pale dots.

taste.summary: Very juicy, fine greenish-white flesh, sometimes tinged pink, with a sweet, low-acid, winey flavour that German pomologists compare to raspberry. Cut flesh browns quickly.
taste.peak: From late September off the tree; keeps to January, longer from higher-altitude sites (de.wikipedia).

tree.notes: Grows strongly when young, then slows once cropping starts; forms a tall, high-arched and rather sparsely branched crown. Crops early, regularly and well.

pollination.notes: Orange Pippin lists group 3; Brogdale records mid-season flowering. Diploid and a reasonable pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist upland sites like the Swiss Mittelland and pre-Alps; fruit from higher orchards keeps longest.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, dry lowlands, and very wet sites where scab and mildew run riot.

health.other: Susceptible to scab and powdery mildew; some susceptibility to fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: Best on moist, fertile soil in a cool, airy position, where its scab and mildew weaknesses are less of a problem. Pair with a group 2-4 pollinator and eat or juice the crop by midwinter.

varieties.name: Bess Pool

origin.place: A wood near Nottingham, Nottinghamshire, England
origin.parentage: Chance seedling, parentage unknown
origin.raised_by: Found by Bess Pool; introduced by the Pearson nursery of Chilwell

varieties.history: Said to have been found as a fruiting seedling in a Nottinghamshire wood by Bess Pool, whose father kept a village inn. The Pearson family's Chilwell nursery took grafts and released it by 1824. Its very late blossom made it a useful apple for frosty sites.

look.description: Handsome, rather tall and slightly irregular fruit, yellow washed and striped with clear red or crimson on the sunny side, with russet around the short, knobbed stalk.

taste.summary: Sweet, gently wine-like flesh, sometimes tinged red under the skin. Old accounts call it tender and juicy, while the National Fruit Collection finds it rather dry and slightly coarse. It stays firm in store until spring.
taste.peak: Orange Pippin: keeps 1-2 months

tree.notes: Hardy and vigorous, forming a big round-headed standard, but slow to start bearing; 19th-century growers called it an irregular, unreliable cropper until the tree is mature.

pollination.notes: Very late flowering: the National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 22 May. Orange Pippin lists group 5. It needs a late-flowering partner such as Edward VII, Court Pendu Plat or Crawley Beauty.

climate.best_climates: Cool, frost-prone parts of central and northern England, where its late bloom misses spring frosts.
climate.poor_climates: Mild-winter or hot-summer regions: a late-blooming, long-keeping English apple is unlikely to get enough chill or keep its texture.

health.other: Its dense blossom clusters on thin stalks were said to be damaged badly by aphids. Otherwise disease behaviour is not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant it where late frosts ruin other apples, and be patient, because young trees bear little. It suits a large standard better than a dwarf tree and needs a late-flowering pollinator.

varieties.name: Bethan

origin.parentage: Thought to be Rajka x Sunrise (raised from seed in 2015)

varieties.history: A small early dessert apple from Karim Habibi's seedling programme, named after his wife Bethan and introduced in 2022.

look.description: Small yellow apple with a red flush and pale cream flesh.

taste.summary: A small, crisp, juicy and sweet early apple with more richness than most September fruit; the RHS fruit specialist Joan Morgan called it pretty and moreish.

tree.notes: Not recorded.

pollination.notes: Self-sterile; group 3 (C in nursery lists).

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: No independent growing information found. Follow the supplying nursery's advice on rootstock and pollination partners.

varieties.name: Beverly Hills

origin.place: University of California, Los Angeles, California
origin.parentage: Melba x Early McIntosh

varieties.history: Bred at the University of California in Los Angeles from Melba x Early McIntosh, selected in 1939 and introduced in 1945 for the mild coastal climate of southern California. A sample is held in the UK National Fruit Collection.

look.description: Pale greenish-yellow apple with an orange-red flush, darker red streaks and russet dots.

taste.summary: A McIntosh-style summer apple: tender, juicy white flesh with a slightly tart, refreshing flavour that sweetens if left to ripen fully on the tree. Useful for cooking as well as fresh, but it does not keep.
taste.storage_change: very short storage life (Pomiferous)
taste.peak: picked early September (NFC)

climate_flavour.note: Pomiferous: suited to warm, low-chill climates (USDA zone 8); about growing, not flavour

tree.notes: Tree characteristics are not well documented.

pollination.notes: No UK flowering group recorded. As a low-chill apple it flowers early; pair with another low-chill variety.

climate.best_climates: Mild-winter, Mediterranean-type coastal climates such as southern California, where it fruits with about 300 chill hours.
climate.poor_climates: Cold-winter areas, where it flowers early and risks frost; in hot humid summers the soft McIntosh-type flesh goes mealy fast.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A home-garden apple for mild coastal climates. Let fruit hang until fully coloured for best sweetness, and use it quickly.

varieties.name: Bietigheimer
varieties.history: A German apple brought to North America around 1870 and received by the UK National Fruit Trials in 1905. It was noted mainly for its huge, handsome fruit. In Germany the name 'Bietigheimer' is also a regional synonym of Roter Stettiner, so take care with identity.

look.description: Very large, broad, ribbed fruit, pale greenish yellow flushed pinkish to deep red, with russet dots.

taste.summary: Coarse, crisp, white flesh that is juicy and acid to subacid; plain as a dessert apple but cooks well.

tree.notes: Spreading to drooping habit at Brogdale; little other tree data.

pollination.notes: Flowers early at Brogdale (about group 2).

climate.best_climates: Temperate central European and north-eastern American conditions where it was historically grown.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No disease data found.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow it as a curiosity for its very large early-autumn cooking apples. Use the fruit within a couple of months of picking.

varieties.name: Binet Rouge
varieties.history: A well-known Norman bittersweet, one of a small 'Binet' group (with Binet Blanc and Binet Violet), long used for Normandy cider and Calvados. Despite the shared syllables it is not thought to be related to the English Dabinett.

look.description: Small cider apple flushed red.

taste.summary: A medium bittersweet with a high sugar content, low acid and moderate tannin, giving a rich, soft, slightly bitter juice valued for Calvados and full-bodied cider.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; a very late apple for milling Nov-Dec
taste.peak: Picked late November (Orange Pippin); mid-October on Salt Spring Island; can take some sweating before pressing

tree.notes: Weak-growing but starts cropping early; reports on yield differ (heavy in some sources, poorly productive in French ones), and it leans towards alternate bearing.

pollination.notes: Needs another cider variety flowering at the same time.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist Atlantic climates with long autumns that ripen its very late fruit.
climate.poor_climates: Warm humid areas with fire blight pressure, and mildew-prone dry sites; short seasons may not ripen it.

health.other: Very susceptible to powdery mildew and fire blight, though notably resistant to canker.

varieties.grow_notes: Use a vigorous rootstock to compensate for its weak growth. Watch for mildew in spring and avoid planting where fire blight is common.

varieties.name: Birgit Bonnier

origin.parentage: Cortland x Lord Lambourne

varieties.history: A Swedish dessert apple from the Balsgård breeding station, released in 1988 and named after the fruit grower Birgit Bonnier, wife of the publisher Albert Bonnier Jr., who ran an organic orchard at Dalarö.

look.description: Medium, flat fruit, pale green to yellowish, flushed and striped orange-red over much of the skin.

taste.summary: Sweet, pleasantly aromatic flesh. Swedish sources call it juicy, though fruit assessed at Brogdale was soft and rather dry.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct, within a month of picking
taste.peak: Keeps about a month after late-September picking (Swedish Wikipedia).

tree.notes: Spreading to drooping habit at Brogdale.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded; both parents flower early to mid season.

climate.best_climates: Southern and central Sweden (Swedish growing zones 1-4) and similar cool, short-summer climates.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot climates.

health.other: Some resistance to scab and mildew is reported.

varieties.grow_notes: An early-autumn dessert apple for cool Nordic-type gardens. Eat the fruit soon after picking, as it keeps only about a month.

varieties.name: Bismarck

origin.place: Disputed: Bismarck (now Collinsvale), Tasmania; Carisbrook, Victoria; or Canterbury, New Zealand

varieties.history: Named after the German chancellor, this apple has three origin stories: the German settlement of Bismarck (now Collinsvale) in Tasmania, the orchard of a German settler named Fricke at Carisbrook in Victoria, or Canterbury in New Zealand, which Hogg recorded. It reached Britain in the 1880s, won a First Class Certificate from the RHS in 1887, and was then widely planted in British and European gardens. It is distinct from a German apple of the same name.

look.description: Large, flattened, ribbed fruit, pale to rich yellow, streaked and often largely flushed bright to dark crimson.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-textured, juicy white flesh with a clean, sharp acidity and a faint perfume. Accounts of cooking disagree: Orange Pippin says it cooks to a golden puree, while growers report a white froth. The last fruit picked, mellowed in store, makes good eating for those who like a tart apple.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Feb for cooking; raw later in the season

tree.notes: Grows strongly when young and then settles; old trees become broad and spreading. It suits bush forms but still needs an occasional firm prune. Crops well and fairly regularly once established.

pollination.notes: Medium-early flowering (National Fruit Collection full bloom around 8 May), so group 3 is inferred and group 2 is possible. Described as partially self-fertile and frost-tolerant in blossom; a partner improves cropping.

climate.best_climates: Temperate climates, from Tasmania and Victoria to Britain and upland central Europe; its wood is described as frost-hardy.
climate.poor_climates: Very hot, humid areas are untested; scab and mildew can be troublesome in damp seasons.

health.other: Somewhat susceptible to scab, canker and mildew; one grower reports brown rot.

varieties.grow_notes: A robust, heavy-cropping cooker for gardens, including colder upland sites. Give it room, or keep it as a bush with occasional firm pruning, and store the fruit for use through winter.

varieties.name: Black Ben Davis

origin.place: Farm of M. Black, Washington County, Arkansas, USA
origin.parentage: Thought to be a seedling or deeper-coloured sport of Ben Davis

varieties.history: Found around 1880 on M. Black's farm in Washington County, Arkansas, and regarded as a more highly coloured seedling or sport of Ben Davis. It was grown as a showy market apple that kept into spring.

look.description: Medium to large, roundish-conical fruit with smooth, glossy skin almost entirely covered in brilliant dark crimson.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse, moderately crisp and moderately juicy white flesh; mildly subacid and sweetish with only a little aroma. Quality is fair to good.
taste.peak: January to May (Beach 1905 via Bard database).

tree.notes: Upright habit at Brogdale; otherwise expected to grow like Ben Davis.

pollination.notes: Flowers late-mid season at Brogdale (group 4-5).

climate.best_climates: Warm continental summers like the Ozarks and US Midwest, where Ben Davis types were widely planted.
climate.poor_climates: Cool maritime summers leave it plain-flavoured.

health.other: No disease ratings found.

varieties.grow_notes: A long-keeping, highly coloured market apple for warm-summer areas. Store it cool and eat from mid-winter.

varieties.name: Black Diamond

origin.parentage: Counted as a member of the Huaniu (Chinese Delicious-type) apple family; exact origin not documented

varieties.history: A very dark, purple-skinned luxury apple grown above 3,500 m in Nyingchi, Tibet, and sold at high prices in upmarket Chinese shops. Sources place it in the Huaniu family, which Chinese Wikipedia treats as Red Delicious grown in Tianshui. It may therefore be a regional product of Delicious-type trees rather than a separate cultivar. The near-black colour comes from strong UV light and big swings between day and night temperatures.

look.description: Glossy, waxy skin coloured deep purple to almost black, with white flesh.

taste.summary: The flesh is fine-grained and crisp, juicy and sweet with only a little acidity. Its taste is typical of the Delicious type it comes from.
taste.best_eaten: From late autumn; stores for months in cold storage

climate_flavour.note: The near-black colour is credited to growing above 3,500 m with large day-night temperature swings and strong UV (en and es Wikipedia).

tree.notes: Reported to need up to eight years to reach full bearing in its Tibetan growing area, where the season is very short; that slowness may reflect the site rather than the tree.

pollination.notes: Not recorded; Delicious-type apples need a cross-pollinator.

climate.best_climates: High, sunny plateau valleys with cold nights and intense UV, which give the near-black colour.
climate.poor_climates: In warm lowland climates it would colour like an ordinary red Delicious-type apple and lose its distinctive look.

health.other: No disease information found; see Red Delicious for the general behaviour of the type.

varieties.grow_notes: The appeal comes from its mountain growing site, not from a special tree, so garden growers elsewhere should expect an ordinary Delicious-type apple. Use a red Delicious strain for the same fruit outside Tibet.

varieties.name: Black Oxford

origin.parentage: Reported as Hunt Russet x Blue Pearmain (not confirmed)

varieties.history: An old Maine apple from Paris in Oxford County, dating to about 1790 and widely grown in the state in the 1800s. It has made a comeback among heritage growers in New England.

look.description: Medium, round fruit of a deep purple, almost black colour under a bluish bloom, like a large plum.

taste.summary: Firm, rather dry white flesh, sweet-sharp at first and growing steadily sweeter over months in store; still firm into early summer. Good for pies, pink sauce and late cider.
taste.storage_change: Grows steadily sweeter over months in store and stays firm into early summer.
taste.peak: Late December to March.

tree.notes: Average vigour spur-bearer; light cropping is reported. Blossom is an unusual pale pink.

pollination.notes: Early to mid-season bloom in Maine; Orange Pippin lists group 4.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter New England conditions like inland Maine.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; short-season far-northern sites may not ripen it fully.

health.other: Some insect and disease resistance is reported; overall disease resistance rated good.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy, long-keeping all-purpose apple for cold northern areas. Pick late, store cool and eat from the New Year when it has sweetened.

varieties.name: Black Twig

origin.parentage: Often said to be a Winesap seedling; unconfirmed

varieties.history: A southern keeping apple from middle Tennessee, known by the early-to-mid 19th century and widely grown in Virginia and the upper South. Many authorities treat Black Twig and Paragon as the same apple; it is distinct from 'Mammoth Black Twig' (the Arkansas variety), with which it is often confused. The name refers to its dark young shoots.

look.description: Medium, roundish fruit, greenish-yellow largely covered with a dull red flush.

taste.summary: Very firm, crisp flesh that is tart and spicy at harvest, rather like a sharper Winesap; it mellows and becomes richer after a couple of months in store. Valued for cider and cooking as well as winter eating.
taste.storage_change: Tart, tannic and sharp at picking; in store the tannins soften and the sugar comes through, giving a sweeter, lightly spiced apple. All three sources say it must be stored (refrigerated) to reach peak flavour.
taste.peak: After a period in (cold) store; available mid-autumn through winter

tree.notes: Vigorous and reputedly drought-tolerant. Like Winesap it is regarded as a poor pollen producer.

pollination.notes: Poor pollen; plant at least one good pollinating variety nearby. UK flowering group not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Hot, long-season upper South: Tennessee, Virginia and the Carolinas.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, short seasons are unlikely to ripen this very late apple.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A late, long-keeping apple for warm regions. Provide a reliable pollinator and leave the fruit to hang late, then store it until mid-winter for the best flavour.

varieties.name: Blenheim Orange

origin.parentage: Chance seedling; parents unknown

varieties.history: Found around 1740 by George Kempster at Woodstock, beside the Blenheim estate, and widely distributed from about 1818; it won the Banksian Medal from the Horticultural Society in 1822. It became one of England's best-loved dual-purpose apples and is a parent of Newton Wonder, Howgate Wonder and Annie Elizabeth among others.

look.description: Big, broad, somewhat flattened apple of golden yellow, flushed and streaked orange-red, with some russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Creamy, crumbly and rather dry flesh with a distinctive nutty, sweet-sharp flavour, traditionally enjoyed with cheese. Sharper early in the season and good for cooking then; it cooks to a stiff purée ideal for apple charlotte.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Jan for eating; usable for cooking from picking
taste.peak: Cooking from late September; eating from October to January (Wikipedia).

tree.notes: A very large, long-lived tree, similar in size to Bramley, and slow to begin cropping. Partial tip-bearer, so renewal-prune rather than spur-prune hard; best on a dwarfing or semi-dwarfing rootstock in gardens.

pollination.notes: Triploid: a poor pollen donor that needs two compatible diploid partners in group 2-4 to pollinate it and each other. Blossom is somewhat frost-susceptible.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist temperate regions such as southern and central England, where old standard trees still crop heavily.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers give soft, poorly flavoured fruit; late frosts can damage the blossom in exposed or low-lying sites.

health.other: Generally robust, with good resistance to canker and fair resistance to scab and mildew. Main drawbacks are its size, slow start and frost-tender blossom.

varieties.grow_notes: Needs space: on vigorous rootstocks it makes a huge tree, so use M26 or MM106 in gardens. Plant two diploid pollinators nearby and be prepared to wait several years for the first good crop.

varieties.name: Bloody Ploughman
varieties.history: A Scottish apple recorded in 1883 from the Carse of Gowrie between Perth and Dundee. Local legend says a ploughman shot for stealing apples from the Megginch estate was sent home with fruit in his pockets, which his wife threw onto a rubbish heap where this seedling sprang up.

look.description: Large, strongly ribbed conical fruit almost entirely covered in bright to purplish blood-red, with darker streaks.

taste.summary: Crisp, rather dry flesh streaked pink near the skin, with a mild but sweet flavour some compare to Red Delicious; one grower notices a raspberry hint in sun-ripened fruit, though Orange Pippin classes its style as sharper. The skin is tough, and it makes a striking dark pink sauce or juice.
taste.peak: Walcot: pick mid September, keeps until November

tree.notes: Fairly vigorous, regular-cropping spur-bearer bred for the Scottish climate.

pollination.notes: Most sources place it in group 4 (D); some list group 3, and at Brogdale it flowers at about the same time as Cox.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist northern climates such as eastern Scotland and northern England, where its deep colour develops well.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers (regularly above about 24 C) are outside its comfort zone and are likely to dull colour and soften fruit.

health.other: Rated about average for disease; no major specific weakness recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the better choices for northern and Scottish gardens. Grow it for its colour, cooking and juice; it needs a pollination partner in group 3-5.

varieties.name: Blue Pearmain
varieties.history: An old American apple of unknown origin, probably from New England, known by the early 1800s and named for the bluish bloom over its dark red skin. Henry David Thoreau wrote admiringly of a Blue Pearmain tree, and in Britain it received an RHS Award of Merit in 1893 and a First Class Certificate in 1896.

look.description: Truncated-conical fruit heavily striped and flushed dark purplish-red, overlaid with a powdery blue-grey bloom.

taste.summary: Dense, very fine-grained flesh with a little crunch but no snap, moist rather than juicy. Sweet with a pear-like flavour and enough acid to leave a lingering tart finish; aromatic and substantial rather than refreshing. Keeps well in cold storage, though very old fruit turns rubbery.
taste.storage_change: After more than two months in cold store the flavours become more concentrated and intense, though the fruit shrivels (Wikipedia citing Pomiferous).

tree.notes: Average vigour; other growth details are not well recorded.

pollination.notes: Mid-season diploid; any group 2-4 diploid will serve.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter, warm-summer north-eastern North America (New England, New York), where it has been grown since the early 19th century; also crops in southern England.
climate.poor_climates: Mild-winter, low-chill regions; hot nights reduce the deep colour.

health.other: Reported to have generally good disease resistance; specific ratings not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy heirloom suitable for colder gardens. Grow it in full sun with a mid-season pollinator, and store the fruit for a few weeks before eating.

varieties.name: Bodil Neergaard

origin.parentage: Seedling of Pigeonnet blanc d'hiver (per the Danish genebank record)

varieties.history: Found around 1850 by a nurseryman named Anderson at Flintinge on Lolland and named after Bodil de Neergaard of the Fuglsang estate. Known in Danish lists from 1913, it reached Sweden through the Alnarp nurseries in 1925 and was still recommended in Denmark in the 1980s.

look.description: Tall, almost pear-shaped conical fruit, waxy greenish-yellow with a faint greyish-orange cheek and conspicuous grey lenticels.

taste.summary: A very juicy late keeper with medium sugar and fairly strong acidity; sources disagree on aroma, the UK collection calling it sweet, aromatic and vinous while the Danish genebank finds the aroma weak. Texture can turn dry and crumbly in English conditions.
taste.peak: January onwards after long storage (Danish genebank; sv.wikipedia says January to April).

tree.notes: Weak to moderate growth with a medium yield. The fruit marks easily, so handle it gently.

pollination.notes: Self-sterile (S-alleles S1S7); Cox's Orange Pippin and Cox's Pomona are listed as pollinators. Full bloom around 10 May at Brogdale.

climate.best_climates: Cool maritime Scandinavian climates such as Denmark and southern Sweden.
climate.poor_climates: Hot or mildew-prone dry sites; very late picking needs a long autumn.

health.other: Unsprayed Danish trials found no scab and strong canker tolerance, but most shoots carried powdery mildew. Fruit bruises easily.

varieties.grow_notes: Choose an airy site and watch for mildew. Pick late and store until the new year, when the fruit is at its best.

varieties.name: Bohnapfel

origin.parentage: Chance seedling of unknown parentage

varieties.history: A chance seedling found in the Neuwied basin on the Middle Rhine in the second half of the eighteenth century. It became one of the backbone varieties of German meadow orchards for juice and Apfelwein, and was among the few varieties officially promoted nationally in 1920s Germany.

look.description: Barrel-shaped fruit, often taller than wide, green ripening yellow-green with brownish-red marbling and short flames; short thick stalk, russet in the stalk cavity.

taste.summary: Hard, coarse and distinctly sour at picking. By February in store it turns juicy, mild and lightly sweet-sharp, and it keeps until June; it is valued mainly for juice and distilling rather than for eating fresh.
taste.best_eaten: Press Nov-Dec; for eating or cooking wait until Feb-Jun after long storage
taste.storage_change: hard and sour when picked; only after-ripening in store makes it mild, juicy and lightly sweet-sour (de Wikipedia)
taste.peak: ready to eat from February, keeps until June (de Wikipedia)

climate_flavour.note: de Wikipedia: on north-facing slopes and at high altitude the fruit does not ripen fully; best when it can ripen completely on the tree

tree.notes: Moderate at first, later strong-growing, forming a large rounded or pyramidal crown; trees can live to a great age. Slow to start cropping and strongly alternate-bearing.

pollination.notes: Mid-early, long-lasting blossom. Triploid: a poor pollen donor, so plant with two diploid partners.

climate.best_climates: Central European lowland and mid-altitude orchard country with cold winters and warm autumns; robust on exposed sites.
climate.poor_climates: High-altitude or north-facing sites where the late fruit fails to ripen fully; very dry or waterlogged soils encourage canker.

health.other: Only slightly prone to scab and generally robust; canker appears on very dry or very wet soils. Strong biennial bearing; triploid.

varieties.grow_notes: A classic standard tree for meadow orchards: plant on vigorous stock with plenty of space and two diploid pollinators. Thin in heavy years to soften the alternation, and avoid waterlogged ground.

varieties.name: Boiken
varieties.history: A north German apple from around Bremen, named after a dike-warden called Boike and known since 1828. The pomologist Oberdieck promoted it, and the German Pomological Society included it among its 50 recommended varieties in 1874.

look.description: Large, flattish, strongly ribbed yellow apple with some red striping.

taste.summary: Snow-white, firm, fine-grained and juicy flesh with high, wine-like acidity and a slight spiciness. Very sharp at picking and long in store; English tasters found little flavour beyond the acid.
taste.peak: en.wikipedia cultivar list: use February to May.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous, forming a tall crown. Reported to adapt to most soils and to do well at higher elevations.

pollination.notes: Late flowering, which helps it escape spring frosts.

climate.best_climates: Cool northern European climates, including frost-prone upland sites where late blossom is an advantage.
climate.poor_climates: Wet sites where scab and canker take hold; hot climates are untested.

health.other: Susceptible to scab and canker.

varieties.grow_notes: A late-flowering keeper for cold, frost-prone gardens. Pick in late October and store until late winter; use it for cooking, drying and juice, or eat it fresh in spring.

varieties.name: Börtlinger Weinapfel

origin.parentage: Chance seedling of unknown parentage

varieties.history: A chance seedling from the village of Börtlingen near Göppingen, said to date from about 1827 and certainly known by the mid-nineteenth century. Long grown only locally, it spread more widely from the 1960s and was named Baden-Württemberg's meadow-orchard variety of the year for 2023.

look.description: Small, round, slightly flattened apple on a noticeably long stalk, largely covered in dark brownish-red over a whitish to greenish yellow ground.

taste.summary: A cider and juice apple with high sugar and relatively modest, fruity acidity, giving a well-balanced juice without a pronounced aroma. The flesh is firm, slightly tough and juicy, greenish-white to yellow.
taste.best_eaten: Press mid Oct to end Nov; also used for sparkling cider and distilling
taste.peak: Picking ripe mid October, processed through November (de.wikipedia)

tree.notes: Strong-growing with a dense crown, steep at first; fruiting shoots arch over into a characteristic hanging canopy. Fruiting wood renews well and crops are regular.

pollination.notes: Flowers mid-early to late, and the blossom is reasonably frost-hardy.

climate.best_climates: Warmer sites within central European orchard country, on well-fed soils.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, exposed or poor-soil sites, where its small fruit stays smaller still; humid summers bring Marssonina leaf fall.

health.other: Generally robust, but susceptible to Marssonina leaf blotch (early leaf drop) and somewhat to scab and mildew.

varieties.grow_notes: A good low-input standard for extensive orchards if given a warm spot and decent soil. Its arching, hanging canopy needs little formative pruning beyond thinning.

varieties.name: Bountiful

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Kent, England
origin.parentage: Reported as a Cox's Orange Pippin seedling, possibly crossed with Lane's Prince Albert; not firmly documented

varieties.history: Raised at East Malling Research Station in Kent in 1964 and released later as a compact, mildew-resistant cooking apple for gardens. It is one of the few British cookers bred in the second half of the 20th century.

look.description: Large, smooth, evenly shaped green apple, sometimes with a light reddish flush where exposed to the sun.

taste.summary: Fairly sweet for a cooker but a little too acid to be an ideal eater, with very firm flesh and not much distinct character raw, though sweet enough to eat when picked ripe in September. Slices hold their shape when cooked and it bakes well whole; it keeps only about a week.

tree.notes: Compact, modest tree that crops heavily and regularly; well suited to small gardens and trained forms. Thin the fruitlets in heavy years.

pollination.notes: Flowers early (about a week before Cox at Brogdale); usually listed in group 3, sometimes group 2.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate gardens such as lowland Britain, where its mildew resistance is a real advantage.
climate.poor_climates: No record from hot climates; expect soft fruit and short keeping in hot summers.

health.other: Bred for resistance to powdery mildew. Capsid bug can cause cosmetic marks on the fruit.

varieties.grow_notes: A low-maintenance cooker for a small plot; on a dwarfing stock it suits cordons or a patio-sized tree. Needs a group 2-4 pollinator nearby.

varieties.name: Bow Hill Pippin

origin.place: Bow Hill, near Maidstone, Kent, England

varieties.history: Raised by A. S. White at Bow Hill near Maidstone and introduced around 1893 by George Bunyard's Maidstone nursery, receiving an RHS Award of Merit the same year. The National Apple Register classes it as a dessert apple, although some nurseries now offer it among cookers.

look.description: Medium-sized, somewhat flattened yellow apple lightly streaked with orange.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse but juicy yellowish flesh with a sweet, aromatic flavour. Little detailed modern tasting information is available.

tree.notes: Growing habit not recorded in sources checked.

pollination.notes: Flowers just ahead of Cox at Brogdale, so group 3; self-fertility unrecorded, so plant with a pollinator.

climate.best_climates: South-east England, where it was raised; presumably similar cool maritime climates.
climate.poor_climates: No performance records outside southern England; hot summers untested.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A Kentish heritage variety for collectors. Grow as a typical English apple on reasonable, well-drained soil with a group 2-4 partner nearby.

varieties.name: Brabant Bellefleur
varieties.history: An old apple of Flemish or Dutch Brabant, noticed in the late 1700s and grown in the Netherlands, Belgium and northern France. It gained an RHS Award of Merit in 1901.

look.description: Medium to large, broadly conical fruit, greenish yellow with an orange-red flush and red stripes, sometimes some russet.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, yellowish-white flesh with a sweet flavour balanced by some acidity and a slight aroma. A late keeper used in the kitchen and for eating.

tree.notes: Fairly vigorous with good crops. Ploidy is uncertain: Orange Pippin lists it as diploid yet a poor pollinator.

pollination.notes: Late flowering (Brogdale dates suggest group 6; Orange Pippin lists 5), which helps it escape spring frost. Pair with another late-flowering variety.

climate.best_climates: Temperate north-west European conditions like the Low Countries; late blossom suits frosty sites.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No disease ratings found.

varieties.grow_notes: A late-flowering, long-keeping kitchen and table apple that is easy for beginners. Plant with another late-blossoming variety and store the fruit for winter.

varieties.name: Braddick Nonpareil
varieties.history: Raised by the Surrey fruit enthusiast John Braddick at Thames Ditton and first exhibited in 1818. Braddick also brought Claygate Pearmain to notice.

look.description: Flattish, rounded fruit, green to greenish-yellow with a brownish orange-red flush and patches of russet.

taste.summary: Firm yellowish flesh with a sweet, aromatic flavour in the nonpareil style.
taste.storage_change: Intensely sharp, even eye-watering, when just picked; sweetens in store, a good winter keeper (Orange Pippin).
taste.peak: Winter, after storage (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Listed as triploid and a regular cropper by Orange Pippin; not independently confirmed. Other growth details not recorded.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from Brogdale flowering dates (similar to Cox). If triploid, it needs two diploid pollinators and is a poor pollen donor.

climate.best_climates: Inferred from its Surrey origin: mild, moist lowland England.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; hot summers likely reduce quality.

health.other: Reported to have some resistance to scab, canker and mildew.

varieties.grow_notes: A rare Surrey heritage apple. Give it a sunny site and, given the reported triploidy, two diploid pollinators flowering in groups 2-4.

varieties.name: Braeburn

origin.place: Waiwhero, Upper Moutere, Nelson, New Zealand
origin.parentage: Chance seedling, probably of Lady Hamilton; pollen parent unknown (Granny Smith is often suggested but unproven)
origin.raised_by: Found on O. Moran's property; developed by Williams Bros

varieties.history: Discovered as a chance seedling on O. Moran's land in the Upper Moutere district of New Zealand and first grown commercially by the Williams brothers at their Braeburn orchard around 1952. It became one of the world's major commercial apples and is a parent of Jazz.

look.description: Smooth, firm fruit with a greenish-yellow ground covered in orange-red to red stripes and flush.

taste.summary: Crisp and very juicy, snapping cleanly without being rock-hard, with a sharp, refreshing edge balanced by real but never sugary sweetness and a rich, spicy depth; new-season fruit can show a faint pear-drop note. Arguably best soon after picking: long-stored fruit stays crisp but may brown at the core, and UK-grown apples often lack the sweetness reached in warmer climates.
taste.storage_change: Orange Pippin: arguably best soon after picking rather than improving in store; pear-drop hint is in new-season fruit. Wikipedia notes a browning disorder in long storage.
taste.peak: Soon after picking; best served slightly below room temperature (Orange Pippin)

climate_flavour.note: Needs a warmer climate and longer season; NFC says fruit usually fails to mature fully in the UK.

tree.notes: Precocious and productive; thin the fruitlets to keep size and reduce alternate cropping. Maidens often have useful feathers. Needs a long, warm season to ripen properly.

pollination.notes: Partly self-fertile, but crops better with a group 3-5 partner.

climate.best_climates: Warm-temperate regions with a long growing season: New Zealand, Chile, southern France, Washington State.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons such as northern Britain, where fruit fails to mature; very cold winters damage the tree.

health.other: Prone to bitter pit and storage browning disorders, canker in damp climates and fire blight; very susceptible to cedar apple rust in North America.

varieties.grow_notes: In the UK, plant only in the warmest southern gardens against a sunny wall or in a sheltered, south-facing spot. Feed calcium where bitter pit is a problem and thin crops for regular bearing.

varieties.name: Braintree Seedling

origin.parentage: Recorded by the National Fruit Collection as a seedling of Gladstone (pollen parent unknown); other sources say parentage unknown

varieties.history: Raised in 1930 by Mrs Humphreys of Braintree in Essex. It remains a local East Anglian variety, conserved in the National Fruit Collection and by the East of England Apples and Orchards Project.

look.description: Broadly conical yellow fruit with a bright orange flush broken by scarlet streaks, and a fair amount of russet.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-textured, crisp cream flesh with a sweet, aromatic flavour.

tree.notes: No reliable growing data found.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering; plant with a group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Inferred from its Essex origin: the relatively dry, sunny lowlands of eastern England and similar temperate climates.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; hot summers likely reduce colour and keeping.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A good local choice for East Anglian gardens. Grow on MM106 or similar in a sunny spot with a mid-season pollinator.

varieties.name: Bramley 20

origin.parentage: Selected less-vigorous clone of Bramley's Seedling

varieties.history: A clone of Bramley's Seedling selected in the second half of the 20th century because it grows less strongly than the standard tree, making a Bramley more manageable in gardens. Fruit and cooking quality match ordinary Bramley; where and by whom it was selected is poorly documented.

look.description: Identical to Bramley's Seedling: large, flattish, green ripening greenish-yellow with broad red-brown stripes on the sunny side.

taste.summary: As Bramley's Seedling: very sharp, cooking down to a pale golden, fluffy purée with a strong apple tang.

tree.notes: Noticeably less vigorous than standard Bramley and reported to start cropping sooner, but still a sizeable triploid tree. Prune as for Bramley, leaving some tip-bearing shoots.

pollination.notes: Triploid like all Bramleys: its pollen is poor, so it needs a diploid partner in groups 2-4, ideally with a third variety to pollinate that partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist maritime climates like England and Northern Ireland, as for Bramley's Seedling.
climate.poor_climates: Hot climates where the fruit softens, loses acidity and suffers bitter pit; spring frost can damage blossom.

health.other: Assumed to share Bramley's susceptibilities, chiefly bitter pit in store and frost-tender blossom.

varieties.grow_notes: Choose this clone where a full Bramley would be too big. Plant two compatible diploid pollinators nearby, feed calcium-deficient soils to limit bitter pit, and avoid frost pockets.

varieties.name: Bramley's Seedling

origin.parentage: Chance seedling grown from a pip; parents unknown

varieties.history: Grown from a pip by Mary Ann Brailsford in her Southwell garden sometime between 1809 and 1813. The cottage later passed to local butcher Matthew Bramley, who let nurseryman Henry Merryweather propagate the tree on condition that it bore his name; it was on sale by the 1860s, won an RHS First Class Certificate in 1893 and became Britain's standard cooking apple, with Co. Armagh's crop holding protected (PGI) status.

look.description: Large to very large, flattish and often lop-sided, green ripening to greenish-yellow, with broad red-brown stripes on the side facing the sun.

taste.summary: Very sharp, with high acidity and little sugar. Cooked, it collapses into a pale golden, fluffy purée whose strong, clean apple tang survives sweetening; after a few months in store it mellows enough for some people to eat raw.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Mar; cooks well straight from the tree
taste.peak: Cooking apple; Scott Farm harvests mid-September into October

tree.notes: Makes a very large, broad, long-lived tree; on vigorous stocks it needs a lot of space. Bears partly on shoot tips, so avoid shortening every shoot when pruning.

pollination.notes: Triploid with poor pollen: plant a diploid partner in groups 2-4, and ideally a third variety so the partner is also pollinated. The blossom is prone to frost damage.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist maritime climates such as England and Northern Ireland, where it crops heavily, keeps its acidity and stores for months; it does well on heavier soils.
climate.poor_climates: Hot or continental summers give softer, less sharp fruit with more bitter pit and sunscald; frosty spring sites damage the early blossom.

health.other: Bitter pit in store is the main fruit disorder; blossom is frost-sensitive and cropping can become biennial. Triploid and partly tip-bearing.

varieties.grow_notes: Choose a semi-dwarfing or dwarfing rootstock unless you want a very large tree, and plant two compatible diploids nearby. Keep the soil well supplied with calcium and pick before heavy frosts to limit bitter pit.

varieties.name: Brenchley Pippin
varieties.history: A Kentish apple raised in the Weald village of Brenchley and first recorded in 1884. Little more is documented about its origin.

look.description: Medium, rather tall fruit with a greenish-yellow ground and a dull brownish flush.

taste.summary: Tender cream flesh with a sweet, aromatic flavour.

tree.notes: No reliable growing data found.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from Brogdale flowering dates, which are a little later than Cox's; plant with a group 3-5 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Inferred from its Kentish origin: mild, moist south-east England.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A local Kent heritage variety. Treat as a typical late English dessert apple: sunny site, reasonable soil and a later-flowering pollinator.

varieties.name: Brettacher Samling

origin.parentage: Usually given as a chance seedling; the National Fruit Collection lists Reinette de Champagne x Jakob Lebel

varieties.history: A seedling from Brettach near Heilbronn (seed reportedly sown around 1900, tree noticed about 1908), spread from the 1920s and still a main orchard apple in Baden-Württemberg. 'Samling' is the Scandinavian word for seedling.

look.description: Large to very large, flattened, ribbed fruit, greenish yellow with a pink flush and red streaks under a thick waxy skin.

taste.summary: Coarse, crisp, very juicy flesh with a refreshing tart acidity and modest sugar. It mellows from Christmas onward and keeps until late spring.
taste.storage_change: Ripens in store; ready from Christmas and keeps until late spring.
taste.peak: From Christmas to April/May.

climate_flavour.note: Pforzheim city variety list says fruit from high, cool sites tastes grassy; it prefers warm soils and a long season.

tree.notes: Strong-growing triploid with sparse branching and a broad, flat crown. Robust and healthy on suitable soils.

pollination.notes: Triploid, so useless as a pollinator; needs two diploid partners. Flowers late-mid season.

climate.best_climates: Warm lowland sites with a long growing season, like the Neckar valley.
climate.poor_climates: High, cold sites (fruit tastes grassy) and cold, wet soils, where canker becomes a problem.

health.other: Generally robust, but canker-prone on cold, wet soils and somewhat susceptible to fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: A big, robust triploid for warm, well-drained orchard sites. Pick late and store cool; the fruit is used for cooking, juice and cider as well as late eating.

varieties.name: Brina

origin.parentage: Open-pollinated seedling of the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois selection PRI 2059-101 (as given on Wikipedia)
origin.raised_by: Istituto Sperimentale per la Frutticoltura, Trento section (later part of CRA-FRU)

varieties.history: A late-season dessert apple released in 1998 by the Trento section of Italy's state fruit-research institute, from a programme breeding for disease resistance. It carries resistance to both scab and powdery mildew; it has remained a minor variety and English-language descriptions are sparse.

look.description: Medium to fairly large fruit with smooth, russet-free skin marked by pale lenticels; described by its breeders as attractive.

taste.summary: Its breeders rate the eating quality highly, but no published tasting notes describing its sweetness, acidity or aroma were found.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous with a spreading habit and heavy production according to the breeders' description.

pollination.notes: Flowers medium-late; the release paper calls it partially self-fertile, so a mid-to-late flowering partner will still improve set. Group number is inferred from that description.

climate.best_climates: Bred and tested in the Alpine valleys of Trentino, where it is picked in the first days of October; suited to similar temperate fruit-growing areas, especially where low-spray growing matters.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in very cold or very hot regions; as a late apple it needs a reasonably long, warm autumn to ripen in cool maritime climates.

health.other: Bred for resistance to apple scab (Vf-derived) and powdery mildew; other susceptibilities are not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A candidate for organic or low-input gardens because of its scab and mildew resistance. Give it full sun and a mid-to-late flowering partner, and thin heavy crops for size. Little UK growing experience is recorded, so treat performance here as untested.

varieties.name: Britemac

origin.place: New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station, New Brunswick, New Jersey, USA
origin.parentage: (Melba x McIntosh) x (Kildare x Langford Beauty), seedlings of open-pollinated crosses
origin.raised_by: Prof. M.A. Blake, New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: Raised in 1934 by M.A. Blake at the New Jersey station as a brighter-coloured McIntosh-type dessert apple. It is now rarely grown.

look.description: Large, broadly conical fruit, greenish yellow brightly flushed and striped red.

taste.summary: Sweet, crisp, juicy white flesh in the McIntosh style; in store it softens and becomes mild.

tree.notes: Spur-bearing; little other tree data.

pollination.notes: Flowers late-mid season (Orange Pippin group 5; Brogdale dates group 4-5).

climate.best_climates: North-eastern US conditions with cool autumn nights, as for other McIntosh types.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Rated resistant to cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: An early-autumn McIntosh-type apple to eat fresh off the tree. Plant with a late-mid season pollinator.

varieties.name: Brown Snout

origin.parentage: Unknown
origin.raised_by: Mr Dent (on whose farm it was found)

varieties.history: Said to have been found on a Mr Dent's farm at Yarkhill in Herefordshire in the mid nineteenth century. Bulmers of Hereford propagated it widely, and it spread through West Midlands orchards and, less often, the West Country.

look.description: Small green fruit with russet patches and a large brown russet patch around the eye, which gives the name.

taste.summary: A mild-to-medium bittersweet: low acid with moderate tannin and firm flesh, making a soft, mellow cider.

tree.notes: Medium-sized tree with a stiffly upright habit; moderately biennial.

pollination.notes: Described as late flowering; group number inferred from that.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist Herefordshire-type climates.
climate.poor_climates: Warm regions where fire blight is common.

health.other: Very susceptible to fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: Avoid in fire-blight areas. Its upright habit suits close planting. Plant with other late-flowering cider apples.

varieties.name: Browns Apple

origin.raised_by: Found by Mr Hill, cider maker and nurseryman of Staverton

varieties.history: Found by Mr Hill, a cider maker and nurseryman at Staverton near Totnes in Devon, and known by the early 1920s. It became one of the standard sharp varieties of West Country cider orchards.

look.description: Medium, flat-round fruit coloured orange-red to red; white flesh often stained pink in well-coloured apples.

taste.summary: A sharp cider apple: fresh, fruity acidity with little tannin. On its own it makes a lively but rather thin cider, so it is mostly blended with bittersweets.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill late Oct-Nov

tree.notes: Very vigorous, which can hold back the first crops; heavy cropping once established, with some tendency to alternate. Fruit drops when ripe.

pollination.notes: A good pollinator for other late-flowering cider apples.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp West Country conditions; considered cold-hardy enough for colder temperate orchards.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, dry summer climates are untested; very short seasons may not ripen it.

health.other: Very resistant to scab; some susceptibility to fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: Its vigour makes it best on a less vigorous rootstock in small orchards. Blend its juice with Dabinett or Yarlington Mill type bittersweets. Gather promptly because ripe fruit drops.

varieties.name: Bulmer's Norman

origin.parentage: Unknown; a French cider variety whose original name was lost

varieties.history: A Norman cider apple imported by H.P. Bulmer of Hereford in the early twentieth century; its French name was lost, so it took the company's name. Its vigour made it a popular choice for frame-working and for early-season commercial orchards.

look.description: Medium, greenish-yellow cider apple.

taste.summary: A bittersweet with sweet, low-acid juice and moderate tannin; useful early in the season to give body to blends.

tree.notes: Very vigorous, spreading, flat-topped triploid; crops heavily but tends to alternate years.

pollination.notes: Triploid, so a poor pollen donor; needs two other compatible varieties nearby to pollinate it and each other.

climate.best_climates: Cool-summer maritime climates such as Herefordshire and Normandy.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, humid areas where scab is severe.

health.other: Very susceptible to scab; triploid; biennial.

varieties.grow_notes: Needs plenty of room or a dwarfing rootstock because of its vigour. Plan pollination carefully as a triploid. Spray or choose an airy site if scab is common locally.

varieties.name: Burgundy

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York, USA
origin.parentage: Sources differ: Macoun x Monroe (National Fruit Collection) or Monroe x (Macoun x Antonovka) (Orange Pippin)
origin.raised_by: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: A very dark red early-autumn apple from the Geneva, New York breeding programme, introduced in 1974.

look.description: Large, round, glossy fruit almost covered in a deep, nearly black-red flush.

taste.summary: Crisp, sweet, subacid flesh that is often stained pink and browns quickly when cut. It does not keep: within weeks it softens and loses quality.
taste.storage_change: Deteriorates after two to three weeks; flesh browns quickly when cut.
taste.peak: Fresh from the tree in September.

tree.notes: Vigorous, regular-bearing spur type; fruit hangs on the tree for about three weeks after ripening.

pollination.notes: Brogdale dates put it in group 4; Orange Pippin lists group 3. A good pollinator for others.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter, cool-to-warm summer regions like upstate New York.
climate.poor_climates: Humid, fire-blight-prone areas.

health.other: Poor disease resistance overall: scab, powdery mildew and cedar-apple rust, and very susceptible to fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: Best for home growers who can spray and who will eat the fruit fresh within a few weeks. Avoid areas with heavy fire-blight pressure.

varieties.name: Bushey Grove

origin.parentage: Queen x Bismarck (both parents uncertain)
origin.raised_by: Good family of Bushey Grove (NFC names Mrs Good; Orange Pippin J.T. Good)

varieties.history: Raised in 1897 at Bushey Grove in Hertfordshire and introduced around 1926 by G.W. King of Sidcup, Kent. It received an RHS Award of Merit in 1922.

look.description: Medium to large, broadly conical fruit, greenish yellow with red stripes.

taste.summary: Very soft, coarse, very juicy flesh with a sharp acidity; a cooker that cooks well.

tree.notes: Vigorous, heavy-cropping tree with attractive blossom; spreading to drooping habit.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering (group 3).

climate.best_climates: South-east English conditions like its Hertfordshire home, ideally on a dry, airy site.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, humid areas where scab is severe.

health.other: Very prone to apple scab.

varieties.grow_notes: A heavy-cropping early cooker; give it an open, airy position and clear fallen leaves to keep scab down.

varieties.name: Butterball
varieties.history: An American ornamental crab of the second half of the twentieth century, named for its abundant butter-yellow fruit. It holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Small rounded fruits about 2.5 cm, bright golden-yellow, some catching a faint orange flush in the sun, crowded along the branches.

taste.summary: Mainly ornamental; the fruit is tart and is used for crab apple jelly rather than eaten.
taste.peak: Fruit ripens in October and persists into winter (Ashridge).

tree.notes: Average vigour with regular, heavy fruiting; the fruit ripens over a period and attracts birds. Light pruning only.

pollination.notes: White single blossom in mid season; a good pollinator for group 2-4 apples.

climate.best_climates: Temperate climates in Britain and northern Europe; tolerates heavier clay soils.
climate.poor_climates: Not well documented; hot, humid regions are likely to increase leaf disease.

health.other: Nursery sources rate its disease resistance as average; no specific weakness well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: Easy for beginners: plant in sun on any reasonable soil, including clay, and prune lightly. Pairs well with mid-season dessert apples as a pollinator.

varieties.name: Calville Blanc d'Hiver
varieties.history: An ancient European apple, most likely French, described in 1598 by the botanist Johann Bauhin in south-west Germany. It became the classic apple of French pâtisserie and was grown by Thomas Jefferson at Monticello.
