look.description: Large, flattened apple with bold ribs running from stalk to eye; pale green ripening to waxy yellow, sometimes with a faint pinkish blush and russet dots.

taste.summary: Juicy, fairly crisp flesh with a distinctly tart flavour, close to Granny Smith in sharpness, balanced by enough sweetness to taste rich; several tasters notice a faint banana note and one finds it slightly grassy. Very high in vitamin C, so cut flesh does not brown. It holds its shape in a tart, or cooks to a rich, sharp puree if cut small, and keeps a month or two.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Mar; needs several weeks in store after picking
taste.storage_change: picked end of October, mature from December (fr Wikipedia)
taste.peak: from December (fr Wikipedia)

climate_flavour.note: NFC: fruits fail to ripen fully in the UK

tree.notes: Demanding: it does best trained against a warm, south-facing wall where the fruit is sheltered from rain. Thin-skinned fruit bruises easily, so handle it gently.

pollination.notes: Mid-late flowering diploid with a short blossom period; pair with a group 3-5 partner.

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer temperate climates with a long autumn: central and southern France, warm parts of Germany, Virginia and similar.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, damp maritime climates such as most of the UK, where fruit often fails to ripen fully and the tree suffers from disease.

health.other: Regarded as demanding and prone to a range of diseases and pests in less than ideal sites; some susceptibility to cedar apple rust in North America.

varieties.grow_notes: In Britain, grow it as an espalier or fan on a dwarfing rootstock against a sunny wall in the south. Pick late, store cool and wait until midwinter for the full flavour.

varieties.name: Calville d'Août
varieties.history: A little-known French summer Calville. It appears in German and French variety lists, and one French list dates it to about 1925 and describes it as a late-summer apple for eating and cooking; little else is documented.

look.description: Not documented in the sources consulted.

taste.summary: Flavour not documented; listed as suitable for both eating and cooking.

tree.notes: No tree data found.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Not documented.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Insufficient information for specific advice; treat as an early-season apple that should be eaten soon after picking.

varieties.name: Calville Rouge d'Hiver
varieties.history: One of the old French Calvilles, known since around 1600 and long grown across France and Germany as a showy winter dessert apple. Its uneven performance and dark skin spotting have pushed it out of commerce, and it now survives mainly in old standard orchards and collections.

look.description: Medium, strongly ribbed, rather tall fruit flushed deep red almost all over; dark spots often appear on the skin.

taste.summary: Soft white flesh with a mild, pleasant sweet-sharp flavour. In a warm, well-chosen site it gains a delicate raspberry-like perfume; grown in cooler or poorer conditions it is rather flat and lacks aroma. Picked very late, it keeps through the winter.
taste.peak: Through the winter (picked very late, keeps 3 months or more)

tree.notes: Tree data not well recorded; quality depends strongly on a warm, favourable site.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Warm, sheltered sites in France and southern Germany with good soil, where the fruit colours and develops its aroma.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, damp or exposed sites, where flavour is poor and scab and canker take hold.

health.other: Susceptible to scab and canker; harmless dark spots on the skin spoil its looks.

varieties.grow_notes: Only worth growing on a warm wall or sunny, sheltered site with good soil. Keep scab under control and store the fruit cool until mid-winter.

varieties.name: Cameo

origin.parentage: Chance seedling in a Red Delicious orchard; thought to be Red Delicious x Golden Delicious

varieties.history: Found in 1987 as a chance seedling in a Red Delicious block owned by the Caudle family near Dryden, Washington. It was propagated commercially in the 1990s and became one of Washington's more widely grown varieties.

look.description: Large fruit with bold red stripes and patches over a cream to orange-yellow ground, dotted with pale lenticels.

taste.summary: Dense, crisp and juicy, balancing sweetness with light tartness and a hint of pear. Orange Pippin's own note calls the flavour fairly bland, but many growers disagree, and individual tasters report strawberry or fresh-pineapple notes. It sweetens over a week or two of storage, browns slowly when cut and keeps its crunch for months in the fridge.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Feb; better after 1-2 weeks in store

tree.notes: Little published garden-growing information.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 3; needs a compatible diploid pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Dry, sunny irrigated fruit regions with cool autumn nights, like central Washington.
climate.poor_climates: Humid eastern North America where cedar-apple rust is rife; cool, short seasons may not ripen it fully.

health.other: Highly susceptible to cedar-apple rust; other disease ratings not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: Best suited to sunny, dry regions. Control cedar-apple rust where junipers grow nearby, and store the crop for a couple of weeks before eating for best sweetness.

varieties.name: Campanino
varieties.history: An old apple of the lower Po valley, first mentioned in 1751 and described by Gallesio in 1815 as the Modena apple. It is still grown around Modena, Ferrara, Mantua, Reggio Emilia, Rovigo and Venice, and is traditional in mostarda and other local preserves.

look.description: Small, neat, rounded fruit, yellow-green with a purplish-red flush and stripes on the sunny side and a little russet netting at the eye.

taste.summary: Very firm, crisp, greenish-white flesh with a sugary but distinctly acid, aromatic flavour; rather dry. It holds its shape when cooked.
taste.best_eaten: Jan-Mar, after a few months of storage
taste.storage_change: Wikipedia: keeps about six months without refrigeration.
taste.peak: en.wikipedia cultivar list: use January to March.

pollination.notes: Late flowering at Brogdale (full bloom around 16 May).

climate.best_climates: The hot-summer, cool-winter plains of north-east Italy where it is a traditional crop.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons may not ripen a late-October apple fully.

health.other: No disease ratings found.

varieties.grow_notes: A late, long-keeping regional apple; the fruit is said to keep about six months without refrigeration. Best suited to warm-summer sites.

varieties.name: Cap of Liberty

origin.parentage: Unknown; a link with Lambrook Pippin has been suggested

varieties.history: An old Somerset cider apple from around Martock. It was little planted after the 1920s and was considered close to extinct by the 1960s, but cider-tree nurseries now offer it again. It is rated a vintage variety, good enough to make a single-variety cider.

look.description: Small, rough-skinned fruit, roughly conical to cylindrical, pale yellow heavily flushed and streaked with red.

taste.summary: A full bittersharp: high in both tannin and malic acid, giving a sharp, astringent juice. Nurseries describe its cider contribution as aromatic, complex and spicy; on its own it makes a fairly light, acidic and slightly bitter cider, so it is usually blended with sweeter fruit.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill within a week or two of picking
taste.storage_change: does not keep; press within a week or two of picking (RHS, Salt Spring)
taste.peak: mill shortly after an early-October harvest

tree.notes: A medium-sized but vigorous tree with a distinctive frame of several long, unbranched, spreading limbs. Crops heavily, but mostly in alternate years.

pollination.notes: Self-sterile; plant near other cider or dessert apples flowering at the same time. Flowering group not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist south-west England cider country and similar cool maritime climates; also grown by cider orchards in coastal British Columbia.
climate.poor_climates: Wet sites with heavy scab pressure ruin the tree; untested in hot continental summers.

health.other: Extremely prone to scab, with some scab and resulting shoot die-back nearly always present; also susceptible to canker.

varieties.grow_notes: Best on an open, airy site where scab is less severe, and in a cider orchard where its sharp, tannic juice can be blended with bittersweets and sweets. Expect alternate-year cropping and press the fruit promptly since it does not keep.

varieties.name: Captain Kidd

origin.parentage: Sport of Kidd's Orange Red (Cox's Orange Pippin x Delicious)
origin.raised_by: Found in the orchard of Robin Osborne

varieties.history: A more deeply coloured bud sport of Kidd's Orange Red, found in 1962 in Robin Osborne's orchard at Twyford in Hawke's Bay and released in 1969. Apart from its redder skin it behaves like its parent, itself a 1924 cross raised by J.H. Kidd at Greytown in New Zealand.

look.description: Medium, conical apple heavily streaked and flushed bright red over yellow, redder than Kidd's Orange Red.

taste.summary: Shares the eating quality of Kidd's Orange Red: very sweet and juicy, honeyed and noticeably sweeter than Cox, with a lively kick that tasters liken to a French dessert wine and occasional pear-drop notes. The dense flesh is firm rather than crunchy. Flavour keeps developing for some weeks after picking; best eaten before the new year.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Jan, after a few weeks in store
taste.peak: November-December (Chris Bowers).

tree.notes: Grows and crops like Kidd's Orange Red; little independent data on the sport itself.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 3, as for Kidd's Orange Red. The RHS lists Kidd's Orange Red and Cox as cross-incompatible, so do not rely on Cox to pollinate it.

climate.best_climates: Sunny temperate climates with cool autumn nights, such as the fruit regions of New Zealand and southern England.
climate.poor_climates: Very short or cool seasons may not ripen a mid-October apple; very warm nights reduce the red colour that is the point of this sport.

health.other: Expected to share the disease profile of Kidd's Orange Red; not separately recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Needs a warm, sunny position to ripen and colour well in Britain. Choose a group 2-4 pollinator other than Cox or its sports.

varieties.name: Carlton

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York, USA
origin.parentage: Autumn Bough x Red Astrachan per the National Fruit Collection (Montgomery x Red Astrachan is also reported)
origin.raised_by: Richard Wellington, New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: Raised in 1912 by Richard Wellington at Geneva, New York, and introduced in 1923 as a late-summer red apple. It is a parent of Niagara and Redhook.

look.description: Medium to large, conical, ribbed fruit, dull yellowish green flushed brownish red and streaked brighter red, with russet dots.

taste.summary: Firm, fine flesh with a subacid flavour leaning slightly acid; low in aroma. A summer apple for eating soon after picking.

tree.notes: Spreading habit at Brogdale; little other data.

pollination.notes: Flowers early at Brogdale (about group 2).

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter north-eastern US conditions like upstate New York.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No disease data found.

varieties.grow_notes: A late-summer eating apple for collections; plant with an early-flowering partner and use the fruit promptly.

varieties.name: Carola

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x unknown

varieties.history: Bred at the Müncheberg fruit research station in East Germany and released in 1962; the National Fruit Collection holds it under the name Kalco.

look.description: Medium to large, flat-conical fruit with prominent ribs at the eye, lemon yellow with red flushing and stripes on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Very juicy, medium-firm, yellowish flesh with a lively sweet, subacid flavour and a fine Cox-like aroma. Eat it from the tree or within a couple of months.
taste.peak: Eat from picking in September; keeps until about December.

tree.notes: Medium vigour at first, weaker with age. Crops very early, sometimes in the second year, and heavily, but tends to alternate after big crops; thinning helps.

pollination.notes: Mid-season (group 3). German sources list Alkmene, Cox, James Grieve, Goldparmäne, Idared and Oldenburg as suitable partners.

climate.best_climates: Central European continental climates on open, fertile soils.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Prone to bitter pit, water core and storage rots; moderately susceptible to scab and mildew; fruit bruises easily.

varieties.grow_notes: A precocious, productive Cox-type for garden trees; thin heavy crops to limit biennial bearing and handle fruit gently. Give it open, fertile soil.

varieties.name: Caroline

origin.place: Blickling Hall, near Aylsham, Norfolk, England

varieties.history: Arose in Lord Suffield's gardens at Blickling Hall in Norfolk, where it was already fruiting by 1822, and was named after Lord Suffield's wife. It is conserved in the National Fruit Collection and by the East of England Apples and Orchards Project.

look.description: Broadly conical fruit, green ripening to yellow, marked with red stripes.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp white flesh with a sweet flavour; a long-keeping dessert apple.

tree.notes: No reliable growing data found.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering period D (group 4) by the East of England Apples and Orchards Project; plant with a group 3-5 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Inferred from its Norfolk origin: the cool, fairly dry lowlands of eastern England.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A Norfolk heritage apple that suits East Anglian gardens. Grow on a semi-vigorous rootstock with a later-flowering pollinator; it can be trained as an espalier or cordon.

varieties.name: Carroll

origin.parentage: Moscow Pear seedling x Melba

varieties.history: A Canadian prairie apple selected in 1947 and released in 1961, bred for extreme winter hardiness from a Russian-type Moscow Pear seedling crossed with Melba. It was chosen as a Manitoba centennial fruit in 1970 and is still grown on the Canadian prairies.

look.description: Mid-sized pale green apple mottled and streaked with rosy red, rather like a brightly coloured Melba.

taste.summary: A soft, mild early apple of Melba type, pleasant fresh and good for sauce and pies; prairie growers note the flesh is slow to brown when cut. It is not as crisp or juicy as commercial western apples.
taste.peak: Ripens about 1 September in Manitoba and keeps 2-3 months (USDA GRIN).

tree.notes: Dwarfish to medium-sized, strongly branched tree that bears annually. Crotch angles can be awkward, so train scaffolds early.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded in sources checked; plant with another hardy early variety.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental interiors such as the Canadian prairies and northern plains, where it survives winters near -45 C.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, humid summers would soften this early, soft-fleshed apple further; little value where better-quality early apples can be grown.

health.other: Rated resistant to cedar-apple rust in Arkansas extension listings. Occasional winter injury in the very coldest prairie winters.

varieties.grow_notes: A choice for gardens in zone 3 where few quality apples survive. Pick as soon as ripe and use within a couple of months; train young trees to wide crotch angles.

varieties.name: Carswell's Orange

origin.parentage: Seedling of Cox's Orange Pippin; pollen parent unknown

varieties.history: Raised in 1938 by J.W. Carswell at Ashtead in Surrey from a Cox's Orange Pippin seed; he also raised Carswell's Honeydew. It is held in the National Fruit Collection but is rarely grown.

look.description: Medium to large conical fruit, yellow with a red flush and scarlet stripes and almost no russet.

taste.summary: Juicy, slightly coarse flesh with a pleasant aromatic flavour that shows its Cox parentage.

tree.notes: Tree characteristics are not recorded in the sources checked.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from Brogdale flowering records, which put it alongside Cox; assume it needs a partner.

climate.best_climates: Southern English conditions like those it was raised in.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented outside Britain; estimates are inferred from its Cox parentage.

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A collector's Cox seedling for southern Britain. Grow in a sunny, sheltered spot on well-drained soil with a group 2-4 pollinator.

varieties.name: Catshead
varieties.history: One of the oldest English cooking apples, already known in the 17th century and named for its boxy, angular outline. Older writers sometimes merged it with the Costard, though Hogg treated them as different apples. It is a parent of both Lord Derby and Peasgood's Nonsuch.

look.description: Very large, squarish, angular fruit with prominent ribs that end in knobs around the eye; pale green with a faint brownish cheek, small russet dots and a greasy skin.

taste.summary: A traditional cooker with juicy, coarse white flesh and a fair amount of acidity, so it needs little added sugar; it cooks down to a textured puree. Raw it is plain, with only a faint perfume, and some tasters find it dry. Keeps a month or two.
taste.peak: picked early October

tree.notes: A strong grower that eventually makes a very large, flat-topped tree. Slow to crop when young but more productive as it ages. Some sources list it as triploid; this has not been confirmed here.

pollination.notes: Flowers alongside Bramley at Brogdale (group 3). If it is triploid as some sources say, it will be a poor pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Traditional English orchards in cool, moist lowland conditions.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are untested; expect softer fruit and shorter keeping.

health.other: Reported to resist scab well; other disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Best grown as a large orchard tree on a vigorous stock where its slow start does not matter. Give it plenty of space and a group 2-4 diploid partner.

varieties.name: Cellini

origin.parentage: Seedling of Nonsuch (pollen parent unknown)

varieties.history: Raised by the Vauxhall nurseryman Leonard Phillips from a seed of Nonsuch and introduced around 1828. Hogg admired it as a showy apple, and it is a parent of Duchess of Bedford, Exquisite and James Lawson.

look.description: Large, flattish, smooth and slightly greasy fruit, greenish-yellow mottled and streaked with orange-red.

taste.summary: Soft, loose, coarse and juicy white flesh with a gentle acidity and a distinctive aniseed-like aromatic note. Mainly a cooker, but eatable fresh when ripe; it soon turns soft.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct, within a few weeks of picking
taste.peak: Orange Pippin: keeps only 2-3 weeks; en.wikipedia list: use October to December.

tree.notes: Average vigour; a spur-bearer that crops heavily and regularly.

pollination.notes: Listed as group 4; full bloom around 12 May at Brogdale.

climate.best_climates: Temperate climates with cool summers, such as southern England.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would hasten its already short life; wet canker-prone sites.

health.other: Some susceptibility to canker reported.

varieties.grow_notes: A reliable, heavy-cropping old garden apple for cooking and early use. Pick in September and use within a few weeks; it is a good pollen source for mid-to-late flowerers.

varieties.name: Centennial

origin.parentage: Recorded by Orange Pippin as Dolgo x Chestnut Crab; not confirmed from a second source

varieties.history: Released by the University of Minnesota in 1957, around the time of the state's centennial, as a large, good-eating crab for very cold gardens. It is grown as much for fresh eating and sauce as for preserves.

look.description: A large crab of roughly 4-5 cm, bright red over an orange-yellow ground.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy and sweet-sharp, good enough to eat fresh like a small dessert apple, and it cooks to a smooth sauce. It does not keep, so use it within a couple of weeks.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-early Sep, fresh from the tree
taste.peak: Mid to late August (UMN); does not store well; keeps 2-3 weeks (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: A naturally small, weak-growing tree that crops heavily, so it suits small gardens without a very dwarfing stock.

pollination.notes: Pale pink blossom; needs a partner but is itself a good pollinator for other hardy apples.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates such as Minnesota and the Canadian prairies, where it is fully hardy.
climate.poor_climates: Low-chill, hot regions; early ripening in summer heat shortens its already short keeping life (inferred).

health.other: Very resistant to scab with some fire blight resistance; main drawback is very poor storage.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant with another hardy apple or crab for pollination. Pick in late August and eat or make sauce quickly, as the fruit does not store.

varieties.name: Champion

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: A Czech Golden Delicious x Cox cross made around 1960 and released in the 1970s; it became an important commercial apple in central and eastern Europe before newer varieties replaced it. Not to be confused with the American 'Champion', a synonym of Collins.

look.description: Large, rounded fruit, greenish-yellow with an uneven orange-red flush and stripes, nearly all red on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Juicy, creamy-white flesh, sweet to very sweet with only gentle acidity and a pleasant, fairly simple flavour. It keeps for several months.
taste.peak: en.wikipedia cultivar list: use October to February.

tree.notes: Moderate vigour; crops early, regularly and heavily, and tends to overset, so thin to keep fruit size. Tolerates pruning well and suits weak to moderate rootstocks.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering diploid; Idared and James Grieve are listed as good pollinators.

climate.best_climates: Warm or moderately warm, sheltered sites in central Europe with deep, moist, fertile soil.
climate.poor_climates: Poor, dry soils reduce quality; wet scab-prone areas without spraying.

health.other: Usually heavily attacked by scab but fairly resistant to powdery mildew; sensitive to some virus diseases.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in a warm, sheltered spot on good soil and thin the fruit. Spray or choose a dry site for scab control.

varieties.name: Charden

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Reinette Clochard

varieties.history: A French Golden Delicious x Reinette Clochard cross raised in 1959 and introduced in the 1970s; Chantecler (Belchard) comes from the same pairing. It is a triploid.

look.description: Green to greenish-yellow, rounded-conical apple with only a trace of red and a little russet.

taste.summary: Fairly crisp, juicy, yellowish flesh with a sweet, honeyed flavour and only modest acidity. Keeps for several months.
taste.peak: en.wikipedia cultivar list: use November to March.

tree.notes: Vigorous but precocious and heavy-cropping.

pollination.notes: Triploid: a poor pollen donor, so plant two other diploid varieties flowering at the same time.

climate.best_climates: Temperate to warm climates, such as France, where a late Golden-type apple ripens fully.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons where a mid-October apple struggles to sweeten.

health.other: Described as having average disease resistance; specific ratings not found.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it room, as it is a vigorous triploid, and two diploid pollinators. Store the fruit for winter use.

varieties.name: Charles Ross

origin.parentage: Peasgood's Nonsuch x Cox's Orange Pippin
origin.raised_by: Charles Ross, head gardener at Welford Park

varieties.history: Raised by the gardener Charles Ross at Welford Park near Newbury and first shown in 1890 as Thomas Andrew Knight. His employer asked for it to be renamed after him in 1899, the same year it won RHS awards; it holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Large, handsome conical apple, pale yellow-green flushed and streaked orange-red; individual fruit can be very big.

taste.summary: Crisp and juicy when picked in September, when it is still fairly sharp; over a few weeks it turns very sweet, with some of Cox's aroma and a pear-like quality (one taster finds a marked orange note). It does not keep: by November the flesh goes dry and almost powdery. Cooked slices only partly break down.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Dec; cook early in the season, eat fresh later
taste.storage_change: Quite sharp in September, sweetens in store; flesh becomes almost powdery as it matures.

tree.notes: Easy, regular-cropping spur-bearer suited to beginners; thin to keep fruit size manageable.

pollination.notes: Group 3; pollinated by most mid-season diploids.

climate.best_climates: Throughout Britain, including cooler northern gardens and thin chalky or limy soils where many apples sulk.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summer climates will soften the large fruit and reduce colour.

health.other: Generally healthy; good scab resistance. Fruit softens fairly quickly once out of cold storage.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the most forgiving dual-purpose apples for British gardens, coping well with chalk and colder sites. Plant with a group 2-4 partner and thin heavy sets.

varieties.name: Chehalis

origin.place: Near the Chehalis River, Oakville, Washington
origin.parentage: Probably a Golden Delicious seedling (open-pollinated)

varieties.history: Found in 1955 by Lloyd Lonborg near the Chehalis River at Oakville in western Washington and widely planted in Pacific Northwest gardens. It looks and tastes much like a large, elongated Golden Delicious, from which it probably descends.

look.description: Big, somewhat elongated greenish-yellow apple, often with a faint pink cheek on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Sweet and juicy with a Golden Delicious character and a honeyed note; crisp at first but the cream flesh turns soft and melting within days of picking. Picked early it is noticeably tart, and the sweetness develops quickly.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct; eat within a few weeks before it softens
taste.storage_change: Tart if picked early, sweetens within a few days, then the flesh softens quickly (Orange Pippin; Brogdale calls it melting).
taste.peak: Mid September to October, soon after picking.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous spur-bearer with a drooping habit at Brogdale; crops regularly. Judge ripeness by a gentle lift - fruit is ready when it parts easily.

pollination.notes: Described as self-fertile by Orange Pippin and USDA Geneva; a partner in group 3 will still improve set.

climate.best_climates: Mild, wet maritime climates like western Washington and British Columbia, where its scab resistance pays off.
climate.poor_climates: Hot regions hasten softening; very cold interiors are untested in the sources consulted.

health.other: Highly resistant to scab and somewhat resistant to mildew, which makes it popular with organic growers in the Pacific Northwest. Fruit softens quickly after picking.

varieties.grow_notes: A good low-spray apple for damp climates. Pick in stages when fruit lifts off easily and use promptly; it makes good pies and dried rings.

varieties.name: Chelmsford Wonder
varieties.history: Arose near Chelmsford in Essex around 1870 and was put on the market about 1890 by the local nursery Saltmarsh & Son. In 1891 the RHS gave it both an Award of Merit and a First Class Certificate; it is still kept in Essex heritage orchards.

look.description: Large, flattish, yellow-skinned fruit with a soft orange-pink to red flush and streaks.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained and juicy flesh with a moderate, clean acidity. A late-keeping cooker that holds well in store.

tree.notes: Tree habit not well recorded in sources checked.

pollination.notes: Flowers with Bramley at Brogdale, so group 3; plant with a group 2-4 partner.

climate.best_climates: East Anglia and similar cool, fairly dry lowland English conditions where it originated.
climate.poor_climates: No records from hot regions; heat would likely shorten keeping life.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A good local heritage choice for Essex and East Anglian gardens. Pick in early October and store cool for use through the winter.

varieties.name: Chenango

origin.place: Lebanon, Madison County, or Chenango County, New York (accounts differ)

varieties.history: A New York apple known from about 1850; it either arose at Lebanon in Madison County or was brought into Chenango County from Connecticut. Valued in its day as a handsome, scented late-summer apple, though too tender to ship.

look.description: Tall, conical, smooth whitish-yellow apple striped and splashed with crimson.

taste.summary: Tender, juicy white flesh with a mild, gently tart, aromatic flavour often said to carry a hint of strawberry. Soft rather than crisp, and it does not keep.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, when the skin turns milky-white
taste.storage_change: Orange Pippin: keeps poorly even when refrigerated.
taste.peak: Orange Pippin: pick when the skin turns milky; ripens over a long period.

tree.notes: Vigorous and precocious; tends to overcrop, so thin and prune firmly. Fruit ripens over a long period and needs several pickings.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering at Brogdale (full bloom around 13 May).

climate.best_climates: Cool to warm summers (below about 30 C), as in New York and New England.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers soften it further; humid sites encourage scab and fruit rots.

health.other: Some susceptibility to scab, mildew and fire blight; some resistance to cedar-apple rust. Fruit can mummify on the tree and bruises easily.

varieties.grow_notes: A fussy but rewarding garden tree. Pick over several passes as the skin turns milky and refrigerate at once; use for eating fresh, pies and sauce.

varieties.name: Cherry Cox

origin.place: Kjer's orchard, Linved, Hjallese (near Odense), Denmark
origin.parentage: Sport of Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: A darker red bud sport of Cox's Orange Pippin found by Mr Roed in a Danish orchard at Hjallese on Funen around 1942. High Weald Nurseries of Crowborough brought it to England in 1951. Apart from colour it is essentially Cox.

look.description: Cox-shaped fruit with much more colour: dark cherry-red stripes and solid red patches over a greenish-yellow ground.

taste.summary: The same rich, aromatic Cox flavour and dense flesh, said by some growers to be slightly sweeter and to hold its quality a little longer in store.

tree.notes: Rather weak-growing; give it a fertile soil and a stronger rootstock than you would for most varieties.

pollination.notes: Group 3. Being genetically Cox, it cannot pollinate Cox or other Cox sports.

climate.best_climates: As for Cox: warm, sunny but temperate maritime summers such as southern England and Denmark.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, cold western sites (disease) and hot continental summers (poor flavour and colour).

health.other: Shares Cox's weaknesses: very prone to scab and canker on heavy or wet soils.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow it where Cox thrives: a warm, sheltered, well-drained site, with spraying or good hygiene against scab. Choose a group 2-4 pollinator that is not a Cox sport.

varieties.name: Chestnut Crab

origin.parentage: Usually given as a Malinda seedling (pollen parent not recorded); Orange Pippin gives Wealthy x Keswick Codlin

varieties.history: Released by the University of Minnesota in 1946 as a hardy, good-eating crab. Its nutty flavour and russeted bronze skin made it a favourite in northern gardens, where it also serves as a pollinator for other hardy apples.

look.description: A large crab, about 5 cm, reddish-bronze over yellow and netted with russet.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy cream flesh, sweet and complex with a distinct nut-like flavour; one grower compares it to a fine white wine. Tasters find little or no tartness, although its juice is classed as on the sharper side. One of the best crabs for eating fresh and good for sauce, but it keeps only two or three weeks.
taste.peak: Scott Farm: long ripening period, early Sep to late Oct

tree.notes: A fairly small tree; the fruit ripens over a period, so it needs more than one picking, and birds like it.

pollination.notes: Needs a pollinator; in turn a useful pollen source for other hardy apples flowering at the same time.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates of the upper Midwest, New England and the Canadian prairies.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer, short-winter regions, where an early-ripening northern variety softens quickly (inferred).

health.other: Generally healthy with some resistance to cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in full sun with another hardy apple for pollination. Pick over two or three passes as the fruit ripens unevenly; it keeps about a month.

varieties.name: Chieftain

origin.place: Iowa Agricultural Experiment Station, Ames, Iowa
origin.parentage: Jonathan x Delicious
origin.raised_by: S. A. Beach, Iowa Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: Raised in 1917 by S. A. Beach at the Iowa station in Ames from Jonathan x Delicious, but not introduced until 1966-67. A hardy, good-keeping Midwestern apple that never became widely known.

look.description: Round, medium to large apple largely covered in crimson flush and stripes over yellow.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, juicy white flesh; sweet with a light acidity that is softer than Jonathan but livelier than Delicious. The flesh is slow to brown.

tree.notes: Average vigour, spur-bearing and regular-cropping; easy for beginners.

pollination.notes: Listed as group 4; full bloom around 12 May at Brogdale.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter continental climates such as the US Midwest; also temperate and warm-summer regions.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season sites where a mid-October apple cannot ripen.

health.other: Some resistance to scab and fire blight; generally healthy.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy, easy dual-purpose apple for cold districts. Pick in mid-October and store for a month or two.

varieties.name: Chisel Jersey

origin.parentage: Unknown; an old Somerset seedling

varieties.history: A nineteenth-century Somerset bittersweet; 'Jersey' is the old county word for a bittersweet apple, and 'Chisel' is usually traced to a dialect word for pebble, a nod to its small, hard fruit. It is widely thought to be one parent of Dabinett.

look.description: Small, hard greenish fruit with a striped red flush; the stalk often sits off-centre.

taste.summary: A full bittersweet: the juice is high in sugar and very high in tannin with little acid, giving heavy astringency and bitterness. Prized for body and mouthfeel in blends rather than for fresh eating.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill in Nov-Dec after a short spell of sweating.

tree.notes: Vigorous and comes into bearing fairly early, but tends strongly towards alternate-year crops. Prone to virus infection, which shows as small, cracked, heavily russeted fruit.

pollination.notes: Late flowering; needs another late-blossoming cider variety nearby.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp maritime climates like Somerset and the English West Country, where long autumns ripen the late fruit.
climate.poor_climates: Areas with short seasons or early autumn frosts, since it is picked very late; hot dry summers are untested for it.

health.other: Susceptible to virus (fruit becomes small, cracked and russeted); marked biennial bearing.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant with other late-flowering cider varieties such as Dabinett or Yarlington Mill. Thinning in heavy years helps to even out its alternate cropping. Use virus-tested stock.

varieties.name: Chivers Delight

origin.parentage: Unknown; sometimes suggested to be a Cox's Orange Pippin seedling
origin.raised_by: Stephen Chivers (Chivers & Sons / John Chivers Farms), Histon

varieties.history: Raised at Histon near Cambridge by the Chivers jam-making family, usually credited to Stephen Chivers in the 1920s (the National Fruit Collection gives 1936 for its introduction). Popular in the first half of the 20th century, it later faded from commerce but remains a garden favourite in East Anglia.

look.description: Medium to large, slightly conical fruit, dull green ripening yellowish, with a streaky golden-orange to brownish flush.

taste.summary: Crisp yellowish flesh, moderately juicy, with a sweet but well-balanced, lightly aromatic flavour (one taster notes a cidery aroma). A good keeper, though the flesh turns dry and fluffy late in storage, and the flavour may not develop fully after a cool, dull autumn.
taste.peak: pick mid October, use November to January (East of England Apples and Orchards Project)

tree.notes: A moderately vigorous, regular-cropping spur-bearer. Its main weakness is canker, so avoid wet, heavy soils and prune out infected wood promptly.

pollination.notes: Sources place it in group 3 or 4 (it flowers about the same time as Cox at Brogdale); any group 3-4 diploid will pollinate it.

climate.best_climates: The relatively dry, sunny lowlands of eastern England and similar cool temperate regions.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, mild western sites encourage canker; hot summers likely reduce quality.

health.other: Rather susceptible to apple canker; good scab resistance reported.

varieties.grow_notes: A reliable late keeper for eastern England. Plant on well-drained soil in full sun, keep an eye out for canker, and store the fruit cool for eating from November.

varieties.name: Christmas Pearmain

origin.place: England (introduced by G. Bunyard & Co., Maidstone, Kent)

varieties.history: Raised by a Mr Manser and first recorded in 1893, then introduced by the Maidstone nursery G. Bunyard & Co. A late-Victorian garden apple valued for keeping to Christmas, as the name suggests.

look.description: Neat, slightly tall pearmain-shaped fruit, golden yellow with a brownish-red flush and darker stripes, lightly dotted with russet.

taste.summary: Firm, fine, crisp and fairly juicy yellow flesh; basically sweet, with enough sharpness and aromatic richness to keep it interesting.
taste.peak: Picked early October (NFC)

tree.notes: A compact, easy-going garden tree that crops well with few problems. Usually described as a partial tip-bearer, so leave some shoot tips when pruning.

pollination.notes: Early-flowering (group 2) and reported to be partly self-fertile; crops better with a group 1-3 partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate gardens in southern and central England.
climate.poor_climates: Early blossom is at risk in frost pockets; hot summers likely give softer, duller fruit.

health.other: Regarded as an easy, relatively trouble-free garden variety; specific disease ratings not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for a small garden on a dwarfing rootstock. Avoid frost pockets because of its early blossom, and plant an early-flowering partner for heavier crops.

varieties.name: Cider Lady's Finger
varieties.history: An old English cider apple of uncertain origin, named for its long, elliptical fruit; 'Lady's Finger' has been attached to several unrelated elongated apples, and different sources link this one to the West Country or to Herefordshire. It appears on the UK statutory list of cider apple varieties and is still pressed as a single-variety cider in the Welsh Marches.

look.description: Distinctly elongated, finger-like fruit, green with a red flush.

taste.summary: Described by cider makers as a mild sharp: fresh acidity with little tannin, giving a light, easy-drinking cider rather than a heavy, tannic one.
taste.best_eaten: Not recorded as a dessert apple; used for cider.

tree.notes: Little published information on tree habit.

pollination.notes: Reported to be self-sterile; plant with another cider variety.

climate.best_climates: Grown in the cool, moist cider country of western England.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No reliable disease data found.

varieties.grow_notes: Treat as a typical West Country cider tree: a sheltered, well-drained site and a compatible pollinator. Because the name has been used for several elongated apples, buy from a source that traces its stock to a known collection.

varieties.name: Clarke Pearmain

origin.place: South-eastern United States (Virginia and North Carolina)

varieties.history: An old Southern eating apple that Thomas Jefferson grew at Monticello. The UK register records it from North Carolina in an 1867 description. It was widely known as Golden Pearmain, a name that other apples also used.

look.description: A medium, rather flat apple. Its yellow skin is flushed orange and striped red, with russet dots that can spread into larger patches.

taste.summary: Its firm, crisp yellow flesh is sweet with mild acidity. One description calls it rich and tender but on the dry side.

tree.notes: One old description calls it a steady, even cropper.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Warm, long-season climates of the American South and mid-Atlantic, where it was traditionally grown.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in cool maritime climates; a russeted Southern apple may struggle to ripen fully in a short English season.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Best for collectors of Jeffersonian or Southern heirloom apples in warm-summer areas. The name Golden Pearmain is shared with other apples, so buy from a nursery that can trace its wood.

varieties.name: Claygate Pearmain
varieties.history: Found growing near Claygate in Surrey by John Braddick, who showed it to the Horticultural Society in 1821. It became a much-admired Victorian dessert apple, likened in flavour to Ribston Pippin, and later received an RHS Award of Merit (1901) and First Class Certificate (1921).

look.description: Broadly conical fruit, green-yellow with a dull orange-red streaky flush and a substantial net and patches of russet; turns yellower in store.

taste.summary: Fairly soft, juicy cream flesh with a rich, aromatic, nutty flavour in the style of Ribston Pippin. Quite tart straight off the tree, it sweetens and deepens after about a month in store, when tasters report tropical, pineapple-like notes. Keeps a month or two.

tree.notes: Average vigour and a regular cropper. Orange Pippin lists it as triploid; that was not independently confirmed, but treat it as a poor pollinator to be safe.

pollination.notes: Group 4. If triploid, as reported, it needs two diploid partners and will not pollinate them in return.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist lowland England and similar temperate climates.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; hot summers likely reduce flavour and keeping.

health.other: Reported to have good general disease resistance, particularly to scab.

varieties.grow_notes: A connoisseur's winter apple for southern English gardens. Plant two diploid pollinators flowering in groups 3-5, and pick late for eating after Christmas.

varieties.name: Clivia

origin.place: Institut für Acker- und Pflanzenbau, Müncheberg, Brandenburg, Germany
origin.parentage: Geheimrat Dr. Oldenburg x Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: Bred at Müncheberg in East Germany from the same parents as Alkmene and released in the early 1960s. It is best known as a parent of Pinova and of several other German apples such as Pilot and Rubinstep.

look.description: Small to medium, slightly conical apple with a smooth, greasy skin striped yellowish-red to reddish-brown over greenish yellow.

taste.summary: Firm, fine, juicy yellowish-white flesh with a sweet-sharp balance and a refined aroma close to Cox's Orange Pippin.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Dec in England; German sources give Dec-Apr
taste.peak: de.wikipedia: eating ripe December to April after mid-October picking (German conditions); NFC picks late September.

tree.notes: Weak-growing with obliquely upright main limbs, few laterals and many short fruiting shoots; the small crown needs firm annual pruning to keep it productive.

pollination.notes: No published group; National Fruit Collection records show it opening with early varieties such as Alkmene and Egremont Russet.

climate.best_climates: Central European and British temperate climates.
climate.poor_climates: Not recorded.

health.other: Low scab susceptibility and good mildew resistance reported.

varieties.grow_notes: Choose a vigorous rootstock or a good soil to offset its weak growth, and prune each winter. Store for a few weeks before eating.

varieties.name: Coccagee

origin.place: Ireland (later common in counties Clare and Limerick)

varieties.history: A very old Irish cider apple. Its name comes from Irish for 'goose dung', after the colour of the skin. Around 1710 it was taken to Somerset near Minehead and became a favoured cider apple across the west of England and Wales. Single-variety Coccagee cider sold at a premium in Ireland. It is now thought lost, though the Gloucestershire apple 'Hen's Turd' has been suggested as a survivor.

look.description: Small to medium, egg-shaped to conical fruit with pale yellow skin flecked with green.

taste.summary: Raw, it was notorious as one of the harshest, most austere apples known, with acidic yellowish-white flesh. Cooked, it is reported to taste rich. It made a pale, straw-coloured cider that was highly prized.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating raw; for cider or cooking

tree.notes: A vigorous tree that could be grown from cuttings struck straight into the ground, as was common in Ireland.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist Atlantic climates: Ireland, the West Country and Wales, where it was historically grown.
climate.poor_climates: No record of performance outside the British Isles.

health.other: Not recorded; the variety is probably extinct.

varieties.grow_notes: Probably not available. If a candidate tree such as 'Hen's Turd' is confirmed, it would suit a wet western cider orchard. Being able to root from cuttings makes it easy to propagate.

varieties.name: Cockle Pippin

origin.place: Godstone, Surrey, England (older accounts say Sussex)

varieties.history: Raised around 1800 by a Mr Cockle, placed at Godstone in Surrey by the National Fruit Collection and in Sussex by Hogg and Bunyard; it was widely grown in both counties during the 19th century. It is often confused with Nutmeg Pippin, which Bunyard regarded as a separate apple.

look.description: Conical, slightly angular fruit, greenish-yellow turning golden, with a faint brownish-orange flush and thin cinnamon russet that thickens towards the base.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, fine-grained flesh, sweet with a mild sub-acid balance and a pleasant aromatic flavour; it can be on the dry side. Bunyard noted it tastes best after a warm summer, and it keeps well into spring.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous and upright, with long, whippy shoots that make it easy to recognise; reported as fertile.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 11 May, so group 3 is inferred. Plant a mid-season partner.

climate.best_climates: South-east England (Surrey and Sussex) and similar mild lowland areas, ideally with warm summers to bring out its flavour.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, dull, short-season areas may leave it under-flavoured; it is untested in hot climates.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A late russet-style keeper for a warm, sunny spot in southern England. Pick in mid October and store it cool until after Christmas.

varieties.name: Coeur de Boeuf
varieties.history: An old French apple whose name means 'ox heart', for its size, shape and dark colour. The UK National Fruit Collection records it as French and very old (its register entry dates it to the Middle Ages, which is hard to verify); a local variety of the same name is conserved in the Haut-Languedoc.

look.description: Large, broad fruit almost entirely streaked dark purplish-red over a pale ground.

taste.summary: Soft, greenish flesh that is often veined with pink, sweetish with a mild acidity and some aroma. Used mainly for cooking and baking.

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not recorded in sources checked.

pollination.notes: Flowers slightly before Cox at Brogdale; treat as group 3.

climate.best_climates: Temperate France and southern England; grown in British collections without special care.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance in very hot or very cold regions.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity for collectors of old French apples, notable for its dark skin and pink-veined flesh. Grow as a standard late-picked apple with a group 2-4 partner.

varieties.name: Collins June
varieties.history: An obscure early American summer apple preserved in the USDA apple collection at Geneva, New York (PI 589149, donated in 1985). Its history is unrecorded; it is a different apple from Collins of Arkansas, whose synonyms include Champion.

look.description: Large, rounded-oblate, greenish-yellow to yellow summer apple.

taste.summary: Soft, cream-coloured flesh with a sub-acid flavour; the USDA rates its eating quality only fair. Low in sugar and juice in Canadian trials.
taste.peak: USDA GRIN: very early, early August.

tree.notes: Recorded as unproductive in the USDA collection.

health.other: Rated fairly susceptible to fire blight (7 on the USDA scale).

varieties.grow_notes: Of collection interest only: a very early, soft yellow apple with light crops. Eat as soon as it is picked.

varieties.name: Colonel Vaughan
varieties.history: An old Kentish apple known since the later 1600s, recorded under the name Kentish Pippin; the National Fruit Collection treats Colonel Vaughan and Kentish Pippin as the same variety.

look.description: Slightly tall, conical fruit with a pale yellow ground largely covered by red flush and stripes, dotted with pale russet.

taste.summary: Firm white flesh, sometimes stained with red, with a sweet to mildly acidic flavour.

tree.notes: No reliable growing data found.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from Brogdale flowering dates, which are close to Cox's; plant with a group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Inferred from its Kentish origin: mild, moist south-east England.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A piece of Kent's orchard history. Grow it like other late English dessert apples: sunny site, decent loam and a mid-season pollinator nearby.

varieties.name: Cornish Aromatic

origin.parentage: Unknown; probably an old local Cornish seedling

varieties.history: A Cornish garden apple that came to wider notice in 1813, when it was shown to the Horticultural Society of London, though it was believed even then to be much older. It is one of the best-known of the West Country heritage dessert apples and is held in the National Fruit Collection.

look.description: Broad, slightly ribbed conical fruit with a golden ground washed and streaked orange-red, often with patches of fine russet.

taste.summary: Firm to very hard, rather dry cream flesh with a rich, sweet-sharp flavour, a spicy, perfumed aroma and a hint of pineapple. Best after a few weeks in store and a good keeper, sometimes lasting into spring; in a cool, dull summer it can stay sharp and less aromatic.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Jan, after a few weeks in store
taste.peak: use October to March (Wikipedia)

climate_flavour.note: Orange Pippin: very enjoyable in a good summer (e.g. 2006)

tree.notes: A fairly strong-growing spur-bearer that crops regularly; prune as a conventional spur-bearing tree.

pollination.notes: UK listings disagree on its flowering group (figures from 2 to 4 are quoted), so pair it with a mid-season group 3 diploid, which should overlap either way.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp maritime climates such as Cornwall, Devon, Wales and Ireland, where its disease tolerance is a real asset.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool summers leave the fruit sharp and dull; there is no record of it doing well in hot continental regions.

health.other: Regarded as resistant to both scab and canker, which is why it suits wet western districts.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the easier heritage dessert apples for wet western gardens. Give it a sunny position, average soil and a mid-season pollinating partner; it needs a reasonably warm autumn to develop its full flavour.

varieties.name: Cornish Gilliflower

origin.place: Cottage garden near Truro, Cornwall, England
origin.raised_by: Brought to notice by Sir Christopher Hawkins

varieties.history: Found growing in a cottage garden near Truro and introduced in 1813 by Sir Christopher Hawkins. 'Gilliflower' is an old name for the clove-scented pink, and the name is usually linked to the clove-like scent of the blossom; Victorian writers ranked it among the best-flavoured English apples.

look.description: Tall, conical and noticeably ribbed, greenish-yellow with a dull red flush and broken streaks plus some russet; some trees give much more russet and less red.

taste.summary: Firm, yellowish, rather dry flesh with a rich, sweet and highly aromatic flavour that has a perfumed edge. Keeps its quality well into the new year in a cool store.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Feb; improves for some weeks after picking
taste.storage_change: Flavour and smell become more floral in storage (Scott Farm); keeps well into the new year (Orange Pippin)
taste.peak: Can be eaten well into the new year (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: A partial tip-bearer with long, bare-ish shoots; unsuited to cordons and espaliers. Often slow to start cropping and yields are modest and sometimes irregular. Renewal-prune rather than shortening every tip.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 4; plant near another group 3-5 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist south-western Britain and Ireland, given a sheltered sunny spot so the late fruit ripens fully.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, exposed northern sites with short autumns, where the late fruit fails to sweeten; hot dry climates are untested.

health.other: Disease scores not well recorded; main grower drawbacks are tip-bearing habit, slow start and light cropping.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow it as a free-standing bush or half-standard and prune lightly because much of the fruit is borne at shoot tips. A warm wall or sunny sheltered site helps the flavour; be patient, as trees can take several years to crop.

varieties.name: Cortland

origin.parentage: Ben Davis x McIntosh
origin.raised_by: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: Bred at the New York State experiment station in Geneva from an 1898 cross and released in 1915. It became one of the main McIntosh-type apples of New York, New England, Quebec and Ontario, valued for its hardiness and for white flesh that is slow to brown when cut.

look.description: Large, flattish apple with a pale green-yellow ground under a dark red flush and stripes; colours best after cold autumn nights.

taste.summary: A McIntosh-type apple with tender, very white, juicy flesh and a sweet, mildly tart flavour, less sharp and more strongly perfumed than McIntosh, with a vinous edge; individual tasters mention blue grape or strawberry. Crispness and sweetness fade quickly after picking and stored fruit turns mealy. Holds its shape in pies and stays white in salads.
taste.storage_change: Sweetness and crispness fade quickly after picking.
taste.peak: Soon after picking

tree.notes: Spreading, somewhat drooping partial tip-bearer that crops heavily; thin fruit to keep size and avoid alternate bearing.

pollination.notes: Group 3; partly self-fertile, but crops better with a group 2-4 diploid partner.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter, sunny-autumn climates such as upstate New York, New England, Quebec and Ontario, where it is hardy and colours deeply.
climate.poor_climates: Mild, cloudy maritime climates give poorer colour and flavour; hot summers make the tender flesh soft and short-lived.

health.other: Susceptible to apple scab and powdery mildew like most McIntosh types; some susceptibility to fire blight and cedar-apple rust. Fruit bruises fairly easily.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for cold inland gardens. Plan a spray or sanitation programme for scab in wet areas, thin heavily after June drop, and prune lightly to keep the fruiting tips.

varieties.name: Cosmic Crisp

origin.place: WSU Tree Fruit Research and Extension Center, Wenatchee, Washington
origin.parentage: Enterprise x Honeycrisp
origin.raised_by: Bruce Barritt, Washington State University (completed by Kate Evans)

varieties.history: Crossed in 1997 at Washington State University's Wenatchee station by Bruce Barritt and taken forward by Kate Evans. Trees went to Washington growers from about 2016-17, with first fruit on sale in 2019, it was the first major variety bred in Washington and was initially restricted to growers in that state.

look.description: Large, dark wine-red fruit speckled with pale lenticels - the 'cosmic' starry look that gave it its name.

taste.summary: Very crisp, firm and juicy with a bright sweet-tart balance; many tasters find the flavour straightforward rather than complex, something like a milder Honeycrisp. The flesh browns slowly and the crunch lasts for months, but fruit held very long in store can turn bland and lose its tartness.
taste.storage_change: Keeps in cold storage for more than ten months; flesh is slow to brown when cut (Wikipedia). No flavour change reported.

tree.notes: Precocious and productive; crop load must be managed to avoid alternate bearing. Fruit set is lower than in most varieties.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 4. Washington State University recommends late-flowering crab apples as pollinators because fruit set is relatively poor.

climate.best_climates: Sunny, dry, irrigated fruit regions with hot days and cool nights, such as central Washington.
climate.poor_climates: Short or cool seasons may not mature it; humid climates are largely untested.

health.other: Prone to 'green spot', a calcium-related, bitter-pit-like skin disorder, and to a physiological leaf blotch and fruit staining. Disease ratings not well published.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant with late-flowering crab apples to improve set and thin consistently to keep cropping annual. Apply calcium sprays to limit green spot. Outside Washington, availability depends on licensing.

varieties.name: Costard
varieties.history: One of the earliest named English apples: costards were bought for Edward I's household in 1292, and street sellers of them were called costardmongers, the origin of 'costermonger'. Grey, green and red costards were described in the 1600s, but by the 19th century the true apple was rare; the National Fruit Collection holds no authenticated tree, so trees sold under the name today may not be the medieval variety.

look.description: Large, tall, conical apple with strong ribs running down the body; dull yellowish green. The name is thought to come from Latin for 'ribbed'.

taste.summary: Old descriptions give tender, greenish-white flesh with a mild sub-acid flavour, suited to the kitchen. Almost no modern tasting information exists for an authenticated tree.

tree.notes: Tudor writers describe the Costard as a large tree to be planted on the north side of an orchard so it would not shade others; modern growing data are lacking.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded; plant with another apple to be safe.

climate.best_climates: Historically grown across lowland England; values here are inferred from its English origin.
climate.poor_climates: No performance data; hot climates untested.

health.other: No disease information available.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow for its history rather than its proven performance, and treat the name with some caution since the authentic medieval variety is thought to be lost. Give it room as a large orchard tree.

varieties.name: Court Pendu Plat
varieties.history: A very old European apple first described around 1613 and thought to be considerably older; it spread across Europe under dozens of names. In England it was nicknamed the 'Wise Apple' because it blossoms so late that it usually escapes spring frosts.

look.description: Distinctly squat, flat apple with a very short stalk, greenish-yellow with a dull orange-red flush and some russet.

taste.summary: Very firm, dense, close-textured flesh that is dry rather than juicy, much like a russet. Strong and fruity when picked, it develops a spiced, aromatic sweetness in store; odd at first bite but moreish, and at its best from midwinter into early spring. Cut flesh browns quickly.
taste.storage_change: Fruity and strong at picking; sweetens and mellows by Christmas; flavour ripens through early winter in store.
taste.peak: From Christmas into early winter; keeps to about March (Walcot)

tree.notes: Moderate vigour, partly tip-bearing and a regular cropper; prune lightly. Its value is very late blossom on frost-prone sites.

pollination.notes: One of the latest-flowering apples (group 6, some tables say 7); needs another late bloomer such as Edward VII or Crawley Beauty.

climate.best_climates: Temperate climates with late spring frosts, from Britain across central Europe; its late bloom suits frost pockets.
climate.poor_climates: Very short-season areas may not ripen this mid-October apple; no strong record from hot, humid regions.

health.other: Generally healthy, with good resistance to scab and mildew on the fruit; little else recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Ideal for cold, frosty gardens where early blossom is often lost. Plant with another late-flowering variety and store the fruit until Christmas for the best flavour.

varieties.name: Court Royal

origin.place: West Country, England (grown in Somerset, East Devon and Herefordshire); exact origin unknown

varieties.history: An old West Country apple whose birthplace is not recorded; it was once planted across Somerset, East Devon and Herefordshire. In the early twentieth century it was also used as an eating apple, but its lasting role has been as a 'sweet' cider fruit that gives sugar to blends.

look.description: Flattish, pale whitish-green apple with a modest orange flush broken into stripes and mottles; a little russet; cream flesh.

taste.summary: A true sweet cider apple: little acid and little tannin, so the juice is soft, sugary and plain, and it ferments quickly. The fruit is lightly crisp and sweet enough to eat fresh, which is why it once doubled as a dessert apple.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Nov; mill soon after picking, it does not need long sweating

tree.notes: Vigorous triploid that makes a large tree, so it suits standard orchard planting rather than small gardens. Cropping regularity is not well recorded.

pollination.notes: Group is approximate (mid-season in NFC records). As a triploid it gives poor pollen, so plant two other compatible diploids nearby.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist maritime regions like the English West Country and Welsh borders, with long gentle autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot summer climates; very cold continental winters and short seasons are not where it was selected.

health.other: Disease record not documented. Triploid, so useless as a pollinator; its size needs space.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it room: on vigorous stocks it becomes a big orchard tree. Pair with two diploid cider varieties that flower mid-season. Useful to add sugar to sharp or bitter blends.

varieties.name: Cox's Orange Pippin

origin.parentage: Chance seedling, possibly of Ribston Pippin

varieties.history: Raised around 1825 by Richard Cox, a retired brewer, in his garden at Colnbrook near Slough, and put on sale by the nurseryman Charles Turner around 1850. It became the benchmark English dessert apple and a parent of a long list of later varieties, from Kidd's Orange Red to Ellison's Orange.

look.description: Medium, slightly conical apple, greenish-yellow to gold with an orange-red to brownish flush and fine red streaks, often with russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Rich and complex: honeyed sweetness balanced by lively acidity, with a floral, almost rose-water perfume, pear-drop esters and a nutty background; tasters also find pear, melon, orange-juice and mango notes. The cream-yellow flesh is juicy but not especially crisp. Flavour deepens for a few weeks after picking and is best before Christmas; it reaches full character only in cool maritime climates such as England or the Pacific Northwest.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Jan; flavour peaks 2-6 weeks after picking
taste.storage_change: best picked fully ripe or within a few weeks; becomes softer and milder with age (Orange Pippin, Wikipedia)
taste.peak: fresh from the tree or within a few weeks, before Christmas (Orange Pippin)

climate_flavour.note: Orange Pippin: true flavour only in England's cool temperate climate, close in the Pacific Northwest and Nova Scotia; continental climates give inferior fruit

tree.notes: A demanding tree: dislikes cold, wet or heavy soils, and blossom and fruit set suffer in cold springs. Prune as a spur-bearer and thin for size.

pollination.notes: Group 3. The RHS lists it as incompatible with Kidd's Orange Red (and its sports) and Holstein; Cox sports cannot pollinate Cox.

climate.best_climates: Warm, sunny but temperate summers with dry autumns, such as south-east England, the Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark and the cooler fruit districts of New Zealand.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, wet western and upland sites where scab and canker run riot, and hot continental summers where the fruit loses flavour, colour and keeping quality.

health.other: Very prone to canker, plus scab and mildew; fruit can crack and suffer bitter pit. Generally needs a good spray or hygiene programme.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in the warmest, best-drained spot available, ideally in the south and east of Britain. Keep the soil fertile but not waterlogged, cut out canker promptly and pick a group 2-4 pollinator that is not a Cox sport or Kidd's Orange Red.

varieties.name: Cox's Pomona

origin.place: Colnbrook Lawn, near Slough, Buckinghamshire, England
origin.parentage: Seedling of Ribston Pippin (pollen parent unknown); thought to be a sister of Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: Raised around 1825 by Richard Cox at Colnbrook Lawn from the same batch of Ribston Pippin seed that is believed to have given Cox's Orange Pippin. It was introduced by Smale's Colnbrook nursery and used as a large dual-purpose apple.

look.description: Big, broad, ribbed fruit with a greasy pale green-yellow skin streaked and mottled with red.

taste.summary: Soft, rather coarse and juicy cream flesh with a sweet, mildly acid flavour; pleasant raw early in its short season and good for cooking.
taste.peak: Picked mid to late September

tree.notes: Little modern growing information; treat as an average old English apple.

pollination.notes: Group inferred from Brogdale flowering records, which show it blooming alongside Cox's Orange Pippin; use a mid-season partner.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist southern England, where it originated.
climate.poor_climates: No evidence from warm or harsh continental climates; soft-fleshed early-autumn fruit is likely to suffer in hot summers.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Mainly a collector's and heritage-orchard variety today. Plant in a sunny spot with a group 3 partner and use the fruit within a couple of months of picking.

varieties.name: Crawley Beauty

origin.parentage: Unknown; the National Fruit Collection notes it appears identical to the French variety Nouvelle France
origin.raised_by: Found in a cottage garden; introduced by J. Cheal & Sons, Crawley

varieties.history: Found around 1870 in a cottage garden at Crawley, Sussex, and introduced by the local nursery J. Cheal & Sons in 1906. It received an RHS Award of Merit in 1912. It is one of the latest-flowering apples grown in Britain, and the National Fruit Collection thinks it may be the same as the French Nouvelle France.

look.description: Medium to large, flattened-round, clean fruit, pale creamy-yellow with a red-orange flush and broken stripes.

taste.summary: Firm, slightly coarse and rather dry flesh. Cooked, it breaks down to a delicately flavoured puree; after storage it softens into a mild, sub-acid eating apple that most tasters find pleasant rather than memorable.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Feb; cook earlier, eat raw after storage
taste.storage_change: Cooked at first; can be eaten fresh after storing.

tree.notes: A healthy, reliable tree that crops heavily and regularly with little attention. Bunyard called it vigorous, while modern growers find it fairly compact. It tolerates many soil types.

pollination.notes: Among the very latest apples to bloom (National Fruit Collection full flower around 29 May). Its self-fertility is disputed, but lone trees often crop, so it is treated as partially self-fertile. Court Pendu Plat flowers at about the same time.

climate.best_climates: Frost pockets and cold, late springs in Britain and similar climates, where its very late bloom escapes frost damage.
climate.poor_climates: Mild-winter regions that cannot supply enough chill for such a late bloomer; untested in hot summers.

health.other: Reported to have good general disease resistance and few pest problems, so it rarely needs spraying.

varieties.grow_notes: An excellent low-maintenance choice for frosty gardens and beginners. Pick in mid October and keep the fruit cool until midwinter.

varieties.name: Creston

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x NJ 381049 (a New Jersey breeding selection)
origin.raised_by: Agriculture Canada research station, Summerland (Pacific Agri-Food Research Centre)

varieties.history: Selected at the Summerland research station in British Columbia between 1969 and 1976 and formally described in 1999. It is a triploid producing large Jonagold-like fruit, used both fresh and for pies and sauce, and remains a minor garden and farm-market apple.

look.description: Large, Jonagold-like apple, yellow with an orange-red flush that often colours poorly; the skin can turn greasy.

taste.summary: Described by its breeders as having good flavour and texture. No pomological tasting notes give specific flavours; Orange Pippin notes that the fruit softens in storage.
taste.storage_change: Orange Pippin's identification note says it softens in storage, while Wikipedia (citing the 1999 release paper) credits good keeping

tree.notes: Triploid; its fruit set is described as self-thinning, which reduces hand-thinning work.

pollination.notes: Triploid with poor pollen: it cannot pollinate other trees, so plant two different diploid pollinators nearby.

climate.best_climates: Bred for the dry interior fruit valleys of British Columbia; grown by home and market growers in Canada and the northern USA.
climate.poor_climates: Little documented; poor colouring is reported, which is likely to be worse in warm-night climates.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: As a triploid it needs two other compatible varieties for pollination and is useless as a pollinator itself. Plant in full sun to help its patchy colour, and use fruit fairly promptly as it can soften in store.

varieties.name: Crimson Beauty

origin.place: Orchard of F. P. Sharp, New Brunswick, Canada
origin.parentage: New Brunswicker x Fameuse according to Wikipedia; the National Fruit Collection gives Duchess of Oldenburg x Fameuse (New Brunswicker is itself a Duchess seedling)

varieties.history: Raised by the New Brunswick pomologist Francis Peabody Sharp, who made deliberate crosses to get apples for short seasons and cold winters; it is often cited as one of the first apples from a controlled cross. Stark Bros later sold it as Early Red Bird.

look.description: Medium apple striped and largely covered in red over greenish yellow; the white flesh may show red veining on the sunny side.

taste.summary: A very early, soft-fleshed apple with a subacid to sharp flavour and little sweetness. Best used quickly, fresh or cooked; it makes a pink sauce.
taste.best_eaten: Early Aug, straight from the tree

tree.notes: Little modern growing data; the National Fruit Collection tree has a drooping habit.

pollination.notes: No published group; National Fruit Collection records show it among the earliest to open (before Egremont Russet), so group 2 or earlier.

climate.best_climates: Short-season, cold-winter regions such as the Canadian Maritimes, for which it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: No firm record; early soft fruit does not store anywhere.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A historical curiosity and very early apple for cold districts. Pick over the tree as fruit colours and use within days. Flowers early, so avoid frost pockets.

varieties.name: Crimson Bramley

origin.parentage: Red-coloured bud sport of Bramley's Seedling

varieties.history: A more highly coloured sport of Bramley's Seedling that appeared in Southwell, Bramley's home town, and was listed in catalogues by 1913. Apart from its redder skin it behaves like ordinary Bramley.

look.description: Bramley's large, flattish shape but with much more of the green-yellow skin mottled and striped red.

taste.summary: As Bramley's Seedling: firm, coarse, juicy and strongly acid, cooking to a fluffy, tangy purée.

tree.notes: Grows like Bramley's Seedling: a large, spreading, partly tip-bearing triploid tree.

pollination.notes: Flowers at the same time as Bramley. Triploid, so it needs a diploid partner in groups 2-4 and cannot pollinate it in return.

climate.best_climates: Cool maritime climates as for Bramley; cool autumn nights bring out its extra colour.
climate.poor_climates: Hot climates where Bramley-type fruit softens and pits, and the red colour develops poorly.

health.other: Assumed to share Bramley's weaknesses: bitter pit in store and frost-sensitive blossom.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow exactly as Bramley, choosing a semi-dwarfing stock for gardens and planting two diploid pollinators nearby. Pick it for its looks if you want a cooker that is attractive on the tree.

varieties.name: Crimson Crisp

origin.place: Cross made at Rutgers, Cream Ridge, New Jersey; selected at Purdue, West Lafayette, Indiana
origin.parentage: Cross between two PRI scab-resistant breeding selections; carries the Vf resistance gene from Malus floribunda 821

varieties.history: Bred by the joint Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) disease-resistant apple programme: the cross was made in 1971, the seedling first fruited in 1979 and was tested as Co-op 39 before release in 2006 under the trade name CrimsonCrisp. It carries the Vf gene and is field-immune to the common races of scab.

look.description: Medium, roundish to slightly flat apple almost entirely covered in glossy deep purplish-red.

taste.summary: Very hard, crisp, breaking yellowish flesh, moderately juicy, with a rich sweet-tart flavour and a slight spicy edge. Can taste quite sharp at picking and mellows over a few weeks in store.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Jan; sharper at picking, sweeter after 2-3 weeks

tree.notes: Moderate to low vigour with upright, rather thin branches; standard (non-spur) growth type that can go biennial if allowed to overcrop. Fruit hangs well on the tree for several weeks.

pollination.notes: The release description says it flowers mid-season just after Golden Delicious (group 4); some UK lists give group 3. Any group 3-5 diploid should overlap.

climate.best_climates: Humid temperate climates where scab is a constant problem, from the US Midwest and north-east to western Europe; trialled across 20 US states and in France and Italy.
climate.poor_climates: Areas with heavy cedar-apple rust or fire blight pressure need care, as it is susceptible to both.

health.other: Vf scab immunity (the resistance can be overcome by races 6 and 7 of the fungus); susceptible to cedar-apple rust and fire blight, and some growers report powdery mildew.

varieties.grow_notes: A low-spray option for gardens where scab ruins other varieties. Keep it away from junipers in rust-prone regions, thin crops to avoid alternate bearing, and leave fruit on the tree a little longer for best sweetness.

varieties.name: Crimson Delight

origin.place: WSU Tree Fruit Research and Extension Center, Wenatchee, Washington
origin.parentage: Splendour x Gala according to the WSU breeding programme (another WSU page calls it a Splendour open-pollinated seedling)
origin.raised_by: Washington State University apple breeding programme

varieties.history: The first apple released by Washington State University's breeding programme, issued to growers in 2009 as WA 2. It was relaunched with managed licensing in 2016 under the brand Sunrise Magic; 'Crimson Delight' was an earlier marketing name.

look.description: Round, Braeburn-sized fruit with an orange-red to pinkish-red blush over most of a yellow ground, marked by large, conspicuous lenticels.

taste.summary: Sweet with moderate acidity and a well-balanced flavour. The flesh is crisp, juicy and very firm, and it keeps that firmness through long storage; flavour is said to improve after a spell in store and a few days at room temperature.
taste.best_eaten: Nov onwards; improves after some weeks in store and holds condition for months
taste.storage_change: Wikipedia: flavour improves with storage and with a few days to a week at room temperature; WSU: firmness hardly drops in storage
taste.peak: out of store from late autumn; keeps months (WSU 13 months CA)

climate_flavour.note: WSU reports good quality in both northern and southern Washington districts; low sunburn risk

tree.notes: Compact grower with average productivity; crops annually if thinned. Late picking raises the risk of splits in the stem bowl.

pollination.notes: Flowering time and pollination needs not published; plant with another diploid of similar season.

climate.best_climates: Developed for irrigated central Washington, where WSU reports good quality from the northern to the southern districts; low sunburn risk suits sunny, dry-summer regions.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented outside Washington; in cool, short-season climates a late-September-to-October apple may struggle to ripen fully.

health.other: Moderately susceptible to powdery mildew and fire blight; little bitter pit or sunburn, but stem-bowl splitting if harvested late.

varieties.grow_notes: A compact, manageable tree for sunny sites; thin to keep it cropping every year and pick on time to avoid stem-end splits. Mostly a licensed commercial variety, so garden trees may be hard to source.

varieties.name: Crimson Gold

origin.parentage: Apple x crab-apple hybrid (applecrab); exact parents unrecorded
