varieties.history: One of Albert Etter's Californian applecrabs, first called Little Rosybloom; Etter died in 1950 before its patent was completed and it was nearly lost until Ram Fishman found it on a single surviving limb around 1970. The name is also loosely applied to other apples in trade (the Czech Svatava and Wickson), which causes confusion.

look.description: Golf-ball-sized apple, mostly covered in ruby red with a plum-like bloom, the yellow ground showing only in shade.

taste.summary: Crisp, very sweet small apple balanced by a good tartness; high in sugar for its size. Keeps its texture even after long cooking, and makes good juice.
taste.peak: Greenmantle Nursery (California): late October to November.

tree.notes: Used as a pollinizer for Honeycrisp, Gala and Fuji in Washington State orchards.

pollination.notes: Blooms mid-season to late; valued as a pollen source for commercial varieties.

climate.best_climates: Mild coastal northern California where it was raised; also grown in Washington State orchards.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No disease ratings found.

varieties.grow_notes: A small, ornamental-looking applecrab for fresh eating, baking and juice, and a useful pollinator. Beware of trees sold under this name that are a different variety.

varieties.name: Crimson King

origin.place: Bewley Down, Chardstock, on the Somerset-Devon border, England

varieties.history: Raised in the late 19th century by John Toucher of Bewley Down, Chardstock, and first recorded in 1895. Planted first in west Somerset, then across Devon and the West Country cider districts.

look.description: Medium to very large, variably shaped fruit, heavily flushed and striped red.

taste.summary: A vintage-quality sharp cider apple: high acid, little or no tannin, giving a light, fruity cider. The big fruit is sometimes used for cooking.
taste.best_eaten: Milled for cider in autumn; also cooks

tree.notes: A vigorous, spreading triploid that bears heavy crops with little biennial tendency.

pollination.notes: Flowered early at Brogdale; as a triploid it is a poor pollen donor and needs two diploid partners.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp West Country cider districts of Somerset and Devon.
climate.poor_climates: Wet sites with heavy scab pressure; hot climates untested.

health.other: Fairly prone to scab.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for the acid component of a cider blend. Give it space, as it makes a big spreading tree, and plant two diploid pollinators.

varieties.name: Crimson Peasgood

origin.parentage: Sport of Peasgood's Nonsuch

varieties.history: A more highly coloured bud sport of the Lincolnshire apple Peasgood's Nonsuch, which Mrs Peasgood raised from seed around 1858. The sport was planted in the National Fruit Trials in 1931; where and by whom it was found is not recorded in the sources checked.

look.description: Very large, flattish, even fruit like Peasgood's Nonsuch but with a much stronger crimson flush and stripes.

taste.summary: As Peasgood's Nonsuch: soft, juicy and moderately sweet with gentle acidity and some aroma. It cooks well, breaking down easily, and is also eaten fresh.

tree.notes: A bud sport, so tree habit should match Peasgood's Nonsuch; not separately documented.

pollination.notes: Peasgood's Nonsuch is in group 3 and the sport flowers at the same time at Brogdale.

climate.best_climates: Temperate English conditions, as for its parent.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to soften the very large fruit; inferred from the parent rather than documented.

health.other: Expected to match Peasgood's Nonsuch; not separately recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Treat it like Peasgood's Nonsuch: a fertile, sheltered site and a group 2-4 pollinator. Grown mainly for its showy colour and large cooking fruit.

varieties.name: Cripps Pink

origin.parentage: Lady Williams x Golden Delicious
origin.raised_by: John Cripps, Western Australian Department of Agriculture

varieties.history: Bred by John Cripps in Western Australia from a 1973 cross aiming to join the long keeping of Lady Williams with Golden Delicious sweetness. Released in the late 1980s, it is sold worldwide under the Pink Lady trademark, with fruit marketed under that name only if it meets strict colour and quality standards.

look.description: Slightly elongated fruit with a clear pink-to-cerise flush over a green ripening to yellow background; smooth, waxy skin.

taste.summary: Very firm, fine-grained and crunchy with a refreshing, almost effervescent sharpness balanced by good sweetness. The acidity mellows in storage and the apple keeps its bite for months.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Apr; improves for a month or more after picking

climate_flavour.note: Wikipedia: needs a long (200-day) season and a hot climate; colour comes from big day-night temperature swings in autumn.

tree.notes: Vigorous tree that needs careful pruning and crop-load management to colour the fruit. Its very long season (about 200 days from bloom to harvest) is the main limit on where it can be grown.

pollination.notes: Flowers early relative to its very late harvest; UK flowering group not confirmed. Needs a compatible diploid flowering at the same time.

climate.best_climates: Long, hot, sunny seasons with a sharp drop to cool nights in autumn: Western Australia, Chile, South Africa, southern France and Spain, California.
climate.poor_climates: Cool or short seasons (most of Britain, northern Europe) where it often fails to ripen or colour before frosts; very warm autumns without cool nights leave the skin poorly coloured.

health.other: Susceptible to fire blight; sunburn on exposed fruit in hot climates. Main weakness in the UK is simply the length of season it needs.

varieties.grow_notes: Only worth trying in Britain on a hot, south-facing wall or in the warmest parts of the south-east, and even then expect patchy ripening. In suitable climates prune to let light into the canopy in autumn so the pink colour develops.

varieties.name: Cripps Red

origin.parentage: Lady Williams x Golden Delicious (same parentage as Cripps Pink)
origin.raised_by: John Cripps, Western Australian Department of Agriculture

varieties.history: A sister seedling of Cripps Pink from John Cripps's Western Australian breeding work, selected for a redder skin and an even later harvest. It is marketed as Sundowner and in some markets as Joya.

look.description: Fairly large fruit with a deep red flush over green-yellow, marked with conspicuous pale lenticels.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy white flesh, sweeter and less acidic than its sister Pink Lady, with a complex flavour and a clean finish. At its best after a spell in cold storage, and keeps well; holds its shape when cooked.
taste.storage_change: becomes sweeter in storage; keeps up to six months cold (Pomiferous)

tree.notes: Average vigour, crops young, with some tendency to alternate bearing; thin heavy crops.

pollination.notes: Reported in flowering group 3; needs a compatible diploid pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Warm, long-season, low-chill fruit regions such as Western Australia and similar Mediterranean climates.
climate.poor_climates: Northern Europe and other short-season areas, where it is unlikely to ripen properly before winter.

health.other: Some resistance to powdery mildew, but susceptible to scab, fire blight and woolly aphid.

varieties.grow_notes: A warm-climate apple that needs a long season; in the UK it is a curiosity rather than a practical choice. Thin to avoid biennial cropping and keep woolly aphid under control.

varieties.name: Crispin

origin.place: Aomori Apple Experiment Station, Kuroishi, Aomori, Japan
origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Indo

varieties.history: Raised in Aomori prefecture, Japan, from a 1930 cross and named Mutsu (after the old name of the region) in 1948. It was renamed Crispin when introduced to UK growers in the late 1960s, and is still sold as Mutsu in Japan and North America.

look.description: Big, slightly lopsided, rather tall fruit; green ripening to yellow-green, sometimes with a faint orange cheek and scattered russet dots.

taste.summary: Very crisp, juicy cream flesh made up of tiny juice-filled cells, firm yet light. Sweet and honeyed like Golden Delicious, with more acidity to balance it and a flowery scent. It sweetens further after a week at room temperature; equally good raw, juiced or cooked, when slices hold their shape.
taste.peak: Keeps 3 months or more (Orange Pippin); keeps up to three months (Wikipedia)

tree.notes: Very vigorous triploid; use a dwarfing rootstock in gardens. Heavy crops of very large fruit; thin to reduce a tendency to alternate bearing.

pollination.notes: Triploid, group 3: needs a group 2-4 diploid partner and is useless as a pollinator itself, so a third variety is needed to pollinate the partner.

climate.best_climates: Temperate climates with long, fairly warm autumns, such as northern Japan, the US north-east and Pacific north-west and southern England.
climate.poor_climates: Very short-season areas where the late fruit does not size or sweeten; humid regions with high fire blight pressure.

health.other: Prone to bitter pit, especially on young trees with light crops; some susceptibility to scab and fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it room or a dwarfing stock, and plant two compatible diploid pollinators nearby. Calcium sprays and even cropping help reduce bitter pit.

varieties.name: Dabinett

origin.place: Middle Lambrook, South Petherton, Somerset, England
origin.parentage: Chance seedling found in a hedge; Chisel Jersey is thought to be one parent

varieties.history: Found as a wilding in a hedgerow at Middle Lambrook in south Somerset by William Dabinett around the turn of the twentieth century. Its compact growth and reliable crops made it the backbone of modern bush-orchard cider planting in England and abroad.

look.description: Small, yellow-green fruit flecked and streaked with dark red.

taste.summary: A medium-to-full bittersweet with plenty of sugar, low acidity and soft, rounded tannin rather than harsh bitterness. Gives a full-bodied cider that stands on its own as a single variety.

tree.notes: Naturally small, spreading tree that comes into bearing early and crops regularly; ideal for bush orchards and small gardens. Usually listed as a vintage-quality variety.

pollination.notes: Late flowering and largely self-fertile, so it crops on its own, though a late-flowering partner helps.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist maritime climates; widely and successfully planted in English, Irish, Pacific Northwest and Australian cider orchards.
climate.poor_climates: Places where autumn ends early, as the fruit is picked late; very hot, humid regions raise disease pressure.

health.other: Generally healthy; good resistance to scab and canker for a cider apple.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the easiest cider apples for a beginner: compact, early-bearing and self-fertile. Suits dwarfing or semi-dwarfing rootstocks in a bush orchard. Leave fruit on the tree until it begins to drop in November.

varieties.name: Danziger Kantapfel

origin.place: Northern Germany or the Low Countries; named after Danzig (now Gdańsk)

varieties.history: An old Calville-type apple of the Baltic and North Sea coasts, reported from the island of Rügen in 1703 and more widely described from the mid-18th century. It remains a favourite of German meadow orchards and was named orchard variety of the year in Baden-Württemberg (2006) and northern Germany (2020). DNA work suggests it may be a parent of Freiherr von Berlepsch.

look.description: Angular, ribbed fruit with a shiny, waxy, silky skin flushed glossy red over most of the surface; flesh sometimes veined with red.

taste.summary: A sweet-sharp, moderately aromatic apple with fairly tender white flesh that can be veined with green and red. Pleasant fresh in autumn and useful in the kitchen; picked at the end of September, it is usable from mid-October until about January.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous with near-horizontal branches forming a broad crown. Valued as an undemanding, productive tree for standard orchards.

pollination.notes: Large pink blossom; flowering time and pollen quality not well recorded.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate and fairly continental climates of northern and central Europe; tolerant of a wide range of sites.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented in hot or low-chill regions.

health.other: Regarded as hardy and undemanding; specific disease ratings not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for a large standard or half-standard tree in a cold or exposed garden. Plant with another diploid apple and give the spreading crown room.

varieties.name: D'Arcy Spice

origin.place: The Hall, Tolleshunt D'Arcy, Essex, England

varieties.history: Found growing in the garden of The Hall at Tolleshunt D'Arcy, Essex, around 1785, and possibly older. The Broomfield nurseryman John Harris put it on sale in 1848 as 'Baddow Pippin'; it remains a symbol of Essex apple growing.

look.description: Uneven, often ribbed fruit, green ripening to gold with a dull orange-red cheek and patches of brownish russet.

taste.summary: Hard and sharp when picked. After a few months in store the firm flesh sweetens and develops its warm sweet-spice character, likened to nutmeg or to mince-pie filling with cinnamon and raisins; fruit often keeps until spring, shrivelling a little without losing flavour. Needs a warm, dry year: in cool districts it may not ripen properly and the flavour stays poor.
taste.storage_change: Hard and sharp when picked; historically stored a month or two before eating, when (after a good year) it sweetens and develops its sweet-spice, mince-pie character (Orange Pippin).
taste.peak: After 1-2 months in store; keeps to the following spring (Orange Pippin).

climate_flavour.note: Orange Pippin: in cooler or less sunny parts of the UK it may not ripen properly and is poorly flavoured; best in the warmer, drier East/South-East.

tree.notes: Weak-growing and slow to come into bearing; crops are often light and vary from year to year. Bears on spurs and tips, so prune lightly.

pollination.notes: Group 4; plant with a group 3-5 diploid. Blossom has good frost tolerance.

climate.best_climates: Dry, sunny lowlands such as East Anglia and south-east England; tolerates light, sandy and even salt-touched coastal soils.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, dull western and northern areas, where the very late fruit stays sharp and lacks spice and the leaves scab.

health.other: Very resistant to mildew; fruit fairly scab-resistant but leaves scab in wet seasons. Main weaknesses are slow, light cropping.

varieties.grow_notes: Needs a warm, sheltered, sunny site and a long season to ripen its very late fruit. Leave on the tree as long as possible, then store until after Christmas before eating.

varieties.name: Dayton

origin.place: PRI co-operative programme (cross at New Brunswick, New Jersey; Purdue, Rutgers and Illinois)
origin.parentage: NJ 123249 x PRI 1235-100 (ancestry includes Melba, Jonathan, Rome Beauty and Malus floribunda)

varieties.history: A scab-immune early apple from the PRI disease-resistance programme: the cross was made in 1966 in New Jersey, the seedling planted in 1969 and selected in 1976, and it was released in 1988 as Co-op 21. It is named after Daniel F. Dayton of the University of Illinois breeding team.

look.description: Glossy, bright medium red over almost the whole of a roundish to slightly flattened fruit.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, fine-grained pale yellow flesh with a sweet, mild, subacid flavour, like Prima but less tart. A good fresh-eating apple for its early season; it holds texture for about a month in a fridge.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, within about four weeks of picking
taste.storage_change: Keeps texture and flavour for about four weeks at 1 C (plant patent).
taste.peak: At harvest, ripening with Prima about four weeks before Jonathan/Delicious.

tree.notes: Moderately upright, vigorous tree similar in habit to Delicious; crops regularly and heavily. Fruit hangs well and ripens over a period.

pollination.notes: Needs a pollinator flowering in mid season.

climate.best_climates: Humid eastern and midwestern US conditions where scab pressure is high; also suited to cool to warm temperate summers.
climate.poor_climates: Very short-season northern sites gain little from it; the fruit does not keep, so it is poor where a storage apple is wanted.

health.other: Carries the Vf scab gene and is field-immune to scab; only slightly susceptible to fire blight and mildew, moderately to cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the easiest early apples for low-spray or organic gardens. Plant with a mid-season pollinator and eat the crop fresh, as it stores only a few weeks.

varieties.name: Decio
varieties.history: A very old Italian apple surrounded by legend: it is said to date back to the time of Attila (around 450 AD) and to be linked with the Roman general Aetius (Ezio). Firm documentary evidence only begins in the Middle Ages, but it is still one of the oldest named apples in cultivation; the National Fruit Collection received it in 1983.

look.description: Small, flattish pale green-yellow apple, sometimes with a light orange-red flush or a few streaks, and russet netting around the stalk and eye.

taste.summary: Fairly soft but dense flesh with little juice and a gently sweet, mildly acid flavour that most modern tasters find lacklustre. Perfectly palatable and keeps into the following year, but its appeal is historical.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Mar; keeps into the new year
taste.peak: Keeps well into the following year (Orange Pippin)

climate_flavour.note: Orange Pippin: should not be picked in the UK until late November, perhaps suggesting a warmer-climate origin.

tree.notes: Little modern growing data in UK conditions.

pollination.notes: Flowering group unclear: one UK listing gives group 5, while National Fruit Collection records show quite early blossom. Not self-fertile.

climate.best_climates: Long warm summers and autumns like those of northern Italy, where the very late fruit can ripen fully.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season or cool northern sites, where the late-hanging fruit may not mature before the frosts.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity for collectors of historic fruit. Give it the warmest, sunniest spot available so the very late crop ripens, and plan for a pollinator that overlaps in flowering.

varieties.name: Delbard Jubilée

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Lundbytorp

varieties.history: Selected by Georges Delbard from his apple crosses and named to mark his 80th birthday and the nursery's 50th year; sources give 1962 or 1964 for its raising. It is a different apple from the Canadian Jubilee (McIntosh x Grimes Golden), though the National Fruit Collection lists it simply as 'Jubile'.

look.description: Large straw-yellow apple almost completely covered in bright red, with a little russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy and sweet with a well-balanced acidity and a pronounced but light aromatic flavour; the breeder claimed a floral scent with hints of banana and hazelnut. It keeps its quality well into late winter.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Mar after a few weeks in store
taste.peak: Harvest mid-late October; keeps until late March (Wikipedia).

tree.notes: Bears good crops of large fruit; growth habit is spreading to drooping at Brogdale.

pollination.notes: Sources disagree: Wikipedia calls it mid-season flowering, while Brogdale records an unusually early 10% flowering date (late April). Choose a pollinator flowering in groups 2-3.

climate.best_climates: Temperate western European climates such as northern and central France and southern England with a long enough autumn to ripen a mid-October apple.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season or very cold areas where mid-October fruit cannot ripen; possible frost risk to blossom if it flowers as early as Brogdale recorded.

health.other: Reported to have generally good disease resistance, but no disease-by-disease ratings were found.

varieties.grow_notes: A late dessert apple for storing: pick in mid-October and keep cool until winter. Provide an early-to-mid season pollinator.

varieties.name: Delbarestivale

origin.parentage: Stark Jon Grimes x Golden Delicious

varieties.history: An early dessert apple bred by the Delbard nursery in central France; the cultivar name is Delcorf and Delbarestivale is its trade name. German sources date its market launch to 1982, and several redder sports (such as Celeste and Monidel) have since been selected.

look.description: Medium to large, somewhat cylindrical fruit with smooth greenish-yellow skin streaked and flushed red on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Aromatic and sweet with gentle acidity; juicy and fairly crisp for an early apple, and it keeps better than most summer varieties.

tree.notes: Vigorous with steep, sparsely branched growth and a strong tendency to crop every other year; thin early. Fruit ripens unevenly, so pick over several passes.

pollination.notes: UK flowering group not confirmed; plant with another diploid.

climate.best_climates: Temperate France and central Europe; its early season helps in places where autumn comes early.
climate.poor_climates: Wet climates with high scab and mildew pressure, where it needs regular spraying.

health.other: Susceptible to scab, powdery mildew and red spider mite; considered unsuited to low-input growing.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the better-flavoured early apples, but needs spraying in damp climates and firm thinning to break biennial cropping. Tie down or spread its upright branches to encourage fruiting.

varieties.name: Delprim

origin.parentage: Recorded as Delbarestivale (Delcorf) x Akane

varieties.history: Raised in the late 1960s by the Delbard nursery at Malicorne in central France, one of several Delbard early apples descended from Delbarestivale. The National Fruit Collection took it in in 1982.

look.description: A red-skinned early apple; detailed descriptions are scarce.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy flesh with a light, moderately aromatic flavour. Like most very early apples it is for eating within a week or so of picking.
taste.best_eaten: Mid-late Aug, within a week of picking
taste.peak: picked mid August, keeps about a week

tree.notes: A fairly vigorous, heavy-cropping spur-bearer; choose a dwarfing rootstock for small gardens.

pollination.notes: Early-flowering (group 2); pair with another early or early-mid season diploid.

climate.best_climates: Temperate France and southern England, where Delbard's early apples were selected and trialled.
climate.poor_climates: Little evidence from other climates; early apples generally soften quickly in hot summers, and its early blossom is at risk in frost pockets.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded. Early flowering exposes the blossom to late frosts.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant away from frost pockets because it blossoms early. Thin heavy sets so the fruit sizes up, and harvest in mid August for immediate eating.

varieties.name: Delrouval

origin.parentage: Delbarestivale (Delcorf) x Akane

varieties.history: A red dessert apple from the French nursery Delbard, combining their Delbarestivale with the Japanese Akane, recorded from 1995. Information outside short French catalogue entries is scarce.

look.description: Small-to-medium fruit with smooth red skin.

taste.summary: No reliable flavour description was found for this variety.

tree.notes: Recommended in France for training as cordons on wires or against a wall.

pollination.notes: French Wikipedia lists it as diploid, self-fertile and in flowering group C (about group 3); a pollinator flowering at the same time will still help set.

climate.best_climates: Not documented; presumably suited to French temperate gardens where it is sold.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: Suited to trained forms such as cordons in small gardens. Little is recorded about its season or health, so treat it as an experimental choice in the UK.

varieties.name: Democrat
varieties.history: A Tasmanian apple first recorded around 1900 and formerly grown in Australian orchards as a late-keeping dessert apple. Not to be confused with an older, unrelated American apple of the same name (also called Varick).

look.description: Dark red flushed apple; fuller details not verified.

taste.summary: Collection descriptions call the flesh crisp, sweet and juicy; detailed tasting notes are scarce.
taste.peak: Picked late October; keeps very long (NFC: over twelve months in Australia; Salt Spring: up to 7 months refrigerated)

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not documented in sources available here.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded; assume a compatible pollinator is needed.

climate.best_climates: Raised in Tasmania's cool-temperate maritime climate; likely to suit similar mild, moist apple regions. Chill figure is inferred from its origin.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; very hot or very cold climates are untested.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage curiosity mainly found in Australian collections. Treat it as a typical late-season dessert apple and give it a long season to ripen.

varieties.name: Detroit Red

origin.place: Said to have been brought to Detroit, Michigan, by French settlers

varieties.history: An old American apple of muddled identity, said to have come to Detroit with French settlers; Thomas Jefferson grew it at Monticello, and the National Apple Register records it from 1842. Detroit Red and Detroit Black may be one variable apple, and old lists confuse several dark red 'Detroit' apples; Orange Pippin even gives north Georgia as its origin.

look.description: Thick-skinned apple almost entirely covered in very dark crimson, sometimes nearly black, with purplish stripes and ribbing around the eye.

taste.summary: Soft, coarse, juicy white flesh, sometimes stained red under the skin, with an aromatic, subacid to tart flavour. Wikipedia calls the quality mediocre.
taste.peak: September (CooksInfo).

tree.notes: Crops somewhat unreliably or every other year.

pollination.notes: No flowering data found.

climate.best_climates: Eastern North American conditions from the Great Lakes to Virginia, where it was historically grown.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; its irregular cropping makes it a poor choice where reliable yields matter.

health.other: No disease ratings found; main documented weakness is irregular or biennial cropping.

varieties.grow_notes: Mainly of historical interest as a Jefferson-era apple. Thin heavy crops to reduce biennial bearing, and check the identity of nursery stock, given the confusion of 'Detroit' names.

varieties.name: Devonshire Quarrenden
varieties.history: An old West Country summer apple first recorded in 1678; it is usually credited to Devon, though the name may point to an origin near Carentan in Normandy. It is believed to be a parent of Worcester Pearmain.

look.description: Small, squat apple almost entirely covered in a dark crimson-purple flush, with a little green showing through.

taste.summary: Very juicy white flesh, sometimes stained pink under the skin, melting rather than crisp. The flavour is sweet, delicate and vinous rather than aromatic; a strawberry note shows in some fruit but is elusive and depends on picking at the right moment. Keeps only a few days.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-early Sep, straight from the tree
taste.storage_change: Keeps only 1-3 days.

tree.notes: Fairly small, spreading, flat-topped tree that bears on spurs; crops well but can slip into alternate-year bearing.

pollination.notes: Early flowering (group 2) and partly self-fertile; blossom is vulnerable to frost, so pair with another early bloomer on a sheltered site.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp south-west England and similar cool maritime climates, where it has been grown for centuries.
climate.poor_climates: Frosty sites damage its early blossom; hot summers would make the soft early fruit go mealy even faster.

health.other: Reported to resist scab well, suiting wet western areas; early blossom is frost-tender. Fruit keeps only days.

varieties.grow_notes: A good early apple for wet western gardens. Avoid frost pockets because it blooms early, and pick and eat the fruit as it colours rather than storing it.

varieties.name: Diana

origin.place: Ontario, Canada (Agriculture Canada, probably the Central Experimental Farm, Ottawa)

varieties.history: A Canadian dessert apple from Agriculture Canada, dated to about 1913 in research-collection records. The UK National Fruit Trials received it in 1967 by a roundabout route from Yugoslavia via Scotland.

look.description: Attractive mid-sized apple with a pale whitish-yellow ground, mostly covered in striped and flushed red.

taste.summary: Soft, juicy white flesh with a McIntosh-like flavour; Brogdale finds it sweet, while USDA Geneva rates it slightly acid and of only poor to fair eating quality.

tree.notes: Crops heavily every year, but ripens unevenly and fruit tends to drop before it is ripe.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records mid-season flowering (early May).

climate.best_climates: Cool continental climates of eastern Canada and the north-eastern US; also grows in southern England.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would worsen its soft texture and pre-harvest drop (inferred).

health.other: Pre-harvest fruit drop and uneven ripening are the main recorded faults.

varieties.grow_notes: Of interest mainly to collectors. Pick in several passes because fruit ripens unevenly and drops early.

varieties.name: Directeur Lesage
varieties.history: An early eating apple grown in Belgium and northern France; the National Fruit Collection received it from France in 1949 but suspects a Belgian origin. Its other name, Précoce de Wirwignes, refers to a village in the Pas-de-Calais.

look.description: Medium, truncate-conical and distinctly ribbed, greenish-yellow with orange-red stripes and flecks.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy, fine white flesh with a fresh sweet-sharp balance. Like most August apples it must be eaten within days.
taste.storage_change: Orange Pippin: keeps only 1-3 days.

tree.notes: A weak-growing spur-bearer that crops heavily and regularly; fruit ripens over a period, so pick over several times.

pollination.notes: Early flowering; an average pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate north-west European climates; reported to be cold-hardy.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; hot summers would shorten its very brief keeping life further.

health.other: Some scab resistance; some susceptibility to powdery mildew.

varieties.grow_notes: An easy, compact early apple for the garden. Pick little and often from early August and eat fresh.

varieties.name: Discovery

origin.parentage: Seedling of Worcester Pearmain; Beauty of Bath is the probable pollen parent
origin.raised_by: Mr Dummer, a fruit-farm worker (spelled Drummer in some records)

varieties.history: Grown from a Worcester Pearmain pip by a farm worker in Langham, Essex, around 1949. It was first called Thurston August, then renamed Discovery and launched in 1962 by the Suffolk nurseryman Jack Matthews of Thurston. It became the standard British supermarket early apple and holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Pale greenish-yellow apple with a glossy bright red flush on the sunny side; the flesh is often tinged pink beneath the skin.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy and fine-textured, more acidic than sweet with a fresh, tangy finish but little depth; a hint of strawberry appears in some years. Best eaten straight from the tree: flavour drops off within about a week and the flesh soon turns woolly, though chilling slows this. Many growers rate it more highly than the official tasting note does.
taste.best_eaten: Mid Aug-early Sep; holds a week or two, longer in the fridge
taste.storage_change: Best fresh: Orange Pippin gives a shelf life of about a week and likes it slightly chilled; Wikipedia says it stores well refrigerated.
taste.peak: Mid August to early September, fresh from the tree

tree.notes: An easy, moderately vigorous garden tree. It carries some fruit at shoot tips, so avoid shortening every shoot when pruning; fruit can stay small on old or overcropped trees.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering (group 3) with frost-tolerant blossom. Needs a diploid partner; some nurseries describe it as partly self-fertile.

climate.best_climates: Cool to mild temperate climates such as lowland Britain and northern Europe; its frost-tolerant blossom suits colder gardens.
climate.poor_climates: Copes with warm summers better than most English earlies, but in hot regions the fruit ripens in peak heat and softens quickly; very cold continental winters are a risk.

health.other: A healthy variety with good scab resistance. Main issues are a short picking window, small fruit if not thinned, and bird and wasp damage on ripe fruit.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the most reliable early apples for gardens and suitable for organic growing. Plant in sun, thin heavy crops, and pick when the background colour turns from green to yellow; pair with a group 2-4 diploid.

varieties.name: Dolgo

origin.place: Brookings, South Dakota, USA (from seed collected in Russia)
origin.parentage: Seedling of the Siberian crab (Malus baccata) raised from Russian seed; pollen parent unknown
origin.raised_by: Niels E. Hansen, South Dakota Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: The plant explorer Niels Hansen gathered Siberian crab seed in Russia in 1897 and selected Dolgo from the seedlings he grew in South Dakota, releasing it in 1917. The name means 'long' in Russian, after the elongated fruit. It became the standard jelly crab of the northern US and Canada and a favourite orchard pollinator.

look.description: Little elongated, egg-shaped fruits around 3 cm long, glossy bright crimson almost all over, hanging in clusters on slender stalks.

taste.summary: Very tart and juicy with a clean, bright fruitiness; just about pleasant raw when fully ripe but really a kitchen crab. It gives a clear, deep ruby jelly that sets well and a vividly coloured juice.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, for jelly and juice soon after picking

tree.notes: Makes a large, open, long-lived tree if not restricted, so choose a dwarfing stock for small gardens. Big, fragrant white blossom makes it worth growing as an ornamental too; pick before the ripe fruit drops.

pollination.notes: Flowers early, heavily and for a long time with plenty of pollen, so it is widely planted as a pollinator for early and mid-season apples. Early blossom can be caught by spring frost in low-lying sites.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates such as the northern US plains, the Canadian prairies and Scandinavia, where its hardiness and clean foliage stand out; also reliable in the mild, damp UK.
climate.poor_climates: Frost pockets, because it flowers early; very hot, humid lowlands with short winters suit it less well.

health.other: One of the healthiest crabs: resistant to scab and cedar-apple rust and fairly tolerant of fire blight. Ripe fruit falls readily and draws wasps if left on the tree.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in full sun on any reasonable, well-drained soil; it shrugs off cold winters. Keep it on a restricting rootstock or prune to an open framework, and use it as a pollinator alongside early-flowering dessert apples.

varieties.name: Domino

origin.place: English Midlands, probably the Southwell area of Nottinghamshire

varieties.history: An early codlin-type cooker first described in 1883, when it was being grown in the orchards around Southwell in Nottinghamshire. Hogg grouped it with Lord Suffield and Golden Spire as quick-bearing, prolific kitchen apples that must be used soon after picking.

look.description: Tall, blunt-conical, strongly ribbed and often lop-sided fruit, plain greenish-yellow with scattered russet dots and no flush.

taste.summary: Soft, juicy, yellowish-white flesh with a mild acidity; cooks quickly to a soft purée. It goes over within a few weeks of picking.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-Sep; use straight from the tree

tree.notes: Recorded as an early-bearing, prolific tree in the codlin tradition; other habit details not recorded.

pollination.notes: Flowers early in the season at Brogdale (a few days before Cox); treat as early group 3.

climate.best_climates: Cool English Midland conditions, where it was a common early orchard cooker.
climate.poor_climates: No records from hot regions; heat would make the soft fruit go over even faster.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Useful for an early supply of cooking apples in August. Pick little and often and use promptly, as the fruit does not keep.

varieties.name: Dorsett Golden

origin.parentage: Chance seedling of Golden Delicious

varieties.history: Found around 1950 in the Nassau garden of Mrs Dorsett on New Providence, Bahamas: a Golden Delicious seedling that could flower and fruit with almost no winter cold. Taken up by growers in Florida, it is now the usual pollination partner for Anna.

look.description: Golden Delicious-like yellow apple, sometimes with a soft pink-red cheek.

taste.summary: Sweet and fairly mild with a Golden Delicious character; lightly crisp and juicy. Flavour is said to be best on fruit ripened in light shade, and it softens quickly after picking.
taste.best_eaten: Immediately after picking (Jun-Jul in subtropical climates)
taste.storage_change: Does not keep: 1-3 days (Orange Pippin); like other early apples it does not stay fresh long (Wikipedia).
taste.peak: Straight from the tree; keeps only 1-3 days (Orange Pippin).

climate_flavour.note: Orange Pippin: a hot-climate early apple with better flavour than expected; flavour is apparently better in slightly shaded fruit.

tree.notes: Average vigour, spur-bearing and extremely precocious, often fruiting in its second year. In Florida it goes briefly dormant around December, which is the time to prune.

pollination.notes: Self-incompatible. Blooms in mid to late winter in warm climates, together with Anna and Ein Shemer, its usual partners.

climate.best_climates: Very mild winters with roughly 100-300 chill hours: central and southern Florida, the Gulf coast, coastal southern California and similar subtropical places.
climate.poor_climates: Anywhere with a real winter: it blooms at the first mild spell and loses its flowers to frost. The SE England harvest date is extrapolated; it is not a variety for the UK.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well documented; very short shelf life is the main drawback.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant with Anna for cross-pollination in frost-free or nearly frost-free gardens. Thin fruit early, keep the tree watered in dry spells, and eat the crop promptly.

varieties.name: Dougherty
varieties.history: An old late apple grown in Australia by 1885 and later widely in New Zealand, from where fruit was exported to Britain. A redder bud sport, Red Dougherty, was found at Twyford, New Zealand, around 1930 and became the commercial form; Red Dougherty is a parent of the New Zealand apple Splendour.

look.description: Medium, roughly truncate-conical fruit, greenish yellow with a red flush; the Red Dougherty sport is coloured a dull red with some russet.

taste.summary: Sweet, with a hint of spice; the Red Dougherty sport has firm, fine-textured, greenish-white flesh.

tree.notes: No reliable tree information found.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Grown historically in Australia and New Zealand, where it ripened late in the season; the figures here are inferred from that range, not measured.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; as a late apple from mild southern-hemisphere regions it may ripen poorly in short, cool seasons.

health.other: Wikipedia credits it with good disease resistance, without specifics.

varieties.grow_notes: Rare in the northern hemisphere and no longer held at the UK National Fruit Collection. Its late season suggests a warm, sunny site if tried in Britain.

varieties.name: Duchess of Bedford

origin.parentage: Cellini x Beauty of Bath

varieties.history: One of the many apples raised by the Laxton Brothers nursery in Bedford, first exhibited in 1918. It combines the Victorian early apple Beauty of Bath with Cellini, and survives mainly in the National Fruit Collection and East of England collections.

look.description: Medium, truncated-conical fruit, green-yellow with orange-red streaks and a noticeably greasy skin.

taste.summary: Pale, soft, fine-textured flesh with gentle acidity and a pronounced aniseed flavour, which one nursery describes as strong; the trait is usually credited to its Cellini parent. An August apple to eat fresh, as it softens quickly.
taste.best_eaten: Mid Aug-early Sep, soon after picking
taste.storage_change: keeps up to two months in cold store (Pomiferous)
taste.peak: pick late August, eat August-September (East of England Apples and Orchards Project)

tree.notes: Little growing data recorded. Prune as a standard spur-bearing dessert apple.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not published; National Fruit Collection blossom dates are mid-season, similar to James Grieve, so a group 3 diploid partner should overlap.

climate.best_climates: Lowland English conditions like the Bedfordshire and Kent sites where it is conserved.
climate.poor_climates: No records from hot or severe-winter regions; soft early fruit like this generally does poorly in hot summers.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A rare Laxton heritage apple for collectors. Grow in full sun on well-drained loam and pick in mid August for eating straight away.

varieties.name: Duchess of Oldenburg
varieties.history: An 18th-century Russian apple, probably from around Tula, that travelled west in the early 1800s: it was in England by the 1820s and reached North America in the 1830s. Its toughness made it a cornerstone of northern breeding, and DNA work shows it in the ancestry of most University of Minnesota apples.

look.description: Flattish, smooth pale yellow apple boldly streaked and splashed with bright red.

taste.summary: Very tart with little sweetness; the flesh is soft and turns mealy within a day or two of ripening, so it is mainly an early cooker. It cooks down quickly into a well-flavoured sauce with a fine aroma, though some growers find pie slices hold together. Keeps only days at room temperature and a few weeks chilled.
taste.best_eaten: Aug, within a week or two of picking
taste.peak: Harvested early-mid August; Scott Farm keeps them in cooler through September; Trees of Antiquity says storage 2-3 weeks

tree.notes: Medium-sized, easy tree that bears young and crops well. The crop ripens in a short window and drops, so pick promptly.

pollination.notes: Early-flowering (group 2, Orange Pippin); pair with another early-to-mid flowering diploid.

climate.best_climates: Severe continental winters - Russia, Scandinavia, the northern US and sheltered prairie sites - and cool maritime areas wanting an early cooking apple.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer and mild-winter regions: fruit ripens fast, softens and colours poorly, and its chill need may not be met.

health.other: Generally healthy, with some resistance to scab and mildew but some susceptibility to fire blight. Main drawbacks are very short keeping and quick softening.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant where an early cooker is wanted in cold country. Pick slightly under-ripe for cooking and use straight away; one tree is plenty because the crop ripens almost all at once.

varieties.name: Duchess's Favourite
varieties.history: Raised about 1800 by the Addlestone nurseryman Mr Cree; the old synonym Duchess of York's Favourite suggests it was named for a duchess of the period, though the exact dedication is not certain. It carries a long list of old synonyms and is a parent of the variety Jennifer.

look.description: Medium, rounded apple, green-yellow with a bright red flush; the flesh may show pink staining.

taste.summary: Sharp and acidic but fairly mild overall, with flesh often stained pink like Beauty of Bath and Discovery. Pleasant straight from the tree in late summer, though newer apples of the same season outclass it.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, fresh from the tree

tree.notes: Old accounts describe it as slow to start bearing but a heavy cropper once established.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not published; National Fruit Collection blossom dates are mid-season, close to James Grieve.

climate.best_climates: Mild south-east England, where it has been grown for over two centuries.
climate.poor_climates: No records from hot or severe-winter regions; red colour and texture of early apples suffer in hot summers.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A Surrey heritage apple for traditional orchards and collectors. Be patient for the first crops, give it a sunny well-drained site, and plant a mid-season diploid pollinator.

varieties.name: Duck's Bill
varieties.history: Known from a single historical source: it reached the National Fruit Trials in 1937 from Fred Streeter, then head gardener at Petworth House in Sussex. Its earlier history is not recorded; the name presumably refers to its narrow, strongly ribbed shape.

look.description: Narrow, tall conical fruit with strong ribs, greenish-yellow with orange stripes over part of the surface.

taste.summary: Firm white flesh with a rich, sweet flavour and a rather chewy bite; a dessert apple for November and December. Acidity and aroma are not recorded in the sources checked.

tree.notes: No growing data recorded.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not recorded; assume it needs a pollinating partner.

climate.best_climates: Presumably the mild lowland climate of south-east England where it was found.
climate.poor_climates: No performance records outside southern England.

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A rare Sussex variety kept mainly for conservation interest. Treat it as a typical English dessert apple: sunny site, decent drainage and a pollinating partner nearby.

varieties.name: Dufflin

origin.place: Kea, near Truro, Cornwall (the National Fruit Collection calls it a Devon apple)

varieties.history: An old West Country cider apple, grown around Kea near Truro in the 19th century; Quiller-Couch mentions Dufflin cider in a story of 1896. Long Ashton Research Station included it in orchard trials in 1957.

look.description: Small to medium, round yellow fruit with no blush and a heavily russeted skin.

taste.summary: Soft flesh with high sugar; sources disagree on class, one calling it bittersharp with the sugar softening it, another listing it as a sweet cider apple. Valued for making and blending cider.

tree.notes: Vigorous and a good cropper.

pollination.notes: Recorded as flowering early at Brogdale, but in a different year from most records, so the group is not certain.

climate.best_climates: Mild, wet south-west England, where its scab resistance is an advantage.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Reported resistant to scab.

varieties.grow_notes: A local cider apple for mild, damp West Country sites. Its cider class is unclear, so taste or test the juice before planning a blend around it.

varieties.name: Dukat

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: A Czech Golden Delicious x Cox's Orange Pippin cross from about 1965, the same parentage as Champion (Šampion). The National Fruit Collection received it from Czechoslovakia in 1974.

look.description: Large, rounded-conical, greenish-yellow apple with a red striped and mottled flush and some russet.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, rather coarse and juicy yellowish flesh with a very sweet flavour and low acidity.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering at Brogdale (full bloom around 10 May).

climate.best_climates: Central European continental climates like Bohemia where it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No disease ratings found.

varieties.grow_notes: A rarely grown Czech dessert apple; little growing advice is published. Pick in mid-October and eat within about two months.

varieties.name: Duke of Devonshire

origin.place: Holker Hall, Cartmel, Lancashire (now Cumbria), England
origin.parentage: Unknown; often thought to be related to Ashmead's Kernel because of its similar look and flavour
origin.raised_by: Mr Wilson, gardener to the Duke of Devonshire

varieties.history: Raised in 1835 by Wilson, gardener on the Duke of Devonshire's Holker Hall estate in north Lancashire, and introduced around 1875. Edward Bunyard considered it essential as a very late dessert apple, and it has stayed a favourite with russet enthusiasts.

look.description: Small to medium, roundish-oval fruit, dull golden-yellow with a faint brownish-red cheek and a heavy net of russet; the stalk is very short and thick.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained, rather dry cream flesh tinged green. The flavour is concentrated and boiled-sweet fruity, with a rich nutty finish. Sweet-sharp in the manner of Ashmead's Kernel rather than the sweeter Egremont Russet; it needs time in store and is best from about December into March.
taste.best_eaten: Feb-Apr, after several months in store

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous and a regular cropper that makes a good standard. Young trees can show variegation in leaves, wood and fruit.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records mid-season bloom (full flower around 11 May), so group 3 is inferred. Any mid-season diploid will pollinate it.

climate.best_climates: Cool, wet northern and western Britain, where its good scab resistance pays off; it was raised on the Cumbrian coast.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot climates; a late russet like this is likely to lose acidity and keeping quality where summers are hot.

health.other: Reported as very resistant to scab and generally healthy, like most russets.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the best late russets for wet northern gardens. Leave the fruit on the tree into October, store it cool, and plan to eat it from February onwards.

varieties.name: Dumelow's Seedling

origin.parentage: Possibly Northern Greening x unknown

varieties.history: Raised by a farmer named Dumelow or Dumeller at Shackerstone, Leicestershire; the original tree was growing by 1800. Shown as 'Dumelow's Crab' in 1818 and soon renamed 'Wellington', it was a leading Victorian keeping cooker and is a parent of Newton Wonder and Lane's Prince Albert.

look.description: Flattish, smooth, pale yellow apple with a light mottled red flush on the sunny side and a few russet dots.

taste.summary: Very firm, crisp, juicy white flesh that is intensely acid. Cooks down to a stiff, pale, strongly flavoured purée, ideal for mincemeat and sauces.

tree.notes: Average vigour, spur-bearing and a regular, good cropper.

pollination.notes: Group 4 (some lists 3); not self-fertile.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate Britain, including the Midlands where it arose; reliably hardy.
climate.poor_climates: No record of use in hot climates; very short seasons may not ripen it for long keeping.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded in modern sources.

varieties.grow_notes: A dependable late cooker for a Midlands or northern garden. Pick in early October and store cool; the fruit keeps its acidity well into spring.

varieties.name: Dunning

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Early McIntosh x Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: Raised in 1923 by Richard Wellington at the Geneva station in New York and introduced in 1938. One of several early Geneva apples combining McIntosh and Cox ancestry.

look.description: Smallish, tall apple heavily striped in glossy dark red over a pale ground, with a waxy bloom.

taste.summary: A very sweet, low-acid early apple; Brogdale's tasting panel found it soft, not very juicy and almost without acidity or aroma, though older descriptions call the flesh firm and crisp with a faint perfume.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, straight from the tree
taste.peak: Late August-September, straight from the tree.

tree.notes: Vigorous, upright-spreading tree of medium productivity with a strong tendency to crop in alternate years.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering at Brogdale (early May).

climate.best_climates: Cool north-eastern North American and north-west European climates suited to its McIntosh parent.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would make the soft early fruit go over even faster (inferred).

health.other: No disease ratings found; strongly biennial.

varieties.grow_notes: Thin fruitlets in heavy years to even out its biennial habit. Eat the crop fresh in late summer, as it keeps only a short time.

varieties.name: Dunn's Favourite
varieties.history: No reliable record of an apple under this exact name was found. It may be a variant name for the Australian Dunn's Seedling, but that could not be confirmed, so this record is a placeholder.

look.description: Not recorded.

taste.summary: No verified tasting notes are available for this name.

tree.notes: Not recorded.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Not recorded.
climate.poor_climates: Not recorded.

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Identity unconfirmed; check the source of any tree sold under this name before planting.

varieties.name: Dutch Mignonne
varieties.history: An old reinette believed to be Dutch, brought to England around 1771 by Thomas Harvey of Catton, Norwich, and distributed by George Lindley about 1820 under the name Dutch Mignonne because its true name was unknown. On the Continent it is the same apple as Reinette de Caux and Grosse Casseler Reinette.

look.description: Medium to large, somewhat flattened greenish-yellow apple with an orange-red flush stippled and striped red, and some russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, juicy cream flesh with a slightly acid, only lightly sweet and faintly aromatic flavour that holds well in store. Useful for both cooking and eating.
taste.storage_change: Orange Pippin: keeps its flavour well in store (3 months or more).
taste.peak: Wikipedia: used November to February; NFC characterisation stores December to March.

tree.notes: Average vigour spur-bearer with a drooping habit.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering.

climate.best_climates: Temperate north-west European climates; described as cold-hardy.
climate.poor_climates: Not recorded.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented in the sources checked.

varieties.grow_notes: A long-keeping dual-purpose reinette. Pick in October and store cool; use for cooking early in the winter and for eating later.

varieties.name: Dymock Red

origin.parentage: Unknown; local historians suggest it descends from the old Herefordshire Redstreak

varieties.history: An old vintage cider apple named after the village of Dymock on the Gloucestershire-Herefordshire border, already well regarded by the late seventeenth century. Long Ashton rated it a vintage-quality apple comparable with Kingston Black, and Bulmers continued to distribute it for cider orchards.

look.description: Small to medium, round to flattish, often lop-sided apple almost covered with dark mahogany red streaked brighter crimson, dotted and patched with cinnamon russet.

taste.summary: Soft, slightly sweet flesh with a pleasant acidity and moderate tannin, giving a balanced juice good enough for single-variety vintage cider. Sources differ on its class: the NFC calls it a bittersweet, while juice data and its comparison with Kingston Black point to a bittersharp.
taste.best_eaten: Mill Oct-Nov; local children ate it fresh
taste.peak: picked late September (NFC)

tree.notes: Medium vigour with thick, twiggy growth.

pollination.notes: Recorded as an early-to-mid season flowerer at the NFC; exact group not established.

climate.best_climates: The Three Counties cider country (Gloucestershire, Herefordshire, Worcestershire): cool, moist, with sunny autumns that deepen its colour.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented outside western England.

health.other: Disease record not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A good heritage choice for a Gloucestershire or Herefordshire orchard. It can stand alone for a single-variety cider or be blended to add balance.

varieties.name: Early Harvest

origin.place: Probably Long Island, New York, USA

varieties.history: An eighteenth-century American summer apple, believed to have originated on Long Island, New York; the synonym Prince's Early Harvest suggests it was distributed by the Prince nursery there. For a century it was one of the most widely planted early apples in the eastern and southern United States.

look.description: Small to medium, smooth pale yellow fruit with whitish specks and only occasionally a faint orange-red cheek.

taste.summary: Tender, crisp, juicy white flesh with a brisk, tangy sub-acid flavour. Best for sauce and pies, and pleasant raw when fully ripe; it goes soft and mealy quickly.
taste.peak: Eat fully ripe; also for sauce (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: Fruit ripens over an extended period, so several pickings are needed; reported to grow on most soil types.

pollination.notes: Not recorded; blossom dates in the US suggest it flowers fairly early.

climate.best_climates: Widely adapted across the eastern US from New York to the upper South, where it was a standard June-July apple.
climate.poor_climates: Not well documented; climate values inferred from its historical range.

health.other: Disease profile not documented; like most summer apples the fruit does not keep.

varieties.grow_notes: A good first apple of the season for sauce and pies. Pick in several passes as the fruit yellows and use within days.

varieties.name: Early Victoria

origin.parentage: Lord Grosvenor x Keswick Codlin

varieties.history: Raised by William Lynn at Emneth in the Wisbech fruit district and introduced by Cross of Wisbech; it gained an RHS Award of Merit in 1899. Officially catalogued as Emneth Early, it remains one of the standard early codlin-type cookers.

look.description: Tall, ribbed, conical codlin apple in plain pale green ripening to yellow-green.

taste.summary: Very tart greenish flesh that is crisp only straight from the tree and soon softens. Cooks quickly to a light, frothy purée and dries well into rings; left to ripen to pale yellow it becomes a passable eating apple with a faint, sweet floral scent. Does not keep.
taste.best_eaten: Cook from late Jul to Aug; thinnings usable from July

tree.notes: Sets very heavily; thin the fruit hard (use the thinnings for cooking) or it falls into biennial bearing.

pollination.notes: Group 3; partly self-fertile but sets better with a group 2-4 partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate Britain, including the north; an early cooker that ripens even in short seasons.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would make the soft early fruit go mealy quickly; little use where cooking apples are needed late.

health.other: Main problem is strong biennial bearing if not thinned; disease scores not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Good early cooker for small gardens. Thin heavily in early summer to keep it cropping every year, and pick over several weeks from late July.

varieties.name: Easter Orange

origin.place: Winchester, Hampshire, England (introduced by Hillier & Sons)

varieties.history: Put on the market by the Winchester nursery firm Hillier & Sons and first recorded in 1897, the same year it gained an RHS Award of Merit. As the name suggests, it was offered as a late-keeping dessert apple for the spring months.

look.description: Truncated-conical, moderately ribbed fruit, yellow almost hidden under a streaky red flush.

taste.summary: Firm, deep cream flesh with a rather chewy texture and an intensely aromatic flavour that develops in store. A good keeper for eating from December into early spring.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Mar; reputedly keeps towards Easter, hence the name

tree.notes: Little modern growing data.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not reliably recorded; plant with another mid-season flowering diploid.

climate.best_climates: Southern England and similar mild maritime climates with a reasonably long autumn.
climate.poor_climates: No records from hot or continental climates; very short seasons may not ripen it properly.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A Victorian keeping apple for a sunny, sheltered site in southern Britain. Pick in early October and store cool and slightly humid so the fruit lasts into late winter.

varieties.name: Ecklinville

origin.place: Ecklinville, near Portaferry, County Down, Northern Ireland
origin.raised_by: Logan, a Scottish gardener at Ecklinville

varieties.history: Raised around 1800 by a Scottish gardener named Logan on the Ecklinville estate near Portaferry on the Ards peninsula. During the 19th century it became widely planted in Ireland and southern Scotland and was a standard early cooker in British gardens.

look.description: Large, flattened, pale lemon-yellow fruit tinged green, with scattered russet dots and sometimes a slight reddish-brown cheek.

taste.summary: Fine-grained, tender white flesh with a very sharp, brisk acidity. Cooks quickly to a smooth froth.
taste.peak: Sept-Oct (Future Forests: pick early Sept, keeps Sept-Oct).

tree.notes: Noted since the 19th century as a great bearer; other habit details not well documented.

pollination.notes: Flowers with Bramley at Brogdale (group 3).

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist, mild maritime climates such as Ireland and Scotland, where it was historically widely planted.
climate.poor_climates: No evidence from hot climates; expect soft fruit that does not keep.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A good early cooker for Irish, Scottish and northern English gardens. Pick from early September and use within a few weeks.

varieties.name: Edelborsdorfer

origin.place: Saxony, Germany (Borsdorf near Leipzig, or the Meissen district)

varieties.history: Regarded as the oldest documented German apple: the Borsdorfer is named in records of the 1500s, and German writers link it to a monastery mention as far back as the 12th century. It was a prestige apple across central Europe and was reputedly a favourite of Queen Charlotte, who had fruit sent to England from Germany.

look.description: Small to medium, flattish fruit, golden yellow with a red cheek on the sunny side and scattered russet dots and veins.

taste.summary: Firm, fine, juicy flesh with a sweet, wine-like flavour; German sources add a faint cinnamon-like spice. A winter apple that is eaten from late autumn and keeps into spring.
taste.peak: From November; keeps until March (de.wikipedia).

climate_flavour.note: de.wikipedia says it needs a warm climate and rich, adequately moist soil.

tree.notes: Forms a rounded crown with long, slender shoots that hang down towards the ground. Very long-lived; foliage small, glossy and leathery.

pollination.notes: German sources call it late-flowering, with blossom that tolerates frost. Group estimated from that and from National Fruit Collection flowering dates; no published group found.

climate.best_climates: Warm, sheltered sites in central Europe with rich, evenly moist soil; the late blossom escapes most spring frosts.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, exposed or dry sites and poor soils, where German growers say the fruit stays small and the tree disappoints.

health.other: Leaves are described as healthy and disease-resistant. Main demand is a warm site and nutrient-rich soil.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a warm, sheltered position on fertile, moisture-retentive soil. Its pendulous shoots need little shortening; thin rather than head back.

varieties.name: Eden

origin.parentage: Linda x Jonamac

varieties.history: A Quebec-bred apple from Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, crossed decades earlier and released around 2006 under the name Eden. Its selling point is flesh that stays white for a long time after cutting, which suits fresh-cut slices and dried chips; fruit also hangs on the tree into winter and has been used for ice cider. Not the same as the English 'Eden' (John Standish x Cox, 1948) held at the National Fruit Collection.

look.description: Rounded, medium-sized fruit (about 150 g) that resists bruising; colour details not confirmed from the sources used.

taste.summary: White, firm, crisp and juicy flesh with a strongly aromatic flavour, balanced between sweetness and acidity and leaning to the sweet side. The cut flesh is very slow to brown.

tree.notes: Semi-vigorous with wide branch angles. Fruit is unusually persistent and can be left hanging long after maturity.

pollination.notes: Flowers about a week ahead of McIntosh; Orange Pippin puts it in group 2.

climate.best_climates: Cool continental and mild, damp temperate climates like its home in southern Quebec.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; as a McIntosh-family apple it is unlikely to do well in hot, humid summers.

health.other: Susceptible to scab; some resistance to mildew and fire blight; some bitter pit reported.

varieties.grow_notes: Needs a regular scab spray programme in wet districts. Plant an early-flowering partner such as another group 2 apple.

varieties.name: Edward VII

origin.parentage: Blenheim Orange x Golden Noble

varieties.history: First recorded in 1902 and introduced by the Rowe nursery of Worcester in 1908; it won an RHS Award of Merit in 1903. Its very late blossom has made it a favourite for frosty sites, and it holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Fairly large, smooth, broad-conical apple, pale green ripening yellow, occasionally with a faint flush.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse, fairly juicy white flesh with a brisk acidity; an excellent late cooker that makes a well-flavoured purée.
taste.peak: Walcot: pick mid October, keeps until April

tree.notes: Average vigour, spur-bearing and a regular cropper; one of the best choices for frost pockets because of its very late flowering.

pollination.notes: Very late flowering (group 6); needs another late bloomer such as Court Pendu Plat or a group 5 variety.

climate.best_climates: Cool, frost-prone temperate areas of Britain and northern Europe, where late blossom escapes spring frosts.
climate.poor_climates: Short cold seasons may not ripen it for storage; hot climates unrecorded.

health.other: Very resistant to scab and generally healthy; suitable for organic growing.

varieties.grow_notes: The obvious cooker for cold, frosty gardens. Pair it with another late-flowering variety, pick in mid-October and store for use through winter into spring.

varieties.name: Egremont Russet
varieties.history: First recorded in 1872; it is often linked to the Earl of Egremont's estate at Petworth in Sussex, though its real origin is unknown. It is now the main commercial russet apple in Britain.

look.description: Flattish-round apple almost completely covered in golden-brown russet, sometimes with a faint orange-bronze cheek.

taste.summary: Dense cream flesh, moist rather than juicy, with a sweet, classically nutty flavour, a little balancing sharpness and a pear-like overtone that some tasters find marked. Crisp at picking, it grows sweeter and nuttier in store but also drier, eventually going woolly or shrivelled; good with cheese and in savoury salads.
taste.storage_change: Flesh is dry rather than juicy and gets drier with keeping (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Fairly compact, upright tree that bears young and regularly; one of the easier russets to grow.

pollination.notes: Group 2; often described as partly self-fertile but crops better with a group 1-3 partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist British and northern European conditions; tolerates colder and wetter sites than Cox.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, dry summers make the dry flesh drier and the fruit smaller; flavour is best in mild climates.

health.other: Generally healthy with good scab resistance; russeted skin loses moisture, so store in a cool, humid place.

varieties.grow_notes: Very reliable in British gardens, including heavier soils and cooler regions. Plant with an early-to-mid flowering partner and pick before the fruit turns too yellow to keep.

varieties.name: Ein Shemer
varieties.history: A low-chill apple from the same Israeli breeding work at Kibbutz Ein Shemer that produced Anna, and named after the kibbutz. Its parentage and release date are not firmly recorded; it is grown mainly as a pollinator and early companion for Anna in warm climates.

look.description: Medium yellow-green to pale yellow apple, occasionally with a faint blush.

taste.summary: Crisp and juicy, on the sharp side with only moderate sweetness; a pleasant early apple rather than a rich one, and it keeps for only a short time.
taste.best_eaten: Straight from the tree (early summer in warm climates)
taste.peak: very early; keeps about a week (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: Precocious, regular and heavy cropping; blossoms very early, ahead of standard apples.

pollination.notes: Group 1 (Orange Pippin) and at least partly self-fertile; the classic pollinator for Anna.

climate.best_climates: Warm-temperate and subtropical climates with mild winters, such as Israel, Florida, the Gulf states and southern California; it sets fruit with very little chilling.
climate.poor_climates: Cold-winter regions, where its early blossom is frosted. The SE England harvest date is extrapolated from its very early season.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well documented; fruit keeps only about a week.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant it mainly as a pollinator for Anna in mild-winter gardens, enjoying its early sharp fruit as a bonus. Thin heavy crops to keep fruit size up.

varieties.name: Elektra

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Geheimrat Doktor Oldenburg

varieties.history: Bred by Professor Martin Schmidt at the Müncheberg research institute east of Berlin, one of a series of German Cox crosses from the 1930s. It was later distributed in eastern Europe and reached the UK National Fruit Trials in 1977.

look.description: Small to medium apple with a dry, slightly rough greenish-yellow skin flushed and dully striped brownish red.

taste.summary: Firm, fine, juicy yellowish flesh that is sweet with little acidity and a refined, Cox-like aroma. Brogdale's panel found it sweet and well balanced, though less aromatic than Cox.
taste.peak: November to February (de.wikipedia); Brogdale store to January/February.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous when young, then weak, forming a small broad-conical crown with few, obliquely upright scaffold branches. Flowers only on spurs; tends to crop biennially.

pollination.notes: Long flowering period; the blossom is sensitive to frost.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate central and north-west Europe with moderate summers, similar to its Cox parent.
climate.poor_climates: Frost-prone sites (tender blossom) and wet sites where canker is rife.

health.other: Very prone to canker; only slightly susceptible to mildew. Blossom is frost-tender. Fruit bruises little and stores well.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a well-drained, sheltered site to limit canker and frost damage, and prune lightly to keep spurs renewed on the small tree.

varieties.name: Elise Rathke

origin.place: West Prussia, near Danzig (Gdansk) or Elbing (Elblag); then Germany
origin.raised_by: Rathke of Praust near Danzig, or A. Duhring of Elbing (sources differ)

varieties.history: A 19th-century apple from West Prussia, first recorded in 1884 and distributed from 1886 by the Spaeth nursery in Berlin. It is best known today as a naturally weeping small tree, often top-grafted as an ornamental standard that also gives edible fruit.

look.description: Small to medium, greasy-skinned fruit, yellow with a pinkish-red flush and streaks and brown dots.

taste.summary: Fine, soft flesh, moderately sweet with little acidity and a light spicy note. Brogdale's assessors found it rather crumbly and dry.

tree.notes: Strongly weeping, forming a broad, half-open umbrella about 3 m tall when top-worked on a stem. Grown as much for its form and pale pink blossom as for fruit.

pollination.notes: No published group found; estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate and Baltic-type climates; a Dutch tree nursery rates it frost-resistant.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, humid districts where scab is severe; performance in hot climates not recorded.

health.other: Very susceptible to scab.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant it where the weeping crown has room to spread, in an open, airy spot to reduce scab. Usually bought top-grafted on a clear stem; little pruning beyond removing upright shoots.

varieties.name: Ellis Bitter

origin.place: Newton St Cyres, near Crediton, Devon, England
origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: A nineteenth-century Devon bittersweet, probably arising on a Mr Ellis's farm at Newton St Cyres in the Crediton area. Its early ripening let commercial growers supplying Bulmers start pressing sooner, and Long Ashton included it in trials.

look.description: Fairly large for a cider apple; conical, yellow with an orange-red striped flush and russet-ringed lenticels.

taste.summary: A mild to medium bittersweet: sweet, low-acid juice with moderate, soft tannin, useful for adding body to early blends.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill in October, it hangs on the tree for only a couple of weeks once ripe.
taste.peak: Picked mid October (NFC)

tree.notes: Very vigorous with a strong tip-bearing habit, so heavy pruning removes fruiting wood. Heavy cropper with some biennial tendency.

pollination.notes: Self-sterile; needs a pollinator flowering at the same time.

climate.best_climates: Mild, wet South West England and similar maritime climates.
climate.poor_climates: Warm humid regions where scab and fire blight are rife.

health.other: Very resistant to mildew but prone to scab and fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it room: it is a strong grower. Prune lightly and renew rather than shortening every shoot, as fruit forms at the tips. Useful to start the cider season before the late bittersweets.

varieties.name: Ellison's Orange

origin.place: Bracebridge and Hartsholme Hall, Lincoln, Lincolnshire, England
origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Calville Blanc
origin.raised_by: Rev. C.C. Ellison and Mr Wipf

varieties.history: Raised near Lincoln by the Reverend C.C. Ellison of Bracebridge with Mr Wipf, gardener at Hartsholme Hall, and first recorded in 1904. Pennells of Lincoln introduced it in 1911 and it won RHS awards in 1911 and 1917.

look.description: Golden-yellow conical apple striped and lightly flushed crimson.

taste.summary: Soft, very juicy, almost pear-textured yellow flesh with a rich, Cox-like fruitiness that is neither very sweet nor sharp, plus an orange-like tang. The aniseed or liquorice note is faint straight off the tree and builds over the following days, so eat it early if you dislike it; it loses crispness and flavour quickly.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct; best within a couple of weeks of picking
taste.storage_change: Aniseed is barely detectable straight from the tree and develops after picking / in storage; keeps about a week.
taste.peak: Within about a week of picking (mid-September)

tree.notes: Easy and productive; can slip into alternate cropping if overloaded, so thin heavy crops.

pollination.notes: Group 4; partly self-fertile and a useful pollinator for mid-late flowering varieties. Blossom tolerates frost well.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate regions, including eastern and northern England and frost-prone sites, thanks to its hardy blossom.
climate.poor_climates: Warm summers make the already soft flesh mealy quickly.

health.other: Good scab and mildew resistance, but prone to canker and attractive to codling moth.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for colder or frostier British gardens. Thin the fruit to avoid biennial bearing, watch for canker, and eat the crop promptly.

varieties.name: Elstar

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Ingrid Marie
origin.raised_by: Institute for Horticultural Plant Breeding (IVT), Wageningen

varieties.history: Bred at the Dutch plant-breeding institute in Wageningen from a 1955 cross and released in 1972. It became one of the leading commercial apples of the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany, with many redder sports such as Elshof and Red Elstar.

look.description: Golden-yellow apple marbled and streaked bright orange-red, with a slightly matt finish and a few russet dots.

taste.summary: Crisp but not hard, juicy cream flesh with an intense honeyed sweetness set against lively acidity; tasters also mention a sherbet-like fizz and a pear note at the finish. Stays firm and sweet for a couple of months and keeps its sharpness for cooking. Opinions vary: many rate it highly, a few find it bland.
taste.storage_change: Trees of Antiquity (not counted): flavour is enhanced by three to four weeks of storage. English Wikipedia: pick early October, keeps until December.
taste.peak: Oct-Dec (English Wikipedia: keeps until December)

tree.notes: Vigorous and quick to crop but strongly inclined to alternate bearing unless thinned early; regular fruit thinning is essential.

pollination.notes: Group 3; partner with another group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cool maritime north-west Europe (Netherlands, Belgium, northern Germany, southern England) with mild summers and cool autumn nights.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers give soft fruit, poor colour and sunburn; it has never succeeded commercially in warm regions.

health.other: Susceptible to powdery mildew and some scab; biennial bearing is the main cultural problem.

varieties.grow_notes: Grows well in most of southern Britain. Thin hard in good blossom years to keep cropping regular, and keep an eye on mildew in spring.

varieties.name: Elton Beauty

origin.place: Ince Orchards, near Chester, Cheshire, England
origin.parentage: James Grieve x Worcester Pearmain

varieties.history: Raised at Ince Orchards near Chester (Elton is the neighbouring village) and introduced by 1952. It shares its parentage with Lord Lambourne and the Swedish Katy.

look.description: James Grieve-shaped fruit coloured almost all over in bright red flush and streaks, with a little russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Soft, fine and very juicy flesh with a lively, fairly sharp and aromatic flavour; best eaten fresh as it does not keep.
taste.peak: Mid-September (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: A rather weak tree that crops heavily; use a vigorous rootstock and thin the fruit.

pollination.notes: Early flowering (group 2); pollinate with a group 1-3 variety.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist north-western England and similar maritime climates.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented outside Britain; soft early fruit is likely to suffer in hot summers.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.
