varieties.grow_notes: Grow on a stronger rootstock than usual because the tree is weak, and keep crops thinned so it does not exhaust itself. Needs an early-flowering partner.

varieties.name: Emilia

origin.parentage: Northern Spy seedling (pollen parent unknown)

varieties.history: One of the Ottawa Central Experimental Farm's early Northern Spy seedlings, dated to about 1915 in research-collection records. The UK National Fruit Trials received it from Ottawa in 1927.

look.description: Medium to large, tall conical apple streaked with red over a pale whitish-yellow to greenish ground.

taste.summary: Crisp but rather coarse, tender cream flesh with a sweet, aromatic, Spy-like flavour; Brogdale's tasting panel found acidity low and aroma modest.

tree.notes: Productive but strongly biennial.

pollination.notes: Flowers fairly late at Brogdale (around 10 May), as befits a Northern Spy seedling.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates such as eastern Ontario and the US north-east.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; late flowering helps it escape spring frosts (inferred from flowering date).

health.other: No disease ratings found; strong biennial bearing is the main recorded fault.

varieties.grow_notes: A collection apple; thin heavily in the 'on' year to temper biennial cropping. Harvest timing is poorly documented: Brogdale gives mid September for ripening but picked in mid October, and USDA Geneva lists it as late.

varieties.name: Emperor Alexander
varieties.history: An old eastern European apple, thought to be Ukrainian and known during the 1700s; it reached Britain in the early 1800s. It spread widely under many names, including Aport, and is the mother of the hardy American variety Wolf River.

look.description: Very large, broad conical apple, greenish-yellow with orange-red streaks and flush; a showpiece fruit.

taste.summary: Sources disagree: English accounts call the flesh coarse, rather dry and fairly acid with little aroma, better cooked than raw, while descriptions of the Aport grown around Almaty give a crisp, fine-grained, sweet-tart apple with a honeyed scent and hints of hazelnut and anise. Softens and turns crumbly in store.
taste.storage_change: Crisp at harvest, becoming softer and crumblier in storage (Aport article); keeps only 2-3 weeks per Orange Pippin.
taste.peak: de Wikipedia: edible November-February

climate_flavour.note: Aport article: growers credit the soil and altitude of the Almaty foothills for its strong honey-like aroma; seedlings unremarkable elsewhere.

tree.notes: A strong, spreading tree from a cold-winter region; the heavy fruit bruises easily and may drop in wind.

pollination.notes: Listed by the RHS in group 3 under the name Alexander.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates with hard winters, such as Ukraine, Russia, Scandinavia and the northern prairies, as well as cool maritime Britain.
climate.poor_climates: Mild-winter or hot-summer regions, where chilling may be inadequate and the large fruit goes soft and mealy.

health.other: Not well recorded; the big fruit bruises easily.

varieties.grow_notes: A historic and very winter-hardy variety for cold gardens or for anyone wanting giant show apples. Give it room to spread and a sheltered spot so the heavy fruit is not blown down.

varieties.name: Empire

origin.parentage: McIntosh x Red Delicious
origin.raised_by: R.D. Way, New York State Agricultural Experiment Station (Cornell)

varieties.history: Raised at the Geneva, New York experiment station from a 1945 cross and released in 1966 by Roger Way. It became a major apple of New York and the north-east, prized as a bruise-resistant, deep red lunchbox apple.

look.description: Medium, rounded apple almost fully covered in dark maroon-red with a light bloom over a pale green ground.

taste.summary: Crisp, crunchy, bright white flesh, juicy and sweet, with the vinous McIntosh character (likened to melon or elderflower) but less acidity. Best fresh from the tree, though it keeps into winter in a fridge and resists bruising; UK-grown or poorly stored fruit can be watery or mealy.
taste.storage_change: Can be stored a short time but best straight from the tree (Orange Pippin); lasts up to ten months in CA store and is slow to brown (Wikipedia).
taste.peak: Straight from the tree (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous spur-bearer with dense growth; open the centre so the fruit colours. Thin to keep fruit size and annual cropping.

pollination.notes: Group 3, partly self-fertile; crops better with a group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter continental climates with sunny autumns and cool nights, such as New York, Ontario and Michigan.
climate.poor_climates: Warm summers and autumns reduce colour and firmness; mild cloudy regions give smaller, duller fruit.

health.other: Susceptible to scab; reasonably tolerant of fire blight, cedar-apple rust and mildew.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy, reliable choice for cold areas. Control scab in wet springs, thin after fruit set, and summer-prune to let light in for colour.

varieties.name: English Russet
varieties.history: Despite its name this is an American russet, recorded from 1842 and also known as Poughkeepsie Russet, which suggests the Hudson Valley of New York. It was valued as a very long-keeping winter apple and for cider, and is sometimes confused with Golden Russet.

look.description: Medium, flattish, slightly ribbed apple, pale green to yellow and more or less covered in russet.

taste.summary: Firm, rather crisp, fine-grained yellowish-white flesh with a mild subacid flavour; rated good rather than outstanding. Its strength is keeping quality rather than flavour.
taste.storage_change: Wikipedia article: keeps exceptionally well; the list gives use January-May
taste.peak: Jan-May (Wikipedia list)

tree.notes: Upright tree according to the National Apple Register; little else is recorded.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: North-eastern US apple country with cold winters and warm summers; inferred from its New York history.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity for keen russet collectors; pick late and store cool to eat from midwinter into spring. Not held at the UK National Fruit Collection, so UK performance is unknown.

varieties.name: Enterprise

origin.place: Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana (PRI co-operative programme)
origin.parentage: Complex PRI hybrid involving McIntosh, Golden Delicious, Starking Delicious, Rome Beauty and Malus floribunda 821 (source of Vf scab resistance)

varieties.history: Released in 1994 by the PRI disease-resistance programme (tested as Co-op 30); the name contains the letters P-R-I. It later became famous as a parent of Washington State University's Cosmic Crisp (Enterprise x Honeycrisp).

look.description: Large, slightly elongated and often lopsided fruit with a glossy red flush over yellow-green; thick, tough skin.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp cream flesh, moderately juicy, with a sharp, slightly spicy flavour at picking that mellows and improves after a month or two in store. Holds up well in cooking.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Mar, after a month or more in store
taste.storage_change: sprightly sub-acid at harvest, mellowing in store; flavour peaks after one or two months in refrigerated storage (Purdue PRI page)
taste.peak: after one to two months in cold store; keeps six months or more (Purdue)

tree.notes: Vigorous and regular-bearing. Very late to ripen, so needs a long, warm autumn.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 4; average pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Long-season continental and humid eastern US climates, including warmer southern apple districts, where its disease resistance and keeping quality shine.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season or cool northern sites where the very late crop may not ripen fully; marginal in northern Britain.

health.other: Scab-immune (Vf) and highly resistant to fire blight, with some resistance to cedar-apple rust and mildew. Thick skin resists insect and storage damage.

varieties.grow_notes: Ideal for organic or low-spray orchards in places with a long autumn. Give it a warm, sunny position, leave the fruit to hang until late October and store before eating.

varieties.name: Envy

origin.parentage: Braeburn x Royal Gala

varieties.history: Raised by New Zealand's HortResearch from the same Braeburn x Royal Gala parentage as Jazz, and patented in 2008-09 as cultivar Scilate. Sold under the Envy trademark, it is grown under licence in New Zealand, Washington State, Chile, Australia and elsewhere.

look.description: Almost entirely bright red with yellow freckling showing through; the skin is notably thick and tough.

taste.summary: Very sweet with low acidity and a faint floral note; crisp, juicy, pale flesh that browns very slowly once cut. Firmness holds well in storage.

tree.notes: Licensed club variety; little published growing information outside commercial programmes.

pollination.notes: Needs a cross-pollinator; UK flowering group not published.

climate.best_climates: Long, sunny seasons with cool autumn nights, as in Hawke's Bay, central Washington and central Chile.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons where a late-October apple will not ripen fully; humid areas with high canker pressure.

health.other: Susceptible to European canker (Neonectria), sometimes carried without visible symptoms; growers have reported russet, shrivel, bitter pit and internal browning.

varieties.grow_notes: A late, long-season apple best left to warm, sunny commercial regions. If grown, choose a free-draining site to reduce canker risk and keep calcium levels up to limit bitter pit.

varieties.name: Esopus Spitzenburg
varieties.history: A chance seedling from the old Dutch settlement of Esopus in the Hudson Valley, known before 1790. It was grown at Monticello by Thomas Jefferson and was one of the most esteemed American dessert apples of the 19th century; it is a parent of Jonathan.

look.description: Tall, slightly tapering fruit, deep yellow almost covered by bright orange-red to red with obscure streaks and conspicuous pale russet dots.

taste.summary: Dense, crisp, buttery yellow flesh, moderately juicy, with a rich, bright sweet-sharp flavour that is spicy and strongly aromatic and improves after some weeks in store. Superb raw and in pies, where slices hold their shape but turn tender.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Feb; improves after a month in store
taste.storage_change: Improves with a few weeks of cool storage, which brings out its full, rich flavour.
taste.peak: After a few weeks of cool storage

tree.notes: Rather slow to bear, with thin, spreading branches and short spurs; crops are often irregular and it needs good soil and care to perform.

pollination.notes: Group 4; plant with another group 3-5 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer, cold-winter continental climates such as the Hudson Valley and similar parts of the eastern and western USA, on fertile, well-drained soil.
climate.poor_climates: Humid, warm areas with high fire blight and scab pressure, and cool, cloudy maritime summers where the flavour does not fully develop.

health.other: Very susceptible to scab, canker and fire blight; a demanding tree for organic growers.

varieties.grow_notes: Worth growing for flavour if you can give it good soil, full sun and a disease-control routine. Thin to even out cropping and prune to keep the canopy open and airy.

varieties.name: Eva

origin.parentage: Anna x Gala

varieties.history: Released in 1999 by the Paraná state agricultural institute IAPAR as one of a group of low-chill apples (with Anabela and Carícia) for warm subtropical parts of Brazil. It ripens in December and January in southern Brazil, ahead of Gala and Fuji, and is now grown even in semi-arid north-east Brazil and other warm-winter countries.

look.description: No reliable description of the fruit's appearance found.

taste.summary: No published tasting notes were found; its value lies in cropping where winters are too mild for most apples.

tree.notes: Reported as highly productive in warm regions; growers in Brazil still often apply dormancy-breaking sprays when winter chill falls short.

pollination.notes: Needs a low-chill partner flowering at the same time; UK flowering group is meaningless for such an early-breaking tree.

climate.best_climates: Subtropical and warm-winter regions with roughly 100-450 chill hours: southern and north-eastern Brazil and similar climates in South America, Africa and the Middle East.
climate.poor_climates: Cold-winter climates such as Britain: chill is satisfied very early, so it breaks bud and flowers early and risks spring frost; harvest time there is not documented.

health.other: No disease information found in the sources consulted.

varieties.grow_notes: A specialist apple for warm-winter gardens, to be paired with another low-chill variety such as Anna or Dorsett Golden for pollination. Not suited to UK gardens.

varieties.name: EverCrisp

origin.parentage: Honeycrisp x Fuji
origin.raised_by: Mitch Lynd for the Midwest Apple Improvement Association (MAIA)

varieties.history: Raised in the late 1990s by Ohio grower Mitch Lynd within the grower-run Midwest Apple Improvement Association, patented as MAIA 1 and sold as EverCrisp. It was promoted from about 2012 and reached wider retail around 2017.

look.description: Fuji-like in shape and look, with a rosy red blush over a cream background and a slightly tougher skin than Honeycrisp.

taste.summary: Very sweet, with a candy-like sweetness, a light tang in the background and a Fuji-like flavour with some Honeycrisp character. Dense and very crisp, a little harder than Honeycrisp, and it keeps its crunch for months in store and for a couple of weeks at room temperature.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Apr; said to eat even better after two or three months in cold store
taste.storage_change: Wikipedia: eats even better after two or three months in cold store and holds crispness for two weeks at room temperature; Fruit Growers News: still crisp and sweet after three weeks in a fruit bowl
taste.peak: after 2-3 months in cold store

tree.notes: A small, spreading tree with wide crotch angles that crops annually and largely self-thins; the original tree set four crops in a row without thinning. Easier to manage than Fuji. Fruit left hanging into November may develop watercore.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not published; plant with another mid-season diploid.

climate.best_climates: Bred for the US Midwest, with cold winters and warm summers and a long autumn; in Indiana it is picked from mid October and can hang into early November.
climate.poor_climates: Its very late season makes full ripening doubtful in cool, short British autumns, as with Fuji.

health.other: No pre-harvest drop or bitter pit recorded in early trials, unlike Honeycrisp; watercore can develop if picked very late.

varieties.grow_notes: Needs a long, warm season to sweeten; in Britain only a warm, sheltered south-facing site is likely to ripen it. The tree is compact and easy, and the fruit stores exceptionally well.

varieties.name: Evereste
varieties.history: A French ornamental crab of the later twentieth century that has become one of the most popular garden crabs and pollinators in Britain. It holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Small rounded fruits about 2.5 cm, yellow heavily flushed orange-red, borne in large numbers and hanging on the tree into December.

taste.summary: Grown above all for show; the fruit is sharp and not an eating apple, but it is used alone or with other fruit to make crab apple jelly, where its pectin helps the set.

tree.notes: Forms a neat, broadly conical small tree, roughly 2.5-3.5 m after ten years, ideal for small gardens. Needs little pruning beyond removing crossing shoots.

pollination.notes: Red buds open to masses of slightly scented white blossom that shed pollen over a long period, making it one of the most popular pollinators for small orchards of mid-season apples.

climate.best_climates: Temperate western Europe including the UK; tolerant of most garden soils.
climate.poor_climates: Not well documented outside temperate Europe; rated hardy to about -20 C, so very severe continental winters may damage it.

health.other: Generally healthy; nursery sources rate its disease resistance as average to good with no single notorious weakness.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice where only one small crab can be planted: it flowers with most group 2-4 apples and stays compact. Plant in sun on any well-drained soil.

varieties.name: Exeter Cross

origin.place: Long Ashton Research Station, Bristol, England
origin.parentage: Worcester Pearmain x Beauty of Bath
origin.raised_by: G.T. Spinks, Long Ashton Research Station

varieties.history: Raised in 1924 by G.T. Spinks at Long Ashton, Bristol, and named in 1953, it was intended as an improved early apple combining Worcester and Beauty of Bath. It is a parent of Redsleeves.

look.description: Small, flat, slightly ribbed apple flushed and striped scarlet over a pale greenish-yellow ground.

taste.summary: Firm and crisp when freshly picked, juicy and sweet with a light, refreshing, moderately aromatic flavour; Orange Pippin notes a sharp edge. It softens and goes over quickly, and Brogdale's panel scored it low on crunch and juice.
taste.peak: August, straight from the tree.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous, upright, tip-bearing tree; prune lightly and renew fruiting shoots rather than spurring back hard.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering at Brogdale (early May).

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist English conditions like those of its Bristol birthplace.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would make an already short-lived early apple go mealy faster (inferred).

health.other: No disease ratings found. Fruit keeps only days.

varieties.grow_notes: Treat as a garden early apple to eat from the tree in August. Being tip-bearing it suits an open-centre bush rather than cordons.

varieties.name: Fall Pippin

origin.parentage: Unknown; links to Holland Pippin or White Spanish Reinette have been suggested but are unproven

varieties.history: An American apple of uncertain origin, documented from the early nineteenth century and widely grown in the eastern states, particularly the Shenandoah Valley, as a late autumn and early winter apple. Its exact birthplace is not known.

look.description: Large to very large, roundish or slightly oblong fruit with thin, clear yellow skin, occasionally with a faint blush.

taste.summary: Tender, juicy, aromatic white flesh tinged yellow, with a rich sweet-sharp balance. Used both raw and for cooking, drying and sauce.
taste.peak: Ripens Aug-Sept; favoured as an early winter apple (Big Horse Creek Farm).

tree.notes: Recorded as a spur-bearing triploid; triploids generally make large trees, so allow space. Other tree traits are not well documented.

pollination.notes: Group 3 triploid and a poor pollinator; plant two compatible diploids nearby.

climate.best_climates: Eastern US temperate climates from New York to Virginia's Shenandoah Valley.
climate.poor_climates: Not well documented; values inferred from where it was traditionally grown.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not documented in sources checked.

varieties.grow_notes: Give this large triploid room and two diploid pollinators. Handle the thin-skinned fruit gently and use it through late autumn and early winter.

varieties.name: Fallawater

origin.place: Pennsylvania (Bucks County according to the National Apple Register)
origin.raised_by: Introduced by a Mr Garber of Columbia, Pennsylvania

varieties.history: A Pennsylvania German farm apple described by 1842 and spread by a Mr Garber of Columbia, Pennsylvania; it collected many local names, including Tulpehocken. It was valued as a huge, productive sauce and drying apple through the Mid-Atlantic states.

look.description: Very large, broad green apple, ripening to yellowish green, with dull red stripes or flush and russet dots; sometimes over 15 cm across.

taste.summary: Firm, coarse, crisp greenish-white flesh with a mild subacid to gently sweet flavour. Best for sauce, pies and drying; USDA Geneva rates it only poor to fair for eating fresh.
taste.peak: November-December (Wikipedia list).

tree.notes: Very productive spur-bearer.

pollination.notes: No flowering data found.

climate.best_climates: Long, warm summers of the eastern US Mid-Atlantic region, where it ripens very late.
climate.poor_climates: Short or cool seasons; at Geneva, New York it ripens only in early November, so it would struggle to mature in cool maritime climates (inferred).

health.other: No disease ratings found.

varieties.grow_notes: A big kitchen apple for warm-summer areas. Give it a long season and a sunny site, and pick last of all.

varieties.name: Falstaff

origin.parentage: James Grieve x Golden Delicious

varieties.history: Raised at East Malling Research Station in Kent in the mid-1960s and released to growers in the 1980s. It became a popular garden apple for its reliable crops and frost-tolerant blossom, and has a redder sport, Red Falstaff.

look.description: Neat golden-yellow apple with a bright red flush and stripes over about half the surface.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy flesh with a fresh sweet-sharp flavour that owes more to James Grieve than to Golden Delicious. Makes good juice.
taste.storage_change: Crunchy and sharp off the tree; mellows and softens somewhat with age but stays juicy (Orange Pippin).
taste.peak: Straight from the tree (Orange Pippin); keeps 1-2 months

tree.notes: Compact-ish, regular-cropping spur-bearer; suits cordons and small trees. Thin heavy crops to keep fruit size.

pollination.notes: Self-fertile, group 3, and a good pollinator for other mid-season varieties; blossom is notably frost tolerant.

climate.best_climates: Cool maritime climates like the UK, including frost-prone gardens thanks to its hardy blossom.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers likely to soften the fruit and reduce colour; little evidence of use in warm regions.

health.other: Generally healthy in UK gardens with only moderate scab and mildew.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the easiest apples for a small UK garden, especially where only one tree fits. Plant in full sun, thin fruitlets in heavy years and prune as a normal spur-bearer.

varieties.name: Fenouillet Gris
varieties.history: An old French russet from Anjou, described as early as 1608 and prized for its anise scent; in England it was called Caraway Russet. It is also sold under the short name 'Anis', which should not be confused with the Russian Anis apples.

look.description: Small, flat and often lopsided fruit, largely covered in grey to reddish-brown russet over a dull yellow and red skin.

taste.summary: Sweet, fine, crisp but rather dry white flesh with almost no acidity and a distinctive anise or musky fennel aroma. An unusual, highly scented dessert apple rather than a juicy one.

tree.notes: Average vigour, regular cropper, spur-bearing.

pollination.notes: Group 4 per Orange Pippin; diploid, an average pollen donor.

climate.best_climates: Warm temperate regions such as western France, and warm-summer climates generally.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, short seasons where late russets struggle to ripen fully.

health.other: Some scab resistance reported; otherwise average disease resistance.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a warm, sunny site so the late fruit ripens and develops its scent. Pick in mid October and store cool; it keeps for three months or more.

varieties.name: Fiesta

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Idared

varieties.history: Raised at East Malling Research Station in 1972 to combine Cox flavour with the easy growing and long storage of Idared. Released in the 1980s, it gained an RHS Award of Merit in 1987 and has been sold in supermarkets as Red Pippin.

look.description: Yellow apple flecked and streaked with orange and red, Cox-like but brighter and more evenly coloured.

taste.summary: Crisp, very juicy cream flesh with a sweet, Cox-like aromatic flavour backed by good acidity; some tasters pick up strawberry, and long-stored fruit can develop odd aniseed or brandy-like notes. Stays firm for months, though the sweetness fades; the skin is tough and the flesh holds firm when cooked. Good for juice.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Jan; best in the first two months
taste.storage_change: The appealing sweetness seems to fade after a while in store, though it stays pleasant (Orange Pippin).

climate_flavour.note: Orange Pippin: in an average year merely a good sweet Cox-style apple, but in a year that suits it close to Cox at its best (season not specified).

tree.notes: Easy, productive spur-bearer, though trees can grow lopsided; thin to avoid small fruit and alternate-year crops.

pollination.notes: Group 3 and partly self-fertile; crops best with another group 2-4 diploid. Blossom has good frost resistance.

climate.best_climates: UK and similar cool maritime climates, where it is a much easier substitute for Cox.
climate.poor_climates: Hot dry summers are likely to give soft, poorly coloured fruit; untested in warm regions.

health.other: Some canker reported in wet soils; bitter pit can show on young, vigorous trees carrying light crops.

varieties.grow_notes: A good Cox alternative for gardeners who struggle with Cox. Plant on well-drained soil, keep crops even by thinning, and store the fruit cool for winter use.

varieties.name: Filippa
varieties.history: Grown from seed at Hundstrup on south Funen by Filippa Johansen, after whom it is named; dates between 1850 and 1881 are given. It won a first-class certificate from the Royal Danish Horticultural Society in 1888, reached Sweden through the Alnarp nursery in 1893, and is a parent of the Swedish apple Aroma.

look.description: Medium to large fruit ripening to greenish-yellow or whitish-yellow.

taste.summary: A sweet-sharp Calville-type apple eaten fresh and pressed for juice and cider; the juice is pale and not very sweet, so it is often blended.
taste.peak: picked mid September (NFC)

tree.notes: Fruit hangs at the ends of long, thin branches and is easily blown off; 30-60% windfalls are common.

pollination.notes: Pollination details not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Cool Scandinavian climates; grown in Swedish zones I-IV.
climate.poor_climates: Windy sites, because of heavy fruit drop; warm-climate performance unknown.

health.other: Good resistance to scab, powdery mildew and canker; main problem is pre-harvest drop.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in a sheltered spot to reduce windfalls, and prune lightly since it fruits at the shoot tips. Collect drops promptly for juice.

varieties.name: Fireside

origin.place: Minnesota Agricultural Experiment Station, Excelsior, Minnesota
origin.parentage: Uncertain: McIntosh x Longfield according to the National Fruit Collection; Wealthy x Northwestern Greening according to Orange Pippin

varieties.history: Selected in 1917 by Charles Haralson at the University of Minnesota's Excelsior station and introduced in 1943 as a large, hardy, late keeping apple for the upper Midwest.

look.description: Large, conical green apple striped scarlet, sometimes with a mottled orange-red flush.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, juicy greenish-white flesh with a sweet, low-acid, mildly aromatic flavour; sweetness improves if left late on the tree. Softens somewhat after long storage.

tree.notes: Drooping habit at the National Fruit Collection; reported to give large annual crops.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental Upper Midwest climates for which it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: Not recorded.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented in the sources checked.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy late apple for cold districts. Leave the fruit on the tree as long as frost allows for best sweetness, then store cool.

varieties.name: Flamenco

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Kent, England
origin.parentage: (Cox's Orange Pippin x Court Pendu Plat) x Wijcik McIntosh

varieties.history: Raised in 1970 at East Malling as part of the 'Ballerina' columnar apple series, which takes its single-stem habit from Wijcik, a compact sport of McIntosh. It is sold as Flamenco and registered at Brogdale as Obelisk.

look.description: Red dessert apple borne close against a single upright stem.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy and rather brisk when picked, mellowing by the New Year according to Brogdale; Orange Pippin rates the flavour as average and on the sharp side.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Jan; sharper early, mellower after store
taste.storage_change: Brisk when picked, becoming mellow by the New Year (NFC).
taste.peak: After Christmas (NFC).

tree.notes: Narrow columnar tree that fruits on short spurs along a single stem; suits pots and small gardens. Brogdale notes a tendency to biennial bearing; Orange Pippin rates cropping light.

pollination.notes: Group 3 per Orange Pippin; Brogdale records quite early flowering (end of April).

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate climates (Orange Pippin lists cold to cool summers).
climate.poor_climates: Warm-summer areas are not recommended by Orange Pippin; poor disease resistance is a drawback in humid climates.

health.other: Orange Pippin rates its overall disease resistance as poor. Sources disagree on keeping: Brogdale says it mellows into the New Year, Orange Pippin gives 2-3 weeks.

varieties.grow_notes: Ideal for a patio container or narrow border; needs no shaping beyond removing any strong side shoots. Feed and water container trees well and supply a group 3 pollinator.

varieties.name: Flanders Cox
varieties.history: No record of this name was found in the UK National Fruit Collection, Orange Pippin or other pomological sources checked. The name suggests a Cox-type apple linked to Flanders, but neither its origin nor its relationship to Cox's Orange Pippin could be confirmed.

look.description: Not recorded.

taste.summary: No reliable tasting notes found for this name.

tree.notes: Not recorded.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Insufficient information to give variety-specific advice; ask the supplying nursery for its origin and pollination group.

varieties.name: Florina

origin.place: INRA Station de Recherches d'Arboriculture Fruitière, Angers, France
origin.parentage: Selection 612-1 x Jonathan; the complex ancestry includes Malus floribunda (source of the Vf scab-resistance gene), Rome Beauty, Golden Delicious, Starking and Jonathan

varieties.history: A scab-resistant apple from the French national research station at Angers, released in the late 1970s and sometimes sold as Querina. Its Vf resistance comes from the crab apple Malus floribunda, and it is widely planted in European organic orchards.

look.description: Medium to large round fruit, washed purplish red over most of a yellow skin; a very handsome apple.

taste.summary: Medium-firm, very juicy flesh with an aromatic sweet-tart balance; some sources find it rather sweet, others rather sharp. Keeps well, though juiciness fades in long storage.
taste.storage_change: de.wikipedia: very juicy at first (implying juiciness fades in store); keeps to December/January.
taste.peak: de.wikipedia: eat December-January; Orange Pippin: keeps 3 months or more.

tree.notes: Vigorous, precocious and productive with a spreading to drooping habit; a partial tip-bearer, so prune lightly. Easy for beginners.

pollination.notes: Needs a partner but is itself a good pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Temperate to warm climates, including western and southern Europe, where its disease resistance makes low-spray growing practical.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons where a mid-October apple may not ripen fully.

health.other: Vf scab resistance; some resistance to mildew, fire blight and woolly aphid. Occasional core mould in store.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the best choices for unsprayed gardens. Plant with another mid-to-late flowering variety and leave the tip-borne fruit buds when pruning.

varieties.name: Flower of Kent
varieties.history: An old English kitchen apple listed by John Parkinson in 1629. It is best known as the variety said to have grown at Isaac Newton's birthplace, Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire, and trees propagated from that line are planted at universities and museums as 'Newton's apple tree'.

look.description: Large, broad-based fruit with blunt ribs around the eye, green turning yellow, striped crimson on the sunny side and russeted around the stalk.

taste.summary: Nineteenth-century accounts describe crisp, very juicy flesh with brisk acidity and rate it a first-rate cooker. Modern tasters of the Newton-line trees tend to find it coarse, mealy and unremarkable.

tree.notes: Described historically as one of the strongest-growing apples and better suited to an orchard than a small garden.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded; plant with a mid-season partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool lowland England, where it has been grown for centuries; Newton-line trees also grow in New England.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers untested; likely to worsen its tendency to soft, mealy flesh.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Grown mainly for its link with Newton rather than for fruit quality. It makes a big tree, so give it space or a semi-dwarfing stock.

varieties.name: Fortune

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Wealthy

varieties.history: Bred in 1904 by Laxton Brothers of Bedford and released in 1931 as Laxton's Fortune; it received an RHS First Class Certificate in 1948. Not to be confused with the American 'Fortune' released by Cornell (Geneva) in 1995.

look.description: Neat, slightly conical apple, greenish-yellow streaked and flushed with bright red.

taste.summary: Fairly firm, slightly coarse, juicy cream flesh with a sweet, aromatic flavour that hints at its Cox parent; best eaten fresh in early autumn.
taste.storage_change: Trees of Antiquity: needs to be left on the tree to ripen fully.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous spur-bearer; tends to crop in alternate years unless thinned in heavy years.

pollination.notes: Group 3; needs a mid-season partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate Britain and similar maritime climates.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers likely to soften the fruit and reduce colour; untested in warm regions.

health.other: Prone to canker on heavy, wet soils; biennial cropping is the other main drawback.

varieties.grow_notes: A good early-autumn eater for well-drained soil. Thin heavy crops to break the biennial habit and keep an eye out for canker.

varieties.name: Foxwhelp
varieties.history: One of the oldest named English cider apples, mentioned by John Evelyn in 1664 and long used to give strength to Herefordshire ciders. The tree throws sports readily, so several clones carry the name (Broxwood, Red, Black and Bulmer's Improved Foxwhelp); the unrelated 'Rejuvenated Foxwhelp' is a different apple. By the 1960s only a few very old trees of the original remained.

look.description: Small to medium, uneven, ridged fruit in deep crimson streaked with yellow; yellow flesh tinged red.

taste.summary: A classic bittersharp: high malic acid with marked tannin and plenty of sugar, giving a strong, rich, coloured juice for blending.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill in Sep-Oct

tree.notes: Upright tree with large, stout branches and distinctive curled, wavy leaves; prone to producing sports on single branches.

pollination.notes: Orange Pippin gives group 5 but treats the clones as one variety; plant with other cider apples.

climate.best_climates: The cool, moist cider country of Herefordshire, Gloucestershire and the Welsh Marches.
climate.poor_climates: Wet sites with heavy scab pressure; little known about hot climates.

health.other: Scab-prone; some susceptibility to canker.

varieties.grow_notes: Check which clone you are buying, as most trees sold as Foxwhelp today are Broxwood or Bulmer's selections. An early bittersharp, so press it with other early fruit or store briefly.

varieties.name: Foxwhelp (Broxwood)

origin.parentage: Thought to be a sport or close seedling of the ancient Foxwhelp; the exact relationship is not proven

varieties.history: A Herefordshire selection of Foxwhelp, the celebrated seventeenth-century West Midlands bittersharp. Several Foxwhelp clones exist; the Broxwood form is generally regarded as the most reliable and is the one most often propagated today.

look.description: Medium, somewhat uneven fruit with a dark crimson flush streaked over a yellow ground.

taste.summary: A powerful bittersharp: high acid and noticeable tannin give a rich, full-bodied, deeply coloured juice that ages well and lifts blends of softer bittersweets.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill late Sep-Oct.

tree.notes: Foxwhelp trees grow upright with stout branches and curled, wavy leaves; the Broxwood clone is reputed to crop more dependably than older Foxwhelp strains.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not reliably recorded; plant with other cider varieties.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist West Midlands and Welsh Marches cider country.
climate.poor_climates: Wet areas with high scab pressure; little documented about hot climates.

health.other: Foxwhelp types are known to be scab-prone.

varieties.grow_notes: An early bittersharp, so pair it with other early-season apples for pressing. Choose an airy site to keep scab down. Check the clone when buying, as 'Foxwhelp' covers several different trees.

varieties.name: Francis

origin.parentage: Seedling of Cox's Orange Pippin; pollen parent unknown

varieties.history: Raised in Essex by F.W. Thorrington from a Cox's Orange Pippin seedling and sent to the National Fruit Trials in 1925; the National Fruit Collection lists it as Francis (Thorrington). Thorrington also raised the Cox seedling Ruby.

look.description: Medium, truncated-conical fruit with a greenish-yellow ground striped and flushed dark red.

taste.summary: Firm, fine, crisp flesh with a very sweet and aromatic flavour in the Cox tradition.
taste.storage_change: Can become more complex in store (Apples & Orchards).

tree.notes: No growing data recorded.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not recorded; plant with a mid-season diploid partner.

climate.best_climates: The relatively dry, sunny south-east and east of England where it was raised.
climate.poor_climates: No records outside England; likely to share Cox's dislike of hot summers and very wet, cold sites.

health.other: Not recorded; as a Cox seedling it may share some of Cox's disease weaknesses, but this is unconfirmed.

varieties.grow_notes: A rare Essex Cox seedling for heritage collections. Give it a sunny, well-drained site and a mid-season pollinator, and store the fruit cool after a mid-October picking.

varieties.name: Freedom

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Macoun x Antonovka-derived selection (given simply as Macoun x Antonovka in some sources)
origin.raised_by: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: Bred at Geneva, New York from a 1958 cross and released in 1983 as a scab-resistant, hardy apple for home and low-spray growers. Its scab resistance is attributed to the Russian Antonovka side of its pedigree.

look.description: Medium-large to large fruit, striped and flushed red so the yellow ground barely shows.

taste.summary: Crisp, very juicy cream flesh with a sweet, sprightly sub-acid flavour that some liken to McIntosh; pleasant rather than intense. It softens and turns mealy soon after picking, so eat it quickly or use it for sauce, drying, juice and cider.

tree.notes: Large, spreading, productive tree that bears early and regularly.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 3; average pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter, humid regions such as New England, New York and the upper Midwest, where its hardiness and scab resistance count.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers give soft, poorly coloured fruit; not suited to low-chill climates.

health.other: Very resistant to scab; some resistance to mildew, fire blight and cedar-apple rust. A short keeper.

varieties.grow_notes: A robust, hardy choice for an unsprayed orchard; give it room or a moderately dwarfing rootstock. Use the fruit within a couple of months.

varieties.name: Freiherr von Berlepsch

origin.place: Grevenbroich, Lower Rhine (district of Düsseldorf), Germany
origin.parentage: Recorded as Ananas Reinette x Ribston Pippin; DNA evidence points to Danziger Kantapfel rather than Ribston as the second parent

varieties.history: Raised around 1880 by the nurseryman Diedrich Uhlhorn the younger and named after Hans Hermann Freiherr von Berlepsch, then head of the Düsseldorf administrative district. It is notable for its high vitamin C content and has been used as a parent in modern breeding.

look.description: Medium, roundish golden-yellow apple marbled and flushed with brownish red, dotted with fine brown lenticels; a redder sport exists.

taste.summary: Intensely flavoured: very juicy, firm, pale-yellow flesh with lively acidity balanced by plenty of sugar and a rich, aromatic finish. Keeps its quality for months in store.
taste.storage_change: keeps its quality for months in store (de Wikipedia)
taste.peak: early January to end of March (de Wikipedia)

climate_flavour.note: de Wikipedia: grows best in very mild sites (about the tree, not explicitly flavour)

tree.notes: Grows strongly when young and needs regular annual pruning to stay productive and open.

pollination.notes: Flowers late (late April to mid May in Germany). Ploidy not confirmed; plant with a late-flowering diploid partner.

climate.best_climates: Mild, warm temperate sites such as wine-growing districts of western and southern Germany, with warm, well-drained soil.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, wet, heavy soils and harsh sites, where canker, fruit rot and collar rot set in.

health.other: On unsuitable sites it suffers from canker, Monilia fruit rot and collar rot (Phytophthora).

varieties.grow_notes: Needs a warm, sheltered position on good soil; avoid cold heavy clay. Prune every year and pick late so the flavour can develop in store.

varieties.name: Frequin Rouge

origin.place: North-western France (old cider variety of Normandy and Brittany)

varieties.history: A long-established member of the French 'Fréquin' family of cider apples, widely planted in Normandy and Brittany for cider and Calvados. It has also been trialled in North American cider programmes.

look.description: Smallish cider apple with an orange-red to red flush, as the name suggests.

taste.summary: A strongly tannic French 'amère' (bitter) apple: very high tannin, low-to-moderate acid and plenty of sugar. Used for weight, colour and grip in cider and Calvados blends rather than on its own.
taste.peak: Early October on Salt Spring Island; press within a few weeks

tree.notes: Fairly large tree that is slow to start bearing; mature trees crop well but tend to alternate.

pollination.notes: Mid-to-late flowering; pair with other French bittersweets.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp Atlantic climates like Normandy, Brittany and south-west England.
climate.poor_climates: Humid sites with heavy disease pressure (scab, canker); hot dry summers untested.

health.other: Susceptible to scab and canker; slow to come into bearing.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant on a reasonably vigorous stock and be patient for the first crops. Thin in heavy years to steady the alternate cropping, and keep canker in check with clean pruning cuts.

varieties.name: Freyberg

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: Raised in 1934 by the amateur breeder J.H. Kidd at Greytown, who also bred Kidd's Orange Red and Gala. After Kidd's death his seedlings passed to New Zealand's DSIR, which released Freyberg in 1959 and named it after Lord Freyberg, then recently Governor-General.

look.description: Flattish, greenish-yellow to yellow apple with at most a faint orange cheek and light russet freckling.

taste.summary: Crisp but not hard, juicy pale flesh with a sweet, refreshing Golden Delicious base. Tasters disagree on the top notes: a pear-like note is the standard description, while others report aniseed or liquorice, banana, lemon or a honeyed finish. Leave it on the tree until it colours towards orange and store a few weeks for the fullest flavour; keeps well.

tree.notes: Weak-growing spur-bearer that crops heavily and regularly; suits small gardens but avoid very dwarfing stocks on poor soil.

pollination.notes: Group 3; partner with a group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Temperate climates with warm, sunny autumns such as New Zealand's North Island and southern England in good years.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons where the mid-October crop does not sweeten fully.

health.other: Some susceptibility to scab and fire blight; otherwise not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A good small-garden tree thanks to its modest vigour and reliable crops. Use a moderately vigorous rootstock on lighter soils and pick in mid-October once the ground colour turns yellow.

varieties.name: Frogmore Prolific

origin.place: The Royal Gardens, Frogmore, Windsor, England
origin.parentage: Possibly a Hawthornden seedling (Wikipedia list)

varieties.history: Raised around 1865 by Mr Ingram in the Royal Gardens at Frogmore, Windsor, as a heavy-cropping early cooking apple. It is now rarely grown.

look.description: Large, broad, truncated-conical greenish-yellow cooker streaked and lightly flushed with red.

taste.summary: Soft, fine-textured white flesh, acid and only moderately juicy, with little distinctive flavour according to Brogdale; a plain early cooking apple.
taste.peak: September-November (NFC, Wikipedia list).

tree.notes: USDA Geneva describes a weak, upright-spreading tree.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering at Brogdale (early May).

climate.best_climates: Southern English garden conditions.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No disease ratings found.

varieties.grow_notes: A historic Victorian kitchen-garden cooker; grow on a vigorous rootstock because the tree itself is weak.

varieties.name: Frostbite

origin.parentage: Reported as a seedling of Malinda

varieties.history: One of the University of Minnesota's oldest selections, kept for decades as MN 447 for breeding before release under the Frostbite name in 2008. It is a parent of Keepsake, which in turn is a parent of Honeycrisp.

look.description: Small to medium apple striped and flushed maroon-red over golden yellow.

taste.summary: Intensely sweet, dense and crunchy, with an unusual flavour tasters struggle to name; comparisons include cane sugar, molasses and caramel apple, with a little tartness behind it. Keeps one to two months and makes a rich, sweet juice or cider.
taste.storage_change: University of Minnesota: 3-4 months in refrigerated storage, though russet cracks can make stored fruit go mouldy. No flavour change reported.

tree.notes: Very hardy; grown mainly for its unusual flavour and for juice. Growth details are not well recorded.

pollination.notes: No UK flowering group recorded; needs a compatible pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cold northern climates such as Minnesota, Wisconsin and southern Canada, where it ripens in cool early autumn.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer and mild-winter regions, where it would lack chill and colour poorly.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity worth growing in cold gardens for its flavour and for blending into sweet juice. Give it full sun and a hardy pollinator.

varieties.name: Fuji

origin.place: Tohoku Research Station, Fujisaki, Aomori, Japan
origin.parentage: Ralls Janet x Red Delicious
origin.raised_by: Tohoku Research Station (Japanese Ministry of Agriculture)

varieties.history: Bred at a government research station in Fujisaki, Aomori, from a 1939 cross and released in 1962. It went on to become the most widely grown apple in the world, dominating production in China, and many better-coloured sports have been selected.

look.description: Large, rounded apple with a yellow-green ground streaked and mottled pinkish-red; colour varies widely between strains and climates.

taste.summary: Very dense, crisp and juicy flesh with high sugar and low acidity, giving a sweet, honeyed flavour; well-ripened fruit may show glassy watercore that tastes especially sweet. Keeps its texture for months.
taste.peak: Nov-Dec in the northern hemisphere (Orange Pippin); keeps very long (Wikipedia).

climate_flavour.note: Needs lots of sunshine to ripen properly (Orange Pippin); thrives with relatively warm summers (Wikipedia); often fails to mature fully in the UK (NFC).

tree.notes: Vigorous and productive but strongly biennial without early fruit thinning; branches spread under heavy crops.

pollination.notes: Usually placed in group 4 (some lists give 3); needs a group 3-5 diploid partner.

climate.best_climates: Long, warm-to-hot growing seasons with cool autumn nights, such as Washington State, northern China, Japan, Chile and New Zealand; moderate chill needs make it possible in milder-winter areas.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons like much of the UK, where the very late fruit often fails to ripen or sweeten fully; hot nights reduce red colour.

health.other: Very susceptible to fire blight and susceptible to scab; prone to sunburn and watercore in hot climates.

varieties.grow_notes: In Britain give it the warmest wall or most sheltered sunny spot available, and only expect good fruit in the south after long, warm autumns. Thin early and hard every year to prevent alternate bearing.

varieties.name: Gala

origin.parentage: Kidd's Orange Red x Golden Delicious

varieties.history: Raised by J.H. Kidd in Greytown, New Zealand in the 1930s; the seedling was later selected by Donald McKenzie and named Gala in the 1960s. It is now one of the most widely planted apples in the world, mostly as redder sports; Royal Gala is strictly one of those sports, though shops use the two names interchangeably.

look.description: Small-to-medium, neatly conical apple; golden-yellow streaked with orange-red in the original, solid red in most modern sports.

taste.summary: Crisp, fine, juicy cream flesh with a sweet, low-acid flavour. Freshly picked home-grown fruit has a surprisingly punchy sweetness with a pear-like note, while supermarket fruit is often bland or soft. Keeps for a few months but gradually loses its crunch.
taste.storage_change: Freshly picked fruit is punchier and pear-like (Orange Pippin); stored fruit tastes slightly less sweet than in-season fruit (Wikipedia).
taste.peak: Straight from the tree (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: Precocious and productive spur-bearer; sets heavily and needs thinning to keep fruit size.

pollination.notes: Group 4, partly self-fertile; crops much better with a group 3-5 diploid partner.

climate.best_climates: Warm, sunny temperate regions such as New Zealand, Washington State, Chile, South Africa and southern Europe, where it sweetens and colours well.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, damp maritime areas (much of the UK) give smaller, blander fruit and heavy canker; hot nights reduce red colour.

health.other: Susceptible to scab and fire blight, and very prone to canker in wet British soils.

varieties.grow_notes: Better suited to warm, dry gardens than wet western ones. Plant on free-draining soil, thin heavily in early summer, and cut out canker lesions promptly.

varieties.name: Gascoyne's Scarlet
varieties.history: Raised by a Mr Gascoyne at Bapchild Court near Sittingbourne and introduced in 1871 by G. Bunyard & Co. of Maidstone; it won an RHS First Class Certificate in 1887. Prized as a showy exhibition and dual-purpose apple, and its pink-tinged flesh gives a rosy juice.

look.description: Large, broad, slightly ribbed apple with a pale cream skin largely covered in pink to bright scarlet with a waxy bloom; flesh often pink just under the skin.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained, rather dry white flesh, sweet with only a light, faintly perfumed flavour; sharper at picking and mellower after storage. Grown more for looks, cooking and coloured juice than for depth of flavour.
taste.storage_change: Sharp when picked, mellows in storage (Wikipedia).

tree.notes: Growers report tip-bearing, which complicates spur pruning. Ploidy is reported inconsistently (some UK lists treat it as triploid, others as an ordinary pollinator).

pollination.notes: Group 4, needs a partner; until its ploidy is confirmed, do not rely on it as the only pollinator for another tree.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate south-east England; traditionally recommended for chalky soils like those of north Kent.
climate.poor_climates: Warm summers would likely spoil the scarlet colour; no record of success in hot regions.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A decorative heritage apple for Kentish-style chalk or loam soils. Prune as a tip-bearer and pick in late September for storing through to the new year.

varieties.name: Gavin

origin.place: John Innes Institute, Bayfordbury, Hertfordshire, England
origin.parentage: Derived from Merton Worcester crossed with scab-resistant crab-apple breeding lines; exact parentage not given in the sources checked

varieties.history: Raised in 1956 by A.G. Brown at the John Innes Institute, Bayfordbury, as one of the first British attempts to breed scab resistance from crab apples into a dessert apple. In looks and taste it resembles its Merton Worcester ancestry (Cox x Worcester Pearmain).

look.description: Small, light yellow apple with a strong red flush.

taste.summary: Firm rather than crunchy flesh with a delicate, aromatic balance of sweet and sharp that leans sweet; more complex than most early-autumn apples. Best within a week or so of picking and past its prime after about a month.
taste.peak: pick early October, use October to December (East of England Apples and Orchards Project)

tree.notes: Tends to make tall, thin, brittle branches that can snap under a crop; prune to build a sturdier framework. Attractive blossom.

pollination.notes: Listed by the RHS in group 3.

climate.best_climates: Wet, scab-prone British and north-west European gardens where its resistance pays off.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented in hot climates; small fruit and English parentage suggest it prefers cool summers.

health.other: Very resistant to scab; brittle wood is its main practical weakness.

varieties.grow_notes: A good low-spray apple for damp areas. Shorten and support long whippy branches so they do not break, and plant with a group 2-4 pollinator.

varieties.name: Geheimrat Dr. Oldenburg

origin.parentage: Recorded as Minister von Hammerstein x Baumanns Reinette; an SNP study instead points to Alexander x Ananas Reinette

varieties.history: Raised at Geisenheim in 1897 and first fruiting in 1904, it became an important parent in German breeding. Alkmene (Early Windsor), Roba, Clivia, Elektra and Apollo descend from it. Not to be confused with Duchess of Oldenburg.

look.description: Medium, tallish fruit, yellow-green to orange with a red flush and stripes on the sunny side. It is slightly ribbed at the eye and has almost no russet.

taste.summary: Loose-textured, juicy, fine-grained flesh with a delicate sweet-sharp balance. German sources call the flavour unusual, almost exotic. British records rate it simply subacid, with softish flesh.
taste.peak: October to December after a September harvest (de.wikipedia).

tree.notes: Forms a medium, airy crown. It starts cropping early and bears reasonably even on poor soil, though it does best with good soil and feeding. The fruit is easily blown off in wind.

pollination.notes: Flowers fairly early at Brogdale, a few days ahead of Wealthy; the group number is inferred from those dates.

climate.best_climates: Sheltered sites in temperate central Europe with good, well-fed soil.
climate.poor_climates: Exposed, windy sites (fruit drop) and poor, wet soils where canker takes hold.

health.other: Prone to canker on poor soils; fruit drops easily in wind.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a sheltered spot and fertile soil, and keep it fed so canker does not get established. Pick promptly in September before wind brings the fruit down.

varieties.name: Gennet Moyle

origin.place: Herefordshire and the Welsh Marches, England

varieties.history: One of the oldest named English cider apples: it was the favourite Herefordshire cider fruit before the Redstreak displaced it in the seventeenth century, and writers of the 1650s-1660s praised both its cider and its cooking. The name combines old words for a mule or hybrid and for a graft, and it was famously propagated by rooting branches cut below a burr knot.

look.description: Roundish, somewhat flattened, obtusely ribbed apple of clear lemon-yellow with a faint russety red cheek and fine russet lines; white to yellowish flesh.

taste.summary: Old descriptions agree on tender, rather dry flesh with a sweet, gently acid flavour and a fragrant scent when fully ripe; its cider was light and pleasant rather than strong. Modern cider-apple tables list it as a sharp or bittersharp, so its classification is unsettled.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Dec for baking and drying; mill soon after picking for a light early cider
taste.peak: Picked late September (NFC); good for baking and drying

tree.notes: Forms burr knots and can be rooted from cuttings, a trait shared with a few very old cider apples. Seventeenth-century growers expected it to fail every other year and found the blossom easily damaged by cold winds.

pollination.notes: Approximate group, from NFC flowering records (mid-season).

climate.best_climates: Drier, shallower soils of the Welsh border country; old writers found it at home even in poor hedgerow ground.
climate.poor_climates: Exposed, windy sites where blossom is damaged; untested in hot or very cold climates.

health.other: Disease record not documented; main recorded weakness is alternate cropping and wind-damaged blossom.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage tree for collectors: shelter it from cold spring winds and expect alternate-year crops. Use the fruit for baking and drying as well as a light cider.

varieties.name: George Cave
varieties.history: Raised in 1923 by George Cave at Dovercourt, near Harwich. The Essex nursery Seabrook & Sons took it up and named it after him in 1945; it remains one of the most reliable very early English eaters.

look.description: Medium, slightly ribbed apple, greenish-yellow with a bright red flush and stripes on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Juicy, fine-textured white flesh with a sharp but pleasant, zingy flavour, stronger than most early apples though without the aromatic depth of later ones. Crisp only on the day it is picked: it softens within hours and goes dry and mealy within days.
taste.best_eaten: Aug, on the day of picking
taste.storage_change: Softens within hours of picking and goes dry and mealy within days.
taste.peak: Straight from the tree in mid-August

tree.notes: Partly tip-bearing and a regular cropper; fruit drops quickly once ripe, so pick over several days.

pollination.notes: Early flowering (usually listed group 2, sometimes 3); partly self-fertile, with frost-tolerant blossom.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate Britain, including colder and more northerly gardens, since it ripens early and its blossom tolerates frost.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would make the quick-softening fruit go mealy even sooner.

health.other: No major weaknesses recorded and considered suitable for organic growing; main drawback is very short keeping and pre-harvest drop.

varieties.grow_notes: A good first apple of the season for a garden. Plant with another early-flowering variety and check the tree daily in August, as ripe fruit falls readily.

varieties.name: George Neal
varieties.history: Raised in 1904 by Mrs Reeves at Otford in Kent and introduced in 1923 by R. Neal & Sons of Wandsworth, London, receiving an RHS Award of Merit the same year.

look.description: Large, flat, ribbed apple, pale green-yellow with a light pinkish flush and stripes.

taste.summary: Rather soft, coarse, juicy greenish flesh with a clean acidity; cooks quickly, collapsing almost completely into a smooth purée.

tree.notes: Little modern growing data recorded.

pollination.notes: Among the earliest to flower in the National Fruit Collection records, consistent with group 2; pair with another early bloomer.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate south-east England, where it was raised.
climate.poor_climates: Early flowering makes it vulnerable in frost pockets; untested in hot climates.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: An early-season cooker for southern gardens. Avoid frost pockets because it blooms early, and use the fruit from August onwards for purées and sauces.

varieties.name: Gewürzluiken

origin.parentage: Chance seedling, parentage unknown

varieties.history: A chance seedling, probably from northern Württemberg, spread widely through the region from about 1885 and became one of its most planted apples alongside the Luikenapfel, with which it is often confused. It is used both as a table apple and for Most (cider/juice).

look.description: Medium to large apple almost covered in strong carmine to dark red, striped brownish red, over a yellow ground, with some russet.

taste.summary: Very juicy, firm white to greenish flesh with a tart, faintly spicy flavour (the name means 'spice Luiken'); Brogdale and USDA Geneva describe it as sweet and subacid. Fruit from cold sites stays poorly coloured and tastes grassy.
taste.peak: November-March (de.wikipedia); NFC store December-March.

climate_flavour.note: de.wikipedia: plant only in warmer sites; in cold sites the fruit does not ripen or colour and tastes grassy.

tree.notes: Wood is susceptible to winter frost damage; plant only in warm sites.

pollination.notes: Flowers fairly late at Brogdale (around 11 May).

climate.best_climates: Warm, sheltered sites in south-west German valleys with long autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, high or frosty sites: the wood suffers winter frost damage and the fruit fails to colour or ripen, tasting grassy.

health.other: Susceptible to winter wood-frost damage.

varieties.grow_notes: Choose a warm, sunny position with a long season; it needs time to colour and develop flavour. Store the fruit until winter before eating.

varieties.name: Ginger Gold

origin.parentage: Chance seedling, probably Golden Delicious x Albemarle Pippin (or another pollen parent)

varieties.history: Found as a seedling in a Virginia orchard that was being replanted after Hurricane Camille in 1969, and named after Frances 'Ginger' Harvey. It became one of the main early-season commercial apples in the eastern USA from the 1980s.

look.description: Large, conical, waxy fruit, pale green ripening to soft yellow, with a long stalk like Golden Delicious.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy cream flesh with a mild flavour, sweeter than tart but a little sharper than Golden Delicious. Slices brown slowly and hold their shape when cooked.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-Sep; keeps several weeks in a fridge

tree.notes: Vigorous to average vigour, precocious and regular. An unusually good keeper for an early apple.

pollination.notes: Group 4 per Orange Pippin.

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer temperate regions such as Virginia and the Carolinas, where it ripens in July-August; also grown in Ontario and Quebec.
climate.poor_climates: Humid areas with heavy fire blight, mildew or cedar-apple rust pressure.

health.other: Susceptible to fire blight and powdery mildew; very susceptible to cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: A good early apple for warmer gardens; pick as soon as the ground colour turns yellow. Watch for mildew and fire blight and avoid planting near junipers where cedar-apple rust occurs.

varieties.name: Gladstone

origin.place: Worcestershire, England (rediscovered at Blakedown Nursery, Kidderminster)

varieties.history: Thought to date from around 1780; it was rediscovered by Mr Jackson of Blakedown Nursery near Kidderminster and sold from 1868 as 'Jackson's Seedling'. After an RHS First Class Certificate in 1883 it was renamed in honour of the Prime Minister W. E. Gladstone.

look.description: Conical, somewhat ribbed apple, mostly covered with a dark red flush and stripes over greenish yellow.

taste.summary: Crisp and juicy when just picked, with a sweet, pleasantly aromatic flavour, but it turns soft and slightly floury within a few days.
taste.best_eaten: late Jul-Aug, straight from the tree
taste.storage_change: Crisp and juicy at first but soon goes soft (NFC); keeps only 1-3 days (Orange Pippin).
taste.peak: Early August, straight from the tree.

tree.notes: Fairly vigorous, partly tip-bearing tree that starts cropping young and bears heavily and regularly.

pollination.notes: Listed in group 4 and partly self-fertile; blossom has some frost resistance.

climate.best_climates: Cool, mild, damp temperate climates such as the English Midlands and west.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would make the very early, quick-softening fruit mealy almost at once.

health.other: Reported to be very resistant to scab and canker; its weakness is that the fruit keeps only a few days.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the earliest English eating apples, best for gardeners who will eat it straight off the tree. Pick little and often as the fruit colours, as it does not keep.

varieties.name: Glockenapfel

origin.place: Uncertain: usually linked to Switzerland, possibly southern Germany or the Altes Land on the lower Elbe

varieties.history: A chance seedling that appeared around the middle of the 19th century; Switzerland, southern Germany and the Altes Land fruit district near Hamburg are all suggested as its birthplace. Named for its tall bell shape, it became an important late-keeping apple in Switzerland and northern Germany and is a traditional choice for strudel.

look.description: Tall, bell-shaped, ribbed fruit with a smooth greenish-yellow skin, dark dots and sometimes a faint orange-red cheek.

taste.summary: Very firm, pale flesh, not very juicy, with pronounced, slightly harsh acidity and a strong aroma. Picked in October but not ready to eat until about December, and keeps around six months; it barely breaks down when cooked, making it a classic strudel and pie apple. One grower found it mild and only lightly sweet.
taste.peak: Picked October, ready to eat from December; keeps in cold store until June (de/en Wikipedia)

climate_flavour.note: German Wikipedia: good fruit quality depends on crop load and a mild climate.

tree.notes: Vigorous when young, settling to moderate growth with a characteristic drooping habit; branches tend to become bare inside, so regular renewal pruning helps. Standard trees tend to alternate, and young wood can be frost-damaged after a heavy crop.

pollination.notes: Flowers fairly early (well before Cox at Brogdale). Described in German sources as partly self-fertile and a good pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist fruit districts of Switzerland, southern and northern Germany with a long growing season and fertile soil.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, exposed sites where wood is frost-damaged, and dry or poor soils that reduce fruit quality.

health.other: Low scab susceptibility but occasionally cankers; prone to bare wood and to frost damage in young shoots after heavy crops.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a warm, sheltered spot on moist, fertile soil and thin the crop to reduce alternate bearing. Pick in mid October and store cold; it is one of the longest-keeping cooking apples.

varieties.name: Gloria Mundi
varieties.history: A giant cooking apple first recorded in the USA in 1804, thought to have been raised in New York though a German origin has also been suggested. Its many names overlap with other huge apples: the National Fruit Collection lists Mère de Ménage as a synonym and vice versa, but the two are held as separate accessions and Bunyard considered them distinct. 'Pound' is also used for other big apples, including Fallawater.

look.description: Very large, broad, ribbed green-yellow apple, sometimes with a faint bronze blush.

taste.summary: Rather soft, coarse, yellowish to greenish flesh with a mild subacid flavour, somewhat dry; valued for size and cooking rather than taste.
taste.peak: NFC store December-March; Wikipedia list uses October-December.

tree.notes: Vigorous, spreading tree that USDA Geneva rates as unproductive; the heavy fruit needs a sheltered site.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering at Brogdale (early May).

climate.best_climates: Sheltered temperate gardens in eastern North America and southern England.
climate.poor_climates: Windy sites, where the huge fruit is blown down (inferred).

health.other: No disease ratings found; poor cropping is the main recorded fault.

varieties.grow_notes: Grown as a curiosity for its enormous fruit. Plant on a sheltered site and thin to single fruits per cluster so they reach full size.

varieties.name: Gloster

origin.place: Obstbauversuchsanstalt Jork, Altes Land, near Hamburg, Germany
origin.parentage: Glockenapfel (Weisser Winterglockenapfel) x Richared Delicious

varieties.history: Crossed in 1951 at the fruit research station at Jork in the Altes Land fruit region near Hamburg and released in 1969, hence the alternative name Gloster 69. It was planted commercially in northern Germany and the Low Countries as a long-keeping red apple.

look.description: Tall, bell-shaped fruit with Delicious-like bumps at the eye, almost wholly covered in dark purplish red with prominent lenticels.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp and juicy greenish-cream flesh with a fairly sharp flavour, tarter than Delicious, finishing with a hint of honey according to one grower. Hangs well on the tree, keeps its crunch for months and mellows slightly in store.
taste.storage_change: Hangs on the tree into winter (Orange Pippin); prone to core rot if stored too long (de.wikipedia).

tree.notes: Undemanding but needs deep soil for good yields. Fruit hangs firmly and resists wind; wood and blossom show little frost damage.

pollination.notes: German sources give early-to-mid May flowering; no UK flowering group found. Plant with a mid-season partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool northern European lowlands such as the Altes Land and the Low Countries, where it colours well and stores into spring.
climate.poor_climates: Areas with fire blight or cedar-apple rust pressure (much of the eastern US) need regular control; probably less well coloured in warm-night climates.

health.other: Susceptible to fire blight and cedar-apple rust; moderately to highly scab-prone; long-stored fruit can develop core rot.

varieties.grow_notes: Best on deep, moisture-retentive soil in an open site. Pick at full colour in October and store cool; watch for scab in wet springs.

varieties.name: Golden Bounty

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Emneth Early (Early Victoria)

varieties.history: Raised around 1940 by A.C. Nash at Scutes Farm, Hastings, from Cox crossed with the early cooker Emneth Early. A Sussex local variety now kept in the National Fruit Collection and the Brighton Permaculture Trust's Sussex collection at Stanmer Park.

look.description: Yellow apple marked with fine, broken orange and red stripes and a little russet.

taste.summary: Firm, fine, crisp flesh with a rich, brisk, sharply aromatic flavour that recalls an early-season Cox with extra acidity.
taste.peak: picked mid September (NFC)

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous and heavy-cropping; other habits not recorded.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from Brogdale flowering records, which match Cox.

climate.best_climates: South-east England and similar mild temperate climates.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented beyond southern England; estimates are inferred from its parents.

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A Sussex heritage apple for a sunny southern garden. Pick in mid-September, eat within a few weeks, and pair with a group 2-4 pollinator.

varieties.name: Golden Delicious

origin.place: Anderson Mullins farm, Clay County, West Virginia
origin.parentage: Chance seedling; often said to be Grimes Golden x Golden Reinette, but unproven
origin.raised_by: Found by Anderson Mullins; introduced by Stark Bros

varieties.history: A chance seedling that appeared on the Mullins family farm in West Virginia around the 1890s. Stark Bros Nurseries bought the tree in 1914 and launched it in 1916; it became one of the world's most planted apples and a parent of Gala, Jonagold, Elstar, Mutsu and many others.

look.description: Long-stalked, slightly conical apple, green-yellow ripening to clear golden-yellow, sometimes with a faint pink cheek; prone to fine russet netting in damp climates.

taste.summary: Left to ripen to golden-green on the tree it is crisp, juicy and richly sweet, with a honeyed, pear-drop note and only modest acidity; a few tasters also pick up a faint ginger or cinnamon warmth. Fruit picked green and held in long storage is the bland, soft, crumbly supermarket apple. Holds its shape when cooked.
taste.storage_change: Fruit picked green and stored for months (supermarket fruit) loses flavour; the true flavour shows only when ripened golden-green on the tree (Orange Pippin, Trees of Antiquity, Chris Bowers)
taste.peak: Ripened on the tree to golden-green; picked early to late October

climate_flavour.note: Chris Bowers: needs higher temperature and light intensity, not successful everywhere in the UK; Orange Pippin: grows well in the UK given a warm, sheltered microclimate

tree.notes: Easy, precocious spur-bearer with wide-angled branches; crops heavily and needs thinning to keep fruit size and annual bearing.

pollination.notes: Group 4, partly self-fertile, and an excellent pollen donor for other diploids.

climate.best_climates: Warm, sunny temperate climates with long seasons (Washington, northern Italy, southern France, Chile), where it ripens to a rich golden colour.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, damp regions such as much of Britain give greener, blander fruit with skin russet; very humid areas bring heavy scab and rust.

health.other: Susceptible to scab, powdery mildew and cedar-apple rust; skin bruises and shrivels easily, and damp springs cause russeting.

varieties.grow_notes: Reliable and productive, but in Britain it needs a warm, sunny site to taste good. Thin crops, pick only when the ground colour turns yellow, and store in plastic bags in a cold place to limit shrivelling.

varieties.name: Golden Delicious Russet

origin.parentage: Presumed russeted sport or selection of Golden Delicious (not verified)

varieties.history: No independent pomological record of this name was found. The name points to a russet-skinned form of Golden Delicious; several russeted sports of Golden Delicious are known (for example Razor Russet from Kentucky), but which one is sold under this name could not be confirmed. Values below assume it behaves like Golden Delicious.

look.description: Golden Delicious-shaped yellow apple with extensive brownish russet over the skin (extent unverified).

taste.summary: Expected to taste like Golden Delicious: sweet, honeyed and low in acid, with the slightly richer, drier mouthfeel that russeted skin often brings. Not independently described.

tree.notes: Assumed to grow like Golden Delicious: precocious, heavy-cropping spur-bearer.

pollination.notes: Golden Delicious is group 4 and partly self-fertile; assumed the same.

climate.best_climates: If it is a Golden Delicious sport, warm temperate regions with long sunny autumns suit it best.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, short British seasons can leave late Golden Delicious types under-ripe and bland.

health.other: Not recorded for this name; Golden Delicious itself is prone to scab, mildew and cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: Treat as Golden Delicious: a warm, sunny site and a long season help, and it is a useful group 4 pollinator. Check the supplier's description of origin before relying on these assumed traits.

varieties.name: Golden Harvey
varieties.history: An old Herefordshire russet thought to date from the 1600s. Its very sugary juice made a strong cider, hence the old name Brandy Apple, and it was also valued as a small, rich dessert apple.

look.description: Small, rounded fruit almost covered with rough golden-brown russet, sometimes with a faint orange-red flush.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp yellow flesh with an intense, sweet yet sharp, rich and aromatic flavour. Its high sugar gives a strong cider.

tree.notes: Vigorous and slow to start bearing.

pollination.notes: Group 3 per Orange Pippin.

climate.best_climates: West of England cider country and similar mild temperate climates.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Rated average for disease resistance; specific weaknesses not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A vigorous tree that takes a few years to crop, so a dwarfing rootstock helps in gardens. Leave the fruit until mid October and store before eating or pressing.

varieties.name: Golden Hornet

origin.parentage: Unknown; usually grouped under Malus x zumi

varieties.history: Introduced around the late 1940s by the Waterer nursery firm in southern England. It became one of Britain's most widely planted ornamental crabs and orchard pollinators; it held the RHS Award of Garden Merit until 2013.

look.description: Small egg- to cone-shaped fruits about 2-2.5 cm, ripening clear golden-yellow and packed thickly along the branches, where they hang on into early winter.

taste.summary: Sharp and somewhat astringent raw with little flavour of its own. Used mainly as a pectin-rich base for jelly, which comes out golden rather than red.

tree.notes: Upright when young, opening out and getting a little straggly with age; about 3-5 m after ten years on a semi-vigorous stock. Heavy crops can weigh branches down.

pollination.notes: White blossom from pink-tinged buds. Nursery sources place it anywhere in groups 3-5, so it overlaps most mid- and late-flowering apples and is a standard pollinator in British orchards.

climate.best_climates: Mild temperate maritime climates such as the UK and north-west Europe, where the yellow fruit display lasts well into winter.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, humid districts encourage scab; warm, humid summers raise the risk of fire blight.

health.other: Some scab in wet seasons and some susceptibility to fire blight where that disease occurs. Lost its RHS Award of Garden Merit in 2013.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a sunny, open spot so the foliage dries quickly and scab stays down. Pick fruit for jelly before it starts to fall, and plant it near mid- or late-flowering apples to earn its keep as a pollinator.

varieties.name: Golden Knob
varieties.history: An old English apple that the National Fruit Collection traces to Enmore Castle in Somerset, in cultivation since the late 1700s. The synonym Kentish Golden Knob points to its later popularity in Kent; a different, unrelated 'Golden Knob' from Berkshire is also recorded.
