varieties.grow_notes: Mostly of historical and breeding interest. Pick in mid-October and store; it suits people who want a very sweet, low-acid apple.

varieties.name: Ingol

origin.place: Obstbauversuchsanstalt Jork, Altes Land, near Hamburg
origin.parentage: Ingrid Marie x Golden Delicious

varieties.history: Crossed in 1954 at the Jork fruit research station in the Altes Land near Hamburg. Its parentage, Ingrid Marie x Golden Delicious, is the same as that of the Dutch Elstar.

look.description: Big, flattish round apple, greenish yellow with a strong red flush and stripes on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Soft, juicy, rather crumbly white flesh with a balanced sweet-sharp flavour; one source calls it pleasantly tart, the National Fruit Collection panel found it only moderately acid with little aroma.
taste.peak: Ready to eat from early October to February (plantura).

tree.notes: National Fruit Collection trees have a drooping habit; little else recorded.

pollination.notes: Late blossom at the National Fruit Collection (about group 5).

climate.best_climates: Raised for the maritime fruit district of northern Germany.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance in hot or very cold regions.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: A large-fruited German dessert apple of the Elstar family. Flowers late, so pair it with another late-blossoming variety.

varieties.name: Ingrid Marie

origin.parentage: Chance seedling; a 2011 DNA study gives Cox's Orange Pippin x Cox's Pomona

varieties.history: A chance seedling found around 1910 in the grounds of a school on Funen and named after the finder's daughter, who died young. Sold in Denmark from 1936 and Sweden from 1946, it became a mainstay of Scandinavian orchards and a parent of Elstar and the Swedish Aroma.

look.description: Round to slightly flattened apple, marbled dark red over most of a yellow-green skin, sprinkled with pale brown lenticels; red often stains the flesh just under the skin.

taste.summary: Tender, juicy, yellowish-white flesh with a fresh sweet-tart balance; Scandinavian sources praise its pleasant aroma and one taster finds a hint of Cox, but Orange Pippin rates the flavour light and rather bland. Best soon after picking, though it can be stored into the new year; a traditional Christmas apple in Scandinavia.
taste.peak: Ripe mid to late September, stores to about January (de.wikipedia); Orange Pippin says best straight from the tree

climate_flavour.note: de.wikipedia: suited mainly to not-too-warm, rather moist sites (site advice)

tree.notes: Grows well in moderately warm, humid climates; avoid poorly drained ground where canker takes hold.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering, assigned to UK group 3 approximately; pollinated by Cox-season diploids.

climate.best_climates: Mild maritime Scandinavia (Denmark, southern Sweden) and similar cool, humid climates such as the UK.
climate.poor_climates: Cold inland areas beyond southern Swedish zones; hot summers are likely to spoil colour and texture.

health.other: Fruit-tree canker is the main weakness, especially on heavy, wet soils.

varieties.grow_notes: Choose a well-drained site and cut out canker promptly. Pair with another mid-season diploid such as Cox or James Grieve.

varieties.name: Irish Peach
varieties.history: An old Irish apple, probably from County Sligo, that reached English nurseries around 1820. Victorian gardeners rated it one of the best-flavoured very early apples, and it has been widely grown across Europe under many translated names.

look.description: Smallish to medium, slightly ribbed round-conical apple, green-yellow with a dull orange-red flush and streaks on the sunny side.

taste.summary: White, very juicy flesh that is soft rather than crisp, with a lively, rather sharp flavour and a distinct peach-like aroma that gives the variety its name. It does not keep: eat within days of picking.
taste.best_eaten: Early-mid Aug, straight from the tree
taste.storage_change: Does not keep.
taste.peak: Mid-August, straight from the tree

tree.notes: A tip-bearer with a spreading, flat-topped habit; unsuitable for cordons or espaliers. Prune lightly, renewing old wood rather than shortening every shoot. Fruit drops when ripe.

pollination.notes: Early-flowering (group 2); needs another early or early-mid season diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist maritime climates such as Ireland, western Britain and Scandinavia, where it ripens slowly enough to keep its flavour.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers make the fruit ripen and soften almost overnight; early blossom is vulnerable in frost pockets.

health.other: Generally healthy. Weaknesses are practical: tip-bearing habit, fruit drop and virtually no keeping life.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for wetter western and northern gardens. Grow as a bush or half-standard rather than a trained form, and visit the tree daily in August as the fruit ripens.

varieties.name: Jamba 69

origin.place: Obstbauversuchsanstalt Jork, Altes Land, near Hamburg
origin.parentage: Melba x James Grieve

varieties.history: Crossed in 1954 by Dr E. Loewel at the Jork fruit research station in the Altes Land and released in 1969, hence the number in its name.

look.description: Tall-round, slightly angular apple, green to yellow-green with a bright red wash and stripes on the sunny side; the skin turns waxy.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy, greenish-white flesh with a lively, fairly sharp and aromatic flavour balanced by good sweetness. An early apple that does not keep long.
taste.peak: Picked mid-August to September in Germany, keeps until October (de.wikipedia).

tree.notes: Medium-sized tree that grows strongly when young and calms down once in full cropping.

pollination.notes: National Fruit Collection blossom dates are mid-season (about group 3-4).

climate.best_climates: Mild, sunny sites in northern European fruit districts.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, exposed sites; no documented performance in hot climates.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: An early-season German dessert apple for a warm, sunny spot. Pick in late August to early September and eat within a few weeks.

varieties.name: James Grieve

origin.parentage: Seedling of Pott's Seedling or Cox's Orange Pippin; pollen parent unknown

varieties.history: Raised in Edinburgh by James Grieve and introduced by his employers, the Dicksons nursery, being first recorded in 1893; it won an RHS Award of Merit in 1897 and a First Class Certificate in 1906. It became a favourite in northern Europe and is a parent of Katy, Lord Lambourne, Greensleeves and Elton Beauty.

look.description: Pale yellow apple flushed and broken-striped with red, with a faint satiny sheen.

taste.summary: Exceptionally juicy, soft, open-textured flesh with a bright, tangy acidity when first picked, good for cooking as well as eating. After a week or two it mellows to a sweeter, gentler apple.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct; sharp and good for cooking when first picked, sweeter after a couple of weeks
taste.storage_change: Sharp and refreshing when picked in early-mid September (good for cooking); after a few weeks it sweetens and becomes quite mild, and the flesh softens.
taste.peak: Sep: sharp at picking, sweeter and milder a few weeks later

tree.notes: Compact-to-moderate spur-bearer that crops early and regularly; adapts well to trained forms. The fruit bruises at a touch and may drop when ripe, so pick carefully over several passes.

pollination.notes: Partly self-fertile and an excellent pollinator for other group 2-4 diploids.

climate.best_climates: Cool, short-summer climates: Scotland, northern England, Germany and Scandinavia, where it crops reliably and keeps its zesty acidity.
climate.poor_climates: Warm wet lowlands encourage canker, and hot summers give soft, quickly-mealy fruit with poor colour.

health.other: Prone to canker on wet, heavy or poorly drained soils; some scab in damp seasons. The fruit bruises very easily.

varieties.grow_notes: A dependable choice for colder and northern gardens and a useful pollinator. Plant on free-draining soil to limit canker, cut out cankered wood promptly, and pick early for cooking or later for dessert.

varieties.name: Jazz

origin.place: Havelock North, Hawke's Bay, New Zealand
origin.parentage: Royal Gala x Braeburn
origin.raised_by: HortResearch (now Plant & Food Research), with ENZA

varieties.history: Bred in Hawke's Bay by the New Zealand government research institute now called Plant & Food Research, from a 1985 Royal Gala x Braeburn cross, and launched commercially in the early 2000s. Jazz is the trademark; the cultivar name is Scifresh, and it is grown only under licence in both hemispheres, including in Kent.

look.description: Medium, slightly conical fruit flushed red to maroon over green-yellow and orange, with fine pale lenticels.

taste.summary: A very hard, dense, crunchy apple with juicy butter-yellow flesh and a strong sweet-sharp flavour led by a pronounced pear-drop note; tasters also report floral, honeyed and occasionally banana or clove hints. Well-coloured fruit tastes best - poorly coloured apples are flatter and closer to Braeburn - and the firmness holds for months in store.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Mar; keeps its crunch well in store
taste.peak: Northern-hemisphere fruit in shops Nov-Dec (Orange Pippin).

climate_flavour.note: Orange Pippin: good red colour is key to the Jazz flavour; poorly coloured fruit tastes like Braeburn.

tree.notes: Average vigour, spur-bearing. A licensed club variety: trees are generally only available to contracted commercial growers, so garden plantings are rare. Needs good light into the canopy for colour.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 3; needs a compatible diploid pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Sunny regions with a long growing season and cool autumn nights, such as Hawke's Bay, Washington, the Western Cape, north Italy and the warmer fruit areas of southern England.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons leave it under-ripe and poorly coloured, which costs it most of its flavour; very hot autumns also limit colour.

health.other: Disease ratings are not well published; both parents (Gala and Braeburn) are prone to European canker and fire blight, and Braeburn to bitter pit, so treat Jazz as at risk of these.

varieties.grow_notes: Only practical where the season is long enough for a late-October harvest with good colour. Grow in full sun with open pruning so light reaches the fruit, and thin early. Pollinate with a group 2-4 diploid.

varieties.name: Jefferis

origin.place: Newlin Township, Chester County, Pennsylvania, USA

varieties.history: A seedling raised by Isaac Jefferis in Chester County, Pennsylvania, around 1830 and named by the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society, which brought it to notice in 1848. It was long regarded as one of the best early-autumn dessert apples of the eastern USA.

look.description: Medium, flattish, thin-skinned fruit, light red with darker red stripes over greenish yellow; skin rather greasy.

taste.summary: Juicy flesh that is crisp yet melting, with a rich, sweetish, mildly acid flavour that recalls pear. An aromatic early-autumn dessert apple.

tree.notes: Bears on spurs and partly at shoot tips; little else recorded.

pollination.notes: No published group found; estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates.

climate.best_climates: Mid-Atlantic US climates like its Pennsylvania home.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded. Thin skin marks easily.

varieties.grow_notes: A partial tip-bearer, so prune lightly and renew rather than spur back hard. Eat soon after picking in September.

varieties.name: Jelly King
varieties.history: A New Zealand crab of the late twentieth century, registered as 'Mattfru' and sold as Jelly King. As the name says, it was selected for jelly-making, with unusually large fruit for a crab, and it holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Large for a crab apple; yellow flushed orange-pink to red, and the fruit persists on the tree after ripening.

taste.summary: Sharp and juicy, rated very good for the kitchen; it makes a well-coloured, well-set jelly and the large fruit is quicker to prepare than tiny crabs.

tree.notes: Vigorous, upright tree that crops heavily; suitable for organic growing and beginners.

pollination.notes: Pale pink buds opening to white blossom; a good pollinator for mid-season apples.

climate.best_climates: Cool to warm temperate climates such as the UK and New Zealand.
climate.poor_climates: Not well documented; rated hardy to about -20 C, so very severe winters may be a limit.

health.other: Rated good overall disease resistance by nursery sources.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in sun on any well-drained soil and give it room, as it is more vigorous than most garden crabs. Pick in late September for jelly; a useful mid-season pollinator.

varieties.name: Jersey Black
varieties.history: An old American apple believed to come from New Jersey and recorded by 1817, once used for cider as well as eating. It is best known today as the second parent, with McIntosh, of Macoun.

look.description: Flattish, ribbed apple almost covered in a very dark brownish to blackish red flush with light russet dots.

taste.summary: Sweet, white, rather coarse flesh, sometimes stained red, with mild acidity and a moderate aroma. Firm when picked but softens in store.

tree.notes: Tree details not well documented; National Fruit Collection trees are spreading to drooping.

pollination.notes: National Fruit Collection blossom dates are mid-season (about group 3).

climate.best_climates: The north-eastern United States and similar climates with warm summers and cold winters; also grown on the coast of British Columbia.
climate.poor_climates: Not well documented outside North America.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: Grown now mostly for its striking near-black colour and its place in Macoun's ancestry. Pick in October; it keeps a couple of months and suits cider blends as well as the fruit bowl.

varieties.name: Jerseymac

origin.place: Rutgers University (New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station), New Brunswick, New Jersey
origin.parentage: N.J. 24 x Julyred
origin.raised_by: Rutgers University / New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: Crossed at Rutgers in 1956, selected in 1961 and released in 1971-72 as an early-summer apple of McIntosh type.

look.description: Red apple, washed rather than striped, with greenish-yellow patches showing through.

taste.summary: Tender, juicy, white flesh with a tart-sweet, McIntosh-like aromatic flavour; crisp when just picked but it softens and does not keep.
taste.storage_change: Does not store well (Orange Pippin).
taste.peak: Eat in August, straight from the tree (Wikipedia list).

tree.notes: Heavy-cropping; flowers very early.

pollination.notes: Among the earliest-blossoming apples at the National Fruit Collection (group 1-2), so it needs an early-flowering partner.

climate.best_climates: Raised for New Jersey's warm-summer climate as an early market apple.
climate.poor_climates: Its very early blossom is at risk in frost-prone sites.

health.other: Reported as very resistant to cedar-apple rust; poor keeping quality.

varieties.grow_notes: An early red eating apple best enjoyed from the tree. Avoid frost pockets because it flowers very early, and pair it with another early-blossoming variety.

varieties.name: Jester

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Kent, England
origin.parentage: Worcester Pearmain x Starkspur Golden Delicious
origin.raised_by: Dr F.H. Alston, East Malling Research Station

varieties.history: Raised by Frank Alston at East Malling in 1966 and released in 1981 as a well-coloured, heavy-cropping modern garden apple. It never became a major commercial variety.

look.description: Smooth, attractive apple with a creamy-yellow ground, flushed and streaked bright red; skin becomes greasy in store.

taste.summary: Crisp to softish, very juicy white flesh with a sweet, light flavour and little sharpness. Pleasant and refreshing rather than complex, and popular with children.

tree.notes: Regular, heavy and early cropper of average vigour; straightforward to prune as a spur-bearer.

pollination.notes: Fairly late flowering, which helps it avoid frost; plant with a group 3-5 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp temperate climates like southern England, where it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: Little grown outside Britain; hot summers likely give soft fruit and poorer colour.

health.other: Reported as having average all-round disease resistance; good blossom frost tolerance.

varieties.grow_notes: An easy, reliable garden apple for southern Britain, good for a family wanting sweet, colourful fruit. Grow on a dwarfing rootstock as a bush or cordon and thin in heavy years.

varieties.name: John Downie
varieties.history: Raised in the 1870s by the Lichfield nurseryman Edward Holmes and named after his fellow nurseryman John Downie. It has long been considered the finest British crab for jelly and is one of the few crabs worth eating raw.

look.description: A comparatively large crab, roughly 3 cm, shaped like an upturned pear; yellow to orange with a bright scarlet flush on the sunny side and a glossy finish.

taste.summary: Sharp, tangy and juicy with more real apple flavour than most crabs, so acid-lovers can eat it straight from the tree. Its fame rests on jelly, which is richly flavoured and a pretty amber-pink to orange-red.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct, for jelly; raw once fully coloured
taste.storage_change: keeps about a month in cold storage (Pomiferous)

tree.notes: Narrow and upright when young, broadening later, so it fits smaller gardens than most crabs (3-5 m after ten years on a semi-vigorous stock). Fruit does not hang as long as the persistent ornamental crabs.

pollination.notes: Generous white blossom from pink buds; a popular pollinator for mid-season apples. UK sources list it in group 3 or 4.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate gardens in Britain and northern Europe on fertile, well-drained soil with good air movement.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, humid areas where scab can disfigure and partly defoliate it; humid summer heat brings fire blight risk.

health.other: Rather prone to apple scab, which can mark the fruit and drop leaves early in wet years, though the crop is still fine for jelly. Formerly held the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

varieties.grow_notes: Site it in sun with free air circulation and clear fallen leaves in autumn to reduce scab. Pick for jelly as soon as the fruit colours, before it drops, and use it as a pollinator for mid-season dessert apples.

varieties.name: John Standish
varieties.history: Thought to have been raised by the nurseryman John Standish at Ascot around 1873 and introduced by Isaac House in 1921; it gained an RHS Award of Merit in 1922. It is the seed parent of the apple Eden.

look.description: Neat, flat-round apple heavily flushed and striped bright red over pale yellow.

taste.summary: Very firm, fine-grained, juicy flesh with a refreshing, moderately sharp flavour and middling aroma.

tree.notes: Tree details not documented; National Fruit Collection trees are spreading to drooping.

pollination.notes: National Fruit Collection blossom dates are mid-season (about group 3).

climate.best_climates: Southern England, where it was raised.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance outside Britain.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: A good-looking late dessert apple for English gardens. Pick in mid October and store until midwinter.

varieties.name: Jonadel

origin.place: Iowa Agricultural Experiment Station, Ames, Iowa, USA
origin.parentage: Jonathan x Delicious
origin.raised_by: H. L. Lantz, Iowa Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: Crossed in 1923 by H. L. Lantz at the Iowa station from Jonathan and Delicious, but not introduced until 1958. It never became widely grown.

look.description: Medium, rather tall fruit with orange-red streaks over greenish yellow and a little russet.

taste.summary: Firm yet tender, fine-grained yellowish-white flesh with a sweet, gently acid and slightly rich flavour.

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not well recorded.

pollination.notes: No published group found; estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates, which are a few days later than average.

climate.best_climates: Raised for the cold-winter, warm-summer Midwest of the USA.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded in the sources used.

varieties.grow_notes: A collector's apple; treat it like Jonathan, with a sunny site and a mid-season pollination partner.

varieties.name: Jonafree

origin.place: PRI co-operative breeding programme (Purdue, Rutgers and Illinois universities), USA
origin.parentage: Complex (PRI 855-102 x NJ 31); ancestry includes Crandall's Rome x Malus floribunda 821, Jonathan, Gallia Beauty, Red Spy and Golden Delicious

varieties.history: A scab-resistant apple from the PRI co-operative programme, which bred the floribunda scab-resistance gene into dessert apples. It was selected in the 1960s and released in 1979 as Co-op 22.

look.description: Medium, rounded fruit almost entirely covered with a bright red flush.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy flesh with a Jonathan-style flavour but noticeably less acid than Jonathan.
taste.peak: Keeps about 10 weeks (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Tree habit not well recorded.

pollination.notes: Early-flowering: Orange Pippin lists group 1 and National Fruit Collection dates are among the earliest; group 2 used as a compromise.

climate.best_climates: Humid eastern and midwestern US climates where scab pressure is high and a spray-free apple is wanted.
climate.poor_climates: Areas with heavy cedar-apple rust, to which it is susceptible.

health.other: Carries the Vf scab-resistance gene; rated susceptible to cedar-apple rust in Arkansas trials.

varieties.grow_notes: Good for low-spray gardens because of its scab resistance, but keep it away from junipers where cedar-apple rust occurs. Needs an early-flowering pollinator.

varieties.name: Jonagold

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Jonathan
origin.raised_by: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station (Cornell University)

varieties.history: Raised from a 1943 cross at the Geneva station and released in 1968. It became hugely popular with European growers, especially in Belgium and the Netherlands, and has produced dozens of redder sports such as Jonagored.

look.description: Large, rounded golden-yellow apple, flushed and striped orange-red over about half the surface.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy, creamy-white flesh with a honeyed sweetness from Golden Delicious, kept lively by plenty of balancing acidity from Jonathan; some tasters note a subtle pear-drop sweetness. Best within a month or two of picking: it softens quickly out of the fridge and turns greasy in long storage, so supermarket fruit is often disappointing.
taste.peak: Picked early to mid October; keeps 1-2 months (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: Vigorous triploid that crops well and early; thin to avoid overcropping and small fruit.

pollination.notes: Triploid, so a poor pollen donor; needs two diploid partners nearby. Sources advise against relying on Golden Delicious (a parent) as its pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cool-summer climates: Belgium, the Netherlands, northern Germany, Pacific Northwest coast, Michigan and New York.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers give soft fruit with poor colour and sunburn, which is why it lost ground in warmer US regions.

health.other: Susceptible to mildew and fire blight; big fruit on light crops may get bitter pit; greasy skin in store.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it space or a dwarfing stock, and two diploid pollinators. Excellent in cool, moist climates; in hot areas choose a red sport and pick on time.

varieties.name: Jonagored

origin.parentage: Sport of Jonagold

varieties.history: A redder-skinned bud sport of Jonagold found by grower Jos Morren at Halen in Belgium and introduced in 1985. It is one of the most widely planted Jonagold sports in Europe; apart from colour it behaves like Jonagold.

look.description: Like Jonagold but with a much fuller, deeper red flush covering most of the fruit.

taste.summary: Same as Jonagold: very juicy, sweet and honeyed with a balancing tang. The extra colour can tempt early picking, which gives a less developed flavour.

tree.notes: As Jonagold.

pollination.notes: As Jonagold: triploid, needs two diploid pollinators.

climate.best_climates: As Jonagold: cool-summer north-western Europe and similar regions.
climate.poor_climates: As Jonagold; it colours more reliably than the parent in warmer autumns, but the fruit still softens in hot summers.

health.other: Same disease profile as Jonagold.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow exactly as Jonagold; choose it over the parent where autumns are too mild for good colour.

varieties.name: Jonalicious

origin.parentage: Believed Jonathan x Red Delicious

varieties.history: A seedling found in 1933 by Anna Morris Daniels at Abilene, Texas, and introduced by Stark Bros. in 1960. It is thought to be a Jonathan x Red Delicious cross.

look.description: Large, bright red apple mottled over a yellow ground.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, juicy cream flesh joining Delicious-style sweetness to Jonathan's tang, with an aromatic finish.

tree.notes: Average vigour.

pollination.notes: Late-flowering: National Fruit Collection blossom dates point to group 6, while Orange Pippin lists group 5.

climate.best_climates: Found in west Texas, so it copes with hot summers and moderate winters; also grown in cooler temperate climates.
climate.poor_climates: Not well documented; very short or cool seasons may not ripen it fully.

health.other: Rated average for disease resistance; no specific weaknesses recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A good keeper for warmer districts. It flowers late, so choose a late-blossoming pollinator.

varieties.name: Jonamac

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York, USA
origin.parentage: McIntosh x Jonathan
origin.raised_by: Roger D. Way, New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: Raised in 1944 by Roger Way at Geneva, New York, and introduced in 1972. It combines McIntosh's white flesh with some of Jonathan's richer flavour, and is itself a parent of the Canadian apple Eden.

look.description: Medium, round fruit largely covered with bright red flush and stripes over pale yellow.

taste.summary: Very white, moderately firm flesh with a McIntosh-type aromatic flavour, sweeter and improved by the Jonathan parent. Orange Pippin also lists honeyed and strawberry notes.

tree.notes: Good cropper with some tendency to alternate bearing; fruit hangs well on the tree.

pollination.notes: Group 2 per Orange Pippin.

climate.best_climates: Cool, cold-winter regions such as New York, New England and eastern Canada, like its McIntosh parent.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers, where McIntosh-type apples go soft and colour poorly.

health.other: Some scab susceptibility; some resistance to fire blight and cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy early-autumn apple for cold districts. Thin the fruit in heavy years to reduce alternate cropping, and use the fruit within a few weeks.

varieties.name: Jonathan

origin.place: Farm of Philip Rick, Woodstock, Ulster County, New York
origin.parentage: Chance seedling, probably of Esopus Spitzenburg
origin.raised_by: Found on Philip Rick's farm; named by Judge Jesse Buel after Jonathan Hasbrouck

varieties.history: Found on a farm at Woodstock in the Hudson Valley and described in 1826 by Judge Buel, who named it after Jonathan Hasbrouck, the man who brought it to his notice. It became one of the great American apples of the 19th and 20th centuries and a parent of Jonagold, Idared and many others.

look.description: Smallish, bright glossy red apple over a yellow ground, with tough waxy skin and a little fine russet.

taste.summary: Crisp, fine white flesh, juicy and tender, with a lively sweet-sharp balance and the spicy, slightly wine-like tang Jonathan is known for. Mellows and softens over a couple of months in store; also cooks well.

climate_flavour.note: Trees of Antiquity (not counted): highly coloured in sunny climates, only striped red in cooler ones - colour, not flavour.

tree.notes: Moderate, twiggy, spreading tree that can droop with crops. Bears on spurs and some tips. Thin to maintain fruit size.

pollination.notes: Partly self-fertile but crops better with another mid-season diploid.

climate.best_climates: Continental climates with warm, sunny summers and dry autumns: the US Midwest and intermountain West, Hungary and central Europe, inland Australia.
climate.poor_climates: Humid regions with fire blight, mildew and cedar-apple rust pressure; very cool maritime summers give small, sharp fruit.

health.other: Very susceptible to powdery mildew, fire blight and cedar-apple rust; fruit prone to 'Jonathan spot' skin lesions in store.

varieties.grow_notes: Best on a sunny, airy site where mildew pressure is low; prune out mildewed tips in spring. Avoid planting near junipers in North America because of rust.

varieties.name: Jubilee

origin.place: Dominion Experimental Farm (later Summerland Research Station), Summerland, British Columbia
origin.parentage: McIntosh x Grimes Golden

varieties.history: Crossed by R. C. Palmer at Summerland in 1926, selected in 1936 and released in 1939. Not to be confused with the French Delbard Jubilee or the English Royal Jubilee; Orange Pippin also uses the name for a Fuji sport.

look.description: McIntosh-shaped, somewhat irregular apple flushed red over greenish yellow with prominent lenticels.

taste.summary: Creamy, crisp, fine-grained, juicy flesh with a sweetish sweet-tart balance when fresh; like McIntosh it loses its crunch and flavour in store.
taste.storage_change: Crisp and well balanced when fresh; like McIntosh it loses crispness and flavour in store (Orange Pippin).
taste.peak: Soon after picking; Wikipedia says it keeps up to three months in cold store, Orange Pippin 1-2 months.

tree.notes: Tree details not documented.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not published.

climate.best_climates: Raised for the dry, sunny Okanagan valley of British Columbia, with hot days, cool nights and cold winters.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented outside western Canada.

health.other: No disease information found; storage quality declines like McIntosh.

varieties.grow_notes: A late McIntosh-family apple from Summerland. Pick about three weeks after McIntosh and eat in the first months after harvest.

varieties.name: Julieta
varieties.history: A low-chill apple from IAPAR's breeding programme in Paraná, made for subtropical southern Brazil. It was published around 2010 as an early cultivar to pollinate the already popular Eva.

look.description: No published description of the fruit's appearance was found.

taste.summary: Its breeder calls the fruit good quality for such an early apple, but no flavour description was found.
taste.best_eaten: At picking or within a few weeks
taste.storage_change: Keeps about 30-45 days in a cold room (ISHS abstract).

climate_flavour.note: Bred for subtropical sites with only 100-500 chill units.

tree.notes: Described as highly productive in its home region.

pollination.notes: Released largely as a pollinator for Eva (IAPAR 75), so the two bloom together in low-chill climates.

climate.best_climates: Subtropical, humid areas that get only about 100-500 chill units, like southern Brazil. It ripens 10-14 days ahead of Eva.
climate.poor_climates: Cold-winter climates, where it would break bud too early and lose its flowers to frost.

health.other: Resistant to Glomerella (Colletotrichum) leaf blotch, the main apple disease of humid southern Brazil.

varieties.grow_notes: For warm-winter gardens only. Plant it with Eva, which it is meant to pollinate. Fruit keeps about a month to six weeks in a cold store.

varieties.name: Julyred

origin.place: New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station, New Brunswick, New Jersey, USA
origin.parentage: (Petrel x Early McIntosh) x (Williams x Starr)
origin.raised_by: G. W. Schneider, New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: An early summer apple from the New Jersey breeding programme, introduced in 1962. It is a parent of Jerseymac and appears in the pedigrees of several later New Jersey apples.

look.description: Large, attractive, rounded fruit, striped and flushed red over pale green.

taste.summary: Soft, white, juicy flesh with a strongly scented, wine-like flavour likened to loganberry. A sweet summer apple to eat straight from the tree.
taste.best_eaten: Aug; within a week of picking

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not well recorded.

pollination.notes: Group 3 per Orange Pippin.

climate.best_climates: Mid-Atlantic and north-eastern US climates, where it provides fruit in July.
climate.poor_climates: Areas with heavy cedar-apple rust pressure.

health.other: Rated susceptible to cedar-apple rust in Arkansas trials; otherwise not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Pick over several passes as fruits colour and eat promptly; like most summer apples it goes soft within a week or so.

varieties.name: Jumbo
varieties.history: Sold in Britain as a cooking apple, but no record under this name was found in the National Fruit Collection database or other pomological sources consulted (the NFC only holds an unrelated Japanese 'Jumbo Ohrin'). Origin and identity are unconfirmed.

look.description: Not recorded.

taste.summary: No reliable tasting description found; listed only as a cooking apple.
taste.storage_change: Keeps very well: fruit put in a fridge in early October was still being eaten in early March with virtually no loss, and later in the season it can be eaten as a dessert apple (Chris Bowers).

tree.notes: No growing data found.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded; plant with a partner of known mid-season group to be safe.

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Too little is documented to give specific advice; grow as a typical British cooking apple.

varieties.name: Jupiter

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Kent, England
origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Starking (a Delicious sport)

varieties.history: A triploid seedling raised at East Malling in 1966 from Cox crossed with the American Starking, and released to growers in 1981. It was one of several attempts to capture Cox flavour in a bigger, easier tree, and it has won an RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: A big, rather tall apple, greenish-yellow under an orange-red flush broken into stripes, with a little russet.

taste.summary: A strong, very fruity Cox-type apple, sweet but noticeably sharper than its parent, with an intense, well-balanced flavour some tasters compare to Topaz. Juicy cream flesh with a green tinge, dense and firm rather than crunchy; it keeps a month or two before softening.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Dec; at its best in the first weeks after picking
taste.peak: Orange Pippin: keeps 1-2 months

tree.notes: A strong-growing triploid that needs room or a dwarfing rootstock. Thin heavy sets to keep size up and to discourage alternate-year cropping.

pollination.notes: Triploid: a poor pollen donor, so it needs one diploid partner in group 2-4 and ideally a second diploid to pollinate that partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool, temperate lowland Britain and north-west Europe, where it gives a Cox-like apple with less trouble than Cox.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer regions are untested and likely to give soft, poorly coloured fruit; very cold continental winters are also outside its known range.

health.other: Generally healthier than Cox, with good mildew and fair scab resistance; fruit does not keep as long as some Cox types.

varieties.grow_notes: A good garden substitute for Cox in southern and central England. Plant with two diploid companions such as Discovery or Sunset, choose M26 or M9 to restrain its vigour, and thin fruitlets in June.

varieties.name: Kaiser Wilhelm

origin.parentage: Possibly a seedling of Harberts Reinette (unconfirmed)
origin.raised_by: Possibly Pastor Johann Wilhelm Schumacher, Ramrath

varieties.history: Grown in the Rhineland from about the 1830s under the name Peter Broich, perhaps raised in a pastor's nursery at Ramrath. In 1875 the teacher Carl Hesselmann of Witzhelden obtained permission from Emperor Wilhelm I to rename it after him, and it became a classic tree of German meadow orchards.

look.description: Large, solid fruit, yellow-green to yellow, with dark red covering from a third to almost all of the skin.

taste.summary: Sweet-sharp with a distinctive raspberry-like aroma; firm and juicy when first picked but becoming drier and somewhat mealy as it stores.
taste.storage_change: Firm and juicy at first, the flesh turns soft (mürbe) and increasingly dry in store (de.wikipedia).
taste.peak: Late October to February, even April (de.wikipedia).

tree.notes: Very vigorous and long-lived; its size and alternating crops make it unsuited to commercial orchards but well suited to large standard trees.

pollination.notes: Triploid, a poor pollen donor; needs two diploid partners. Described as mid-season flowering (UK group assigned approximately).

climate.best_climates: Temperate central European lowlands and hills with moderate rainfall and well-drained soil.
climate.poor_climates: Heavy, wet soils, which encourage canker.

health.other: Fairly resistant to scab and mildew but notably prone to bitter pit; canker on wet, heavy ground.

varieties.grow_notes: Best as a large standard or half-standard on a well-drained site, with two diploid pollinators nearby. Avoid waterlogged clay.

varieties.name: Kalmar Glasäpple

origin.place: Grown around Kalmar, south-east Sweden; origin disputed (Sweden or Germany)
origin.parentage: Unknown; possibly the same as the old Spanish/German Gelbe Spanische Renette (White Spanish Reinette)

varieties.history: A Swedish heritage apple cultivated since the 18th century, named after Kalmar. Its origin is disputed, and it may be identical to the old White Spanish Reinette (Gelbe Spanische Renette); the UK National Apple Register files 'Kalmar Glassapple' among that variety's synonyms.

look.description: A light yellow apple, about 78 mm wide and 65 mm tall, on a short stalk.

taste.summary: A balance of good acidity and sweetness; it is at its best after a period in store, reaching full ripeness in early December.
taste.storage_change: picked early October, fully ripe in early December, keeps one to two months (sv and en Wikipedia)
taste.peak: early December onwards

tree.notes: No reliable tree information found.

pollination.notes: Late flowering; needs a pollinator that blooms at the same time. Group number inferred from 'late blossoming'.

climate.best_climates: The mildest southern Swedish growing zones (zones I-II) and comparable cool temperate climates.
climate.poor_climates: Recommended only for southern Sweden, so colder inland or northern climates are too harsh; hot climates untested.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: A late-flowering heritage apple for cool-temperate gardens; pick in early October and store until December. Pair with another late-flowering variety.

varieties.name: Kandil Sinap
varieties.history: Thought to have arisen in Crimea in the early nineteenth century; some sources link it to Turkey. It is famous for its exceptionally tall, narrow, almost cylindrical shape.

look.description: Strikingly tall, slim, cylindrical apple with smooth, porcelain-like creamy yellow skin flushed and striped red.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy, fine-textured, snow-white flesh that is sweet with refreshing acidity and a slightly winey, perfumed flavour.

tree.notes: Upright, regular and heavy-cropping spur bearer.

pollination.notes: Mid-season blossom (group 3).

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer climates such as its Black Sea homeland; listed for zones 6-9 and also succeeds in coastal British Columbia.
climate.poor_climates: Not recommended for very cold-winter regions.

health.other: No specific weaknesses documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A conversation piece with genuinely good flavour. Give it a warm, sunny site, pick in mid October and store for winter eating.

varieties.name: Kanzi

origin.parentage: Gala x Braeburn (reportedly the sports Gala Must and Braeburn Hillwell)

varieties.history: Bred in Belgium from a Gala x Braeburn cross made around 1992 at the Nicolai nursery with the University of Leuven, and released about 2002 as cultivar Nicoter. It reached European shops under the Kanzi trademark (Swahili for 'hidden treasure') in 2006 and is a sibling of Jazz in parentage, though a separate seedling.

look.description: Gala-like but more conical, with a bright pinkish-red flush and streaks over yellow; smooth skin.

taste.summary: Firm, fairly crisp and very juicy, with a mild, clean flavour that leans sharp rather than sweet and a light, vinous aftertaste. More delicate and less pronounced than its sibling Jazz; some tasters find a nectarine-like fruitiness, others want more sweetness.
taste.storage_change: flesh browning comes easily with wrong storage (de Wikipedia)

climate_flavour.note: de Wikipedia: colours poorly where day and night temperatures differ little

tree.notes: Medium-sized tree with regular annual crops; fruit on a tree ripens fairly evenly. A licensed club variety mostly limited to contracted growers.

pollination.notes: Needs a cross-pollinator; UK flowering group not published.

climate.best_climates: Temperate north-west European fruit regions (Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, northern Italy) with sunny autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, cool sites with heavy scab and canker pressure; hot climates likely reduce colour and acidity.

health.other: Susceptible to scab and not resistant to canker; prone to internal flesh browning if stored badly.

varieties.grow_notes: Needs a routine scab programme in wet climates and a free-draining soil to limit canker. Ripens around the same time as Golden Delicious, so it suits sunny southern sites in the UK.

varieties.name: Karmijn de Sonnaville

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Jonathan (some German sources suggest Belle de Boskoop as the pollen parent)

varieties.history: Raised in 1949 by Piet de Sonnaville at Wageningen and released in 1971. It never became a major commercial apple because it is awkward to grow, but enthusiasts prize its intense flavour; an Irish orchard grows it for juice.

look.description: Medium to large apple flushed carmine red over yellow-green, often with considerable russet.

taste.summary: A Cox-type apple with even more intensity: high in both sugar and acid, with a rich, spicy, strongly aromatic flavour. Crisp and juicy, and it becomes more complex after a few weeks in store.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Dec, after a few weeks in store
taste.storage_change: Orange Pippin: flavour becomes more complex in storage.
taste.peak: de.wikipedia: picked October, at its best through December.

tree.notes: Vigorous triploid that needs good soil, a good site and careful management; can be difficult to grow.

pollination.notes: Triploid: a poor pollen donor that needs two other compatible varieties nearby for good fruit set.

climate.best_climates: Warmer, drier temperate areas, similar to those that suit Jonathan.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, scab-prone districts; cold, poor sites.

health.other: Very susceptible to scab; fruit russet can be severe; codling moth damage reported.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in a sunny, well-drained, sheltered spot with two pollinators. Expect to manage scab, and leave the fruit in store for a few weeks to reach full flavour.

varieties.name: Katy

origin.parentage: James Grieve x Worcester Pearmain

varieties.history: Bred at the Balsgard fruit-breeding station in southern Sweden in 1947 and released in 1966 as Katja; it is sold as Katy in Britain. It combines the juiciness of James Grieve with the bright colour of Worcester Pearmain and became a popular garden and juicing apple.

look.description: Bright scarlet flush over most of a pale yellow-green skin; a glossy, eye-catching apple.

taste.summary: Very juicy, pale cream flesh on the softer side of crunchy, with a mild apple flavour, a refreshing touch of acidity and, in a good year, a hint of strawberry inherited from Worcester Pearmain. Pleasant rather than deep; it softens within a week or so (keep it chilled) and gives an attractive pink-orange juice.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, within a week or two of picking
taste.storage_change: Refreshing straight from the tree but goes soft after a while; best kept in the fridge and eaten cool (Orange Pippin)
taste.peak: Late August-early September for a few weeks; stores until October (Walcot)

climate_flavour.note: Orange Pippin: one of the best for northern areas with short seasons, ripens even in a poor summer

tree.notes: A vigorous, regular and heavy-cropping spur-bearer; thin fruitlets to maintain size. Ripe fruit tends to drop.

pollination.notes: Mid-season (group 3) and a good pollinator for others; some nurseries call it partly self-fertile, but a partner improves crops.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate and northern climates such as Scandinavia, Scotland and northern England, and mild damp areas generally; blossom is frost tolerant.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers soften the fruit and reduce colour; it is not suited to low-chill regions.

health.other: Good general disease resistance. Fruit drops when ripe and keeps only briefly.

varieties.grow_notes: An easy, productive tree for colder or wetter gardens and a good juicing apple. Thin heavy crops, pick as soon as the fruit colours fully, and pair with any group 2-4 diploid.

varieties.name: Keepsake

origin.place: University of Minnesota Fruit Breeding Farm, Excelsior, Minnesota, USA
origin.parentage: Frostbite x Northern Spy

varieties.history: Released by the University of Minnesota in 1978 as a very hardy, long-keeping winter apple. Its homely, irregular looks kept it out of supermarkets, but it found fame as a parent of Honeycrisp.

look.description: Small to medium, lumpy and irregular fruit, mostly covered with red flush and streaks.

taste.summary: Very hard, crisp, fine-grained and juicy light-yellow flesh with a strongly aromatic, sweet and spicy flavour. It mellows in store and is at its best in mid-winter.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Mar; peaks in Jan-Feb after storage
taste.storage_change: Hard at picking; mellows in store and reaches peak quality in mid-winter.
taste.peak: January-February; keeps into April (Orange Pippin), about 6 months (Univ. of Minnesota).

tree.notes: Medium vigour and easy to manage; comes into bearing early but tends to crop biennially.

pollination.notes: Group 4 per Orange Pippin.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates such as Minnesota and the northern US and Canada, where it is very hardy.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season districts where it cannot be left to mid-October; untested in hot climates.

health.other: Good general disease resistance; some resistance to fire blight and cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: Pick late and store cool; it needs two or three months in store to reach full flavour. Thin in heavy years to curb biennial cropping.

varieties.name: Kent

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Maidstone, Kent, England
origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Jonathan
origin.raised_by: H.M. Tydeman, East Malling Research Station

varieties.history: Raised in 1949 by H.M. Tydeman at East Malling as a later-keeping, Cox-flavoured apple, and released as Malling Kent. It holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Large greenish-yellow apple flushed and striped orange-red, with a little russet.

taste.summary: Juicy, slightly coarse white flesh with a sweet-sharp, aromatic flavour in the Cox mould, sharpened by its Jonathan parent. Keeps its flavour well into the new year.

tree.notes: Tree habits are poorly recorded; treat as an ordinary spur-pruned dessert apple.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records show it flowering with Cox; pair with another group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Southern and eastern England and similar cool, temperate climates with a long enough autumn for a mid-October harvest.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season northern sites where it may not ripen; hot summers likely to reduce flavour and colour.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A good late-keeping Cox substitute for southern gardens; it needs a warm, sheltered site to finish ripening in mid-October. Store cool to enjoy it through the winter.

varieties.name: Kentish Fillbasket
varieties.history: An old cooking apple thought to come from Kent and known before 1820. Hogg warned that some earlier writers, including Miller and Forsyth, used the name for a different apple, the Kentish Codlin. By Bunyard's time (1920) it was already rarely grown.

look.description: Very large, flattened, irregular and slightly ribbed fruit, yellow-green to pale yellow with a reddish-brown flush broken by deeper red stripes.

taste.summary: Tender, juicy, greenish-white flesh with a brisk, clean acidity, well suited to cooking. It was rated a first-class kitchen apple for the midwinter months.

tree.notes: A strong, vigorous tree that grows large and crops abundantly, according to 19th-century accounts.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 9 May, so group 3 is inferred (group 2 is possible). Plant a mid-season partner.

climate.best_climates: South-east England and similar mild, cool-summer lowland climates.
climate.poor_climates: No record of performance outside southern England; values are inferred from its origin.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Best suited to a large orchard standard, where its vigour and size are an advantage. Pick in mid October and store for cooking through to the new year.

varieties.name: Kentish Quarrenden
varieties.history: Offered as a late-season eating apple, but no independent pomological description was found: it is not listed, even as a synonym, in the UK National Fruit Collection or National Apple Register data. The name hints at a link with the Quarrenden apples, but the best-known of them, Devonshire Quarrenden, is an August apple, and no connection is documented.

look.description: Not recorded in available sources.

taste.summary: No reliable tasting description found in independent sources.

tree.notes: Not recorded.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Presumably south-east England, if it is a Kentish variety; unverified.
climate.poor_climates: Not recorded.

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Insufficient independent information; treat as a typical English dessert apple and pair with a mid-season pollinator until its flowering time is known.

varieties.name: Kermerrien
varieties.history: A traditional Breton cider apple from Finistère, in use since the nineteenth century around Quimper and Carhaix. It is a staple of the Cornouaille cider orchards.

look.description: Medium-sized cider apple with an orange to orange-red flush.

taste.summary: French sources and juice analyses class it as a bitter apple: very juicy and strongly scented, with high tannin and little acid. One English-language source calls it an acidic blending apple instead, so its role is reported inconsistently; the analytical data point to bittersweet.
taste.peak: Salt Spring: about three weeks of sweating at most

tree.notes: Average vigour with an upright-spreading habit. Sources disagree on how quickly it comes into bearing.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not reliably recorded; plant with other Breton or Norman cider varieties.

climate.best_climates: Mild, wet Atlantic climates like western Brittany and Cornwall.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hard continental winters or hot, dry summers.

health.other: Reported to be fairly resistant to scab and mildew; otherwise little documented.

varieties.grow_notes: Suited to low-input orchards in mild, damp regions. Blend it with sweeter or sharper fruit to balance its strong tannin.

varieties.name: Kerry Pippin
varieties.history: An Irish early dessert apple on record since 1802 and known in England by 1819. Hogg credited its wider spread to Robertson, a Kilkenny nurseryman who died in 1839, and ranked it among the finest early dessert apples.

look.description: Small, neat oval fruit with a glossy pale yellow skin, streaked and flushed bright red on the sunny side, sometimes with a trace of fine russet.

taste.summary: Hard, very crisp yellowish flesh with a brisk, sugary and aromatic flavour of the sub-acid type. Older writers found it very juicy, while the National Fruit Collection describes it as rather dry. Best eaten soon after picking.

tree.notes: A hardy, medium-sized tree that 19th-century growers recommended for dwarfing stocks, bush forms and espaliers. Cropping was described as good by Hogg and moderate by Bunyard.

pollination.notes: Flowers early: the National Fruit Collection records full bloom in the first week of May, so group 2 is inferred. Assume it needs an early-to-mid flowering partner.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp maritime climates like Ireland and western Britain, where it has long been grown.
climate.poor_climates: No record of use in hot regions; an early, small dessert apple like this would likely ripen soft and colour poorly in warm summers.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for a small garden tree or trained form in Ireland or western Britain. Pick at the end of August and eat within a few weeks, and plant an early-flowering partner nearby.

varieties.name: Keswick Codlin

origin.place: Gleaston Castle, near Ulverston, Lancashire (now Cumbria), England
origin.parentage: Chance seedling found on a rubbish heap
origin.raised_by: Introduced by John Sander, nurseryman of Keswick

varieties.history: Discovered as a seedling growing on a rubbish tip at Gleaston Castle near Ulverston and recorded in 1793. A Keswick nurseryman, John Sander, distributed it, and it became a standard early codlin across northern Britain; it is a parent of Emneth Early.

look.description: Ribbed, conical, pale greenish-yellow codlin, sometimes with a slight pinkish-orange cheek.

taste.summary: A sharp, acidic early codlin. The National Fruit Collection describes the flesh as soft, coarse and fairly dry, but growers eating it fresh off the tree report a crisp, eye-watering snap and plenty of juice. It collapses to a pale puree when cooked, makes good jelly, and keeps only about a week.
taste.peak: picked mid August; does not keep (Wikipedia)

tree.notes: Crops young and heavily but can slip into alternate bearing; thin heavy sets. Very pretty blossom.

pollination.notes: Early flowering; partly self-fertile, but a group 1-3 partner gives better crops.

climate.best_climates: Cool, wet, northern and upland Britain, where it has a long record of reliable cropping; also grown historically in northern and eastern Europe.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would push its already early, soft fruit to drop and go mealy quickly.

health.other: Good general disease resistance and tolerance of wet sites; skin can carry superficial fungal spotting.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the best early cookers for the north and for exposed or damp gardens. Begin picking thinnings for cooking in late July and use the main crop through August.

varieties.name: Kidd's Orange Red

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Delicious

varieties.history: Raised in 1924 by amateur breeder J.H. Kidd at Greytown in New Zealand and brought to Britain around 1932. Crossed with Golden Delicious it gave Gala, making it one of the most influential apples of the 20th century.

look.description: Conical, yellow apple largely covered with an orange-red flush and stripes, often with a little russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Dense, firm cream flesh that bites cleanly and keeps releasing juice, with a honeyed sweetness richer than Cox and an aromatic depth likened to a sweet dessert wine with a lively finish. Firm and slightly chewy rather than crunchy; best eaten before the New Year.
taste.peak: Best before the New Year (Orange Pippin); Chris Bowers says November-December; Walcot stores until January

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous spur-bearer; generally easier to grow than Cox.

pollination.notes: Flowers with Cox; any group 2-4 diploid will do.

climate.best_climates: Temperate climates with warm, sunny autumns: New Zealand, southern England and similar, where it ripens and colours fully.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, wet, short-season areas where it may not ripen fully; hot climates likely reduce colour.

health.other: Usually healthier than Cox, with less scab, but can get mildew.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for anyone who loves Cox but struggles with its diseases. Plant in a warm, sunny spot so it ripens fully by mid-October.

varieties.name: King Byerd
varieties.history: A Cornish apple of unknown age, received by the UK National Fruit Trials from Cornwall in 1954 and still held at Brogdale. Used mainly for cooking but also eaten fresh once it has mellowed in store.

look.description: Large, tall, noticeably ribbed apple, green ripening to yellow, streaked with orange-red and flecked with grey russet.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, fine-textured cream flesh. Sharp with some sweetness when picked, mellowing in store to a sweeter, still-brisk flavour by midwinter.
taste.best_eaten: Jan-Mar for eating fresh; cook from picking
taste.storage_change: sharp-sweet at picking, mellowing to a sweeter balance by January-March (Wikipedia)
taste.peak: Jan-Mar (Wikipedia)

tree.notes: No reliable tree information found.

pollination.notes: At Brogdale it reaches full bloom around mid May, similar to group 4 varieties.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist south-west England and similar cool maritime climates.
climate.poor_climates: Humid sites with high scab pressure; hot climates untested.

health.other: Scab is the main recorded problem.

varieties.grow_notes: A late, long-keeping dual-purpose apple for the south-west; give it an open, airy position to reduce scab. Pick in late October and store for eating after Christmas.

varieties.name: King Cole

origin.parentage: Believed Jonathan x Dutch Mignonne

varieties.history: Raised by R. G. Cole at Lang Lang in Victoria, Australia, and first shown in 1912. It is believed to be a Jonathan x Dutch Mignonne cross.

look.description: Smooth-skinned apple with a bright, Jonathan-like red flush and stripes over greenish yellow, with the odd russet patch.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained, greenish-white flesh with a brisk, moderately sharp flavour and modest aroma.
taste.peak: Keeps until January (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Tree details not documented; National Fruit Collection trees have a drooping habit.

pollination.notes: National Fruit Collection blossom dates are mid-season (about group 3).

climate.best_climates: Raised in southern Victoria's mild temperate climate; also fruits in south-east England.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance in very cold or very hot regions.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: A late-keeping Australian dessert apple. Pick in mid October; in a cool store it lasts well into the new year.

varieties.name: King David

origin.parentage: Chance seedling; thought to be Jonathan x Winesap or Arkansas Black

varieties.history: Found in 1893 growing in a hedgerow in north-west Arkansas and introduced by Stark Bros in 1902. A dark-red southern apple that is enjoying renewed interest among heritage growers for its flavour and fire-blight resistance.

look.description: Almost entirely covered in deep, dark red, with a few pale dots; firm, glossy fruit.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse yellowish flesh with an intense sweet-tart, spicy, Winesap-like vinous flavour; individual tasters pick out a heady Muscat-grape finish and even a caramel note. Sweetens somewhat in store and keeps a month or two. Good fresh, cooked or in cider, where it adds a soft astringency.

tree.notes: Vigorous, upright and productive; comes into bearing early and crops regularly.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering diploid.

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer climates such as the US South and Midwest, where it colours deeply and ripens fully.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season, cool maritime sites where a mid-October apple may not develop its full sugar.

health.other: Highly resistant to fire blight with some resistance to scab and cedar-apple rust; some bitter pit reported.

varieties.grow_notes: A useful choice for warm, humid areas where fire blight limits other varieties. Give it a sunny site and space for its upright growth.

varieties.name: King of the Pippins

origin.place: Probably France (as Reine des Reinettes); origin disputed

varieties.history: An 18th-century apple whose origins are muddled: the British national collection treats it as identical to the French Reine des Reinettes, and in England it seems to have been sold first as Golden Winter Pearmain before the nurseryman Kirke of Brompton renamed it. It was widely planted across Europe in the 19th century and carries well over a hundred synonyms.

look.description: Neat, slightly conical golden fruit with an orange flush streaked in red and freckled with russet dots.

taste.summary: Firm, juicy, yellowish flesh with a brisk sweet-sharp balance and a light aromatic, almond-like note; it is sharper when picked and mellows in store. Holds its shape when cooked, which is why the French favour it for tarte Tatin.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Jan; sweeter after a few weeks in store
taste.storage_change: Sharp when picked and sweetens in storage (Orange Pippin). German Wikipedia: picked from late September, it needed some weeks in store before eating.
taste.peak: Oct-Jan (German Wikipedia); Dec-Mar (French Wikipedia)

tree.notes: A fairly compact, upright, easy tree that crops well; heavy years can be followed by lighter ones, so thin in big years.

pollination.notes: Partly self-fertile but sets better with a group 3-5 partner; a useful pollinator for other diploids.

climate.best_climates: Temperate western Europe, from southern England through France and the Low Countries, where it has been grown for over two centuries.
climate.poor_climates: Very wet, scab-prone sites can mark the fruit; extreme continental cold is outside its documented range.

health.other: Some scab susceptibility; otherwise regarded as a trouble-free garden tree.

varieties.grow_notes: A versatile choice for anyone wanting one tree for both the fruit bowl and the kitchen. Grows well on ordinary soils in sun; prune as a spur-bearer and thin in heavy-crop years to avoid alternate bearing.

varieties.name: Kingston Black

origin.place: Kingston St Mary, near Taunton, Somerset, England
origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: Named after the parish of Kingston St Mary near Taunton, it was well known in Somerset by the nineteenth century and by the mid twentieth was one of the most widely grown cider apples in the West Country. It is the classic example of a balanced bittersharp capable of a fine single-variety cider.

look.description: Small, rounded fruit, yellow and red-streaked on the shaded side, deep maroon-purple where sunlit, with patches of grey russet.

taste.summary: The benchmark bittersharp: sharp, tannic and sugary all at once, so its juice is well balanced on its own. Ciders from it are full, fruity and long-lived.

tree.notes: Slow to come into bearing and a shy, erratic cropper; sources differ on how strongly biennial it is, some calling it markedly so.

pollination.notes: Self-sterile; plant with a mid-season flowering cider apple.

climate.best_climates: Somerset-like mild maritime climates with long, mild autumns and good drainage.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, cold or high-disease sites, where canker and scab overwhelm it; humid regions with cedar-apple rust.

health.other: Prone to canker and scab, and to cedar-apple rust in North America; not well suited to organic growing.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a warm, free-draining, sheltered spot and good air movement to limit canker and scab. Be patient: it can take years to crop and yields are modest. Worth growing for the quality of the juice rather than the quantity.

varieties.name: Knobby Russet
varieties.history: Brought to notice in 1820 by Haslar Capron of Midhurst in Sussex. It is best known for its grotesque appearance: lumpy, warty fruit almost entirely coated in russet.

look.description: Knobbly, warted and lumpy fruit, nearly covered in rough russet over a golden-orange ground.

taste.summary: A warty, potato-like russet with a sweet flavour. Descriptions of the flesh disagree: Wikipedia calls it soft and creamy, while other accounts find it firm, rather dry and fairly strongly flavoured, more a curiosity than a juicy dessert apple. In season from October to about March.
taste.best_eaten: Midwinter, after a spell in store
taste.peak: In season October to February/March (Wikipedia)

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not well recorded.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records show it flowering about a week before Cox; plant with a group 1-3 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Southern England and similar mild, temperate climates.
climate.poor_climates: Not recorded outside Britain; early flowering makes frost pockets risky.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded; early blossom is exposed to spring frost.

varieties.grow_notes: Grown mainly as a conversation piece and late keeper. Avoid frost pockets because it flowers early, and pick late for winter storage.

varieties.name: Kronprinz Rudolf

origin.parentage: Chance seedling
origin.raised_by: Johann Klöckner (some accounts credit Franz Pfann)

varieties.history: A Styrian apple from seed sown in 1863, named after Crown Prince Rudolf of Austria and exhibited at the Vienna World's Fair of 1873. Two accounts compete over who raised it, naming either Johann Klöckner or Franz Pfann.

look.description: Medium, roundish to slightly flattened, smooth apple, greenish-yellow to greenish-white with a bright red washed cheek on the sunny side and a little russet in the stalk cavity.

taste.summary: Very juicy, fine and fairly soft white-to-cream flesh; sweet with a light, refreshing tartness and a delicate spicy perfume.
taste.peak: Harvest October; stores until March (de.wikipedia).

tree.notes: Fertile and regarded in Austria as suitable for rough, exposed sites. Reports on vigour conflict (strong in Austrian sources, weak in others). Sensitive to copper sprays.

pollination.notes: Listed as group B (2) and self-sterile; Brogdale records early flowering.

climate.best_climates: Cool Alpine-foothill climates such as Styria, including harsher upland sites.
climate.poor_climates: Little information from hot or mild-winter regions.

health.other: Moderately susceptible to scab; leaves are damaged by copper fungicides.

varieties.grow_notes: A traditional Austrian dessert apple for cool, exposed gardens. Avoid copper-based sprays and plant an early-flowering (group 1-3) partner.

varieties.name: Lady Alice

origin.parentage: Chance seedling; reportedly a shoot from the seedling rootstock of a damaged Red Delicious tree
origin.raised_by: Found by orchardist Don Emmons; developed by Rainier Fruit Company

varieties.history: Found in 1979 in a Red Delicious orchard near Gleed, Washington, where a shoot from a damaged tree's rootstock was allowed to fruit. Rainier Fruit Company markets it as a trademarked late-winter apple; accounts differ on whether it was named for the finder's mother or for Rainier co-founder Alice Zirkle.

look.description: Medium, roundish-oblate apple with thin skin: a pink to orange blush and bright red streaks over a creamy yellow ground that deepens in store.

taste.summary: Sweet with a touch of tartness and a rich, complex, heirloom-style flavour, with hints of honey and almond. Dense and crisp; slow to brown when cut and holds its shape in hot baking.
taste.best_eaten: Sold Feb-May after storage, at its best around March
taste.storage_change: stored after harvest and sold February-May, peaking in March (Wikipedia)
taste.peak: March

tree.notes: A proprietary commercial variety; no published tree information found.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Irrigated central Washington, with hot, dry summers and cold winters.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: Grown commercially under licence in Washington; garden trees are rarely offered. Its flavour is developed by storage, so it is eaten in late winter and spring.

varieties.name: Lady Henniker

origin.place: Thornham Hall, near Eye, Suffolk, England
origin.parentage: Unknown; selected from seedlings grown from cider-pomace pips
origin.raised_by: John Perkins, gardener to Lord Henniker

varieties.history: Between 1840 and 1850 Lord Henniker's estate at Thornham Hall made large amounts of cider. His gardener John Perkins sowed bushels of pips from the pressings and thinned the seedlings over many years until this favourite was left. It was shown in 1873, received an RHS First Class Certificate and became a popular Victorian garden apple.

look.description: Large, angular, often slab-sided fruit with ridges round the eye; golden-yellow with a light red flush broken by crimson streaks on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Tender yellow flesh with a gentle perfume. Bunyard compared its flavour to Blenheim Orange, but the National Fruit Collection found it coarse, rather dry and fairly acid. Mainly a cooker that breaks down to a pale, well-flavoured purée needing little sugar; some growers also enjoy it raw as a sweet-sharp apple.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Jan; cooks to a pale purée
taste.peak: picked early October; keeps 3 months or more

tree.notes: A vigorous, upright, long-lived tree that crops heavily and regularly. Being triploid, it makes a large tree, so allow room or choose a dwarfing rootstock.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 4 (D). Triploid, so it gives poor pollen: plant two different diploid partners from groups 3-5 that can also pollinate each other.

climate.best_climates: Lowland eastern and southern England and similar mild, temperate climates, where old trees go on cropping for a century.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer regions are untested; probably less suited to very short, cold seasons because it is picked fairly late.

health.other: Generally healthy, with some scab resistance. Triploid vigour means big trees, and very old specimens can develop heart rot in the main limbs.

varieties.grow_notes: Best as a half-standard or standard where it has room. Plant two compatible diploid pollinators nearby, and pick in October for winter cooking.

varieties.name: Lady Northcliffe
varieties.history: An English dessert apple of the early twentieth century, generally attributed to the Allgrove nursery at Langley, Buckinghamshire, and named after the wife of the newspaper owner Lord Northcliffe. Little has been published about it, and details here could not be cross-checked.

taste.summary: Reported as a crisp, juicy, sweet dessert apple, but no detailed tasting notes could be verified for this record.

tree.notes: Growth habit not documented in the sources consulted.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not verified; plant with another apple flowering at a similar time.

climate.best_climates: Presumably the cool, moist lowlands of southern England where it was raised (inferred from origin).
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; like most English dessert apples it is unlikely to suit hot or low-chill climates.

health.other: Disease profile not documented in the sources consulted.

varieties.grow_notes: Treat as a typical English garden dessert apple: sunny site, well-drained soil, and a compatible pollinator nearby. Check with a specialist nursery for its flowering group before planning pollination.

varieties.name: Lady of Wemyss
varieties.history: An old Scottish cooking apple, on record since 1831; the National Fruit Collection holds it as 'Lady of the Wemyss'. The name points to the Wemyss estates of Fife, but no reliable account of its exact birthplace was found.

look.description: Large, broad apple, ribbed from eye to base, pale or yellowish green with a dull orange-red to mauve-red flush and russet flecks.

taste.summary: Hard, fine-textured greenish-yellow flesh with a distinctly acid flavour, used as a cooker.

tree.notes: No reliable growing data found.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates (early May, alongside Grenadier); treat as mid-season and provide a partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool Scottish and northern British conditions, where it originated.
climate.poor_climates: No record of performance in warm climates; assume it prefers cool summers.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage choice for Scottish and northern collections. Little is documented about the tree, so grow on a moderately vigorous rootstock and treat as a standard spur-bearing cooker.

varieties.name: Lady Sudeley

origin.raised_by: Mr Jacob, a cottager at Petworth

varieties.history: Raised around 1849 by a Petworth cottager named Jacob and later introduced by George Bunyard and Co. of Maidstone in 1885, a year after it won an RHS Award of Merit. A showy Victorian garden apple, it is a parent of Benenden Early and Laxton's Beauty of Bedford.

look.description: Handsome, distinctly ribbed fruit, golden yellow boldly striped and flushed with orange-red to scarlet.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained and juicy yellowish flesh with a lively, slightly sharp flavour of good quality. Best eaten straight from the tree; it softens within about a week.
taste.storage_change: Orange Pippin: unusually for an early apple it keeps a week or so in the fridge.

tree.notes: Average vigour with attractive blossom. The wood is brittle and branches can snap under a heavy crop, so thin fruit and support laden limbs.

pollination.notes: Fairly late-flowering for an early apple (group 4) with frost-resistant blossom; partly self-fertile but crops better with a group 3-5 diploid partner.

climate.best_climates: Southern and central England and similar mild climates; its later, frost-resistant blossom helps in gardens with spring frosts.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would hasten softening and dull the striped colour; no records from hot regions.

health.other: Reported to have good general disease resistance. Main weakness is brittle wood that breaks under heavy crops.

varieties.grow_notes: A decorative early apple for gardens, good in sites where late frosts catch earlier blossom. Thin the fruit in heavy years to protect the brittle branches, and pick over a few weeks from late August.

varieties.name: Lady Williams

origin.parentage: Chance seedling, probably of Granny Smith; the pollen parent is thought to be Jonathan or Rokewood.
origin.raised_by: Found on the orchard of Arthur and Maud Williams

varieties.history: Came up as a chance seedling around 1935 on the Williams family orchard at Donnybrook in Western Australia and was named after Maud Williams, who recognised its promise. Its fame rests on its offspring: crossed with Golden Delicious it gave Cripps Pink (Pink Lady) and Cripps Red.

look.description: Green apple turning yellowish-green, with a red to pinkish-red flush over part of the skin.

taste.summary: Very firm, crisp, dense flesh with a sharp, Granny Smith-like edge that rounds into a balanced sweet-sharp flavour after some months in store. A late, long-keeping apple rather than one to eat off the tree.
taste.storage_change: Tart if harvested early; mellows when left on the tree into early winter (Trees of Antiquity).
taste.peak: Very late; picked as late as February in southern California (Orange Pippin).

climate_flavour.note: Very well suited to warm climates and unlikely to ripen in cooler ones (Orange Pippin); rarely reaches maturity in the UK (NFC); suited to low-chill sites (Trees of Antiquity).

tree.notes: Needs a very long, warm growing season; in cool climates the fruit may not ripen before winter.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 2 (Orange Pippin); pair with another early-flowering diploid.

climate.best_climates: Long, warm, sunny seasons with mild winters: south-west Western Australia, Mediterranean-type climates and the warmer apple districts of California and South Africa.
climate.poor_climates: Short or cool seasons: in places like the UK it ripens so late (November) that fruit is often under-ripe and exposed to frost.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well documented outside Australia.

varieties.grow_notes: Only worth planting where the season is long and warm enough to finish a very late apple. Pick as late as safely possible and store cold; flavour develops over the winter.

varieties.name: Lakeland

origin.place: University of Minnesota Fruit Breeding Farm, Excelsior, Minnesota, USA
origin.parentage: Open-pollinated seedling of Malinda

varieties.history: One of the University of Minnesota's mid-century hardy apples, introduced in 1950 from a Malinda seedling. A general-purpose apple for cold northern gardens.

look.description: Medium to large, broadly conical fruit, flushed and streaked dark purplish red over yellowish green, with a waxy skin.

taste.summary: Fine-textured, juicy cream to yellow flesh, sometimes tinged red, with a sweet and mildly acid flavour. A good all-round apple for eating, pies and sauce.
taste.peak: Keeps until December (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not well recorded.

pollination.notes: Group 2 per Orange Pippin.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter northern climates such as Minnesota, for which it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; hardy northern apples generally do less well in hot summers.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded in the sources used.

varieties.grow_notes: Mainly of interest for very cold gardens. Use early fruit for cooking and let the rest store until December.

varieties.name: Landsberger Reinette

origin.place: Landsberg an der Warthe, Brandenburg, then Prussia (now Gorzow Wielkopolski, Poland)
origin.parentage: Seedling, reportedly of Harberts Reinette

varieties.history: Raised around 1840-1850 by Councillor Burchardt at Landsberg on the Warthe, then in Prussian Brandenburg and now Gorzow Wielkopolski in Poland. It received a First Class Certificate from the RHS in 1882 and was widely planted in Germany and eastern Europe.

look.description: Smooth, fine-skinned apple ripening from yellow-green to pale straw-yellow, with fine brown dots and a light orange-red tinge on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Soft, fine-textured and very juicy white flesh, sweet and refreshing with a gentle, slightly winey tang but little aroma. Bruises easily.
