taste.peak: de Wikipedia: ripe from November, keeps to end of January

tree.notes: Strong-growing tree that makes a good standard; crops early and abundantly.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records show it flowering just before Cox; plant with another mid-season variety.

climate.best_climates: Cool, continental central and northern Europe, where it was raised and is valued for reliable cropping.
climate.poor_climates: Warm, dry sites encourage powdery mildew; wet, poor soils encourage canker.

health.other: Mildew can be a problem in warm, dry places and canker on wet, hungry soils; fruit bruises easily.

varieties.grow_notes: Prefers a cool site and is not fussy about soil, but avoid waterlogged or very poor ground where canker sets in. Handle the soft fruit gently at picking.

varieties.name: Lane's Prince Albert

origin.parentage: Recorded as Russet Nonpareil x Dumelow's Seedling
origin.raised_by: Thomas Squire; introduced by John Lane (nurseryman, Berkhamsted)

varieties.history: Raised around 1840 by Thomas Squire in Berkhamsted and named, by tradition, after Prince Albert passed through the town. The local nursery of John Lane released it in 1850; it won an RHS First Class Certificate in 1872 and remains one of the classic English cookers, holding an RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Large, smooth, bright green apple ripening yellowish, striped and lightly flushed with red on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Very juicy, soft white flesh with a strong, clean acidity. It cooks to a sharp puree that keeps a little texture, and it softens and sweetens somewhat in store; flesh browns quickly once cut.
taste.storage_change: Keeps very well, 3 months or more; browns quickly when cut (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Fairly weak, compact tree with a spreading, somewhat drooping habit, which makes it suitable for small gardens. Crops young and regularly.

pollination.notes: Mid-to-late flowering (group 3 in most lists, 4 in some). A good pollinator for others; needs a partner. Blossom is sensitive to frost.

climate.best_climates: Throughout Britain, including the north, Scotland and the wet west; hardy to roughly -20 C and fine in mild damp climates.
climate.poor_climates: Frost-prone hollows can damage its blossom; hot climates are untested and would likely shorten storage.

health.other: Main weakness is powdery mildew; otherwise a healthy tree with good scab resistance.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for a small garden that wants one reliable cooker; its modest vigour suits bush or cordon forms. Prune out mildewed shoot tips in spring and keep the tree open to airflow.

varieties.name: Laxton's Epicure

origin.parentage: Wealthy x Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: Crossed by the Laxton Brothers of Bedford in 1909 and released in 1929; it won an RHS Award of Merit in 1931 and later the Award of Garden Merit. It brings some of Cox's flavour to an apple that ripens several weeks earlier.

look.description: Smallish truncated-conical apple, greenish-yellow streaked and mottled with brownish to bright red.

taste.summary: Sweet, juicy and aromatic, with a fine-grained, moderately crisp texture and something of the Cox richness in it. Flavour is best when the apples are left to ripen fully on the tree, and it fades within a couple of weeks.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-mid Sep; does not keep long
taste.storage_change: does not store well (Pomiferous)
taste.peak: pick late August, use August-September (East of England Apples and Orchards Project)

tree.notes: A rather small, very precocious tree with large leaves that will set fruit even on unpruned one-year shoots. Thin heavy crops to keep fruit size.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering (group 3); plant with another group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate gardens such as most of Britain; ripening in late summer, it is picked before autumn weather sets in.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, high-rainfall districts raise the risk of canker; hot summers would give soft fruit with little colour.

health.other: Disease resistance slightly above average overall, but canker can be a problem in wet districts.

varieties.grow_notes: A good Cox-flavoured early apple for small gardens because the tree stays compact and crops young. Grow on well-drained soil, thin the fruit, and leave apples on the tree until fully ripe for the best flavour.

varieties.name: Laxton's Superb

origin.parentage: Wyken Pippin x Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: Raised by the Laxton Brothers nursery in Bedford in 1897 and introduced in 1922 after RHS awards in 1919 and 1921. It was widely planted in British orchards and gardens through the mid-20th century as a hardier, later-keeping alternative to Cox.

look.description: Greenish-yellow apple flushed dull crimson-purple with darker streaks, and a little russet.

taste.summary: Dense, sweet, very 'appley' cream flesh with a hint of Cox aroma but less acidity and complexity. Sources disagree on texture: Orange Pippin finds it firm rather than crisp and not very juicy, while growers and older descriptions call it very juicy, so season and ripeness seem to matter. Keeps one to two months.
taste.peak: Picked early October; stores until January (Walcot); keeps 1-2 months (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: Vigorous and hardy, but notoriously biennial: thin blossom or fruit hard in 'on' years to keep it cropping annually.

pollination.notes: Usually listed in group 4, though at Brogdale it opens about the same time as Cox.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate climates including northern Britain, where it is hardier and more reliable than Cox.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to give soft, poorly coloured fruit.

health.other: Main weakness is strong biennial bearing; scab can be troublesome in wet years.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy, productive Cox-style keeper for colder gardens. Thin heavily in a big blossom year, and grow on a dwarfing stock to keep its vigour manageable.

varieties.name: Leathercoat Russet
varieties.history: An old English russet known in the 1500s; 'leathercoats' are mentioned by Shakespeare in Henry IV Part 2. The name has long been confused with Royal Russet, which the national apple register lists under Leathercoat Russet as a synonym, so trees sold under this name may not all be the same apple.

look.description: Conical fruit, slightly ribbed at the eye, covered in dark brown russet with occasional patches of yellowish-green showing through.

taste.summary: Crisp, greenish flesh with a sweet, gently sharp (subacid) flavour. Detailed modern tasting notes are scarce.

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not recorded in available sources.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded; not currently held in the National Fruit Collection.

climate.best_climates: Inferred: mild, moist English lowland climates where it has been grown for centuries.
climate.poor_climates: Not recorded; hot dry summers are likely to give small, dry fruit.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage curiosity rather than a well-characterised garden apple. Treat as a typical English russet: a sunny, sheltered site, good drainage and a mid-season pollinator.

varieties.name: Lemon Pippin
varieties.history: An old apple, probably English though a Norman origin has been suggested, on record since the mid-eighteenth century. Its name comes from the lemon-like shape and colour of the fruit, which often has a fleshy knob at the stalk end; it spread widely in Europe under names such as Englischer Quittenapfel.

look.description: Oval, lemon-shaped fruit, often with a fleshy swelling at the stalk, ripening to clear lemon-yellow with fine russet dots.

taste.summary: Firm, rather dry, coarse flesh that is moderately sharp with a faint aroma. It keeps its shape when cooked, suiting pies and slices, and was traditionally used for drying and preserves; by late winter it is acceptable eaten raw.

tree.notes: Average vigour, spur-bearing and regular.

pollination.notes: Late-ish flowering (group 4); pair with another group 3-5 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Temperate western Europe; long grown in England and across continental collections.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance in hot climates; short cool seasons may not let it finish ripening for storage.

health.other: Reported as having good general disease resistance; specific susceptibilities not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity worth growing for its unusual lemon-shaped fruit and long keeping. Pick in October and store cool; use for cooking first and eat the remainder raw in late winter.

varieties.name: Liberty

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Macoun x PRI 54-12 (a Purdue selection carrying Malus floribunda scab resistance)
origin.raised_by: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station (R.C. Lamb)

varieties.history: Crossed at Geneva, New York in 1955 and released in 1978 as a disease-resistant McIntosh-type apple. It became one of the standard low-spray apples for home and organic orchards in North America.

look.description: Dark red, striped colour over almost the whole fruit, with a little russet in the stalk cavity.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy, pale yellow flesh with a sprightly, vinous McIntosh-family flavour, sharper and better balanced than many of its relatives. Improves for a few weeks after picking and makes a pink-tinged sauce.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Dec; improves a few weeks after picking

tree.notes: Sets far more fruit than it can size; thin hard or apples stay small and the tree slips into alternate bearing.

pollination.notes: Orange Pippin lists group 2; other lists place it mid-season, so pair it with a group 2-3 partner.

climate.best_climates: Humid, cold-winter regions such as the north-eastern US and upper Midwest, where its scab and rust resistance saves a lot of spraying; also fine in the UK.
climate.poor_climates: Very hot summers give softer, less well coloured fruit, as with other McIntosh relatives.

health.other: Carries the Vf scab-resistance gene (immune to common scab races, though Vf-breaking races exist in parts of Europe). Main cultural problem is overcropping.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the best choices for an unsprayed garden apple. Thin fruitlets to one per cluster, and plant with an early-to-mid season partner.

varieties.name: Ligol

origin.place: Research Institute of Pomology and Floriculture, Skierniewice, Poland
origin.parentage: Linda x Golden Delicious
origin.raised_by: S. Zagaja, A. Przybyła and J. Krzewiński at Skierniewice (seedlings from crosses by W. Dzięcioł)

varieties.history: Selected at Skierniewice in 1972 from seedlings of Linda x Golden Delicious crosses made in the 1960s, and entered in the Polish national variety register in 1997. It became one of Poland's most widely grown commercial apples and is also planted in Lithuania and neighbouring countries.

look.description: Large to very large, glossy fruit, ribbed at the eye and somewhat irregular, with a diffuse carmine blush over greenish-yellow.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy flesh that is sweet with a delicate tartness, scoring well with consumer panels. Holds its firmness unusually well through long storage.
taste.storage_change: Flesh stays firm a long time in store (Polish Wikipedia).
taste.peak: Picked early October in Poland, eating-ripe a few weeks later; keeps to Feb-Mar (Apr in CA)

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous with a dense, pyramidal crown that needs thinning out. Fairly resistant to bark diseases and winter cold.

pollination.notes: Flowers mid-season (approximately group 3) and is a good pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter continental climates of central and eastern Europe, where it is frost-hardy and stores into spring.
climate.poor_climates: Areas with heavy fire blight pressure, and hot summers that would soften the fruit and dull its colour.

health.other: Very susceptible to fire blight; moderately susceptible to scab and mildew. Stores well with good resistance to storage rots.

varieties.grow_notes: Suits an open, sunny site in a cold-winter climate; thin the dense crown for light and air. Avoid areas where fire blight is common.

varieties.name: Limbertwig

origin.place: Southern Appalachians, USA (North Carolina, Georgia, Tennessee, Virginia)
origin.parentage: Not a single clone: a family of related Appalachian seedlings sharing a drooping habit and similar fruit

varieties.history: Limbertwig is a group name for a family of old Appalachian apples, recorded before the 1830s, whose trees share long, drooping, limber branches. Dozens of local strains exist (Old Fashioned, Red, Royal, Victoria, Brushy Mountain, Kentucky and others); this record describes the group in general and the Old Fashioned type in particular, which is said to come from north Georgia in the early 1800s.

look.description: Medium fruit with rather rough, thick, greenish-yellow skin washed with dull to deep red; appearance varies between strains.

taste.summary: Firm to hard, yellowish, aromatic flesh with a distinctive flavour that improves in storage; Limbertwigs are valued more as long keepers and for pies, jelly and cider than as showy dessert apples. Flavour differs from strain to strain.

tree.notes: The defining feature is the weeping, limber-branched habit; branches bend down under crop, so leave headroom and avoid heavy heading cuts that spoil the form.

pollination.notes: Not recorded for the group; plant with another late-season apple.

climate.best_climates: Upland South: the Blue Ridge and Smoky Mountains and surrounding foothills, with hot summers and cool mountain nights.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, short-season climates may not ripen these late apples; climate values are inferred from region of origin.

health.other: Disease profile not documented and likely varies between strains.

varieties.grow_notes: Choose a named strain from a heritage nursery, since 'Limbertwig' covers many different trees. Give the weeping tree room, pick late and store the fruit for winter use.

varieties.name: Limelight

origin.parentage: Discovery x Greensleeves

varieties.history: Raised around 1985 by the Kent fruit breeder Hugh Ermen at Faversham and released in 2000. Bred as a compact, disease-resistant green dessert apple for gardens.

look.description: Smooth, clear lime-green fruit ripening to pale yellow, without any red flush.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp and juicy with a clean, refreshing sweetness and enough acidity to keep it lively; tasters place it somewhere between Golden Delicious and Granny Smith. Best eaten soon after picking.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct, within a few weeks of picking
taste.peak: picked mid September, keeps 2-3 weeks (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: Weak-growing and compact, so suited to small gardens, patio containers and cordons; crops regularly.

pollination.notes: Needs a diploid partner flowering in group 2-4.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist British gardens, where its scab and mildew resistance pays off.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented in hot or continental climates; a green apple bred in Kent is unlikely to enjoy hot summers.

health.other: Good resistance to scab and mildew is reported, though scab can still appear in wet years.

varieties.grow_notes: An easy, low-spray apple for a small garden. Because the tree is weak-growing, give it a semi-vigorous rootstock such as MM106 or M26 in poorer soil, and plant near another mid-season diploid.

varieties.name: Linda

origin.parentage: Langford Beauty x unknown (open-pollinated)

varieties.history: A Langford Beauty seedling from the Central Experimental Farm in Ottawa that first fruited in 1908, was selected in 1914 and introduced around 1925. It is a parent of Karmen and Lindel.

look.description: Large, rounded pale yellow apple with a deep carmine flush and stripes.

taste.summary: Fine, tender, juicy white flesh that is fairly sweet with gentle acidity and some aroma; one grower notes a strawberry-like flavour. The NFC panel found it rather acid and soft.

tree.notes: Vigorous tree; National Fruit Collection trees have a drooping habit.

pollination.notes: National Fruit Collection blossom dates are early mid-season (about group 2-3).

climate.best_climates: Bred for the cold winters of eastern Ontario; also grown in coastal British Columbia.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented in hot-summer regions.

health.other: No disease information found; short storage life.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy Canadian autumn apple. Allow room for a vigorous tree and eat the crop within a couple of months of picking.

varieties.name: Liveland Raspberry

origin.place: Livonia (Livland Governorate of the Russian Empire, now Latvia/Estonia)

varieties.history: A Baltic apple from the old Livland province, recorded before 1870 and among the 'Russian' apples imported to the American Midwest (credited to A. G. Tuttle of Baraboo, Wisconsin); it was formally introduced in the US in 1883. It is often linked to the ancestry of Melba and is a parent of Joyce.

look.description: Waxy, pale cream apple flushed and striped light crimson; the white flesh is often stained pinkish red.

taste.summary: Fine, very tender white flesh tinged red, mildly sweet with gentle acidity and a light perfume. Unusually for a summer apple it stays pleasant on and off the tree for a short while.
taste.storage_change: Holds its quality on and off the tree better than most apples of its season (Albemarle CiderWorks).

tree.notes: Naturally small, upright and compact tree even on its own roots; inclined to crop every other year.

pollination.notes: National Fruit Collection blossom dates are early mid-season (about group 2-3).

climate.best_climates: Cold continental and northern climates: the Baltic, Scandinavia, the upper Midwest and New England, where its winter-hardiness matters.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers ripen summer apples like this too fast and soften them; it has little advantage in mild climates.

health.other: Biennial bearing is the main recorded fault.

varieties.grow_notes: A compact, very hardy early apple for cold gardens. Thin the fruit in heavy years to even out cropping and eat it within days of picking.

varieties.name: Lobo

origin.place: Central Experimental Farm, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada
origin.parentage: McIntosh, open-pollinated seedling

varieties.history: Raised at Ottawa in 1898 from McIntosh seed and released in 1930. It became widely grown in Scandinavia, Poland and the Baltic region as a hardy, attractive McIntosh-type apple.

look.description: Large, flattish apple flushed and faintly striped dark red with a bloom; the short, stout stalk is often tinged red.

taste.summary: White, juicy McIntosh-type flesh, sweeter and less acid than McIntosh, with a gently vinous character; some tasters find strawberry and caramel hints. Accounts of texture differ: some growers praise its satisfying crunch and say it keeps late, while others find it softens and turns mealy within a few weeks. Cooks well in pies and sauce.
taste.peak: Mid-September to November (La Pomme du Quebec); picked mid September (NFC)

tree.notes: Hardy and a regular cropper. Watch for canker and scab, both common on this variety.

pollination.notes: Average pollinator. Swedish growers pair it with mid-season varieties such as Cox's Orange Pippin, Discovery, James Grieve and Katja.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter, cool-summer climates such as eastern Canada, Scandinavia and the Baltic, where it is fully hardy and colours deeply.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers give soft, poorly coloured fruit; wet, mild regions encourage scab and canker.

health.other: Susceptible to scab and frequently affected by canker; fruit softens quickly after picking.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for cold, northern gardens. Plant on well-drained soil to limit canker, keep the canopy open against scab, and use the fruit soon after picking.

varieties.name: Lodgemore Nonpareil

origin.parentage: Seedling; parents not recorded
origin.raised_by: Mr Cook of Lodgemore; introduced by Clissold

varieties.history: Raised around 1808 by a Mr Cook at Lodgemore near Stroud and put into circulation by Clissold, hence its other name. It is one of the Gloucestershire heritage apples conserved by local orchard groups.

look.description: Small, flattish apple, green ripening to golden yellow, with a light orange-red flush and quite a lot of russet dots and patches.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp and juicy yellowish flesh with a sweet, perfumed, rich flavour typical of the nonpareil type.
taste.best_eaten: Jan-Apr, after a long rest in store

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not well recorded.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records show it flowering about ten days after Cox, close to Edward VII; choose a late-flowering partner (group 5-7).

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist western England and similar; its very late flowering helps it escape spring frosts.
climate.poor_climates: Not recorded outside Britain; hot summers are likely to shorten its keeping life.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Useful in frosty gardens because it blooms so late, but it needs a late-flowering pollinator. Pick in early October and store cool for eating after Christmas.

varieties.name: Lodi

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Montgomery x Yellow Transparent
origin.raised_by: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: Bred at the Geneva station in New York and released in 1924 as an improved Yellow Transparent: larger, firmer and keeping a little longer. It is still grown as an early sauce and pie apple, especially in the northern US.

look.description: Large, smooth, pale green to greenish-yellow apple with no blush.

taste.summary: Juicy, crisp-tender white flesh with a sharp, tangy flavour. Turns soft quickly but cooks down to an excellent smooth sauce.
taste.best_eaten: Aug, within a week or two of picking
taste.storage_change: Orange Pippin: keeps about a week.

tree.notes: Bears young and heavily but tends to alternate; thin hard in heavy years. Ploidy unconfirmed (one source lists it as triploid).

pollination.notes: Early flowering; reported as a poor pollinator, so pair it with another early-flowering variety.

climate.best_climates: Cold northern climates (northern US, Canada, upper Midwest) where an early, hardy cooking apple is wanted.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers make the fruit soften and drop even faster; low-chill regions unsuitable.

health.other: Highly susceptible to cedar-apple rust; overall disease resistance reported as poor.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy early cooker for cold gardens. Thin fruit to reduce biennial bearing, keep it away from junipers in North America, and use the crop promptly.

varieties.name: London Pippin
varieties.history: One of the oldest named English apples, recorded in 1580 and thought to have arisen in Essex or Norfolk. The alternative name Five Crowned Pippin refers to the five prominent knobs around the eye; it was later grown in Somerset as Royal Somerset and travelled widely in Europe under many names.

look.description: Flattish fruit ribbed along the sides and crowned with five bold ridges at the eye; yellow with a dull brownish-red flush on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Crisp, firm, white flesh with moderate acidity and little perfume. Used chiefly for cooking through the winter; its juice has also gone into Somerset cider, where it rates as a low-tannin sweet type.

tree.notes: Little modern growing information.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates, which match the group 4 Lemon Pippin; use a mid-to-late flowering partner.

climate.best_climates: Lowland England and similar temperate climates; long established in European collections.
climate.poor_climates: No reliable evidence for hot or very cold climates.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A historic keeper for heritage orchards. Pick in mid-October, store cool and use for cooking from midwinter onward.

varieties.name: Lord Derby

origin.parentage: Catshead x unknown (a seedling of Catshead, per the National Fruit Collection)

varieties.history: Raised by a Stockport nurseryman named Witham and first recorded in 1862; the National Fruit Collection gives Catshead as one parent. Its near-certain annual cropping made it a staple market cooker in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and it is still a common garden alternative to Bramley.

look.description: Large, tall, boldly ribbed fruit with ridges round a crowned eye; smooth, shiny dark grass-green, ripening to greenish-yellow, with a few russet dots and lines.

taste.summary: A sharp, rather coarse and dry cooker. It is distinctly acidic if picked early and milder once the skin yellows. It bakes well and makes a textured purée; Bunyard noted that the cooked flesh turns a deep golden-red.
taste.storage_change: Acidic if picked young, milder once fully ripe and yellowing (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: A sturdy, upright, vigorous spur-bearer that crops heavily almost every year. It tolerates cold, heavy soils and northern gardens.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 4, with blossom that resists frost well. Plant a group 3-5 diploid partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool, wet temperate climates, including northern England, Wales and frost-prone sites, where its hardy blossom and disease resistance pay off.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot climates. Some growers in the far north of Scotland find the fruit bland there.

health.other: Very resistant to scab, but brown rot can spoil fruit on the tree and in store. The flesh browns quickly once cut.

varieties.grow_notes: A tough, dependable cooker for heavy clay, cold or damp gardens where Bramley struggles. Thin the fruit for size, and remove brown-rotted fruit promptly.

varieties.name: Lord Grosvenor
varieties.history: Its origin was never recorded; it was regarded as a new apple around 1872. Hogg grouped it with the pale, early English codlin-style cookers such as Keswick Codlin and Stirling Castle. It is a parent of Emneth Early (Early Victoria).

look.description: Large, tall-conical fruit, strongly and irregularly ribbed with a puckered eye; even pale straw-yellow that fades almost to white when ripe.

taste.summary: Soft, white, juicy flesh with a clean, sharp acidity. A codlin-type cooker for late summer, used straight from the tree.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-Sep, for cooking soon after picking
taste.peak: Picked mid August (NFC).

tree.notes: Bunyard rated it among the most prolific of all apples, though not a strong grower, and said it usually needs fruit thinning to give well-shaped apples. He found it did well on dry soils.

pollination.notes: No published group found. Estimated as group 3 from National Fruit Collection flowering dates, which put it in bloom alongside Lord Hindlip. Plant a group 2-4 partner.

climate.best_climates: Temperate British gardens, including drier eastern soils; an early cooker that ripens even in short or cool seasons.
climate.poor_climates: Little information. Soft early fruit is unlikely to keep or travel well in hot weather.

health.other: Disease behaviour is not well recorded. The main problem is overcropping, which leads to small, misshapen fruit.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow it for an early supply of cooking apples, and thin the fruitlets hard in heavy-setting years. It tolerates a drier site better than many cookers.

varieties.name: Lord Hindlip

origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: A Worcestershire seedling of unknown parentage, introduced by Watkins of Hereford. It received an RHS Award of Merit in 1896 and a First Class Certificate in 1898. Bunyard saw it as a strong candidate for the late-season market dessert apple growers wanted.

look.description: Regular, small-to-medium conical fruit, nearly covered by a dark crimson flush and stripes over greenish-yellow, with patches of fine russet netting.

taste.summary: Firm, very fine-grained, juicy white flesh with a balanced sweet-sharp taste and a hint of the old Victorian aromatic richness. Eaten in October it can taste muted and watery; the flavour builds in store, peaking after the New Year and lasting into spring. Holds its shape when cooked.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Mar; at its best after a couple of months in store
taste.storage_change: benefits from storage; flavour best early in the new year and still passable in May (Orange Pippin)
taste.peak: early in the new year (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: A slender, upright-spreading spur-bearer of average vigour that crops well and regularly; easy for beginners.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 3; plant any group 2-4 diploid nearby.

climate.best_climates: Western and southern Britain and other mild, damp temperate areas with an autumn long enough to ripen a mid-October apple.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season northern sites may not ripen it fully. Hot summers are untested and probably poor for colour.

health.other: Rated as having good general disease resistance, with some resistance to scab.

varieties.grow_notes: A good late keeper for a sheltered, sunny garden. Leave the fruit on the tree until mid-October and store it cool, then eat from midwinter.

varieties.name: Lord Lambourne

origin.parentage: James Grieve x Worcester Pearmain

varieties.history: Raised by the Laxton Brothers of Bedford in 1907 and released in 1923, after winning the RHS Bunyard Cup in 1921 and an Award of Merit in 1923. It still holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit. A brighter-coloured sport (Lady Lambourne) and a russeted sport (Russet Lambourne) are also known.

look.description: Neat, evenly rounded medium fruit; greenish-yellow with an orange-red flush and darker red stripes over about half the skin, sometimes with a little russet.

taste.summary: Juicy, fairly crisp cream flesh. Sweetness is balanced by a lively James Grieve acidity and a gentle English aromatic flavour. Less complex than the later aromatic apples, but one of the earliest of the type.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Nov; best within a few weeks of picking
taste.peak: Picked mid to late September; stores until November (Walcot), 2 months refrigerated (Salt Spring)

tree.notes: A neat, easy, beginner-friendly tree that crops early and regularly. Being a partial tip-bearer, prune lightly and leave some unpruned one-year shoots.

pollination.notes: Early-flowering (group 2) and partly self-fertile, but crops better with a group 1-3 partner. The blossom has some frost tolerance.

climate.best_climates: Cool to mild, damp temperate climates such as the UK and Ireland, including the north and Scotland.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, dry summers: growers in arid inland areas report split fruit and weak growth.

health.other: Rated very resistant to scab and fairly resistant to canker. Fruit can crack after drought.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the most reliable early dessert apples for a small garden. Suits most soils in a sunny spot; water in dry spells to prevent fruit splitting, and thin heavy sets on young trees.

varieties.name: Lord Suffield

origin.place: Boardman Lane, Middleton, near Manchester, Lancashire, England

varieties.history: Raised by Thomas Thorpe, a hand-loom weaver of Middleton near Manchester, and released around 1836. It was named after Lord Suffield, then lord of the manor of Middleton. It was a leading early codlin in Victorian times until Early Victoria and other varieties replaced it.

look.description: Large, tall, ribbed conical codlin with smooth pale greenish-yellow skin, occasionally with a faint red tinge.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy white flesh with a sharp, fresh acidity; it collapses completely to a fluffy froth when cooked. It is used for cooking straight from the tree and does not keep.
taste.peak: Used from August to November (Wikipedia)

tree.notes: A small, compact, twiggy tree that bears very young and very heavily, but tends to be short-lived.

pollination.notes: Early flowering: the National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 4 May, so group 2 is inferred (it may also overlap group 1). Use an early-blooming partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool, northern English conditions such as Lancashire, where early codlins were valued for their reliable early crops.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, heavy soils make its canker worse, and hot climates would soften and rot this early, tender fruit even faster.

health.other: Very prone to canker, and the fruit is apt to rot on the tree. Trees are short-lived.

varieties.grow_notes: Worth growing only for heritage interest or an early cooking crop, on well-drained soil with prompt removal of cankered wood. Pick and use the fruit as soon as it sizes up in August.

varieties.name: Lucombe's Seedling

origin.place: Lucombe, Pince & Co. nursery, St Thomas, Exeter, Devon

varieties.history: Raised by the Exeter nursery Lucombe, Pince & Co. and described in 1831; it was once widely grown in Devon and Cornwall under local names such as Kirton Fair and Newquay Prizetaker.

look.description: Large, angular pale yellow-green apple streaked with crimson and dotted with dark spots, on a short thick stalk.

taste.summary: Firm, juicy white flesh with a pleasant subacid flavour and a spicy note; used both for the kitchen and for eating.
taste.peak: Use October to January (Wikipedia list).

tree.notes: Not very vigorous.

pollination.notes: National Fruit Collection blossom dates are mid-season (about group 3).

climate.best_climates: The mild, moist south-west of England, where it was popular.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance outside England.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: A West Country heritage apple worth growing in Devon and Cornwall orchards. The tree is modest in vigour, so a more vigorous rootstock suits it.

varieties.name: Macoun

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: McIntosh x Jersey Black

varieties.history: Bred at the Geneva station in New York State, described in 1918 and released in 1923. It was named after W. T. Macoun, the Canadian Dominion Horticulturist, and remains a much-loved New England autumn apple despite its short season.

look.description: Flattish apple almost covered in a dark purplish-red flush and stripes, often with a bluish bloom.

taste.summary: Very crisp, tender, snow-white flesh that bursts with sweet juice and a strong vinous perfume typical of the McIntosh family, with just a little tartness. Best fresh; it loses its snap quickly out of cold storage.
taste.storage_change: Trees of Antiquity: at its best picked and eaten straight from the tree. Orange Pippin: keeps about a week.
taste.peak: Straight from the tree, mid-September onwards

climate_flavour.note: Trees of Antiquity: dark purplish-red blush in cooler summer climates (colour).

tree.notes: Upright and vigorous; strongly inclined to crop every other year and to set small fruit unless thinned early. The short stem makes fruit prone to drop before harvest.

pollination.notes: Needs a diploid partner in group 2-4.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter, cool-autumn regions such as New England, upstate New York, Ontario and Quebec, where it colours deeply and keeps its crunch.
climate.poor_climates: Warm or hot autumns give poorly coloured, soft fruit; in mild maritime Britain it grows but is seldom planted.

health.other: Scab-prone like McIntosh; marked biennial bearing and pre-harvest drop are the main grower complaints. Fruit bruises easily.

varieties.grow_notes: Worth growing where winters are cold and autumns crisp. Thin hard every year to break the alternate-bearing habit and to get decent size, and pick promptly before the fruit drops.

varieties.name: Magnum Bonum

origin.parentage: Seedling grown from seed of the Hall apple

varieties.history: Raised in 1828 in Davidson County, North Carolina, when John Kinney planted seeds of the Hall apple. It became a long-standing southern favourite for early autumn and was grown commercially in Virginia for a time.

look.description: Small to medium yellow apple largely covered with light and dark red streaks and many small pale dots.

taste.summary: Fine-grained, crisp, juicy white flesh, often pink-stained under the skin, with a well-flavoured, aromatic sweet-sharp balance; one grower in England found it a little sharper than Cox. Regarded as one of the best early-autumn southern dessert apples.
taste.peak: Ripens Sept-Oct, keeps fairly well (Big Horse Creek Farm).

tree.notes: Described as a hardy and productive tree; other details are not well documented.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: The piedmont and mountains of the upper South (North Carolina, Virginia), with hot summers and moderate winters; reported to do well in mild south-west England too.
climate.poor_climates: Not well documented; chill and hardiness figures are inferred from its North Carolina origin.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A good early-autumn dessert apple for warm-summer regions. Plant with a pollinator of similar season; the fruit keeps reasonably for a few weeks if stored cool.

varieties.name: Maiden Blush
varieties.history: An old New Jersey apple, recorded before 1817 and later grown across the northern and southern United States. Valued for drying because its slices stay pale, and for sauce and pies.

look.description: Flattened, pale lemon-yellow apple with a sharply defined crimson blush on the side that faced the sun.

taste.summary: Fine, tender, moderately crisp white flesh with a sharp flavour that softens as the fruit ripens. Better for cooking and drying than for long storage.
taste.storage_change: Orange Pippin: sharp at first, mellowing as it ripens. Beach: after December it may look sound but quality is poor.
taste.peak: Beach: September to December.

tree.notes: Little modern growing information.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Eastern US conditions from the North to the South; old nursery catalogues gave picking dates for both regions.
climate.poor_climates: Humid areas with heavy scab pressure.

health.other: Susceptible to scab; rated resistant to cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: A useful heritage apple for drying, sauce and pies. Pick from late August and use within a couple of months.

varieties.name: Maidstone Favourite

origin.parentage: Alexander x Beauty of Bath

varieties.history: Raised by the Maidstone nursery of George Bunyard and Co. and given an RHS Award of Merit in 1913. A Kent early apple from the same firm that introduced Lady Sudeley, now rare outside collections.

look.description: Smallish to medium, flattish, very even fruit, pale green-yellow prettily striped with carmine red.

taste.summary: Fine-textured, juicy and sweet, with a pleasant and slightly distinctive aromatic flavour. An apple for eating within days of picking.

tree.notes: Little growing data recorded. Prune as a normal spur-bearing dessert apple.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not published; National Fruit Collection blossom dates are early-to-mid season, similar to Beauty of Bath.

climate.best_climates: Kent and similar mild south-east English conditions where it was raised.
climate.poor_climates: No records from hot or very cold regions; soft early fruit generally fares badly in hot summers.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A Kent heritage apple for collectors and local-variety orchards. Grow in sun on well-drained loam with an early or mid-season diploid pollinator and pick in mid August.

varieties.name: Maigold

origin.place: Swiss Federal Agricultural Research Station, Wädenswil, Switzerland
origin.parentage: Fraurotacher (Franc Roseau) x Golden Delicious
origin.raised_by: F. Kobel, Swiss Federal Agricultural Research Station, Wädenswil

varieties.history: Selected from a cross made in 1944 at the Swiss federal fruit research station in Wädenswil and released for propagation in 1964. A late-keeping Swiss dessert apple of the post-war decades, it is a parent of Mairac.

look.description: Medium to large, tall conical and often lopsided fruit, green ripening to gold with a bright orange-red flush on the sunny side; skin turns waxy when ripe.

taste.summary: Crunchy, firm, fine-grained and juicy, with a sweet but balanced flavour and honeyed, pear-like notes; tasters report a citrus edge appearing as it keeps. Bruises less readily than most.
taste.storage_change: Slightly honeyed at first, mellowing to a citrus taste in storage; keeps well and resists bruising (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Little published growing data in English.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records it flowering with Golden Delicious (about group 4). Diploid and self-sterile.

climate.best_climates: Central European climates such as the Swiss lowlands, with autumns warm enough to ripen a mid-October apple.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons where a mid-October apple may not sweeten fully; no data from hot climates.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: Treat as a late dessert apple for a warm, sheltered spot. Pick in mid October, store cool, and plant with a group 3-5 diploid pollinator.

varieties.name: Major

origin.place: South Devon and the Blackdown Hills, Somerset, England
origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: A long-established bittersweet of nineteenth-century or earlier date, found in old farm orchards across South Devon and on the eastern side of the Blackdown Hills. Rated as of vintage quality.

look.description: Medium, typical 'Jersey'-type fruit with a pinkish-red flush.

taste.summary: A full bittersweet: high tannin, low acid and good sugar, giving a well-structured cider that can stand alone.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill late Sep-Oct.

tree.notes: Triploid; young trees grow very vigorously, so it is unsuited to the most vigorous rootstocks.

pollination.notes: Triploid, so a poor pollen donor; plant with two other compatible varieties.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp South West England.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No reliable disease data found.

varieties.grow_notes: Use a moderate rootstock to tame its vigour. As an early bittersweet it pairs with early sharps for the first pressings. Remember it needs two pollinators as a triploid.

varieties.name: Malinda
varieties.history: An old Vermont apple of unknown parentage that became important as a hardy parent in the University of Minnesota breeding programme. It appears in the ancestry of Haralson, Beacon, Keepsake, Sweet Sixteen and, more distantly, Honeycrisp.

look.description: Conical, somewhat angular yellow apple with a mottled red blush. Sources disagree on size (small in one list, above medium in Beach).

taste.summary: Dense, juicy flesh that is very low in acid, with a mild sweetness and a pear-like flavour. Long-keeping; rated only fair for quality.
taste.peak: Beach: February to March.

tree.notes: Little growing information; valued for winter hardiness.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Cold northern climates with heavy snowfall, such as Vermont and Minnesota.
climate.poor_climates: Not recorded.

health.other: Not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: Mainly of interest as a historic hardy parent of Minnesota apples. Store the fruit until late winter, when it is at its best.

varieties.name: Malus sieversii

origin.place: Tian Shan and Dzungarian Alatau mountains of Central Asia (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Xinjiang, China)
origin.parentage: Wild species; the principal ancestor of the cultivated apple (Malus domestica)

varieties.history: The wild apple of the Central Asian mountains, named after the botanist Johann Sievers and first described by Ledebour (as Pyrus sieversii) in 1833. Genome sequencing in 2010 confirmed it as the main wild ancestor of the domestic apple, which spread west along the Silk Road. Its fruit forests near Almaty are a conservation priority and the species is classed as vulnerable.

look.description: Very variable from tree to tree: small to medium fruit up to about 7 cm across, in shades from green and yellow to red.

taste.summary: Seedlings vary enormously, from small, sour or astringent crabs to sweet fruit as good as many cultivated apples; there is no single flavour for the species.

tree.notes: Wild trees reach 5-12 m, sucker from the roots and take 6-8 years from seed to first fruit. Many trees colour red in autumn, unlike most domestic apples.

pollination.notes: Self-incompatible like the domestic apple; any compatible apple or crab flowering at the same time can pollinate it.

climate.best_climates: Continental mountain foothills with cold winters and warm summers, like its native Tian Shan.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, humid lowlands and mild-winter regions far from its mountain habitat.

health.other: Wild populations are an important source of disease-resistance and stress-tolerance genes for breeders, but individual trees vary widely.

varieties.grow_notes: Grown mainly by collectors and breeders, usually from seed, so every tree is different. Treat it as a large crab or wildlife tree with plenty of space, and graft from a known good selection if you want edible fruit.

varieties.name: Mank's Codlin
varieties.history: Raised by Kewley at Ballanard on the Isle of Man, where it first fruited in 1815. It spread under many names, including Eve Apple in Scotland and Irish Codlin. It was long a standard cooking apple in northern England, and later reached the Netherlands and Germany.

look.description: Medium, conical, slightly five-sided codlin, smooth and pale yellow, with an orange-red cheek where it gets sun and often a fleshy swelling beside the stalk.

taste.summary: Firm, white, juicy flesh with a brisk acidity and a faint perfume. Picked young it is a sharp cooker that softens when cooked, and by autumn it is mellow enough to eat raw.

tree.notes: A small, compact, very hardy and healthy tree that crops extremely young (nursery trees fruited two years from grafting) and heavily. It suits espaliers and dwarfing stocks.

pollination.notes: Early flowering (National Fruit Collection full bloom around 5 May), so group 2 is inferred. Plant an early-blooming partner.

climate.best_climates: Exposed, cool and wet areas such as the Isle of Man, northern England, Scotland and Ireland; it tolerates shallow soils.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would hurry this early, soft-keeping fruit; it has no record of use in warm regions.

health.other: Long described as a hardy, healthy tree, but specific disease ratings are not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the best old cookers for windy, northern or upland gardens and thin soils, and a good small tree for trained forms. Thin heavy crops so the tree does not exhaust itself.

varieties.name: Mannington's Pearmain

origin.raised_by: Mr Turley (grew the seedling); introduced by John Mannington

varieties.history: Grew from pips in cider pomace thrown out in Mr Turley's garden at Uckfield around 1770, and was put on the market by John Mannington in 1847.

look.description: Roundish greenish-yellow to golden apple with a brownish-red or pinkish flush and some russet.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained, moderately juicy flesh with a rich, sweet, subtly aromatic flavour and a hint of nuttiness.
taste.peak: Use November to March (Wikipedia list).

tree.notes: Reasonably vigorous and a reliable cropper; National Fruit Collection trees have a drooping habit.

pollination.notes: National Fruit Collection blossom dates are mid-late (about group 4).

climate.best_climates: South-east England, where it arose; also grown in coastal British Columbia.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance in hot or very cold regions.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: A Sussex late keeper for heritage collections. Pick in mid October and store until the new year, when the flavour is richest.

varieties.name: Mantet

origin.place: Dominion Experimental Station, Morden, Manitoba, Canada
origin.parentage: Tetofsky x unknown (National Fruit Collection); Orange Pippin gives McIntosh x Tetofsky

varieties.history: Selected in 1928 at the Morden station in Manitoba and introduced in 1929; the name joins 'Man' for Manitoba and 'Tet' for Tetofsky. Bred as a hardy early apple for the Canadian prairies, it is a parent of State Fair.

look.description: Medium to large, narrowly conical and strongly ribbed yellow apple streaked with orange-red.

taste.summary: Tender, fine, creamy flesh that is sweet, juicy and tangy with a good aroma, notably full-flavoured for such an early apple. It turns soft and mealy within days of picking.
taste.storage_change: Orange Pippin: keeps only 1-3 days and soon turns soft and mealy.
taste.peak: Eat from the tree in August.

tree.notes: Spreading habit; very cold-hardy.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering; needs a partner.

climate.best_climates: Cold prairie and northern climates; grown successfully as far north-east as Nova Scotia.
climate.poor_climates: Does not perform well in warm climates.

health.other: Not well documented; growers report scab in unsprayed trees.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the best-flavoured early apples for very cold gardens. Pick over several times as fruit colours and use at once, for eating or sauce.

varieties.name: Margil

origin.place: Probably continental Europe (possibly France); grown in England by 1750

varieties.history: A very old dessert apple, probably of continental European origin, known in England before 1750 and also widespread in Germany and France under Muscat Reinette names. Recent DNA pedigree work has suggested it may be a parent of Cox's Orange Pippin, which would fit their similar flavour.

look.description: Small, conical and noticeably ribbed, orange-gold with streaks of deep red and patches of russet.

taste.summary: Small, russet-flushed apple with a strong, clean, intensely aromatic Cox-style flavour that is sweet and well balanced; some tasters find a pineapple note. Older accounts call the flesh firm and rather dry, but modern growers report it crisp, juicy and never woolly. Keeps one to two months.
taste.storage_change: Albemarle CiderWorks (not counted): keeps well in storage and becomes greasy.
taste.peak: Nov-Feb (Wikipedia)

tree.notes: Average vigour; mainly a spur-bearer with some tip-bearing, so prune lightly. Crops regularly.

pollination.notes: Flowers with Cox; pair with any group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Mild temperate maritime climates; reported to do well in northern districts where Cox struggles.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers likely to make the already dry flesh drier; little record of it in warm regions.

health.other: Some scab resistance reported, with some susceptibility to canker.

varieties.grow_notes: A connoisseur's apple for anyone who wants Cox-like intensity with fewer problems. Because it partly tip-bears, prune lightly, and grow it in a sunny, sheltered spot.

varieties.name: McIntosh Red

origin.parentage: Chance seedling, possibly of Fameuse (Snow Apple) or Saint Lawrence

varieties.history: Found as a wild seedling by the settler John McIntosh while clearing land at Dundela, Ontario, in the early 1800s (the national collection gives 1796). His son Allan began grafting and selling it in the 19th century, and it became the classic apple of eastern Canada and New England and a parent of Macoun, Spartan, Empire and many others.

look.description: Pale green-yellow fruit flushed and striped bright red, with a waxy bloom on the skin.

taste.summary: Bright white, very juicy flesh that is crunchy when fresh but soon softens, with a simple sweet flavour, refreshing acidity and the vinous, perfumed note likened to wild grapes that defines the McIntosh family. The vinous character fades within a few weeks of storage and the flesh can go mealy; it collapses to a smooth sauce when cooked.
taste.storage_change: Keeps reasonably but the vinous flavour fades quickly in store (Orange Pippin); can turn mealy if stored below 2 C (Wikipedia).
taste.peak: Straight from the tree, mid-September onwards.

climate_flavour.note: Best flavour in colder apple regions (Orange Pippin); grows best where nights are cold and autumn days clear, otherwise poor colour and soft flesh (Wikipedia).

tree.notes: Vigorous, spreading and productive; fruit drops readily as it ripens, so pick on time. Stop-drop sprays are routine in commercial orchards.

pollination.notes: Early-flowering; pair with another group 1-3 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter, cool-summer regions: Ontario, Quebec, the Maritimes, New England and the upper Midwest, where cool autumn nights give its bright red colour.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers and warm nights give poor colour and soft fruit, and its scab susceptibility is a burden in humid maritime climates such as Britain.

health.other: Very prone to apple scab; pre-harvest drop and soft, easily bruised fruit are the other weaknesses.

varieties.grow_notes: Best in cold, continental gardens; in damp mild areas expect to manage scab. Plant in an open, airy site, thin crops, and harvest promptly to beat fruit drop.

varieties.name: Médaille d'Or

origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: First propagated around 1865 by the nurseryman Godard at Bois-Guillaume outside Rouen, it won a gold medal from the Seine-Inférieure horticultural society in 1873, hence the name. It reached England in the 1880s.

look.description: Small golden-yellow apple marbled with fine brown russet, often heavier on the sunny side.

taste.summary: A full bittersweet with exceptionally high sugar and tannin and little acid; the juice is rich and aromatic but intensely astringent, so it is usually blended.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous, spreading tree; productive but tends to crop in alternate years.

pollination.notes: Very late flowering; choose an equally late pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Mild Atlantic climates like Normandy and western England, with long autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season areas where its very late fruit cannot ripen.

health.other: Some scab resistance; some fire blight susceptibility; biennial.

varieties.grow_notes: Use sparingly in blends for sugar and tannin. Plant with other very late bloomers such as Dabinett or Stoke Red. Its late blossom avoids most spring frosts.

varieties.name: Medina

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Deacon Jones x Delicious

varieties.history: Raised in 1911 by Richard Wellington at the Geneva station in New York and introduced in 1922-23 as a larger, later Delicious-type apple.

look.description: Ribbed, flattish golden-yellow apple with orange-red to red mottling and streaks.

taste.summary: Tender, fairly coarse yellowish flesh, sweet with low acidity and a pronounced perfumed aroma in the Delicious style.

tree.notes: Tree details not documented.

pollination.notes: National Fruit Collection blossom dates are mid-season (about group 3-4).

climate.best_climates: Bred for western New York; warm-summer, cold-winter climates.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance outside the north-eastern US and English trials.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: A Delicious-style keeper of mainly historical interest. Pick in mid October and store for early winter eating.

varieties.name: Melba

origin.place: Central Experimental Farm, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada
origin.parentage: McIntosh seedling; the pollen parent is often given as Liveland Raspberry but is not firmly documented
origin.raised_by: W. T. Macoun, Central Experimental Farm

varieties.history: Raised in 1898 by W. T. Macoun at Canada's Central Experimental Farm in Ottawa and released in 1909; it is generally said to be named after the opera singer Nellie Melba. It won the American Pomological Society's Wilder Medal in 1927 and became a leading summer apple in Canada and Scandinavia.

look.description: Pale yellow apple washed and striped with pinkish to crimson red, with a whitish bloom and somewhat ribbed shape.

taste.summary: Snow-white, crisp and juicy flesh that softens fairly quickly, with a sweet, lightly tart, wine-like flavour and the perfumed skin aroma typical of the McIntosh family. Also makes good sauce.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-early Sep; eat soon after picking or use for sauce
taste.peak: Picked mid August (NFC).

tree.notes: Very productive and bears young, but strongly inclined to alternate cropping; thin hard in heavy years. Fruit bruises easily.

pollination.notes: UK flowering group not reliably published; National Fruit Collection blossom dates are early-to-mid season, similar to Beauty of Bath.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter continental and northern climates such as eastern Canada, the northern US and Scandinavia, where it is very winter-hardy.
climate.poor_climates: Hot humid summers bring soft fruit, poor colour and heavy scab pressure; mild, wet maritime climates also favour scab.

health.other: Susceptible to scab like other McIntosh offspring; strongly biennial; fruit bruises easily.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the hardiest good-quality summer apples, worth growing in cold districts. Thin fruit every year to curb biennial bearing, and spray or choose an open, airy site where scab is common.

varieties.name: Melon

origin.place: East Bloomfield, Ontario County, New York, from seed brought from Connecticut

varieties.history: Grew from seed carried from Connecticut to the orchard of Heman Chapin at East Bloomfield, New York, around 1800, and was introduced in 1845. It was regarded in the 19th century as a first-rate dessert apple.

look.description: Medium to large, broadly conical apple with pale whitish-yellow skin striped and partly flushed red.

taste.summary: Fine-grained, crisp yet very tender and very juicy yellowish flesh, sweet with gentle acidity and a noticeable aroma. Quality falls away if kept much past mid-winter.
taste.storage_change: Beach (1905): if kept past January in ordinary storage it soon loses flavour and quality.
taste.peak: Beach: October to February, best before late winter.

tree.notes: Little modern growing information.

pollination.notes: Late-ish flowering; plant with another mid-to-late variety.

climate.best_climates: Long-established in New York State and New England conditions.
climate.poor_climates: Not recorded.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage dessert apple for collectors. Pick in mid-October and eat before late winter, when flavour declines.

varieties.name: Melrose

origin.place: Ohio Agricultural Experiment Station, Wooster, Ohio
origin.parentage: Jonathan x Red Delicious
origin.raised_by: Freeman S. Howlett, Ohio Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: Bred by Freeman Howlett at Wooster from a cross made in the 1930s and introduced in 1944; it is the official state apple of Ohio. It found a second home in Europe, where it became a significant late-keeping variety in Belgium, northern France and Poland.

look.description: Broad, flattish fruit streaked and flushed dark red over yellow-green, with patches of russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse but juicy cream flesh with a Jonathan-like sweet-sharp balance, milder than Jonathan; some tasters notice pineapple. Plain when first picked and then best in pies, it develops a fuller, fruity aroma after two or three months in store, from around Christmas.
taste.storage_change: best after Christmas, when it develops its fruity aroma (Orange Pippin)
taste.peak: after Christmas (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: Vigorous, vase-shaped tree that crops heavily and regularly; scab control is usually needed.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 3; average pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter continental and north-west European climates (Ohio, Belgium, Poland) with cool autumns that colour the fruit and a long enough season to finish it.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, humid areas without a spray programme because of scab; warm-night regions give poorer colour.

health.other: Scab is the main problem; slightly prone to mildew; some resistance to cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it space or a semi-dwarfing rootstock and an open, airy site to limit scab. Pick in mid October and store for several weeks before eating.

varieties.name: Mère de Ménage
varieties.history: Known in Britain by the late 1700s, but its origin is uncertain. Bunyard considered it most probably Continental (it was grown in Belgium as Queen Emma) but distinct from the French apple of the same name. It was widely grown in East Anglia as a long-keeping kitchen apple. Old catalogues often confuse it with Gloria Mundi and other giant cookers.

look.description: Very large, irregular, ribbed, flat-conical fruit; almost covered with dull brownish-crimson and broad darker stripes, scattered with conspicuous pale dots.

taste.summary: Firm, coarse, greenish flesh with a brisk, sharp flavour, juicy when fresh but drier in store. A first-rate cooker in its day and a good keeper.
taste.peak: Early October; keeps 3-4 months refrigerated (Salt Spring)

tree.notes: Bunyard describes a vigorous tree that grows large and spreading, with only moderate cropping. Give it room.

pollination.notes: No published group found. Estimated as group 3 from National Fruit Collection flowering dates. Ploidy is unrecorded, so plant two partners to be safe.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate lowlands of eastern England and the Low Countries, where it was traditionally grown.
climate.poor_climates: No record from warm climates. A late, large apple that probably needs a long, mild autumn.

health.other: Disease responses are not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage curiosity for a large garden or orchard. Plant it on a vigorous rootstock with plenty of space, and store the fruit cool for winter cooking.

varieties.name: Meridian

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Maidstone, Kent, England
origin.parentage: Falstaff x Cox's Orange Pippin
origin.raised_by: Dr Frank Alston, East Malling Research Station

varieties.history: Bred at East Malling by Frank Alston from Falstaff and Cox and introduced in 1999 as a Cox-flavoured apple that is easier to grow. It has been sold mainly to gardeners rather than commercial growers.

look.description: Clean, smooth apple with a green-yellow ground, flushed and striped orange-red, with little russet.

taste.summary: Crisp and exceptionally juicy, with a delicate, well-balanced sweet-sharp flavour in the Cox mould but with less depth; tasters pick out hints of lemon and melon. Best within two or three weeks of picking.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Nov, within a few weeks of picking
taste.peak: Keeps 2-3 weeks (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: Average vigour, regular and heavy cropping spur-bearer; thin in heavy years.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cool, temperate English-type climates; bred for gardens in southern Britain.
climate.poor_climates: Little grown outside Britain; hot summers are likely to soften fruit and dull colour.

health.other: Good general disease resistance with some resistance to scab and mildew; some susceptibility to woolly aphid.

varieties.grow_notes: A low-fuss alternative to Cox for gardens in southern and central Britain. Plant with any mid-season pollinator and eat the fruit fairly soon after picking, as it does not keep long.

varieties.name: Merton Delight

origin.place: John Innes Horticultural Institution, Merton, London, England
origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Golden Pippin (National Fruit Collection); Orange Pippin gives Cox's Orange Pippin x Golden Russet
origin.raised_by: M. B. Crane, John Innes Institution

varieties.history: One of the Merton seedlings raised by M. B. Crane at the John Innes Institution in the 1930s from a Cox cross. It was not taken up commercially and was dropped from British trials in 1959.

look.description: Medium, flattish yellow fruit with pinkish-red stripes.

taste.summary: Tender, crisp, creamy flesh with a sweet to gently acid flavour.

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not recorded.

pollination.notes: No published group found; estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates and its Cox parentage.

climate.best_climates: Southern English conditions, where it was raised and trialled.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A rare collection apple; grow as for Cox, with a group 3 partner and a sheltered site.

varieties.name: Merton Russet

origin.place: John Innes Horticultural Institution, Merton, Surrey (now south London), England
origin.parentage: Sturmer Pippin x Cox's Orange Pippin
origin.raised_by: M.B. Crane, John Innes Horticultural Institution

varieties.history: A deliberate cross made in 1921 by M.B. Crane at the John Innes institute in Merton, combining the long-keeping Sturmer Pippin with Cox. It was named in 1943 and is kept in the National Fruit Collection, but it never became a commercial apple.

look.description: Medium, truncated-conical fruit with a yellow ground largely overlaid by russet, showing some red flush through it.

taste.summary: Small golden russet from a Sturmer Pippin x Cox cross, with very crisp, juicy, deep-yellow flesh and a complex sweet, spicy flavour. A late apple that holds its quality into the winter.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Feb, after some weeks in store

tree.notes: Little published growing data. Both parents are diploid spur-bearers, so treat it as a normal spur-pruned diploid until it shows otherwise.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 2 and flowers early at Brogdale; pair with an early-to-mid flowering diploid (groups 1-3).

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate lowland Britain and similar maritime climates with long, mild autumns to finish a mid-October apple.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot or very cold climates; very short seasons may not ripen it, and hot summers are likely to blunt its acidity.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded. Its Cox parent passes on canker and mildew susceptibility to many offspring, so watch for both.

varieties.grow_notes: A collector's russet for a sunny, sheltered garden in southern Britain. Plant with an early-flowering partner, pick in mid October and store cool to eat after Christmas.

varieties.name: Merton Worcester

origin.place: John Innes Horticultural Institution, Merton, Surrey (now London), England
origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Worcester Pearmain
origin.raised_by: M. B. Crane, John Innes Institute

varieties.history: Crossed at the John Innes Institute at Merton in 1914, it was not named until 1947 and reached growers around 1948; the RHS gave it an Award of Merit in 1950. The hope was a Worcester with Cox's aroma, but it turned out much more like its Worcester parent. It is a parent of the scab-resistant Gavin.

look.description: Broadly conical, greenish-yellow apple mostly covered in red, hard to tell apart from Worcester Pearmain.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained and juicy, with a pleasant sweet flavour. Growers describe it as an improved Worcester rather than a Cox, lacking the aromatic depth that was hoped for.
taste.peak: September-October, soon after an early-September pick (Wikipedia list).

tree.notes: Reported as a regular cropper; was grown on a small commercial scale in England. Little else is recorded about the tree.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 10 May, a few days ahead of Cox, so group 3 is inferred. Orange Pippin rates it an average pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cool maritime summers like southern and central England, where Worcester types colour well and keep their freshness.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to soften the fruit and dull its colour; mild-winter regions will not meet an English apple's chill requirement.

health.other: No specific disease record found; parent Worcester Pearmain is known for some scab tolerance but mildew susceptibility.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow it as you would Worcester Pearmain: an open sunny site and a mid-season diploid partner. Pick in early September and eat within a few weeks.

varieties.name: Michaelmas Red

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Kent, England
origin.parentage: McIntosh x Worcester Pearmain
origin.raised_by: H. M. Tydeman, East Malling Research Station

varieties.history: Raised in 1929 by H. M. Tydeman at East Malling from McIntosh x Worcester Pearmain, the same cross that produced Tydeman's Early Worcester. The National Fruit Collection lists it as Tydeman's Michaelmas Red; the name refers to ripening around Michaelmas (29 September).

look.description: Medium, truncate-conical fruit with greenish-yellow skin largely covered by streaked red.

taste.summary: Rather soft, very juicy greenish-white flesh with a sweet, refreshing, vinous flavour that shows its McIntosh parentage.

tree.notes: Little growing information is recorded; it is rarely planted outside collections. Both parents are diploid.

pollination.notes: No published group found. Estimated as group 3 from National Fruit Collection flowering dates; plant a group 2-4 partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate climates like south-east England. Its McIntosh and Worcester parents both colour best with cool autumn nights.
climate.poor_climates: Warm-night regions are likely to give poorly coloured, soft fruit (inferred from its parents).

health.other: Disease behaviour is not recorded for this variety.

varieties.grow_notes: A collector's early-autumn dessert apple. Grow it like Tydeman's Early Worcester in a sunny, open spot, and eat the fruit fresh because the soft flesh does not keep long.

varieties.name: Michelin

origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: Raised by the Yvetot nurseryman Legrand, it first fruited in 1872 and was named after the cider pomologist Henri Michelin. Herefordshire's Woolhope Club brought it to England in the 1880s, and despite being scarce in France it became one of the most planted English cider apples of the twentieth century.

look.description: Small-to-medium green apple, similar to Brown Snout but without the russet patch at the eye.

taste.summary: A medium bittersweet with good sugar, low acid and fair tannin; reliable but rather neutral, so it is usually blended rather than used alone.

tree.notes: Valued for dependable, regular heavy crops without strong biennialism; a long-standing commercial partner for Dabinett.

pollination.notes: Partly self-fertile; often used as a pollinator in bush cider orchards.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist maritime climates; widely grown in English and New World cider orchards.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season areas; humid regions with heavy scab pressure.

health.other: Scab reports vary from some resistance to moderate susceptibility.

varieties.grow_notes: A reliable workhorse cider apple for blending. Grows well in intensive bush orchards. Pick when fruit starts to drop.

varieties.name: Miller's Seedling
varieties.history: Raised in 1848 by James Miller at Newbury in Berkshire and given an RHS Award of Merit in 1906. Popular with Victorian and Edwardian gardeners as a sweet, juicy early apple; a redder sport, Red Miller, also exists.

look.description: Pale greenish-yellow, flattish apple with a light pink-red flush and fine red stripes on the sunny side.

taste.summary: White, very juicy flesh, crisp but light when first picked and soon softening, with a sweet, refreshingly tart and fragrant flavour. It bruises at the slightest knock and goes waxy within about a week, so eat it straight from the tree.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-mid Sep, fresh from the tree
taste.peak: Picked late August (NFC).

tree.notes: Crops very heavily in its 'on' years and then rests, so thin fruitlets hard to even out cropping.

pollination.notes: Usually placed in early flowering group 2 (one guide gives 3); partly self-fertile but sets better with a partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool, mild temperate climates like southern and central England.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers make the soft, easily bruised fruit deteriorate even faster; no records from hot regions.

health.other: Average disease resistance. Main faults are a strong biennial habit and fruit that bruises very easily.

varieties.grow_notes: A rewarding sweet early apple for gardens if thinned every year to avoid feast-and-famine cropping. Handle the fruit gently and eat or juice it within a week of picking.

varieties.name: Milton

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York, USA
origin.parentage: Yellow Transparent x McIntosh
origin.raised_by: Richard Wellington, New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: Crossed in 1909 by Richard Wellington at Geneva and introduced in 1923 by the New York State Fruit Testing Association. An early-autumn McIntosh-type apple.

look.description: Medium, ribbed, conical fruit, pale yellow largely covered by a deep cherry-red flush.

taste.summary: Soft, fine and very white flesh, juicy and sweet with low acidity and a hint of raspberry.

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not well recorded.

pollination.notes: Group 2 per Orange Pippin; early-flowering at Brogdale.

climate.best_climates: Cool north-eastern US and Canadian climates suited to its McIntosh and Yellow Transparent parents.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; soft early fruit is unlikely to stand hot weather.

health.other: Rated very resistant to cedar-apple rust in Arkansas trials; other diseases not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Eat soon after picking. Pair with another early-flowering apple for pollination.

varieties.name: Minnehaha

origin.place: University of Minnesota Fruit Breeding Farm, Excelsior, Minnesota
origin.parentage: Originally recorded as a Malinda seedling; a 2022 DNA pedigree study (Luby et al., cited by Wikipedia) indicates Wealthy x (Ben Davis x Fameuse).

varieties.history: The first apple released by the University of Minnesota breeding programme, selected in 1914 and introduced in 1920. Its recorded pedigree was revised by DNA work a century later.

look.description: Flattish yellow apple streaked with dark red.

taste.summary: Rather soft, coarse flesh with a mildly acid, faintly sweet flavour, according to the National Fruit Collection; little else is recorded about its eating quality.

tree.notes: Little documented beyond its Minnesota origin; bred for winter hardiness.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 9 May, so group 3 is inferred (group 2 is possible). Self-fertility not recorded; assume a partner is needed.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates with short warm summers, such as Minnesota and the upper Midwest, for which it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, humid summers are likely to give soft, poorly coloured fruit; mild-winter regions will not satisfy its chilling need.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: Of mainly historical interest as the first Minnesota-bred apple. Treat as a hardy mid-season dessert apple and provide a pollination partner.

varieties.name: Mio

origin.parentage: Worcester Pearmain x Oranie
origin.raised_by: Emil Johansson, Alnarp horticultural research station

varieties.history: Crossed in 1932 at Alnarp in southern Sweden and sold from 1956; named after Astrid Lindgren's children's book 'Mio, min Mio'. A popular early-autumn garden apple in Sweden.

look.description: Medium to large, ribbed, conical fruit, mostly red-striped over a pale green ground; skin becomes greasy.

taste.summary: Soft, white flesh tinged with pink, sweet with a light acidity. The National Fruit Collection found the flavour rather insipid in Kent.

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not well recorded.

pollination.notes: Swedish sources call it medium-early flowering and list James Grieve, Katja, Melba and Transparente Blanche among good partners.

climate.best_climates: Southern and central Sweden (Swedish zones I-IV) and similar cool northern climates.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; in the milder, warmer English climate its flavour was judged dull.

health.other: Good scab resistance reported in Sweden.

varieties.grow_notes: A garden apple for cool northern climates; pick in early September and use promptly.

varieties.name: Mollie's Delicious

origin.place: New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station, New Brunswick, New Jersey
origin.parentage: (Golden Delicious x Edgewood) x (Red Gravenstein x Close); not a sport of Red Delicious despite the name
origin.raised_by: G.W. Schneider, New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station (Rutgers)

varieties.history: Crossed in 1948 in the Rutgers apple programme in New Jersey and released in 1966. Despite its name it has no connection with Red Delicious; Golden Delicious and Gravenstein sit in its pedigree, and it was later used as a parent in the PRI scab-resistance programme that produced Williams' Pride.

look.description: Big, tall, strongly ribbed fruit with a yellow skin washed and mottled with pinkish to bright red.

taste.summary: Sweet and mild, reminiscent of a fresher, slightly sharper Golden Delicious, with cream flesh that is juicy and fairly crisp when picked at the right moment but can turn soft and starchy if picked early or left too long. Noted for a pleasant lingering aftertaste.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, fresh from the tree; keeps better than most earlies in a fridge
taste.storage_change: quality holds at least 10 weeks under refrigeration (Orange Pippin)
taste.peak: picked late August (NFC)

tree.notes: Little UK growing data. In the southern USA it has a reputation as one of the few good apples that fruits reliably in mild-winter areas.

pollination.notes: Sources differ: Brogdale records it flowering a few days after Cox, while Orange Pippin lists group 5. Plant with a group 3-5 diploid partner.

climate.best_climates: Warm-temperate areas with hot summers and fairly mild winters, such as the US mid-Atlantic and upper South, where it ripens well ahead of the worst heat.
climate.poor_climates: Colour is slow to develop where nights stay warm, so fruit may stay mostly green in the Deep South; in cool, dull summers the fruit may lack sweetness. Chill figure is an estimate from its reported success in mild-winter regions.

health.other: Rated very resistant to cedar-apple rust by the University of Arkansas. Other disease behaviour poorly recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A good early apple for warmer gardens where Cox-types struggle. Give it full sun to help the blush develop and a mid-to-late flowering partner; pick when the ground colour turns from green to yellow.

varieties.name: Monidel

origin.parentage: Red-coloured bud sport of Delbarestivale (Delcorf)

varieties.history: A redder-skinned bud sport of Delbarestivale (Delcorf), the early French dessert apple raised at the Delbard nurseries. It is treated as the same apple as its parent apart from the stronger red colour.

look.description: Yellow apple heavily striped and flushed red, redder overall than ordinary Delbarestivale.

taste.summary: As Delbarestivale: sweet, juicy and fairly crisp, with a gentle aromatic quality and low sharpness. Best eaten soon after picking.
