tree.notes: Grows as a narrow single column with short fruiting spurs, needing almost no pruning; ideal for pots and very small spaces.

pollination.notes: Early flowering; pair with another early-to-mid diploid, such as another Ballerina.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate gardens such as the UK and northern Europe, where it was bred and tested.
climate.poor_climates: Little evidence from hot-summer regions; McIntosh-type colour and texture usually suffer in heat.

health.other: Disease resistance described as average; specific ratings not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow in a large container or a sunny border where space is tight; keep the leader single and simply remove any side shoots that grow long. Feed and water well, as columnar trees in pots dry out quickly.

varieties.name: Polly
varieties.history: A Cornish apple sent to the National Fruit Trials in 1954; nothing more is known of its origin. Not to be confused with Polly Prosser (a Cox seedling) or the Somerset apple Polly Whitehair.

look.description: Broad, rounded-conical apple with a greenish-yellow skin and little or no russet.

taste.summary: Soft white flesh with a sweet, gently acidic flavour; usable both raw and in the kitchen.
taste.peak: Picked early September (NFC).

tree.notes: No published growing data.

pollination.notes: Brogdale flowering dates are close to Cox, so group 3 is assumed.

climate.best_climates: Mild, wet south-west England, where it originated; likely suited to other mild maritime areas.
climate.poor_climates: No records outside the UK; climate values are inferred from origin.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded, though Cornish local varieties are often chosen for tolerance of damp conditions.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for a heritage collection in the south-west. Use the fruit promptly as the flesh softens quickly; plant with a group 2-4 partner.

varieties.name: Polly Prosser

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Duke of Devonshire

varieties.history: Raised in Maidstone, Kent, in 1946 by J.H. Cooper from Cox crossed with the late-keeping Duke of Devonshire. It is held in the National Fruit Collection but is little known outside heritage collections.

look.description: Medium-large, flattish, slightly ribbed fruit, green-yellow with orange streaks.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse yellowish-white flesh with a sweet, mildly acidic and rich flavour. Few further tasting notes are published.
taste.peak: picked early October (NFC)

tree.notes: No published growing data.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not published; it flowers mid-season at Brogdale.

climate.best_climates: South-east England, where it was raised.
climate.poor_climates: No record of performance elsewhere.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded; its Cox parent often passes on canker and mildew susceptibility.

varieties.grow_notes: A Kentish heritage apple for collectors. Grow it like Cox, in a sheltered sunny site with good drainage, and plant a mid-season pollinator nearby.

varieties.name: Pomme Gris

origin.place: St Lawrence valley, Quebec (French Canada); possibly derived from a French grey reinette

varieties.history: An old russet apple of French Canada, long grown around Montreal and the St Lawrence and thought by some to descend from a French grey reinette. It was among the apples planted by Thomas Jefferson at Monticello and remains a heritage favourite in north-eastern North America.

look.description: Small, flattish apple covered in grey-brown to golden russet.

taste.summary: A rich, sweet, nutty russet with firm, fine flesh and a sprightly finish; improves for a few weeks after picking.
taste.peak: Very late (early November); keeps 2-3 months refrigerated (Salt Spring)

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not well recorded.

pollination.notes: Pollination details not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter north-eastern North America (Quebec, New England, New York); also grown historically in Virginia.
climate.poor_climates: No reliable reports; very warm, low-chill regions are unlikely to suit it.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy heritage russet for cold gardens. Plant with another diploid that flowers at a similar time and store the fruit cool to bring out its flavour.

varieties.name: Porter's Perfection

origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: Associated with Charles Porter of East Lambrook in south Somerset and introduced in the early 1900s. A late bittersharp valued for blending and occasionally for single-variety cider.

look.description: Conical fruit with a pale cream ground mostly covered by a dark red flush.

taste.summary: A bittersharp with high acid and fairly mild tannin; tart if picked early or grown in a cool spot, it needs a few weeks of storage before milling.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; store about a month, then mill Dec.

tree.notes: Vigorous, heavy-cropping tree with some tendency to alternate years.

pollination.notes: Needs a compatible pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp maritime climates with long autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season regions; the very late fruit needs a long autumn.

health.other: Generally healthy, with some resistance to scab and canker.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the last cider apples to pick; let the fruit mellow in store before pressing. A good source of acid to balance bittersweets.

varieties.name: Pott's Seedling
varieties.history: Raised by Samuel Potts at Ashton-under-Lyne around 1849. It has been suggested as the unconfirmed parent of James Grieve. The National Fruit Collection also lists Holland Pippin and Dean's Codlin among its synonyms.

look.description: Large, plain pale green to yellow apple with a glossy skin that bruises easily.

taste.summary: Soft, fine, greenish-white flesh with a clear acidity. Cooks down to a smooth puree that needs little sugar, while holding enough acid to keep slices from browning.
taste.peak: September-October (Wikipedia list).

tree.notes: Grower reports mention crops that vary from year to year and a tree that stayed healthy without spraying.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 12 May, so group 3 is inferred.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist northern English climates like the one it was raised in.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; probably unsuited to hot or mild-winter regions.

health.other: No formal disease ratings found. The fruit bruises easily.

varieties.grow_notes: An early cooking apple from north-west England. Handle the fruit gently and use it within a few weeks.

varieties.name: Poveshon

origin.place: Slopes of the Watchung Mountains, Essex County, New Jersey, USA

varieties.history: An 18th-century New Jersey cider apple, grown in the same Essex County district as Harrison and Campfield both before and after the Revolution. William Coxe described it in 1817. It was long counted as lost, but a possible survivor was found in upstate New York in 2015 and still needs confirming.

look.description: A small, flat apple with smooth deep-red skin streaked lengthwise with darker red blotches and dotted with small pale spots. The flesh is rich yellow.

taste.summary: Old descriptions call the yellow flesh sweet and unusually dry. It was valued mainly for early-season cider rather than for eating.
taste.best_eaten: Pressed for early cider as it ripens and drops in Sep-Oct

tree.notes: Old accounts describe a very straight tree with upright branches that cropped heavily.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: The humid continental climate of northern New Jersey, where it was a standard cider apple.
climate.poor_climates: No records outside the north-eastern United States.

health.other: Not recorded; the fruit drops when ripe.

varieties.grow_notes: Only of interest if the 2015 candidate tree is confirmed and propagated. Gather fallen fruit promptly for pressing.

varieties.name: Prairie Spy

origin.place: University of Minnesota Fruit Breeding Farm, Excelsior, Minnesota
origin.parentage: Not firmly recorded. One source gives Wealthy x Northwestern Greening; Northern Spy ancestry has been suggested but not confirmed.

varieties.history: Grown from seed planted in 1914 at the University of Minnesota fruit breeding farm, selected in 1923 as Minnesota 1007 and named in 1940. The name borrows from Northern Spy, but its parentage remains uncertain.

look.description: Large, roundish apple with a yellow ground streaked and flushed red.

taste.summary: Firm, dense, crisp flesh with a rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavour that improves after some weeks in store. Excellent for baking and pies, and one of the longest keepers among hardy apples.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Mar, after a few weeks in store
taste.storage_change: Orange Pippin: keeps 3 months or more; no flavour change given.

tree.notes: Slow to start bearing - expect several years - but crops well once established.

pollination.notes: No UK flowering group recorded; needs a compatible diploid pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cold northern climates (zone 3-5) with a long enough autumn to ripen a late apple, such as Minnesota and the northern Great Lakes.
climate.poor_climates: Very short seasons where a late apple will not mature, and hot or mild-winter regions where it lacks chill and colours poorly.

health.other: Generally reported as healthy, but specific scab and fire blight ratings are not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: Be patient: plant it on a dwarfing rootstock if you want fruit sooner. Leave fruit on the tree as long as frosts allow, then store cold for winter baking.

varieties.name: Priam

origin.place: Purdue University, Lafayette, Indiana (PRI co-operative programme)
origin.parentage: PRI 14-126 x Jonathan

varieties.history: A scab-resistance selection from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois co-operative breeding programme, crossed at Purdue (French Wikipedia dates the work to 1951) and introduced in 1974. It is the parent of the French cultivars Judaine and Judeline.

look.description: Medium conical apple, bright red flushed and striped over a pale yellow-green ground, with a short stalk.

taste.summary: Juicy yellow flesh with a sweet-sharp balance and fairly pronounced acidity, in the style of its Jonathan parent.
taste.peak: Keeps well through January (Orange Pippin); about 3 months at 2 C (fr.wikipedia).

tree.notes: Average vigour; Orange Pippin lists it as a tip-bearer, so prune lightly and renew rather than spur-prune.

pollination.notes: Group 3 (Orange Pippin).

climate.best_climates: Inferred: temperate climates similar to the US Midwest and France, where low-spray growing benefits from its scab resistance.
climate.poor_climates: No documented reports; fields inferred from its origin.

health.other: Bred for scab resistance in the PRI programme and rated as having good disease resistance; other susceptibilities not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: Suited to low-spray orchards because of its scab resistance. As a tip-bearer it is better as a bush or half-standard than as a cordon.

varieties.name: Prima

origin.place: PRI co-operative breeding programme (Purdue, Rutgers and Illinois universities), USA
origin.parentage: PRI 14-510 x NJ 123249; a complex PRI selection whose ancestry includes Malus floribunda (source of the Vf scab gene) with Rome Beauty, Melba, Golden Delicious and Wealthy

varieties.history: One of the first scab-resistant apples released by the joint Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) programme, introduced in 1970; the 'PRI' letters are hidden in its name. Its Vf resistance has since been overcome by new scab races in several regions, so it is no longer the trouble-free garden apple it was once sold as.

look.description: Medium to large, roundish-conical fruit, a dark red flush over a yellow ground; size is variable.

taste.summary: Juicy, cream-white flesh with a gentle, fruity balance of sugar and mild acidity; pleasant rather than memorable straight from the tree. It does not keep, losing quality within a few weeks even under refrigeration.
taste.peak: Straight from the tree; Wikipedia and Orange Pippin both say it keeps poorly, even refrigerated.

tree.notes: A robust, productive spur-bearer; fruit hangs well and does not drop readily. Has some tendency to crop biennially, so thin heavy crops.

pollination.notes: Flowers early-mid season at Brogdale (full bloom around 8 May); needs a compatible early or mid-season pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Continental and temperate climates of the American Midwest and north-east where it was bred, and similar summers in Europe.
climate.poor_climates: Areas where Vf-breaking scab strains are established, and wet warm regions with heavy cedar-apple rust pressure.

health.other: Bred as scab-immune (Vf) but that resistance has broken down in many areas, so it now scabs badly where new races occur. Highly susceptible to cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: Still a useful low-spray tree where its scab resistance holds, but check local scab experience before relying on it. Eat or process the fruit promptly; it is a short-season apple, also used for drying, sauce and cider.

varieties.name: Primate
varieties.history: An old New York summer apple thought to have arisen with Calvin D. Bingham at Camillus around 1840, and once highly regarded as an early eating apple across the north-eastern United States. It gathered many local names, among them July Apple, Powers and Scott.

look.description: Medium to large, smooth, pale green to whitish-yellow apple, often ribbed, sometimes with a faint red or orange cheek.

taste.summary: Fine, tender, white flesh that is crisp when first picked, with a lively tart, lightly aromatic flavour typical of the early American summer apples. It softens and loses its edge quickly.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-early Sep, straight from the tree

pollination.notes: Early-flowering at Brogdale (full bloom around 7 May); pair with another early or mid-season variety.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter, warm-summer north-eastern North America where it originated; ripens in late July in mild California sites.
climate.poor_climates: Little documented; as a soft summer apple it will not hold on the tree in hot spells.

health.other: No reliable disease ratings found. Soft fruit bruises easily and keeps only days.

varieties.grow_notes: A garden tree for an early fresh apple; pick as soon as the fruit comes away easily and eat within a week or two. Plant with an early-flowering partner.

varieties.name: Primrose Pippin

origin.parentage: Seedling from the Keepers Nursery programme (seedling 82); parents not published

varieties.history: Karim Habibi's best-regarded seedling so far, named after his eldest child. It was shown to the RHS Fruit Group in 2023 and was released for ordering in May 2025. It is sold under the trademark Primrose Pippin. As yet it has only been grown in Kent.

look.description: Yellow skin that develops a red striped flush late in the season; roughly round-oblong with a long thin stalk.

taste.summary: A modern-style crisp, juicy apple with more sugar (about 18% by refractometer), acidity and fruitiness than most late-season supermarket types. The raiser and the RHS fruit specialist Joan Morgan both describe the balance as excellent.

tree.notes: No published growing data found.

pollination.notes: Self-sterile; group 3 (C in nursery lists).

climate.best_climates: Only trialled in Kent so far.
climate.poor_climates: Not yet known; a mid-November pick needs a long season.

health.other: No significant fungal susceptibility seen in Kent trials; not yet tested elsewhere.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant with another group 2-4 apple. Because it ripens very late, give it the warmest, most sheltered spot you have.

varieties.name: Primus

origin.parentage: Reinette Rouge Etoilee x Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: Raised in 1935 at Wageningen in the Netherlands from the Dutch Sterappel (Reinette Rouge Etoilee) and Cox's Orange Pippin.

look.description: Large, conical yellow apple striped orange-red, with russet dots and streaks and a slightly greasy skin.

taste.summary: Soft, coarse, creamy-white flesh with a very sweet flavour.

tree.notes: No tree description found.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 12 May, so group 3 is inferred.

climate.best_climates: Cool maritime north-west European climates like the Netherlands (inferred).
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: A rarely grown Dutch Cox seedling; treat it like a Cox-type dessert apple with a mid-season partner.

varieties.name: Priscilla

origin.place: Purdue University, Lafayette, Indiana (PRI co-operative programme)
origin.parentage: Starking Delicious x PRI 610-2 (Vf scab resistance from Malus floribunda)

varieties.history: One of the earliest releases (1972) of the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois programme that bred scab resistance from a Japanese flowering crab into dessert apples. It was intended as a disease-resistant apple with some Delicious character.

look.description: Waxy, bright red blush over a yellow ground, slightly conical in the Delicious manner.

taste.summary: Crisp, fairly juicy flesh with a sweet but noticeably tart flavour that varies from year to year; descriptions range from mild and Delicious-like to pleasantly sharp. Good fresh off the tree, it also holds its shape when baked, makes a pink-tinged sauce and keeps one to two months.

tree.notes: Average vigour with a spreading, flat-topped habit; regular cropper suited to beginners and organic growers.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 3; plant with another group 2-4 variety.

climate.best_climates: Humid continental climates of the eastern and midwestern US where scab, rust and fire blight are routine problems.
climate.poor_climates: Little documented performance in hot, low-chill or very cool maritime regions.

health.other: Scab-immune (Vf) and very resistant to fire blight and cedar-apple rust; some susceptibility to canker.

varieties.grow_notes: A dependable low-spray apple for the home garden. Give it full sun and a mid-season pollinator; chill and hardiness figures are estimates from where it is grown.

varieties.name: Pristine

origin.place: Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana (PRI co-operative programme)
origin.parentage: Camuzat x Co-op 10; scab resistance (Vf) traces back to Malus floribunda 821

varieties.history: Released in 1994 by the joint Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) disease-resistance breeding programme after testing as Co-op 32. It was aimed at providing a scab-immune early yellow apple to replace older summer varieties.

look.description: Clear, glossy lemon-yellow apple, sometimes with a faint warm blush on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy, firm yellow flesh that is Granny Smith-tart if picked a few weeks early, mellowing at full ripeness to a gentle tartness with sweetness beneath; one grower notes a pear-like flavour with a citrus bite. Unusually good for such an early apple but best eaten within a week or two; also good for sauce.
taste.best_eaten: Aug, within a week or two of picking
taste.storage_change: Does not keep fresh very long (Wikipedia).

tree.notes: Fruit ripens over an extended period, so pick in several passes. Thin to discourage alternate bearing.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 4; needs a partner.

climate.best_climates: Humid continental climates of the US Midwest and East, where an early scab-immune apple is valuable.
climate.poor_climates: Its short shelf life limits it everywhere; little evidence of performance in hot, low-chill regions.

health.other: Scab-immune (Vf); some resistance to mildew but only moderate tolerance of fire blight and cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: A good low-spray summer apple: plant in sun with a mid-to-late flowering partner and harvest in stages. Eat or process quickly as it does not keep.

varieties.name: Profusion

origin.parentage: Usually given as Malus 'Lemoinei' x Malus sieboldii

varieties.history: A Dutch purple-leaved crab from the Boskoop nursery district, introduced in the late 1930s and widely planted in Europe and North America for its wine-red spring blossom. Improved selections are sold as 'Profusion Improved'.

look.description: Tiny ox-blood red fruits about 1.5 cm, on long stalks in clusters, persisting on the tree into winter.

taste.summary: Grown purely for ornament; the tiny fruit is sharp and is mostly left for birds or added in small amounts to mixed crab jelly for colour.
taste.best_eaten: Not an eating apple; display Sep-Dec

tree.notes: Young leaves are purple, maturing to bronze-green; deep wine-red flowers fade to pink. Grows to roughly 3-5 m after ten years.

pollination.notes: Long flowering period with abundant pollen; a good partner for early-flowering apples.

climate.best_climates: Temperate climates of north-west Europe and the northern US, in open, airy sites.
climate.poor_climates: Damp, sheltered sites where scab and mildew build up on the foliage.

health.other: Some susceptibility to canker and powdery mildew, and scab can spoil the leaves in wet seasons.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in an open, sunny position with good air flow to keep leaf disease down. Its early, long blossom makes it a useful pollinator for early-flowering apples.

varieties.name: Pumpkin Sweet

origin.place: Orchard of S. Lyman, Manchester, Connecticut

varieties.history: A very large sweet apple from the Lyman orchard in Manchester, Connecticut, recorded by 1834 and widely grown in New England and New York for baking. Many large sweet apples were sold as 'Pound Sweet', and the Apples of New York treats that name for this one as a synonym.

look.description: Very large rounded yellow apple marbled with green, with a dull brownish flush and pale scarf-skin streaks near the stalk.

taste.summary: Distinctly sweet and almost without acid, with an odd, characteristic flavour and firm yellowish flesh. Brogdale tasters found it very sweet but low in aroma, juice and crunch; its main traditional use is baking, where it holds together and turns rich.
taste.peak: Oct-Jan (Apples of New York via Bard AppleDB); prized for baking.

tree.notes: Orange Pippin lists it as a tip-bearer. Keeping quality varies widely with place and season.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records full bloom around 13 May, which corresponds to group 4.

climate.best_climates: New England and New York, where it was long a farmhouse baking apple.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; mild-winter regions are probably unsuitable for this northern heirloom.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow it for baking and drying rather than fresh eating. As a tip-bearer it suits an open-centre tree with light renewal pruning.

varieties.name: Queen Cox

origin.place: Appleby Fruit Farm, Kingston Bagpuize, Berkshire (now Oxfordshire), England
origin.parentage: Colour sport of Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: A more highly coloured clone of Cox's Orange Pippin, found at Appleby Fruit Farm, Kingston Bagpuize, and received by the National Fruit Trials in 1953. It became one of the standard commercial Cox clones. A separate self-fertile selection is sold under a similar name.

look.description: Typical Cox shape and russet freckling, but more of the skin is covered by a deeper orange-red flush and stripes than in standard Cox.

taste.summary: Like Cox, with firm, juicy, slightly acid flesh and a rich, aromatic flavour that brings floral, pear-drop and honeyed notes into balance. It improves for a few weeks after picking.
taste.peak: Picked late September (NFC)

tree.notes: Grows and crops like ordinary Cox: a spur-bearer of medium vigour that needs good soil, shelter and attentive disease control.

pollination.notes: Flowers with Cox in group 3. Standard Queen Cox needs a pollinator; only the separately sold self-fertile selection can set fruit alone. Good partners include Egremont Russet, Discovery and Worcester Pearmain.

climate.best_climates: Warm, sheltered sites in southern England and similar cool-summer maritime climates on well-drained soil.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, wet districts encourage canker and scab, and hot summers give poorly coloured, soft fruit with less aroma.

health.other: Shares Cox's weaknesses: canker, scab and mildew, along with some bitter pit and cracking.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow it as you would Cox: a sunny, sheltered site on fertile, free-draining soil, with spraying or careful hygiene against scab and mildew. Choose it over standard Cox mainly for better colour.

varieties.name: Quinte

origin.parentage: Crimson Beauty x Red Melba

varieties.history: Released in 1964 by the Smithfield Experimental Farm in Ontario as an early summer apple. It found a niche in cold climates such as Sweden but is too light-cropping for commercial use.

look.description: Medium, slightly tall yellow apple mostly washed with light red.

taste.summary: Tender, creamy-white flesh, sweet but with a clear tart edge; one Swedish account compares the texture to sorbet. A good early apple that should be eaten straight from the tree.
taste.peak: Straight from the tree in August; keeps 2-3 weeks (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Low yields keep it out of commercial orchards (Swedish Wikipedia).

pollination.notes: Early flowering: Orange Pippin lists group 2 and the National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 6 May. Swedish sources name Discovery, Katja, Summerred and White Transparent as pollinators.

climate.best_climates: Cold-temperate climates such as Ontario and southern to central Sweden (Swedish zones I-IV).
climate.poor_climates: Areas with heavy cedar-apple rust pressure; hot summers would hurry and soften an already short-lived early apple.

health.other: Susceptible to cedar-apple rust (Orange Pippin) and powdery mildew (Swedish Wikipedia).

varieties.grow_notes: An early-August apple for cold gardens. Plant with another early-flowering variety and eat the fruit within a couple of weeks.

varieties.name: Rajka

origin.place: Institute of Experimental Botany, Strizovice, Czech Republic
origin.parentage: Sampion x a scab-resistant selection (given as Katka in some sources, Jolana x Rubin in others)
origin.raised_by: Institute of Experimental Botany, Czech Academy of Sciences

varieties.history: Bred at the Czech Institute of Experimental Botany (the programme that also gave Topaz) for resistance to apple scab; the cross dates from the early 1980s and it was released in the 1990s. Through its Sampion parent it descends from Golden Delicious and Lord Lambourne.

look.description: Attractive medium-to-large, roundish-conical fruit almost entirely covered in bright deep red over a yellow ground, with a little russet in the stalk cavity.

taste.summary: Fairly crisp, open-textured cream-yellow flesh that snaps cleanly, with a sweet flavour and good acidity much like Elstar; after a good summer it can carry a hint of strawberry. Juicy and pleasant rather than complex, and it keeps a few weeks.

climate_flavour.note: Orange Pippin: the strawberry hint shows only in a good summer.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous, spurs freely, comes into bearing early and crops regularly; fruit holds well on the tree. Suited to organic growing.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering (group 3) and a good pollinator for other group 2-4 diploids.

climate.best_climates: Central European and British temperate climates, including damp western areas where its scab resistance is a real advantage; suggested as suitable for cooler regions.
climate.poor_climates: Low-chill or very hot regions; warm nights are likely to reduce its strong red colour.

health.other: Scab resistant (Vf) and tolerant of mildew. Birds can damage the fruit. Vf resistance has broken down to new scab races in some regions.

varieties.grow_notes: An easy, healthy garden apple that needs little spraying, even in wet areas. Plant with a group 2-4 partner, thin if the set is heavy, and pick in early October.

varieties.name: Ralls Janet
varieties.history: A Virginia apple associated with Caleb Ralls's orchard in Amherst County around 1800; one story has Thomas Jefferson passing on scions he received from the French envoy Edmond-Charles Genet. Introduced to Japan around 1870 and renamed Kokko in 1900, it was the backbone of Aomori's apple industry for decades and is the mother of Fuji.

look.description: Medium, roundish to blunt-conical apple, greenish-yellow mottled and streaked with pink to dark red, often with a heavy bloom and a little russet near the stalk.

taste.summary: Dense, crisp, yellowish flesh with a lively sweet-tart balance and a pleasant scent when cut. A long keeper, though it turns mealy by late spring unless cold-stored; also used for pies, apple butter and blending into cider.

tree.notes: Vigorous, wide-spreading tree whose growth slows once in full bearing. Colours poorly and needs a long season to ripen.

pollination.notes: One of the latest apples to blossom (at Brogdale about a week after Golden Delicious; in Japan about five days after Fuji), which lets it escape spring frosts - hence the name Neverfail. Pair with another late-flowering diploid.

climate.best_climates: Long, warm seasons such as Virginia and the American mid-South, and northern Japan, where it was long the main commercial apple.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season or very cold areas (considered unsuitable for Hokkaido); poorly drained, acid soils encourage bark disease.

health.other: Very susceptible to blossom fire blight and somewhat to scab and bitter rot, but highly resistant to collar rot. Prone to rough-bark disease on wet, acid soils in Japan.

varieties.grow_notes: A useful apple for frost pockets because it blooms so late, provided the summer is long enough to ripen it. Pick in late October and store cold; avoid it where fire blight is common.

varieties.name: Rave

origin.place: University of Minnesota Horticultural Research Center, Excelsior, Minnesota
origin.parentage: Honeycrisp x MonArk
origin.raised_by: University of Minnesota apple breeding programme (David Bedford, James Luby)

varieties.history: Bred at the University of Minnesota by crossing Honeycrisp with the early Arkansas apple MonArk, and trialled as MN55. It is a managed (licensed) variety: Stemilt in Washington State markets it as Rave from about 2017-18, while Minnesota growers sell the same apple as First Kiss.

look.description: Bright red flush with some streaking over a yellow ground; a Honeycrisp-type look on a smaller, earlier fruit.

taste.summary: Very crisp, shattering, juice-laden flesh in the Honeycrisp mould, with a brighter tart edge than its parent balanced by good sugar. An eating apple only: the flesh collapses when cooked.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-Oct; fresh, or from cold store
taste.storage_change: Pleasantly tart when picked early, well balanced at full maturity; stores up to 6 months (University of Minnesota).
taste.peak: Mid-Aug to early Sept in Minnesota (UMN); sold Aug-Oct (Stemilt).

climate_flavour.note: Wikipedia: fruit quality depends on climate, site and growing practice; Stemilt credits long sunny days in central Washington for its colour.

tree.notes: Fruit tends to drop before it is fully ripe, so crops need watching and picking promptly. Propagation is restricted under licence, so trees are rarely available to home growers outside Minnesota (where it is sold as First Kiss).

pollination.notes: No published UK flowering group; plant with another apple flowering at the same time.

climate.best_climates: Bred for Minnesota winters and grown commercially in the hot, dry, irrigated orchards of central Washington, where it ripens in midsummer.
climate.poor_climates: Little record outside the northern US; untested in mild maritime climates such as the UK, and its pre-harvest drop is a nuisance anywhere.

health.other: Main documented weakness is pre-harvest fruit drop. Disease ratings not published in the sources checked.

varieties.grow_notes: Mainly a commercial club apple; where trees are available, give it a sunny site and pick over several passes as fruit colours, because ripe apples fall readily. Chill hours and hardiness are estimates from its Minnesota origin.

varieties.name: Raxao
varieties.history: A traditional Asturian cider apple, one of the local varieties approved for the protected 'Sidra de Asturias' designation and characterised by the regional agricultural research service. It is regarded as one of the more valuable varieties for cider making.

look.description: Fairly large, flattened-round fruit, yellow-green with orange-brown and red colouring streaked purple-red; cream flesh.

taste.summary: Belongs to the acid group of Asturian cider apples: a clearly sharp juice with good sugar and only modest phenolics, giving a slight bitter edge. Valued for freshness and acidity in the typical Asturian blend.

tree.notes: Very vigorous and slow to come into bearing; productive once established but strongly inclined to alternate cropping.

pollination.notes: Flowers very late by Asturian standards (early-to-mid May there), which helps it escape spring frost; pair with other late-flowering cider apples.

climate.best_climates: Mild, humid Atlantic climates like the Asturian valleys, with long autumns for its November ripening.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season or early-frost regions where its very late fruit cannot ripen; cold-hardiness untested.

health.other: Low susceptibility to brown rot, canker and mildew in Asturian trials; main drawback is strong biennial bearing.

varieties.grow_notes: Needs space and patience: a big tree that is slow to start. Thin heavily in 'on' years to reduce alternation. Late flowering makes it a good choice for frost-prone valleys.

varieties.name: Red Astrachan

origin.place: Russia (name refers to Astrakhan); reached Sweden from Russia

varieties.history: An old Russian summer apple that was brought to Sweden around 1780, introduced to England in 1816 and to the United States in 1835. Its hardiness and early ripening made it one of the most widely planted summer apples across North America in the 19th century, from New England to the South.

look.description: Medium, flattish fruit washed and streaked deep crimson over pale green-yellow, with a bluish waxy bloom.

taste.summary: Juicy, crisp white flesh, often tinged red, with a brisk tart flavour and some aroma. Good eaten straight from the tree but goes mealy within days; best known as a sauce and pie apple.
taste.best_eaten: Aug, within a few days of picking
taste.storage_change: Very short storage; like all early apples it does not keep (Orange Pippin, Wikipedia).
taste.peak: Ripe from late July to mid August in the US (Wikipedia, historical table).

tree.notes: Hardy, vigorous and productive. Fruit ripens unevenly over a few weeks and falls readily, so pick in several rounds.

pollination.notes: Early flowering; plant with another early-to-mid season diploid. UK flowering group not confirmed.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter continental climates (Russia, Scandinavia, northern US) and, as an early apple, widely across the eastern US including the South.
climate.poor_climates: Mild, very wet climates encourage scab; low-chill subtropical areas are unsuitable.

health.other: Susceptible to scab and fire blight, and to summer fruit rots; blossom can be frosted.

varieties.grow_notes: A tough, hardy tree for cold sites. Pick over several passes as the fruit colours and use it at once for sauce or pies.

varieties.name: Red Autumn Calville
varieties.history: An old Calville listed from 1670 and traditionally credited to the Auvergne. German sources identify it with a 'true red apple' grown in the Stuttgart court garden by 1565. It was once common across Central Europe but is now rare. Some fruit rattle when shaken because the seed cavity is so large.

look.description: Large, tall, ribbed fruit flushed pale to dark red over yellow. The white flesh is stained red just under the skin.

taste.summary: Tender, juicy, somewhat coarse flesh with a sweet, mildly acid flavour. Its strong aroma recalls raspberry and strawberry, and it makes a pale red juice. It also bakes well, keeping its shape with a creamy texture.
taste.best_eaten: An autumn apple, eaten fresh or baked

tree.notes: Needs good, deep soil and a warm position, plus regular spraying, because it is prone to disease and pests.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Warm, sheltered sites on deep fertile soils in France and southern Germany.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, exposed or thin-soiled sites, where its disease problems get worse.

health.other: Generally prone to diseases and pests; needs plant protection.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant against a warm wall or in a sheltered sunny spot on rich soil and expect to spray. Grow it for the red-tinged flesh and berry aroma, not for easy cropping.

varieties.name: Red Delicious

origin.parentage: Chance seedling of unknown parentage (Yellow Bellflower has been suggested)

varieties.history: Found around 1880 by Jesse Hiatt on his farm near Peru, Iowa, and first called Hawkeye. Stark Brothers bought it and launched it as Delicious in 1895, and it was renamed Red Delicious after they acquired the unrelated Golden Delicious. Repeated selection of ever-redder sports such as Starking made it the leading US apple for most of the 20th century, at some cost to flavour.

look.description: Tall, strongly conical fruit with five prominent bumps at the eye, dark crimson-red over most of the skin (striped in the original, solid in modern sports).

taste.summary: Sweet, juicy flesh with a light crispness, very little acidity and only a faint aroma, sometimes likened to slightly over-ripe melon, under a thick, tough skin. Freshly picked fruit from a warm climate is refreshing, but stored supermarket fruit is often mealy and bland.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Jan; eat fresh, as texture declines in ordinary store
taste.peak: harvested mid-fall; best fresh (Wikipedia)

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous; many commercial strains are compact spur types. Precocious and productive.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 4 and a good pollen donor; crab apples and Golden Delicious are common orchard partners.

climate.best_climates: Sunny continental climates with hot days and cool autumn nights, such as central Washington State, where it colours deeply and develops full sweetness.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, cloudy maritime climates such as Britain, where it ripens late, colours poorly and tastes thin; very hot nights also spoil colour.

health.other: Fairly resistant to cedar-apple rust; moderately susceptible to scab. Prone to watercore when left late on the tree.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow it only where summers are warm and sunny; in Britain it is a curiosity rather than a reliable cropper. Plant with a group 4 partner.

varieties.name: Red Falstaff

origin.parentage: Sport of Falstaff (James Grieve x Golden Delicious)

varieties.history: A redder-skinned colour sport of Falstaff, the James Grieve x Golden Delicious apple raised at East Malling. It shares Falstaff's reliability and holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit; details of exactly where and when the sport was found are not well documented.

look.description: Medium, roundish fruit with a bright red to orange-red flush over much of the yellow skin, redder than ordinary Falstaff.

taste.summary: Crisp and very juicy, with a sweet-sharp balance that combines the zest of James Grieve with Golden Delicious sweetness. Good fresh or pressed for juice.
taste.peak: Picked late September-October; stores until January or longer (Chris Bowers), until March (Walcot), 1-2 months (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: Regular, heavy cropper that can overcrop and give small fruit, so thin in good years. Blossom is relatively frost-resistant.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 3. Described as self-fertile, but crops better with a group 2-4 partner; also a good pollinator for others.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate gardens throughout Britain and northern Europe; frost-tolerant blossom makes it useful in colder spots.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer regions, where fruit is likely to soften quickly and colour less.

health.other: Some susceptibility to scab; Falstaff is generally regarded as fairly healthy and mildew-tolerant.

varieties.grow_notes: A dependable garden apple that suits small trees and cordons on dwarfing stocks. Thin fruitlets to keep size up and regular cropping.

varieties.name: Red Jade

origin.place: Brooklyn Botanic Garden, New York, USA
origin.parentage: Open-pollinated seedling of the German weeping crab 'Exzellenz Thiel'

varieties.history: Raised in the 1930s at Brooklyn Botanic Garden from seed of the weeping crab 'Exzellenz Thiel' and introduced in the early 1950s. Some databases list it as German, probably because its seed parent came from Germany.

look.description: Small, glossy, egg-shaped bright red fruits about 1.5 cm, strung like beads along the hanging branches and lasting well into winter.

taste.summary: An ornamental crab; the small fruit is sharp and mostly left for birds, though it can go into mixed crab jelly.
taste.best_eaten: Not an eating apple; display Sep-Dec

tree.notes: A small weeping tree with a wide, flat-topped crown; usually top-worked on a clear stem. Thin the hanging shoots so the head stays open and sheds rain quickly.

pollination.notes: White blossom from pink buds in spring; its exact flowering group was not found in the sources consulted.

climate.best_climates: Temperate climates of the north-eastern US and north-west Europe, in sunny, airy sites.
climate.poor_climates: Humid, wet districts where leaf diseases can defoliate it.

health.other: Prone to apple scab, with some susceptibility to powdery mildew and fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: Use it as a focal weeping tree in sun, with a support stake while the head forms. Keep the canopy thinned and clear fallen leaves to reduce scab.

varieties.name: Red James Grieve

origin.place: Seabrook's orchards, Boreham, near Chelmsford, Essex, England
origin.parentage: Sport of James Grieve
origin.raised_by: Found in the orchards of W.P. Seabrook

varieties.history: A redder bud sport of the Scottish apple James Grieve, found around 1922 in W.P. Seabrook's orchards at Boreham in Essex. A separate German red sport (Erich Neumann's Roter James Grieve, 1953) is sometimes also sold as Red James Grieve.

look.description: James Grieve shape and size, but with a much heavier flush and stripes of red over pale yellow.

taste.summary: As James Grieve: very juicy, soft-textured flesh with a lively, refreshing acidity when first picked that mellows to a sweeter balance after a week or two.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct; sharp at picking, softer and sweeter a little later

tree.notes: Tree identical to James Grieve: moderate vigour, reliable heavy crops. Fruit bruises very easily, so handle and store gently.

pollination.notes: As James Grieve: group 3, partly self-fertile and a good pollinator for other mid-season apples.

climate.best_climates: Cool northern climates: Scotland, northern England and northern Europe, where the parent is valued as a reliable early cropper.
climate.poor_climates: In hot summers the soft fruit drops and deteriorates fast; canker is a problem on wet, heavy soils.

health.other: Canker-prone like James Grieve, particularly on wet ground; fairly resistant to mildew. Fruit bruises easily.

varieties.grow_notes: Suits colder and northern gardens where Cox fails. Avoid waterlogged soils because of canker, and pick over several passes as fruit ripens unevenly.

varieties.name: Red Pineapple

origin.place: Sieglitzer Berg on the Elbe, Germany

varieties.history: A German dessert apple found by Richter at Sieglitzer Berg on the Elbe and described in 1854. It spread to Scandinavia and eastern Europe and is still widely grown in Denmark, where it is recommended for gardens as one that can crop without spraying.

look.description: A medium, conical apple that is mostly covered in red over yellow, with a slightly greasy skin and almost no russet.

taste.summary: Fine, firm yellowish-white flesh, stained pink under the skin, with a sweet, gently acid flavour. No source found ties the 'pineapple' name to any particular pineapple note.

tree.notes: Danish growers rate it as suitable for unsprayed garden growing.

pollination.notes: Flowers around the same time as Wealthy at Brogdale (about 8 May); group inferred from those dates.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate northern Europe: Germany, Denmark and further east, where it is widely grown.
climate.poor_climates: No records from hot-summer climates.

health.other: Reported to be healthy enough to grow without pesticides in Denmark; specific disease ratings not published.

varieties.grow_notes: A good low-input garden apple for cool climates. Pick in late September; the National Fruit Collection still holds it, so true wood is available.

varieties.name: Red Sauce

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Deacon Jones x Wealthy

varieties.history: Raised in 1910 at the Geneva station in New York State and introduced in 1926. Its distinction is red-stained flesh that colours the juice and gives a pink sauce when cooked.

look.description: Large conical fruit, largely flushed and striped red over pale green; the flesh is often stained pink to the core.

taste.summary: Coarse, rather dry flesh with a mild, lightly acid flavour; more interesting for its pink colour than its eating quality. Cooks to a rosy sauce.
taste.peak: Harvest late Sept-early Oct, keeps until November (Chris Bowers).

tree.notes: No reliable growing data recorded.

pollination.notes: Flowers fairly late at Brogdale; group estimated from collection flowering dates (borderline 3/4).

climate.best_climates: Bred for New York's cold-winter, cool-autumn conditions; grows in the UK national collection in Kent.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance in hot or very cold regions.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity for cooks who want naturally pink apple sauce. Treat as an ordinary mid-season diploid: sunny site, a pollinator in group 3-5, spur pruning.

varieties.name: Red Sentinel

origin.parentage: A selection within Malus x robusta (hybrids of Malus baccata and Malus prunifolia)

varieties.history: A British selection of the hybrid crab group Malus x robusta, valued for clusters of glossy dark red fruit that cling to the branches through winter. It holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Tiny, glossy, cherry-like fruits about 2 cm, scarlet deepening to dark red, in dense clusters that often last until late winter.

taste.summary: Sharp and not for eating raw; it can be used for jelly, but it is grown mainly for its long winter fruit display and as food for birds.

tree.notes: Vase-shaped to rounded tree reaching about 3-5 m after ten years. Fruit commonly persists into the new year, giving late-winter colour and bird food.

pollination.notes: Plain white blossom early in the season; a good pollinator for early- and mid-flowering apples.

climate.best_climates: Temperate maritime climates like the UK, where the fruit can hang on the tree all winter.
climate.poor_climates: Little information outside the UK; early flowering may be frosted in cold hollows.

health.other: Rated as having good overall disease resistance; foliage and fruit usually stay clean in Britain.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in full sun on any well-drained soil; it needs only light pruning. Useful as a pollinator for early-flowering apples while adding winter interest.

varieties.name: Red Windsor

origin.parentage: Red-skinned sport of Alkmene (Early Windsor), itself Geheimrat Dr Oldenburg x Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: A redder-skinned mutation of the German apple Alkmene, which is sold in Britain as Early Windsor. Known first as Red Alkmene, it was renamed Red Windsor in 1998 and has an RHS Award of Garden Merit; it has also been marketed in supermarkets as Sweet Lilibet. Where and by whom the sport was found is not well documented.

look.description: Medium apple largely covered in bright red, with faint Cox-like striping and a little russet showing through.

taste.summary: Crisp, very juicy, firm yellowish flesh with an aromatic, Cox-like flavour that is tangier and cleaner-tasting than Cox; most tasters find it refreshingly sharp, and it gains a honeyed sweetness only when fully ripe. A short keeper, best eaten within a week or so of picking.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct, within a few weeks of picking
taste.storage_change: Keeps about 1 week; flesh oxidises (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Moderate vigour and a reliable, regular cropper; popular for small gardens and containers.

pollination.notes: Early flowering and reported to be self-fertile or partly so; crops better with an early partner. Blossom is vulnerable to frost.

climate.best_climates: Cool, mild British and northern European gardens, including the north and Scotland where it is widely planted.
climate.poor_climates: Frost pockets damage its early blossom; hot climates are outside its known range.

health.other: Good scab resistance inherited from Alkmene; early blossom is frost-tender.

varieties.grow_notes: An easy, healthy Cox-style apple for beginners. Avoid frost hollows because it blooms early, and pick when the fruit is fully red and parts easily from the spur; eat soon after.

varieties.name: Redfree

origin.place: Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana (PRI co-operative programme)
origin.parentage: Raritan x PRI 1018-101 (Vf scab resistance from Malus floribunda)

varieties.history: Released in 1981 by the PRI disease-resistance programme, tested as Co-op 13. It was meant as a scab-immune early red apple for home and low-spray growers.

look.description: Glossy, bright red over most of the skin with a yellow-green ground beneath.

taste.summary: Crisp and juicy straight from the tree, with a fresh, sweet flavour, a little zing and an overall mild character; some tasters detect an unusual note they put down to its crab-apple ancestry. It softens in storage within a few weeks and opinions vary, one grower finding it soft and flavourless. Dries well.
taste.peak: picked early September, keeps 2-3 weeks

tree.notes: Average vigour and regular bearing. Fruit ripens over several weeks, so plan more than one picking.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 3; a good pollinator for others.

climate.best_climates: Humid continental climates of the US Midwest and East where scab and rust are common.
climate.poor_climates: No clear record of performance in very hot or low-chill climates; a short keeper anywhere.

health.other: Scab-immune (Vf) and very resistant to cedar-apple rust; some resistance to mildew and fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: Easy, low-maintenance early apple for a sunny garden. Pair with a group 2-4 partner and harvest over several weeks.

varieties.name: Redgold

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Richared Delicious

varieties.history: Raised by F.A. Schell at Cashmere in the Wenatchee district of Washington from Golden Delicious crossed with Richared, and introduced in 1946 (sold by Stark as Stark Redgold).

look.description: Medium, tall and strongly ribbed apple in the Delicious style, mostly covered by a pinkish-red flush over pale yellow.

taste.summary: Tender yellow flesh with a very sweet, low-acid flavour; Orange Pippin calls it one of the sweetest apples, and home growers praise it as sweet and juicy.
taste.peak: Keeps for weeks in the refrigerator (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Little published growing information; home growers report heavy crops of rather small fruit.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records full bloom around 10 May, which corresponds to group 3.

climate.best_climates: Inferred from its Washington origin: sunny temperate climates with warm days and cool autumn nights.
climate.poor_climates: No documented reports.

health.other: No published ratings; one UK grower reports heavy scab in a wet year.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow like Golden Delicious in a sunny, open site. Thin heavy crops to keep up fruit size.

varieties.name: Redwell

origin.place: University of Minnesota Fruit Breeding Farm, Excelsior, Minnesota
origin.parentage: Uncertain: the National Fruit Collection records Scott's Winter x unknown; Orange Pippin gives a Wealthy x Alexander seedling.

varieties.history: Raised around 1911 at the University of Minnesota fruit breeding farm and released in 1946. Sources disagree about its parentage.

look.description: Large, slightly elongated apple, streaked red to orange-red over yellow-green.

taste.summary: Soft, greenish to cream flesh with a mild, gently acid flavour; described as smooth and mellow, good for eating and baking.
taste.peak: Keeps until January (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: No tree description found.

pollination.notes: Fairly late flowering: the National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 15 May, so group 4 is inferred.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates like Minnesota, for which it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers and mild winters (inferred from its origin).

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy, mild-flavoured Minnesota apple that keeps until about January. Plant with a later-flowering partner.

varieties.name: Regent

origin.place: University of Minnesota Fruit Breeding Farm, Excelsior, Minnesota
origin.parentage: Daniels Red Duchess x Delicious (National Fruit Collection); Orange Pippin gives Haralson x McIntosh

varieties.history: Released by the University of Minnesota in 1963-64 as a hardy, long-keeping apple for eating and cooking. Its published parentage differs between sources.

look.description: Medium to large, conical apple striped bright red over yellow-green.

taste.summary: Crisp, crackling and juicy cream flesh, sweet and honeyed but with plenty of acidity for balance. Holds its shape when cooked, with a light, sweet, fruity flavour.
taste.peak: Stores 4-5 months (University of Minnesota).

climate_flavour.note: Orange Pippin lists it for cool summers (20-24 C).

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous and easy to train (University of Minnesota); precocious, spur-bearing heavy cropper (Orange Pippin).

pollination.notes: Orange Pippin lists group 3; the National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 11 May.

climate.best_climates: Cool-summer continental climates such as Minnesota and the northern US; rated moderately hardy there.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers (inferred); the very coldest Minnesota sites, where it is only moderately hardy.

health.other: Susceptible to apple scab; some fire blight susceptibility; very resistant to cedar-apple rust (Orange Pippin).

varieties.grow_notes: A good keeper for cold gardens that crops early and heavily. Spray or site it for scab control, and thin heavy crops.

varieties.name: Reinette Clochard
varieties.history: A traditional apple of Gâtine in Poitou, originating at Secondigny and widely grown in Deux-Sèvres, Vendée and Charente. INRA Bordeaux crossed it with Golden Delicious in 1958, producing the commercial varieties Chantecler (Belchard) and Charden.

look.description: Medium, somewhat flattened apple with a rough skin, deep yellow when ripe and freckled with small brown russet spots.

taste.summary: Firm, juicy cream flesh with a sweet-sharp balance that leans to the sweet side; it also holds its shape in cooking and gives a sweetish juice. A very long keeper that lasts into March, though it shrivels and softens toward the end of storage.
taste.peak: Picked mid to late October; keeps 3 months or more (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: Upright spur-type tree with short internodes and moderate vigour; crops heavily almost every year, unlike many old varieties.

pollination.notes: Described as late-flowering and so escaping spring frosts, though one French catalogue lists it in early group B. Suggested partners include Reine des Reinettes, Reinette de Caux, Grand'Mère and Chailleux.

climate.best_climates: Mild, sunny Atlantic west of France (Poitou, Vendée, Charente) with warm summers and mild winters.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented in cold continental or very low-chill climates.

health.other: Fairly little troubled by scab; other disease behaviour not recorded. Harvest date for SE England inferred from its late season.

varieties.grow_notes: A regular-cropping keeper suited to a warm, sunny site. Its compact spur habit makes it easy to manage; store fruit cool and humid to delay shrivelling.

varieties.name: Reinette du Canada
varieties.history: Despite the name this is an old French apple, probably from Normandy, already listed in France by 1771; it received an RHS Award of Merit in 1901. This is the white (lightly russeted) Canada Reinette; the grey, heavily russeted Reinette Grise du Canada is treated as a separate variety, though some sources lump them.

look.description: Large, broad, irregular and faintly ribbed apple; greenish-yellow with patchy russet and sometimes a slight orange-brown flush on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse, somewhat dry flesh. Picked early it is tart and keeps its shape in cooking (a classic strudel apple); after some months in store it turns softer, sweeter and aromatic, and eventually mealy.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Mar; tart for cooking at first, sweeter for eating after storage
taste.storage_change: Tart at picking and best for cooking then; after storage it becomes softer and sweeter (en.wikipedia) and eventually mealy (de.wikipedia).
taste.peak: December to March/April (Wikipedia list; de.wikipedia).

climate_flavour.note: de.wikipedia: needs warm, moist, nutrient-rich sites.

tree.notes: Vigorous, forming a broad crown (German Wikipedia; Orange Pippin). As a triploid it needs plenty of room.

pollination.notes: Orange Pippin lists group 4; Wikipedia says it blooms about three days after Cox, while National Fruit Collection records put full bloom close to Cox (about 13 May). Triploid: a poor pollen donor, so plant two compatible diploids.

climate.best_climates: Warm, sheltered sites with moist, rich, clay-containing soils in temperate Europe (German Wikipedia).
climate.poor_climates: Cold, exposed or dry, poor sites (German Wikipedia).

health.other: No reliable disease ratings found for the white form; flesh becomes mealy in long storage.

varieties.grow_notes: A big, vigorous triploid: give it room, a warm site and rich, moist soil, and two diploid pollinators. Use early fruit for cooking and keep the rest for eating after Christmas.

varieties.name: Reinette Grise du Canada

origin.place: France; some authors argue for the St Lawrence valley, Quebec
origin.parentage: Unknown; the russeted form of Reinette du Canada

varieties.history: The grey, russeted form of the Reinette du Canada, a large old reinette that French lists date to the early 1800s. Despite the name its Canadian origin is unproven and it has been grown mainly in France, Switzerland and northern Italy, where the Reinette du Canada is still a commercial cooking and eating apple.

look.description: Large, irregular, flattened-round to slightly conical fruit almost wholly covered in cinnamon-brown russet over a greenish-yellow ground.

taste.summary: Fine, dense, lightly crisp flesh, juicy and sweet in the russet manner, with a pleasant sharpness and a distinctly spicy perfume. A mainstay of French cookery: it bakes whole without collapsing, stews to a textured puree that needs little sugar, and keeps a month or two.

tree.notes: Very vigorous with a drooping habit and strong wood; cropping can be irregular. Undemanding of fertiliser.

pollination.notes: Triploid, a poor pollinator; French nurseries put it in flowering group D (mid-late) and suggest Idared, James Grieve or McIntosh as partners.

climate.best_climates: Temperate France, Switzerland and the Alpine valleys of northern Italy, with warm summers and well-drained soil.
climate.poor_climates: Wet sites with heavy soils; triploid vigour makes it unsuitable for very small gardens.

health.other: Resistant to scab but prone to bacterial canker; the Reinette du Canada group is notorious for bitter pit in storage.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it plenty of room or a dwarfing stock, plus two diploid pollinators. Keep calcium and water supply even to limit bitter pit.

varieties.name: Reinette Rouge Etoilée
varieties.history: First described in 1830, probably from the Maastricht area on the Dutch-Belgian border, and spread along the Lower Rhine. Its deep red, star-speckled skin made it a traditional polished Christmas apple. It is a parent of Primus, Koningin Juliana and Atalanta.

look.description: Rounded apple washed purple-red to dark red with a bluish bloom and many conspicuous pale star-shaped lenticels.

taste.summary: Firm, fine, rather dry white flesh, sometimes pink-tinged under the skin, with a mild sweet-sour flavour and a faint perfume. Generally rated more beautiful than tasty; it goes mealy by mid-winter.
taste.storage_change: Keeps until about mid-January, then turns mealy (de.wikipedia).
taste.peak: October-December (Wikipedia list).

tree.notes: Strong-growing with a tall, rounded crown; slow to start bearing (German Wikipedia mentions 10-12 years on standard trees), then crops reasonably well.

pollination.notes: Orange Pippin lists group 4; German Wikipedia describes late, long flowering, while National Fruit Collection records put full bloom close to Cox (12-14 May). Poor pollination can make crops irregular.

climate.best_climates: Humid north-west European lowland climates with deep, moist soils.
climate.poor_climates: Dry sites and light soils (German Wikipedia).

health.other: Generally robust and frost-hardy (German Wikipedia); some canker resistance and some scab susceptibility (Orange Pippin). Prone to lenticel spotting and codling moth.

varieties.grow_notes: Grown mainly for its striking winter colour. Give it deep, moist soil and patience, as it is slow to begin cropping.

varieties.name: Reinette Simirenko

origin.place: Platonov khutir near Mliiv, Cherkasy region, Ukraine
origin.raised_by: Found in the orchard of Platon Simirenko; described and spread by his son Lev Simirenko

varieties.history: A chance seedling noticed by Lev Simirenko in his father's orchard near Mliiv and named for the father; Ukrainian sources date its description to 1880, the National Fruit Collection to 1895. It became the most widely planted winter apple of the Soviet Union and still makes up a large share of Ukrainian orchards.

look.description: Bright green, waxy, flattish apple with conspicuous pale or russeted dots and small warty russet spots, sometimes a faint brownish-red cheek in hot districts.

taste.summary: Dense, very juicy greenish-white flesh with a wine-like sweetness, moderate acidity and a pleasant spicy aftertaste; underripe fruit is sour and slightly astringent. It improves in store and is at its best from late winter into spring.
taste.best_eaten: Jan-May, after some weeks in store
taste.storage_change: Unripe fruit is sourish and slightly astringent; this goes as it ripens, and the flavour improves in store (uk.wikipedia).
taste.peak: Late winter into spring; keeps until June (uk.wikipedia).

tree.notes: Vigorous tree with a dense, broad crown. In southern orchards it often fruits on the current season's growth as well as on spurs. Trunk and limbs are easily winter-damaged, but the crown regrows quickly.

pollination.notes: Self-sterile. Ukrainian growers use Idared, Golden Delicious, Antonovka and similar varieties as pollinators. Brogdale records full bloom around 10 May (group 3).

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer steppe and forest-steppe climates: southern and central Ukraine, Crimea, the Caucasus and Central Asia, where it tolerates heat and drought well.
climate.poor_climates: Places with severe winters, where the trunk suffers frost damage; humid regions with heavy scab and mildew pressure.

health.other: Below-average resistance to scab and powdery mildew; poor winter hardiness of the wood.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a warm, sheltered site and protect the trunk in cold winters. Plant a compatible pollinator, and pick in early to mid autumn for long storage into spring.

varieties.name: Renown

origin.parentage: Peasgood's Nonsuch x Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: One of the apples raised by Charles Ross, head gardener at Welford Park near Newbury, from Peasgood's Nonsuch and Cox. It received an RHS Award of Merit in 1908.

look.description: Large, uneven conical apple mostly covered in red flush over yellow.

taste.summary: Firm, pale yellow flesh with a sweet, mildly acid flavour; usable both for dessert and cooking.

tree.notes: No tree description found.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 14 May, close to Cox, so group 3 is inferred.

climate.best_climates: Southern English conditions like those at Welford Park (inferred).
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: A rare Edwardian Charles Ross apple; grow it like Cox with a mid-season pollinator.

varieties.name: Rescue

origin.parentage: Usually given as an open-pollinated seedling of Blushed Calville

varieties.history: A very hardy applecrab selected at the federal experimental farm at Scott, Saskatchewan, and released in the 1930s for prairie gardens where ordinary apples could not survive the winters. It is still recommended for the coldest parts of the Canadian prairies.

look.description: Small, around 3.5-4 cm, yellow-green with a deep red blush and stripes.

taste.summary: Crisp and juicy with a tart-sweet balance, good eaten fresh from the tree; it turns mealy within a few weeks. Also used for sauce and preserves.
taste.storage_change: Goes mealy quickly and stores only about 3 weeks (Alaska Pioneer Fruit Growers); keeps better if picked as it ripens.
taste.peak: Mid to late August, fresh

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not well documented in the sources consulted; valued above all for its winter hardiness.

pollination.notes: Plant with another hardy apple or crab for pollination.

climate.best_climates: Severe continental climates with short summers, such as the Canadian prairies and northern plains.
climate.poor_climates: Warm or hot regions, where an early crab like this ripens in the heat and goes mealy almost immediately (inferred).

health.other: Disease ratings not documented in the sources consulted; main fault is the short life of the ripe fruit.

varieties.grow_notes: A choice for gardens too cold for standard apples. Pick as soon as ripe in August and eat or process quickly; plant another hardy apple or crab nearby for pollination.

varieties.name: Reverend W. Wilks

origin.parentage: Peasgood's Nonsuch x Ribston Pippin

varieties.history: Raised by the Veitch nursery firm, at its Langley grounds, from Peasgood's Nonsuch crossed with Ribston Pippin. It was named after the Rev. William Wilks, then secretary of the RHS and the raiser of the Shirley poppy. It received an RHS Award of Merit in 1904 and a First Class Certificate in 1910, and is still a common garden cooker.

look.description: Very large, broad, slightly conical fruit; smooth pale creamy or milky green-white skin with a light flush and a few soft red stripes.

taste.summary: Crisp, fine-grained, juicy white flesh with a delicate sweet-sharp flavour and a pleasing scent; most tasters find it fine raw, though one found it too bitter to eat uncooked. Cooks quickly to a pale, smooth puree needing little sugar, browns very fast once cut, and keeps only a few weeks unless stored cool and airy.
taste.peak: Late August, keeps 2-3 weeks (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: A stout, dwarfish spur-bearer that crops young and very heavily, but tends to alternate heavy and light years. Thinning in heavy years helps even this out. Well suited to small gardens and trained forms.

pollination.notes: Early-flowering (group 2). Orange Pippin lists it as self-fertile, but it sets better with a group 1-3 partner.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp temperate climates throughout the UK, including cooler northern gardens, since it ripens early.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are untested. As an early cooker its main risk is short storage rather than a failure to ripen.

health.other: Good general disease resistance (some resistance to scab, canker and mildew). The main faults are biennial bearing, short keeping and fast-browning flesh.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the best early cookers for a small garden or a cordon. Thin heavily in 'on' years to limit biennial cropping, and use or freeze the fruit within a few weeks of picking.

varieties.name: Rhode Island Greening

origin.place: Green's End, near Newport (now Middletown), Rhode Island
origin.raised_by: Attributed to a tavern keeper named Green

varieties.history: One of the oldest American apples, said to have come from a seedling grown around 1650 by a tavern keeper named Green near Newport, Rhode Island. It became a leading 19th-century New York apple, is still grown commercially in the north-eastern US for pies and sauce, and is Rhode Island's state fruit.

look.description: Large, flattish, often ribbed fruit with greasy grass-green skin turning greenish yellow, occasionally a faint orange cheek, and russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Large, hard, firm flesh, less juicy than many, with a clean, strong tartness softened by a little sweetness; tasters pick out cider, grape and lemonade-like citrus hints. Best mellowed in store before eating raw, and at its finest cooked, holding its shape in pies and making excellent sauce.
taste.best_eaten: Cook Oct-Feb; raw after a few months in store
taste.storage_change: Tart when freshly picked (best for cooking); mellows in store into a rich eating apple, keeping into spring (Salt Spring, Wikipedia).
taste.peak: Cook from picking; eat fresh after storage

tree.notes: A large, vigorous, spreading tree that is slow to come into bearing and tends to crop biennially. Triploid, so it gives no useful pollen.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 3; triploid, so plant two different diploid pollinators that flower in groups 2-4.

climate.best_climates: Humid continental climates of New England, New York and the Great Lakes, with cold winters and warm summers.
climate.poor_climates: Warm, humid regions with heavy fire blight pressure, and low-chill climates.

health.other: Very susceptible to fire blight; some susceptibility to cedar-apple rust. Triploid.

varieties.grow_notes: Needs plenty of room and two diploid pollinators. Expect to wait several years for the first crops; thin heavy crops to reduce alternate bearing.

varieties.name: Ribston Pippin

origin.place: Ribston Hall, near Knaresborough, Yorkshire, England
origin.parentage: Seedling from pips brought from Rouen, Normandy

varieties.history: Grew from pips sent from Rouen and planted at Ribston Hall in Yorkshire in the early 1700s. It was a celebrated Victorian dessert apple and is almost certainly a parent of Cox's Orange Pippin. It holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Medium, irregular roundish-conical fruit, often lopsided, yellow with an orange-red flush and red streaks over a light network of russet.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained flesh with a strong, aromatic flavour that is more robust, if less refined, than its offspring Cox; sources note a pear-like taste and one grower a pronounced lemon tang. At its best about a month after picking, but it does not stay crisp for long and browns quickly when cut.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Jan; best after a month in store
taste.storage_change: Flavour is at its best about a month after picking (Orange Pippin).
taste.peak: About a month after picking (Orange Pippin).

climate_flavour.note: Wikipedia: weather during ripening causes water-coring, and in very hot weather the fruit ripens prematurely.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous, long-lived spur-bearer. Triploid, so its pollen is of little use to other varieties.

pollination.notes: Generally listed in flowering group 2 (some sources give 3). Triploid: plant two diploid pollinators flowering in groups 1-3.

climate.best_climates: Cool, mild temperate climates across England, from its Yorkshire home to the south, on well-drained soils.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers soften the fruit and dull its flavour; heavy, wet soils encourage canker.

health.other: Prone to canker, especially on wet, heavy soils. Triploid.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant on well-drained soil to limit canker, and provide two early-flowering diploid pollinators. Pick in late September and let the fruit mature in store for its best flavour.

varieties.name: Rokewood

origin.place: Rokewood district near Ballarat, Victoria (Western Australia is also suggested)

varieties.history: An Australian apple from the Rokewood district near Ballarat, dating from about the 1870s. Because it ripened at the start of the southern winter and kept well, it was shipped to London and sold before the English crop arrived; it is also in the ancestry of Lady Williams.

look.description: Small to medium, truncated-conical apple; green-yellow skin largely covered by streaked orange-red to deep red.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, greenish-white flesh with a sweet, mildly acid flavour. Valued above all as a very long keeper.

climate_flavour.note: Wikipedia list: not suited to England; it ripens very late (March-April in Australia).

tree.notes: Recorded as a vigorous tree and a regular, heavy bearer.

pollination.notes: In Kent the National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 6 May, suggesting group 2; an Australian heritage orchard lists it as group 3.

climate.best_climates: Long, warm growing seasons of south-eastern Australia such as Victoria, where it ripens in March-April.
climate.poor_climates: England and similar cool, short-season climates: it ripens too late and is described as unsuited there.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: A very late, long-keeping apple for warm-summer regions. In Britain it struggles to ripen; elsewhere pick as late as possible and store.

varieties.name: Rome Beauty

origin.parentage: Unknown; arose as a shoot from below the graft of a nursery tree bought by Joel Gillett

varieties.history: Joel Gillett noticed an odd tree among grafted stock he had bought around 1816, and his son Alanson planted it beside the Ohio River. First called Gillett's Seedling, it was renamed after Rome Township in the 1830s; the original tree was lost to a flood in 1860. It became one of the main American baking apples of the early 20th century and has given many redder sports.

look.description: Big, smooth, glossy apple with a thick skin, mottled and streaked bright red over a greenish-yellow base, dotted with pale lenticels.

taste.summary: Firm, solid, rather dry flesh with a mild sweetness and a little tartness; unremarkable raw, though one taster found a rose-like note. It shines in the oven, holding its shape when baked whole, and turns dry and mealy if kept long without cold storage.
taste.peak: picked mid October (NFC)

climate_flavour.note: NFC: fruits do not mature well in the UK

tree.notes: Bears a good part of its crop on the shoot tips, so avoid heavy tipping-back in winter pruning. Comes into bearing young and crops heavily.

pollination.notes: Late flowering, which helps it miss spring frosts. Often described as partly self-fruitful in North America but crops better with a late-flowering partner.

climate.best_climates: Long, warm summers with late springs, as in the Ohio valley, the Virginias and irrigated parts of the US West, where late bloom avoids frost.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons give small, poorly finished fruit; humid areas with junipers nearby bring heavy cedar-apple rust.

health.other: Very susceptible to cedar-apple rust and also prone to scab, powdery mildew and fire blight; needs a spray programme where these are common.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a sunny, open site and a long season. Prune lightly to renew fruiting wood rather than shortening every shoot, because of its tip-bearing habit. Keep it well away from junipers (red cedar) in North America.

varieties.name: Rosa Mantovana

origin.place: Probably the Kaltern (Caldaro) district, South Tyrol, Italy

varieties.history: An old winter dessert apple of the Adige valley, known in German as Kalterer Böhmer and in Italian as Rosa del Caldaro or Rosa Mantovana. German sources equate the names, but the National Fruit Collection marks Rosa Mantovana as a doubtful synonym, so the identity is not fully settled. In 1929 it supplied over a quarter of South Tyrol's apple deliveries, before newer varieties pushed it out after the 1950s.

look.description: Flattened, somewhat lopsided and ribbed apple, pale greenish-yellow ripening to a waxy yellow, with a bright, unstriped red to carmine flush on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Fine, rather soft white flesh that is sweet with gentle acidity and a delicate, slightly perfumed and mildly winey flavour. Pleasant rather than juicy.
taste.peak: Picked early October (NFC)

tree.notes: Recorded as upright-growing; little modern information on vigour or cropping.

pollination.notes: Recorded as early flowering in the National Apple Register and at Brogdale (as Rosa del Caldaro).

climate.best_climates: Sunny Alpine valleys such as the Adige around Bolzano and Kaltern, with warm days and cool autumn nights.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented outside its home region.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage choice for collectors of Alpine and Italian apples. It flowers early, so pair it with a group 1-3 partner, and keep the fruit cool until midwinter.

varieties.name: Rosemary Russet
varieties.history: An English russet of unknown parentage, first described in print in 1831 and praised by Robert Hogg later in the century as a dessert apple of the very first rank. It never became as widely planted as Egremont Russet but holds an RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Tapering, slightly flat-topped fruit, green-yellow with a faint brownish-red cheek and a thin coat of pale brown russet that is heaviest around the eye and the long stalk.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained and juicy, with a lively balance of sugar and acid and a rich, aromatic finish. Sharper than most russets when first picked, it rounds out and sweetens after a few weeks in store.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Feb, after some weeks in store

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous with an upright habit; a regular-bearing spur type that suits restricted forms and standard winter spur pruning.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering (National Fruit Collection records it in bloom with Bramley and Cox); any group 2-4 diploid will pollinate it.

climate.best_climates: Cool to mild temperate climates such as lowland England, where a long autumn lets it build sugar before picking.
climate.poor_climates: Very short, cool seasons may leave it too sharp; in hot humid regions disease pressure and early softening are likely problems.

health.other: Generally considered a healthy garden tree with some resistance to scab and canker; suitable for low-spray growing.
