varieties.grow_notes: Plant on the warmest, sunniest wall or slope you have, because it needs a long season to ripen. Pick as late as frost allows, store cool and humid, and leave it until after Christmas before tasting.

varieties.name: Styre
varieties.history: One of the most celebrated old cider apples of the Forest of Dean, with a name that may be Anglo-Saxon. It declined from the mid-19th century, was called almost extinct by 1898, and the last known tree was felled at Halmore in 1968. Pomologists are still looking for survivors.

look.description: Small, pale yellow fruit with a red flush on the sunny side, on a very short stalk.

taste.summary: A bittersharp cider apple, high in both acid and tannin. The flesh is sharp at picking but turns sweet and almost honeyed after keeping. It made a famously smooth, long-keeping and deceptively strong cider.
taste.storage_change: Acidic when picked; becomes sweet, honeyed and edible after keeping (en and fr Wikipedia).

tree.notes: A very large, vigorous, upright tree that tended to make wood rather than fruit. It could be propagated without grafting by rooting shoots from the crown. It was probably triploid, which may explain its later poor fruiting.

pollination.notes: Probably triploid, so a poor pollen donor.

climate.best_climates: The mild, moist west of England around the Forest of Dean.
climate.poor_climates: No records outside its home district.

health.other: Not recorded; the variety is believed extinct.

varieties.grow_notes: Not available; believed extinct since 1968. Any candidate tree from the Forest of Dean or Severn Vale should be reported to local orchard groups.

varieties.name: SugarBee

origin.parentage: Open-pollinated Honeycrisp seedling (pollen parent unknown, presumably bee-carried)

varieties.history: Chuck Nystrom grew it from Honeycrisp seed collected in 1994 and picked it out in 2004 at his Minnesota orchard. The cultivar, first numbered B-51 and later CN 121, is now grown under licence in Washington State and sold as SugarBee. It went on sale in 2016, and the name refers to its bee-pollinated origin.

look.description: A medium to large, often lopsided conical apple. Bright red is washed over a yellow-green base with a few darker stripes and pale lenticels, plus a little russet in the stalk cavity.

taste.summary: Very sweet and only mildly acid, with crisp, crunchy, juicy flesh. Tasters describe caramel, honey and molasses notes with a light floral, fruity touch. It is sweeter than Honeycrisp.
taste.storage_change: Keeps up to about five months in cold storage and longer in CA, outlasting Honeycrisp (patent; Wikipedia).

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous and upright to spreading, with average productivity, according to the plant patent.

pollination.notes: Blooms at the same time as Honeycrisp; group taken from Honeycrisp.

climate.best_climates: Found in southern Minnesota and grown commercially in central Washington; suits cold-winter continental climates.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in warm-winter or humid maritime climates.

health.other: The patent says it is susceptible to all the usual pests and diseases of central Washington and notes no special resistance.

varieties.grow_notes: A licensed club apple, generally not sold to home gardeners. It ripens about ten days after Honeycrisp and stores for around five months in cold storage.

varieties.name: Summer Rambo

origin.place: Probably near Rambures, Picardy, France (traditional account)

varieties.history: An old French summer apple, Rambour d'Ete, said to take its name from the village of Rambures in Picardy; some accounts place it as early as the sixteenth century. Carried to North America, it became a popular early-season apple in Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia, but its poor keeping kept it out of commercial trade. It is distinct from the autumn-ripening Rambo, and the French name Rambour Franc is applied inconsistently to it and to a different later apple.

look.description: Large, squat, often lopsided or ribbed fruit, greenish-yellow washed and striped with pinkish to carmine red on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Coarse, breaking, exceptionally juicy flesh with a subacid, aromatic, slightly honeyed flavour and a noticeable touch of tannin. Good eaten off the tree but soon turns soft, keeping only about a week; prized above all for sauce, and also good for pies and drying.
taste.storage_change: does not store; keeps about a week
taste.peak: late August to early September (Orange Pippin), early August in the US (Wikipedia)

tree.notes: Vigorous and productive, bearing partly at shoot tips; tends to alternate heavy and lighter years. Thin heavy crops to keep fruit size and reduce biennialism.

pollination.notes: Listed as triploid in one database, so plant two diploid pollinators flowering at about the same time.

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer temperate regions such as the Mid-Atlantic states and northern France, where it ripens reliably in late summer.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, wet summers give watery fruit and more scab; the soft fruit is unsuited to shipping anywhere.

health.other: Average overall disease resistance; some susceptibility to scab, but some resistance to fire blight is reported. Fruit bruises and softens fast.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a warm, open site and room to spread. Pick over several passes as the fruit colours, using greener fruit for cooking, and eat or process the crop within a week or two.

varieties.name: Summerfree

origin.parentage: Reported on Wikipedia as PRI 1956-6 x Ed Gould Golden (the same parentage given for Golden Orange, possibly an error)
origin.raised_by: Istituto Sperimentale per la Frutticoltura, Trento section (later part of CRA-FRU)

varieties.history: One of three scab-resistant apples released in 1996-97 by the Trento section of Italy's state fruit-research institute, with Golden Lasa and Golden Orange. Unlike its sisters it is an early apple, ripening at the end of August in Trentino.

look.description: A smooth-skinned, attractive early apple averaging about 175 g.

taste.summary: No published tasting notes were found.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous with a spreading habit.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Northern Italian fruit valleys; an early season means it ripens even where autumns are short.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Bred for scab resistance (Vf); other susceptibilities not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: An early, scab-resistant apple for low-spray growing, said to store unusually well for its season. UK experience is lacking, so treat it as experimental.

varieties.name: Summerred

origin.parentage: Open-pollinated seedling of Summerland (McIntosh x Golden Delicious)
origin.raised_by: K.O. Lapins, Canada Department of Agriculture, Summerland

varieties.history: Selected in 1961 by K.O. Lapins at Summerland, British Columbia, from open-pollinated seedlings of the McIntosh x Golden Delicious selection Summerland, and named in 1964. It was later tested successfully in south-central Alaska, where the original tree survived -40 F without protection.

look.description: Uniform, slightly elongated apple almost covered in a bright solid red, with prominent lenticels.

taste.summary: Soft to moderately firm, very juicy cream flesh with a refreshing, mildly winey sweet-tart flavour reminiscent of McIntosh. Reports of aroma vary from fragrant to faint.

tree.notes: Crops regularly year after year according to Alaskan trials; National Fruit Collection records a drooping habit.

pollination.notes: Diploid; a good pollinator for McIntosh, Golden Delicious and Delicious. Group estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates (full bloom around 5 May).

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter, short-season regions such as interior British Columbia and southern Alaska, where an early red apple is valuable.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers and mild winters; frost pockets because it flowers early.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A very hardy early apple for cold gardens; use a hardy rootstock where winters are severe. Pick in late August and eat within a few weeks.

varieties.name: Sundance

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Co-op selection 1050 NJ 1 (ancestry includes Winter Banana, McIntosh, Rome and Malus floribunda)
origin.raised_by: Purdue University, Rutgers University and University of Illinois (PRI)

varieties.history: A disease-resistant yellow apple from the PRI cooperative programme, tested as Co-op 29 and released in 2004. Its scab resistance comes ultimately from the crab Malus floribunda.

look.description: Clear yellow apple, occasionally with a light blush; skin can be thick.

taste.summary: Very firm, crisp, breaking cream flesh with a full, spicy and sprightly flavour, more tart than sweet at harvest with lemony notes; it mellows and sweetens in storage.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Mar, after a few weeks in store
taste.storage_change: Tart at harvest; mellows and sweetens in refrigerated storage, keeping texture for five months or more (Cummins, Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Vigorous spur-bearer; fruit hangs well on the tree.

pollination.notes: Needs a mid-season diploid partner.

climate.best_climates: Humid eastern and midwestern US conditions where scab, rust and fire blight are rife; a nursery quotes a modest chill need of about 500 hours, so it also suits warmer districts.
climate.poor_climates: Very cold zones below about zone 5, and short summers that cannot ripen a mid-October apple.

health.other: Field immune to scab and highly resistant to cedar-apple rust and fire blight; moderately resistant to powdery mildew.

varieties.grow_notes: An excellent low-spray apple for organic or humid gardens. Let it hang until fully yellow, then store; flavour improves after a few weeks.

varieties.name: Sunflare

origin.parentage: Honeycrisp x Cripps Pink
origin.raised_by: Washington State University apple breeding programme

varieties.history: WSU made the cross in 1998 at its Columbia View research orchard near Wenatchee and selected the seedling, numbered WA 64, after long trials. It was named Sunflare in 2024. Trees went to Washington growers from 2026, it is reserved for the state for at least a decade, and fruit is expected in shops around 2029.

look.description: A small to medium, two-coloured apple with a pink blush over yellow to yellow-orange skin and noticeable lenticels.

taste.summary: A balanced sweet-tart apple with a firm, crunchy, juicy bite. It is less hard than Cripps Pink, getting its crispness from Honeycrisp and its flavour and firmness from Cripps Pink.
taste.best_eaten: From harvest; keeps 9-12 months in controlled-atmosphere storage
taste.storage_change: Stores 9-12 months in controlled atmosphere and resists bruising (en.wikipedia).

tree.notes: Still being trialled by growers; no published tree description yet.

pollination.notes: Not published.

climate.best_climates: The sunny, irrigated semi-arid fruit districts of central Washington where it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: Not yet tested outside Washington; it shows some sunburn in strong sun.

health.other: Not prone to bitter pit and resists bruising. Mildly susceptible to mildew, flesh browning and sunburn.

varieties.grow_notes: Licensed to Washington growers only for now. It is picked about when Golden Delicious is, roughly two weeks before Cosmic Crisp.

varieties.name: Sunrise

origin.place: Agriculture Canada Research Station, Summerland, British Columbia
origin.parentage: McIntosh x Golden Delicious, with an unnamed selection also in the pedigree
origin.raised_by: Summerland Research Station (Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada)

varieties.history: Released in 1991 by the Summerland research station in British Columbia, the programme that also produced Spartan. The name was earlier used for an unrelated Victorian English apple from Welford Park, Berkshire; the widely sold modern tree is the Canadian one.

look.description: Smooth, clean apple with a long stalk; pale green-yellow skin flushed bright pinkish-red on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Remarkably crisp for an August apple, with fairly juicy white flesh and a sweet-sharp flavour that stays fairly acidic; one taster notes a slight pear flavour. Best chilled and eaten within a week of picking, as it browns fast and can turn mealy.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep; ripens over several weeks on the tree
taste.peak: Late August; keeps about a week refrigerated, best slightly chilled (Orange Pippin, Salt Spring)

tree.notes: Easy, reliable cropper. Fruit ripens over a long period so it can be picked as needed; training as an espalier helps colour.

pollination.notes: Early flowering (group 2); needs a pollinator that flowers early, and is exposed to spring frost.

climate.best_climates: Sunny, dry continental-temperate valleys like the Okanagan, and southern England, where it gives one of the better early crops.
climate.poor_climates: Wet climates encourage scab; very hot nights limit the McIntosh-type red colour, and early flowering risks frost in late-spring areas.

health.other: Somewhat susceptible to scab; shows some mildew resistance.

varieties.grow_notes: A good beginner's early apple. Plant with another early-flowering variety, give it sun for colour, and pick over several weeks from late August.

varieties.name: Sunset

origin.parentage: Seedling of Cox's Orange Pippin, pollen parent unknown

varieties.history: Raised around 1918 by G. C. Addy at Ightham in Kent, almost certainly from a Cox pip, and named in 1933. It received an RHS Award of Merit in 1960 and an Award of Garden Merit, and is the standard 'easy Cox' for gardens.

look.description: Cox-like fruit: golden-yellow with an orange-red flush and stripes and light russet patches.

taste.summary: Crisp cream flesh with a sweet, aromatic Cox-like flavour and gentle acidity. Flavour is very variable: excellent in good years (reportedly better on M9 than MM106 rootstock) but disappointing in poor ones. Does not keep well, softening after a few weeks, though it lasts about a month in a fridge.
taste.storage_change: Does not keep especially well; lasts about a month in a refrigerator.

climate_flavour.note: Orange Pippin: flavour can be very disappointing in a poor year, though it stays crisp and sweet; reportedly better on M9 than MM106.

tree.notes: A compact, moderate grower that crops heavily and regularly; fruit stays small unless thinned.

pollination.notes: Partly self-fertile, with frost-resistant blossom; crops better with a group 2-4 partner and is a good pollinator itself.

climate.best_climates: Throughout Britain, including cooler, wetter and more northerly gardens where Cox fails.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer regions are untested and likely to soften the fruit and dull its colour.

health.other: Far healthier than Cox, with fair canker resistance, though scab can still appear; small fruit if not thinned.

varieties.grow_notes: The best choice for a Cox-style apple in a small or northern garden. Thin to one or two fruits per cluster in June and store in a cool place or fridge.

varieties.name: Suntan

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Kent, England
origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Court Pendu Plat
origin.raised_by: Dr Frank Alston, East Malling Research Station

varieties.history: Raised at East Malling in 1955 from Cox crossed with the ancient late-flowering Court Pendu Plat. It is a triploid with Cox-like aroma but more acidity, and it once held the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Large, slightly flattened gold-yellow apple flushed and striped with orange-red, rather like an oversized Cox.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse, fairly juicy cream flesh with an intense, aromatic Cox-type flavour that is both very sweet and distinctly sharp. Keeps well for a month or two and mellows in store; yellower fruit is said to taste better than red-flushed.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Jan, after a few weeks in store
taste.storage_change: Trees of Antiquity: stores well into Christmas.

tree.notes: Very vigorous, spreading triploid; choose a dwarfing rootstock for small gardens. Crops heavily and regularly once established.

pollination.notes: Late flowering (group 5) and triploid, so it needs a late-flowering diploid partner, and a third variety if that partner also needs pollinating. Its own pollen is poor.

climate.best_climates: Frost-prone temperate gardens where its late blossom escapes spring frosts, such as much of lowland Britain.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to reduce colour and aggravate bitter pit; very short seasons may not ripen it well.

health.other: Fairly prone to bitter pit, so calcium sprays and even cropping help; resistant to scab and mildew, with some susceptibility to canker.

varieties.grow_notes: Useful where late frosts spoil earlier blossom. Plant with a diploid that flowers in groups 4-6 (Edward VII is a classic choice), give it room or a dwarfing stock, and keep watering and cropping even to limit bitter pit.

varieties.name: Surprise

origin.place: Uncertain; circulating in European collections by 1831
origin.parentage: Thought to descend from the red-fleshed wild apple Malus niedzwetzkyana of Central Asia

varieties.history: A small red-fleshed apple recorded in the London Horticultural Society's garden in 1831 and taken to the Ohio Valley by German settlers around 1840. It was judged of little worth for eating but became an ancestor of later pink- and red-fleshed apples, including Pink Pearl. Not to be confused with Surprise (Veitch) at the National Fruit Collection, a large cream-fleshed apple, nor with Landsberger Reinette, which has also been called Surprise.

look.description: Small, round apple with dull pale green to whitish-yellow skin hiding pink to red-stained flesh.

taste.summary: Very tart; its interest is the pink-red flesh rather than eating quality.

climate_flavour.note: Wikipedia: did better on the US West Coast with long seasons, hot days and cool nights than in the Midwest or East (growth, not explicitly flavour).

tree.notes: Little growing information. A tree survived in a Michigan orchard into the 1950s.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Reported to do better on the US West Coast, with long seasons of hot days and cool nights.
climate.poor_climates: Reported as poorly suited to the US Midwest and East.

health.other: Not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: Mainly of interest to collectors of red-fleshed apples and breeders. Check the source of any tree carefully, as the name is shared by at least two other apples.

varieties.name: Swaar

origin.place: Esopus, Hudson River valley, New York

varieties.history: Said to have been raised by Dutch settlers near Esopus on the Hudson River in the 18th century; the name is the Dutch word for heavy, after its dense fruit. It was in print by 1804 and became one of New York's celebrated winter dessert apples.

look.description: Heavy, flattish, somewhat ribbed fruit, greenish ripening to dull gold, heavily freckled and patched with russet, sometimes with a faint dull flush.

taste.summary: Dense, fine-grained creamy flesh that is sweet and richly aromatic with a nutty depth, the qualities that made its name among 19th-century American growers. Best after a spell in store.
taste.storage_change: Best after mellowing 4-6 weeks in store, when it softens and the flavour 'explodes' (Trees of Antiquity).
taste.peak: After 4-6 weeks in store; keeps 3-6 months (Trees of Antiquity).

tree.notes: A vigorous spur-bearer. Historically noted as needing good, deep soil to give its best fruit.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering; any group 2-4 diploid will do.

climate.best_climates: Humid continental climates with warm summers and cold winters, like the Hudson Valley where it originated.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, short British summers may leave it less rich than in New York; little information from hot southern regions.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not well recorded in modern sources.

varieties.grow_notes: A historic American keeper for enthusiasts. Give it a deep, fertile soil and full sun, pick in October and store until midwinter, when the flavour is at its best.

varieties.name: Swazie

origin.raised_by: First tree at the nursery of Isaac Swayze

varieties.history: A late-18th-century Ontario apple whose first tree grew at Isaac Swayze's nursery near Niagara-on-the-Lake. It is described in The Apples of New York (1905) and may be the same as 'Golden Gray'. Do not confuse it with the French-Canadian Pomme Grise.

look.description: A small to medium apple; the name 'golden grey apple' suggests a russeted golden skin, but no direct description was found.

taste.summary: Considered a high-quality dessert apple, but no fuller tasting notes were found.
taste.storage_change: Keeps well through the winter (en.wikipedia).

tree.notes: No tree description found.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: The Niagara fruit belt of Ontario and similar Great Lakes climates.
climate.poor_climates: No records outside eastern North America.

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A rare Canadian heirloom for collectors. It keeps well into winter.

varieties.name: Sweet Alford

origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: A Devon cider apple reputed to date from the eighteenth century, grown as a high-quality sweet. Rated a vintage variety capable of single-variety cider.

look.description: Small, flattened-conical apple with waxy pale yellow skin, a pink flush and russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Sweet, juicy, fairly crisp white flesh with only a faint astringency; the juice is sweet and makes a soft, mild bittersweet-leaning cider that balances sharper fruit.

tree.notes: Little published information on tree habit.

pollination.notes: Reported to blossom in mid spring; group not reliably recorded.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp South West England; also grown in North American and New Zealand cider collections.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No reliable disease data found.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow it to sweeten and soften blends built on bittersharps. Plant with another mid-season flowering cider variety.

varieties.name: Sweet Bough
varieties.history: An early American sweet apple described by 1817 and widely grown in eastern North America under many names; also once wrongly sold as 'Washington'.

look.description: Large, conical to oblong pale greenish-yellow apple, occasionally with a faint blush.

taste.summary: Very tender, juicy white flesh with a honeyed, almost acid-free sweetness and only slight aroma. Admirers value it as an early sweet apple; critics find it one-dimensional and soon mealy.
taste.peak: Aug-Sep, keeps only a few weeks (Bard AppleDB; Trees of Antiquity).

tree.notes: Small tree and heavy bearer with large, strongly scented blossom; responds well to thinning.

pollination.notes: Listed by a US nursery as mid-season flowering (taken here as group 3); needs a partner.

climate.best_climates: Eastern North American summers; a US nursery lists it for zones 5-9.
climate.poor_climates: No specific reports.

health.other: Described as disease-hardy; a low-spray grower in Massachusetts reports it largely disease-free.

varieties.grow_notes: A compact, productive tree for an early sweet apple; thin the fruitlets for size and eat within a couple of weeks of picking.

varieties.name: Sweet Coppin

origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: An old Devon cider apple, probably nineteenth century or earlier, grown to supply sugar to blends. It is held in the National Fruit Collection.

look.description: Conical, pale green-yellow fruit.

taste.summary: A pure sweet: sugary juice with very little acid or tannin, used to soften sharper or more tannic fruit in a blend.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill soon after picking in Nov.
taste.storage_change: Keeps only 1-3 days (Orange Pippin).
taste.peak: Ripens early November (NFC, Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Fairly small tree with a biennial tendency; fruit drops when ripe and does not keep.

pollination.notes: Needs a mid-season flowering pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp South West England.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season areas where very late fruit will not ripen.

health.other: Some mildew susceptibility; fruit keeps poorly.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow as a blending sweet alongside bittersweets and bittersharps. Press quickly after gathering because the fruit does not store.

varieties.name: Sweet Delicious

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Deacon Jones x Delicious
origin.raised_by: Richard Wellington, New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: Raised in 1911 by Richard Wellington at Geneva from Deacon Jones crossed with Delicious; a sister of Orleans from the same cross.

look.description: Large, ribbed, truncate-conical greenish-yellow apple flushed reddish orange with red streaks and many russet dots.

taste.summary: Firm, fine, creamy-white flesh that becomes melting; very sweet with an aromatic flavour and little acidity.
taste.peak: Excellent keeper (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: Little modern growing information.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records full bloom around 15 May, which corresponds to group 4.

climate.best_climates: Inferred from its New York breeding: temperate climates with warm summers.
climate.poor_climates: No documented reports.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: A very sweet keeping apple for collectors; grow like Delicious in a sunny, open site with a mid-season pollinator.

varieties.name: Sweet Sixteen

origin.parentage: MN 447 (later released as Frostbite, a Malinda seedling) x Northern Spy

varieties.history: Released by the University of Minnesota in 1977 from a cross of the old breeding selection MN 447 (later named Frostbite) with Northern Spy. Its unusual candy-like sweetness gave it a cult following among northern home growers.

look.description: Medium to large, roundish-conical apple with bright red stripes and flush over a yellow ground.

taste.summary: Very sweet, crisp and juicy, with yellow flesh and a striking flavour often likened to cherry candy or sugar cane; anise notes come through after a spell in store. Acidity is low to moderate.
taste.peak: ripens mid to late September; stores 5-8 weeks (Wikipedia)

tree.notes: Very vigorous, so a dwarfing or semi-dwarfing stock helps. Fruit tends to drop before harvest; pick promptly once ripe.

pollination.notes: Needs another apple or crab flowering at the same time; fragrant, long-lasting white blossom.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates of the upper Midwest, New England and southern Canada; reported hardy into zone 3.
climate.poor_climates: Low-chill, hot climates where northern-bred apples get too little winter cold.

health.other: Some resistance to scab, fire blight and cedar-apple rust; pre-harvest fruit drop is its main fault.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow on a restricting rootstock to tame its vigour, in full sun with a pollinator nearby. Pick as soon as the fruit is ripe to beat the drop; flavour develops further over a few weeks in store.

varieties.name: Sweet Society

origin.parentage: A Cox-type cross by the amateur breeder Hugh Ermen

varieties.history: A Cox-type dessert apple bred by Hugh Ermen and introduced in 2004 among the varieties the RHS chose to mark its bicentenary.

look.description: Small, yellow-green with a good red flush and russet streaks, like a well-coloured Cox.

taste.summary: A Cox-like apple, sweet, rich and aromatic. The fruit are small, so crops need thinning.
taste.peak: Picked late September, stores to December (Frank P Matthews)

tree.notes: Compact, bushy and free-spurring.

pollination.notes: Unknown.

health.other: Unknown.

varieties.grow_notes: No independent growing advice available; ask the supplying nursery for its experience with the tree.

varieties.name: Sweet Winesap

origin.parentage: Unknown; not a sport of Winesap despite the name

varieties.history: A 19th-century Pennsylvania apple that was long cultivated in western New York by the early 1900s and shipped to southern markets. It is unrelated to Winesap and was sometimes confused with Lady Sweet.

look.description: Attractive, uniform apple almost covered in bright light red with carmine stripes over a pale yellow-green ground.

taste.summary: Firm, fairly fine, moderately crisp and juicy white flesh with a pronounced sweet, low-acid flavour, good for eating and for baking.

tree.notes: Little growing information recorded.

pollination.notes: No UK flowering group recorded.

climate.best_climates: Eastern US fruit districts such as Pennsylvania and western New York.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; probably short, cool summers that do not ripen a mid-October apple.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage sweet apple for baking and fresh eating; keeps two to three months chilled. Pair with a mid-season pollinator.

varieties.name: SweeTango

origin.parentage: Honeycrisp x Zestar!
origin.raised_by: University of Minnesota (David Bedford, James Luby)

varieties.history: Bred at the University of Minnesota from a 1988 Honeycrisp x Zestar! cross and patented in 2008 as cultivar Minneiska. It is sold as SweeTango and grown under a managed licence by a growers' cooperative in the northern USA and Canada.

look.description: Medium to large fruit with a red flush and streaks over yellow-green.

taste.summary: Explosively crunchy and juicy in the Honeycrisp mould but with a livelier sweet-tart balance; tasters describe floral, lightly spicy notes (one found a trace of cinnamon) and citrus hints have also been reported. Best eaten soon after harvest: fruit left at room temperature turns mealy and bland within a week or two, and it does not bake well.

climate_flavour.note: University of Minnesota says fruit quality can be affected by climate and site, hence its release as a managed variety.

tree.notes: Bears young. A managed variety, so trees are mostly restricted to licensed growers.

pollination.notes: Needs a cross-pollinator; UK flowering group not published.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter northern regions with cool summer nights: Minnesota, Michigan, New York, Quebec, Nova Scotia and similar.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer, mild-winter areas where its Honeycrisp heritage suggests soft, poorly coloured fruit.

health.other: Disease ratings not well published.

varieties.grow_notes: Bred for cold northern orchards. Pick as soon as ripe and eat within a few weeks, as it does not keep its best texture for long.

varieties.name: Sweetie

origin.parentage: Royal Gala x Braeburn (the US plant patent gives the cross as Braeburn x Royal Gala)
origin.raised_by: Allan G. White; introduced by Prevar Ltd

varieties.history: A New Zealand Gala-Braeburn cross bred in Hawke's Bay, patented as PremA280 and released through Prevar under the trademark Sweetie. It was meant to be an early, very sweet alternative to Gala, and it is also grown under licence in Washington State.

look.description: Medium to large, conical, often lopsided fruit, striped and flushed dark red over most of a yellow skin, with prominent pale lenticels.

taste.summary: Very sweet with low acidity, firm and crisp, with very juicy cream-coloured flesh. The flavour has a faint spicy note but is mild and does not linger. The breeders' description rates the aroma higher than retail tasting notes do.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous with wide branch angles and a spreading habit, according to the plant patent.

pollination.notes: Flowers mid to late season in New Zealand; UK group not established.

climate.best_climates: Warm, sunny temperate fruit districts such as Hawke's Bay and central Washington; it ripens a few days to a week before Royal Gala.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in cold-winter or cool maritime climates.

health.other: The patent reports no notable resistance or susceptibility.

varieties.grow_notes: A licensed commercial variety, not usually offered to home gardeners. As an early Gala-season apple it is best eaten fresh rather than kept long.

varieties.name: Sylvia

origin.parentage: Gyllenkroks Astrakan x Worcester Pearmain (per Swedish sources)

varieties.history: A Swedish summer apple raised at the Balsgård breeding station in Skåne. It reached modest commercial planting in Sweden, with a few thousand orchard trees recorded.

look.description: Slightly glossy apple in pink and yellow.

taste.summary: Juicy, fairly firm flesh with a sweet, aromatic and only slightly tart flavour; collection tasters found it sweet and low in acid. It keeps only briefly.
taste.storage_change: Keeps only a short while after ripening in August (sv.wikipedia).
taste.peak: August.

tree.notes: Little growing information recorded.

pollination.notes: Swedish sources list partners such as James Grieve, Transparente Blanche, Sävstaholm, Alice and Cortland. Group estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates (full bloom around 10 May).

climate.best_climates: Cool northern European summers; grown in Swedish zones I-IV.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers, where an early apple turns soft and loses quality quickly.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: An early-August eater for cool gardens. Pick as soon as the fruit colours and eat promptly.

varieties.name: Taliaferro

origin.place: Near Williamsburg, Virginia, USA (probably Doncastle's Ordinary)

varieties.history: A Virginia apple found by Major Richard Taliaferro in a field near Williamsburg before 1778. It may have come from the Robinson family property, which explains the alternative names. Thomas Jefferson rated it the finest cider apple he knew. It appears to be lost, though 'Nelson County Crab', 'Highland County' and 'Red Coat' have been suggested as surviving forms.

look.description: A small to medium, flattened apple with straw-coloured to whitish skin and faint red streaks.

taste.summary: Jefferson found it very juicy and good to eat. He praised its cider above all others, comparing it to fine wine or Champagne.

tree.notes: No tree description survives.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: The warm, humid Virginia Piedmont and Tidewater where it was grown.
climate.poor_climates: No records outside Virginia.

health.other: Not recorded; probably extinct.

varieties.grow_notes: Not available as such; growers interested in Jefferson's cider should try the candidate survivors with caution, since none is confirmed.

varieties.name: Tartu Rose
varieties.history: An Estonian apple once treated as a native variety. Hansman's Estonian pomology (1970) later judged it probably the same as the American Wealthy. The UK National Fruit Collection received it as 'Rozovoe iz Tartu' from the Vavilov Institute in 1976. That clone ripens in mid-August, about a month before Wealthy at Brogdale, and is crisp rather than soft, so the two may not be the same and its identity is still open.

look.description: Small, broad-conical fruit with a pale whitish-yellow base, partly flushed and striped red, with a little russet.

taste.summary: In the UK the white flesh is firm, crisp and juicy but has little flavour. No tasting notes from Estonia were found.
taste.best_eaten: Straight from the tree in August

climate_flavour.note: The NFC says the fruit has little flavour in the UK, implying it does better in its Baltic home climate.

tree.notes: No tree description found.

pollination.notes: Flowers early at Brogdale (late April), well before Wealthy; group inferred from those dates.

climate.best_climates: Cold Baltic climates such as Estonia's, where it was grown and probably tastes better than in England.
climate.poor_climates: Mild maritime climates such as south-east England, where it gives little flavour.

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Mainly of interest to Baltic or cold-climate growers. In the UK, other early apples taste better. Check whether your tree is really Wealthy.

varieties.name: Telstar

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Kidd's Orange Red (per UK National Fruit Collection; another source gives Kidd's Orange Red x Cox)

varieties.history: Raised in 1934 by J. H. Kidd at Greytown in New Zealand's Wairarapa, the breeder also responsible for Kidd's Orange Red and Gala, but not named until 1965. If the national collection's parentage is right it shares both parents with Gala; it is little grown and survives mainly in collections.

look.description: Truncated-conical, somewhat ribbed fruit, greenish-yellow streaked with orange.

taste.summary: Firm, coarse cream flesh with a sweet, rich flavour and only mild acidity; described as strongly flavoured and sweeter than Cox.

tree.notes: No reliable growing data recorded.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from Brogdale flowering dates (borderline 3/4).

climate.best_climates: Raised in the temperate Wairarapa of New Zealand and grown in the UK national collection in Kent; little else recorded.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A rarity for collectors of Kidd's New Zealand apples. Treat as a standard mid-season diploid: sunny site, pollinator in group 2-4, spur pruning.

varieties.name: Ten Commandments

origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: A Herefordshire apple recorded in 1883. The name comes from the ring of ten red dots, the cut vascular strands, that appear around the core when the fruit is sliced across.

look.description: Medium apple, often entirely red, with large pale lenticels; flesh tinged red under the skin and ten red spots around the core.

taste.summary: Mild and mostly sweet with only gentle tannin; pleasant enough to eat and cook, and in cider it adds a pink tinge. Some tasters note an unusual, almost balsamic flavour.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct; keeps only a few weeks.

tree.notes: Little published information on growth habit.

pollination.notes: Reported as early flowering; needs a compatible early-blossoming pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist western England.
climate.poor_climates: Frost-prone sites may catch its early blossom.

health.other: No reliable disease data found.

varieties.grow_notes: Sources disagree on its cider class (sweet or mild bittersweet); it is best treated as a dual-purpose apple and blended with bittersweets for cider. Avoid frost pockets because it blooms early.

varieties.name: Tentation

origin.parentage: Grifer (Blushing Golden) x Golden Delicious

varieties.history: Bred by the Delbard nursery in France from a 1979 cross (Orange Pippin dates its development to about 1990) and protected as the cultivar Delblush. A group of New Zealand growers took it up from the late 1990s to supply northern markets in summer, and it is also grown in Europe, including Kent.

look.description: Golden-yellow to light greenish-gold apple dotted with many lenticels and carrying an orange to pinkish flush on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Sweet and crisp, essentially a Golden Delicious type; its full aroma is said to develop only a month or more after picking. Opinions range from rich to pleasant but slightly bland, with sweetness outweighing acidity.
taste.storage_change: fr Wikipedia: needs 30-40 days after harvest to develop its full aroma
taste.peak: from about 4-6 weeks after picking

climate_flavour.note: Orange Pippin finds the orange flush more prominent on southern-hemisphere fruit; no flavour effect reported

tree.notes: Medium vigour with an open shape; starts cropping early and bears regular, plentiful crops.

pollination.notes: Diploid and not self-fertile; plant with another diploid of similar flowering time.

climate.best_climates: Sunny temperate regions such as France and New Zealand; it is also grown commercially in Kent. The orange flush is reported to be stronger on southern-hemisphere fruit.
climate.poor_climates: Dull, cool seasons may leave it pale and less flavoursome, like other Golden Delicious types.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow like Golden Delicious: full sun, fertile, well-drained soil and a diploid pollinator. Pick when the skin turns golden and store for a few weeks before eating so the aroma can develop.

varieties.name: Tolman Sweet

origin.parentage: Unknown; sometimes said to be Sweet Greening x a russet, without firm evidence

varieties.history: An old New England sweet apple of uncertain origin, recorded by the early 1820s and grown for well over a century in New York and New England. Its exceptional winter hardiness made it a favoured grafting stock as well as a baking apple.

look.description: Pale butter-yellow, roundish fruit with faint russet dots and a distinctive line running down one side like a seam.

taste.summary: Firm, rather dry flesh with an intensely sweet, low-acid flavour; fairly plain raw but prized for baking, boiling and pickling, which bring out its richness. Also used in sweet ciders.
taste.peak: Wikipedia (1905 data): in ordinary storage November-January

tree.notes: Hardy, long-lived and productive, though inclined to crop in alternate years. Fruit hangs well on the tree.

pollination.notes: Plant with a pollinator; UK flowering group not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter northern New England, northern New York and similar climates where tenderer varieties fail.
climate.poor_climates: Hot southern regions; not a variety for warm, low-chill areas.

health.other: Disease behaviour poorly documented; fruit bruises readily and needs careful handling.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the hardiest old New England apples, good for cold sites. Thin in heavy years to reduce biennial cropping, and handle the fruit gently.

varieties.name: Tom Putt

origin.place: Devon or Somerset/Dorset, England (associated with Combe House, Gittisham, and with Trent)
origin.raised_by: Attributed to Thomas Putt of Combe, Gittisham, or his nephew Rev. Thomas Putt, rector of Trent

varieties.history: A late-eighteenth-century West Country apple named after the Putt family: either 'Black Tom' Putt, a barrister of Combe House, Gittisham, or his nephew the Rev. Thomas Putt of Trent. Grafted everywhere in Devon and Somerset gardens and orchards (hence the nickname 'Cottage Apple'), it picked up many local names and is now somewhat variable.

look.description: Large, broad, strongly ribbed fruit with a greasy skin, pale yellow almost covered by bright crimson-red stripes and blotches.

taste.summary: Sharp and juicy with a slightly bitter edge when picked, mellowing into a brisk, fragrant eating apple after a few weeks. It cooks well and makes a sharp cider with low tannin.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Nov; cook or press from picking, eat fresh once it has mellowed
taste.peak: In use September to November (NFC).

tree.notes: Vigorous, wide-spreading and quick to crop. Generally regular, though some Devon growers found it less reliable.

pollination.notes: Triploid: a poor pollinator. Needs two diploid partners flowering mid-season.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp temperate climates with cool summers, such as south-west England; growers report good crops as far north as Aberdeenshire.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summer climates are untested; fruit keeps poorly in warm conditions.

health.other: Generally healthy with some scab resistance; triploid; fruit does not keep long.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it room, as it spreads widely. Plant two diploid pollinators nearby. One of the most versatile West Country apples for kitchen, table and cider.

varieties.name: Tompkins King

origin.place: Warren County, New Jersey, USA (popularised in Tompkins County, New York)

varieties.history: Brought around 1804 to Jacksonville in Tompkins County, New York, where Jacob Wycoff grew it and it took the county's name. Liberty Hyde Bailey later found the Tompkins County tree had been grafted, which points to an earlier origin in Warren County, New Jersey. It became a major New York and Pacific Northwest commercial apple in the nineteenth century.

look.description: Very large, somewhat irregular fruit, yellow largely covered with orange-red to red flush broken by darker carmine stripes and pale dots.

taste.summary: Coarse-grained but crisp, juicy yellowish flesh with a delicate, mild and faintly floral flavour; growers find it very sweet with only a light tartness, although one listing classes it on the sharper side. Good raw, cooked (it needs little added sugar) and pressed for fresh juice; at its best in autumn and early winter, though well-stored fruit can last longer.
taste.peak: picked mid October; keeps 1-2 months

tree.notes: Vigorous, spur-bearing triploid that makes a large tree. Its own root system is reputedly weak, so it is best on a strong rootstock or top-worked onto a hardy framework.

pollination.notes: Triploid, so it is a poor pollen donor: plant two other compatible diploids (group 2-4) to pollinate it and each other.

climate.best_climates: Cool-temperate regions with good summers: upstate New York, the Hudson Valley and the Pacific Northwest, where it was grown commercially.
climate.poor_climates: Very cold interior winters can injure the tree; hot southern summers give soft fruit with weaker colour.

health.other: Poor own-root growth and somewhat limited winter hardiness are the main grower complaints; keeps less well than the classic New York winter apples.

varieties.grow_notes: Graft onto a vigorous, well-anchored rootstock and allow plenty of room for a big spreading tree. As a triploid it needs two diploid pollinators nearby. Eat or cook the crop by midwinter.

varieties.name: Topaz

origin.place: Institute of Experimental Botany, Czech Republic
origin.parentage: Rubin x Vanda
origin.raised_by: Jaroslav Tupy, Institute of Experimental Botany

varieties.history: A scab-resistant apple from the Czech Institute of Experimental Botany, released in the 1990s. Both parents are Czech, and through them it descends from Lord Lambourne, Golden Delicious and James Grieve. It is now a mainstay of European organic orchards and holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit. Not to be confused with an unrelated older English 'Topaz' raised by Seabrook in Essex in the 1930s.

look.description: Medium, rounded apple with yellow skin largely covered in a striped orange-red to crimson flush, sometimes with a little russet in the stalk cavity.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy cream flesh with a bold, tangy sweet-sharp balance, likened to Lord Lambourne or James Grieve but much crunchier; tasters also note spicy complexity, and one picked out something close to blackcurrant. A favourite with lovers of sharper apples, it keeps a month or two and mellows slightly in store.
taste.peak: Picked October-November; keeps 1-2 months (Orange Pippin), until March (Walcot), 4+ months refrigerated (Salt Spring)

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous, upright spur-bearer that crops early and heavily. Fruit size drops if the crop is not thinned in late May or June.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering; a reasonable pollinator for other group 2-4 diploids.

climate.best_climates: Central and western European climates with damp springs, where its scab resistance lets it be grown with little spraying; also does well in cooler parts of North America.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, humid summers favour leaf-blotch diseases it is vulnerable to, and warm nights weaken its colour.

health.other: Very resistant to scab (Vf gene) with moderate mildew resistance. In continental European orchards it has proved susceptible to Marssonina leaf blotch, which can cause early leaf fall.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the best choices for an unsprayed garden apple. Grow in full sun with a mid-season partner, thin fruitlets firmly to keep the apples a good size, and clear fallen leaves in autumn to reduce leaf-spot diseases.

varieties.name: Tower of Glamis
varieties.history: A Scottish cooker known before 1800 and once grown commercially in the Carse of Gowrie between Perth and Dundee, hence its synonym Carse of Gowrie. It was also taken up in continental and Russian collections.

look.description: Large, conical, strongly ribbed apple with greasy yellow skin, faintly tinged reddish-brown and dotted with russet.

taste.summary: Crisp, fairly fine, firm greenish-white flesh, juicy with a sharp but distinctly perfumed flavour. Cooks down to a well-flavoured puree.

tree.notes: A vigorous tree that crops regularly; as a triploid it needs room and a good pollination set-up.

pollination.notes: Early flowering and triploid, so a poor pollen donor; plant two early-flowering diploids nearby.

climate.best_climates: Cool eastern Scotland and northern Britain, as in the Carse of Gowrie orchards; also held in colder continental collections.
climate.poor_climates: No record of use in hot climates; early blossom is at risk in frost pockets.

health.other: Disease ratings not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy, heritage cooker for Scottish and northern orchards. Site it away from frost hollows because it flowers early, and provide two compatible pollinators.

varieties.name: Transcendent
varieties.history: An old American crab of uncertain origin, already grown in the first half of the nineteenth century and long planted across the northern states for preserves and cider. Its extreme susceptibility to fire blight later limited its use.

look.description: Large for a crab (around 4-5 cm), somewhat ribbed, golden-yellow with a crimson cheek.

taste.summary: Cream-yellow, juicy flesh with a mildly acid but noticeably astringent flavour; it softens quickly. Used for jelly, pickling, sauce and as a tannic addition to cider blends.

tree.notes: Large, spreading, very hardy tree that crops heavily. Prune out any fire blight strikes promptly, well below the visible damage.

pollination.notes: Pale pink blossom in mid season. Needs another apple or crab nearby and is described by one source as a poor pollen donor.

climate.best_climates: Cold northern climates with dry summers, where its hardiness is an asset and fire blight pressure is low.
climate.poor_climates: Warm, humid regions, where fire blight can kill limbs or whole trees.

health.other: Extremely susceptible to fire blight, its major weakness. Fruit keeps only about a week.

varieties.grow_notes: Best in cold, dry-summer areas away from pear and other fire blight hosts. Use the fruit within days of picking for jelly or juice.

varieties.name: Transparente de Croncels

origin.place: Croncels, a suburb of Troyes, Aube, France
origin.parentage: Reported as a seedling of Antonovka
origin.raised_by: Baltet Frères nursery (Charles and Ernest Baltet)

varieties.history: Raised in 1869 by the well-known Baltet nursery at Troyes, in its Croncels district, reportedly from a seed of the Russian Antonovka. Its pale, almost translucent skin gave it its name, and its hardiness made it a popular early autumn cooker in eastern France and central Europe.

look.description: Medium to large, pale matt yellow fruit fading to near white, peppered with light grey dots, giving a translucent look.

taste.summary: Juicy, coarse-grained white-yellow flesh that is only slightly crisp, with a gently acid flavour and a fairly delicate aroma. Excellent cooked; for eating raw it must be taken straight from the tree, because fruit picked too ripe turns floury, and it bruises easily.
taste.storage_change: Keeps no more than about a month (de.wikipedia).
taste.peak: Sept-Oct (de.wikipedia).

climate_flavour.note: de.wikipedia: aroma ranges from slight to fine depending on site; in a rough climate the fruit does not ripen.

tree.notes: Very vigorous and productive; fruit drops readily, so it is usually grown as a standard in a sheltered spot. Fruit bruises easily and travels badly.

pollination.notes: A good pollinator, flowering a few days before Golden Delicious; compatible with James Grieve, Lord Lambourne, Grenadier and Cox's Orange Pippin.

climate.best_climates: Cool and continental climates of eastern France and central Europe; very resistant to winter cold.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to hasten mealiness in an already short-lived fruit; windy sites cause drop.

health.other: Robust against most diseases and pests apart from codling moth; main drawbacks are fruit drop, bruising and short storage.

varieties.grow_notes: A tough, cold-hardy tree for any soil. Site it out of the wind, pick before full ripeness and use the fruit quickly, mostly for cooking.

varieties.name: Tremlett's Bitter

origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: A nineteenth-century bittersweet from the Exe Valley in Devon, named after the Tremlett family. It became one of the standard early bittersweets for commercial cider orchards.

look.description: Medium, firm, conical fruit, yellow with a heavy deep red flush.

taste.summary: A full bittersweet with a very high tannin load and little acid; the juice is markedly astringent and bitter, so it is normally blended to give body and structure.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill Oct, keeps up to three weeks.

tree.notes: Comes into bearing at three to four years and crops heavily; sources differ on whether it is regular or biennial.

pollination.notes: Blossom is reported to tolerate frost fairly well; needs a pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp South West England and similar maritime areas.
climate.poor_climates: Humid regions with heavy scab pressure.

health.other: Scab reports conflict: some growers find it prone, others fairly resistant.

varieties.grow_notes: A precocious, productive early bittersweet for blending. Use only a modest share in a blend, as its tannin can dominate. Space for good airflow to keep scab down.

varieties.name: Tropical Beauty
varieties.history: A low-chill apple sold by US nurseries for subtropical gardens. Nursery descriptions commonly give South Africa as its origin, but this and its breeding history could not be verified for this record.

look.description: Usually described as red-blushed; fuller details not verified.

taste.summary: Sold as a sweet-tart eating apple for warm climates; reliable independent tasting notes were not found.

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not documented in sources available here.

pollination.notes: Low-chill apples flower very early in the season; pair it with another low-chill variety such as Anna, Dorsett Golden or Ein Shemer.

climate.best_climates: Marketed for mild-winter subtropical gardens (roughly 250-350 chill hours) such as Florida, the Gulf coast and southern California.
climate.poor_climates: Cold-winter regions, where a low-chill apple blooms too early and is frosted.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: Only for mild-winter gardens. Plant alongside another low-chill apple for pollination and treat it like Anna for thinning and watering.

varieties.name: Tsugaru

origin.place: Aomori Apple Experiment Station, Aomori, Japan
origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Jonathan (pollen parent identified by DNA in 1990)

varieties.history: From a 1930 cross at the Aomori Apple Experiment Station, selected from seedlings raised in the 1940s, provisionally named Aori 2 in 1970 and registered as Tsugaru in 1975. Its unknown pollen parent was shown by DNA work to be Jonathan. It is Japan's leading early apple and second only to Fuji in production.

look.description: Medium-large round apple, pale yellow almost covered with red and darker red stripes.

taste.summary: Sweet and very juicy with low acidity and a mild, gentle flavour; the dense, fine flesh softens fairly quickly. Some tasters find it bland.
taste.peak: picked late October in UK (NFC)

tree.notes: Productive but notorious for dropping fruit before harvest; Japanese growers use stop-drop sprays. Colour is poor in hot weather, so better-colouring sports are widely planted.

pollination.notes: Self-incompatible (S3S7). Brogdale records flowering in early May, around group 2-3.

climate.best_climates: Northern Japan (Aomori, Nagano, Hokkaido) and similar climates with cool late-summer nights.
climate.poor_climates: Hot late summers spoil the colour and speed softening; a poor keeper anywhere.

health.other: Main faults are heavy pre-harvest drop, short storage life and poor colour in warm weather.

varieties.grow_notes: Pick promptly as the fruit loses its green tinge, because it drops readily, and eat within a few weeks. Brogdale records a much later picking time (late October) than Japanese sources, so test ripeness by taste.

varieties.name: Tumanga

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Schoener aus Nordhausen

varieties.history: Bred at Muencheberg in the 1930s (German Wikipedia gives 1935, Orange Pippin 1930) from Cox's Orange Pippin and Schoener aus Nordhausen, and marketed in East Germany from 1960 as Tumanga; in the West and at Brogdale it is known as Auralia. It is a parent of Pikkolo.

look.description: Small-to-medium, flat apple with smooth yellowish-green skin and a mottled orange-red cheek.

taste.summary: Juicy, tender, fine-grained yellowish-white flesh with a delicate sweet-sharp balance and a pleasant aromatic, perfumed character from its Cox parent. The flavour builds in store and is best from mid-winter to March.
taste.storage_change: Flavour strengthens in storage through to March (Orange Pippin).
taste.peak: Dec-Mar (de.wikipedia eating ripeness).

tree.notes: Strong grower forming a broad pyramid with dense, drooping branches; bears on short spurs and also laterally on one- and two-year wood. Described as a regular bearer.

pollination.notes: Blossom is described as hardy and long-lasting. Brogdale records full bloom around 14 May, which corresponds to group 4.

climate.best_climates: Central European continental climates like Brandenburg, where it was bred for commercial growing.
climate.poor_climates: Inferred: hot summers, where Cox-type aromas fade; humid sites favour mildew.

health.other: Prone to powdery mildew but fairly scab-resistant; the fruit bruises easily in handling and transport.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it room, as it is vigorous and spreading, and an airy site to limit mildew. Pick carefully in October and store cool for eating after Christmas.

varieties.name: Twenty Ounce
varieties.history: An American apple of uncertain origin, probably New York or Connecticut, that came to wider notice around 1844. It was grown across the north-eastern US for its very large fruit, valued for cooking and for market display.

look.description: Very large, roundish to slightly oblong fruit, green to yellow, splashed and striped with bright red.

taste.summary: Large, juicy apple tart enough that most growers prefer it baked or in sauce, though fully ripe fruit is listed as sweet-sharp with a honeyed character. Older accounts call the flesh coarse and fairly tender, whereas modern growers find it firm and crisp enough to hold its shape in the oven.
taste.peak: Late September-early October

tree.notes: A strong, spreading tree that bears partly on the tips of shoots, so avoid shortening every lateral at pruning time.

pollination.notes: Mid-season blossom in National Fruit Collection records; pair with a group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter, warm-summer climates of the north-eastern US and southern Ontario, where it was a standard orchard apple.
climate.poor_climates: Mild, damp maritime climates may give less colour; little information from hot regions.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not well recorded; very large fruit may need support or thinning to avoid limb breakage.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage cooker for anyone wanting really big apples. Give it room and full sun, prune lightly because of its partly tip-bearing habit, and use the fruit within a couple of months of picking.

varieties.name: Tydeman's Early Worcester

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Kent, England
origin.parentage: McIntosh x Worcester Pearmain
origin.raised_by: H.M. Tydeman, East Malling Research Station

varieties.history: Bred in 1929 by H.M. Tydeman at East Malling and introduced in 1945 as an earlier-ripening alternative to Worcester Pearmain. It is the seed parent of Folkestone.

look.description: Bright, almost wholly crimson-red apple with faint streaks over a yellow ground, resembling an early Worcester.

taste.summary: Crisp, fine white flesh that is very juicy, with a sweet, vinous flavour that shows the McIntosh side of its parentage. Short-lived: it softens within a couple of weeks.

tree.notes: Vigorous with long, whippy, sprawling shoots; partial tip-bearer, so prune with renewal methods rather than hard spur pruning.

pollination.notes: Group 3; needs a pollinator such as James Grieve or Cox.

climate.best_climates: Southern and eastern England and other cool temperate areas with reasonably dry summers.
climate.poor_climates: Humid climates favour the mildew it inherited from McIntosh; heat softens the fruit quickly.

health.other: Prone to powdery mildew; moderate scab. Fruit drops and goes soft if left on the tree.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it room or a vigour-controlling rootstock because of its sprawling growth. Remove mildewed shoot tips in spring and pick as soon as the fruit colours fully.

varieties.name: Tydeman's Late Orange

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Kent, England
origin.parentage: Laxton's Superb x Cox's Orange Pippin
origin.raised_by: H. M. Tydeman, East Malling Research Station

varieties.history: Raised at East Malling by H. M. Tydeman in 1930 and introduced in 1949. It was intended as a long-keeping apple with Cox-type flavour, to follow on after Cox in store.

look.description: Conical, Cox-like fruit, greenish-yellow with a brownish orange-red flush and a little russet.

taste.summary: Very firm, crisp and fairly juicy cream flesh with a rich, aromatic flavour in the Cox style. Quite sharp early in the season, it becomes sweeter and more rounded by midwinter.
taste.storage_change: Intensely rich, aromatic and quite sharp in December; later it mellows and sweetens, losing some of its scent, and keeps to April (Orange Pippin). Salt Spring (not counted) agrees: sharp for about eight weeks after harvest, subtler in store.
taste.peak: Dec-Jan, after several weeks in store (Trees of Antiquity: around Christmas)

tree.notes: A spur-bearing tree; thinning the fruitlets helps keep the apples a good size.

pollination.notes: Flowers slightly after Cox, in the same window as Laxton's Superb; partners from groups 3-5 work.

climate.best_climates: Southern and eastern England and similar temperate climates with a long autumn to finish the fruit before mid-October picking.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons may not ripen it fully; hot climates are untested.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded; with Cox as a parent, watch for scab and canker.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for anyone who loves Cox and wants fruit into spring. Grow in a sunny, sheltered spot on well-drained soil with a group 3-5 pollinator, pick in mid-October and keep the fruit cool until after Christmas.

varieties.name: Upton Pyne
varieties.history: Raised by George Pyne of Denver Nurseries, Topsham, and introduced in 1910, named after the Devon village of Upton Pyne. Fruit was shown at the RHS in 1933.

look.description: Large, conical golden-yellow apple striped and mottled with pinkish orange.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse and juicy flesh with a fairly sharp flavour carrying a delicate pineapple note. Mainly a cooker, it cooks to a purée, but it can be eaten fresh later in the season.
taste.peak: In season December to March (en.wikipedia).

tree.notes: Upright tree described as a regular bearer.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records full bloom around 11 May, which corresponds to group 3.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist south-west England, where it originated and is still grown locally.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; listed as suited to cool summers.

health.other: Some resistance to scab.

varieties.grow_notes: A good Devon dual-purpose apple for wetter western gardens. Store the fruit until after Christmas for fresh eating.

varieties.name: Uttwiler Spätlauber

origin.parentage: Thought to be a local chance seedling

varieties.history: A rare Swiss apple known around Uttwil on Lake Constance since about 1750 and conserved by ProSpecieRara. It became famous in the 2000s when an extract of its plant stem cells, noted for the fruit's very long keeping life, was marketed for anti-ageing cosmetics.

look.description: Smooth, glossy green apple turning greenish-yellow only late, with brownish-red tones on sunny sides; the skin darkens in long storage.

taste.summary: Firm, crunchy flesh with a sour flavour and only a faint spiciness; an acidic all-purpose apple used mostly for cooking and cider.
taste.best_eaten: Winter into the following summer; keeps up to a year
taste.storage_change: Keeps up to a year; the skin darkens to brown-black in storage (Wikipedia).

tree.notes: Grows vigorously and healthily, bears early and readily, and often forms blossom on summer shoot growth.

pollination.notes: No flowering group recorded.

climate.best_climates: Central European conditions with moderately moist soil and warm, dry, sunny summers, as around Lake Constance.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; probably very short cool summers that fail to ripen a mid-October keeper.

health.other: Described as a healthy tree with modest soil and climate demands; specific disease data lacking.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity for collectors and cider makers. It is undemanding and fruitful; pick in mid October and store cool, where it keeps exceptionally long.

varieties.name: Venus Pippin

origin.place: Devon or the Tamar Valley, south-west England

varieties.history: An old south-western English apple, thought to have been raised around 1800 in Devon or the Tamar Valley; around Launceston it was known as Plum Bidy. It is recommended locally for Cornish orchards.

look.description: Smooth, pale yellow to green-yellow apple with only an occasional pink flush.

taste.summary: Very tender, soft and coarse cream flesh with a slightly sweet, slightly sharp flavour and little aroma. Sharp enough to cook to a purée when first picked, it is briefly a pleasant eater before going over.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-early Sep; cook early, eat soon after

tree.notes: Little growing information recorded.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates (full bloom around 14 May).

climate.best_climates: Mild, wet south-west England, where it is a recommended local variety.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; hot summers would hasten its already short life.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A West Country heritage apple for local orchards. Pick in early August, use the first fruits for cooking and eat the rest promptly.

varieties.name: Vilberie
varieties.history: A traditional French cider apple, dated to the first half of the 19th century, that was brought to Herefordshire by the Woolhope Naturalists' Field Club at the end of the 19th century. It is still grown in English cider orchards for its full bittersweet juice.

look.description: Small, flattish, strongly ribbed yellow apple flushed and streaked orange.

taste.summary: A full bittersweet cider apple: sweet, very tannic juice with low acidity, giving a full-bodied cider.
taste.best_eaten: Mill Nov-Dec, within a few weeks of picking

tree.notes: Vigorous, open-spreading tree; precocious and heavy cropping.

pollination.notes: Very late flowering (full bloom late May at the National Fruit Collection), so pair with other late cider apples.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp cider districts of western England and north-west France; late bloom avoids spring frost.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season climates that cannot ripen a mid-November apple.

health.other: Appears susceptible to powdery mildew; some fire blight susceptibility.

varieties.grow_notes: A late, heavy-cropping bittersweet for cider orchards. Plant with other late-flowering cider varieties and watch for mildew; shake fruit down in November and mill soon after.

varieties.name: Virginia Beauty

origin.place: Piper's Gap, Carroll County, Virginia, USA

varieties.history: Grew from a seed planted around 1810 on the Safewright farm at Piper's Gap in the Blue Ridge of south-west Virginia; the original tree lived until about 1914. It was once a well-known southern winter apple that competed with Red Delicious in local markets, but is now rare.

look.description: Medium to large, often lopsided fruit with smooth skin almost covered in dark red to purplish red.

taste.summary: Fine-grained, tender, juicy greenish-yellow flesh with a sweet, mild flavour; prized as a late dessert apple that holds well into winter.
taste.peak: Oct-Feb; a good keeper (Big Horse Creek Farm).

tree.notes: Tree characteristics are not well documented.

pollination.notes: Not recorded; plant with another apple of similar season.

climate.best_climates: Upland South and Mid-Atlantic regions with long, warm growing seasons and cold winters, like its Blue Ridge home.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons (including much of Britain) may not ripen this late apple fully; estimates here are inferred from its origin.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A late, long-keeping southern apple: give it the warmest site you have and a long season. Store the fruit cool for winter use.

varieties.name: Vista Bella

origin.place: New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station, New Brunswick, New Jersey
origin.parentage: Complex: includes Julyred, Williams Early Red and Starr

varieties.history: Raised in 1956 in the Rutgers programme in New Jersey. Its name ('beautiful view') reflects its unusually good performance in trials in the Guatemalan highlands, and it is still grown on a small commercial scale as one of the earliest apples of summer.

look.description: Pale yellow-green skin heavily flushed and striped dark red, turning almost solid crimson in sun when fully ripe.

taste.summary: Light, juicy, creamy-white flesh with a fruity McIntosh-like flavour that reminds some tasters of slightly under-ripe raspberries. Excellent off the tree but loses crispness and flavour within days.
taste.best_eaten: Aug (from late Jul in warm years), straight from the tree; keep in the fridge
taste.storage_change: Flavour and crispness decay very rapidly after picking (Orange Pippin); eat within a few days (Salt Spring).
taste.peak: Straight from the tree; keep in the fridge and serve cool (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: Comes into bearing early and crops well. Fruit ripens over a short window and must be picked promptly.

pollination.notes: Early flowering (group 2); pair with another early bloomer.

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer regions where an apple in midsummer is valued: the US mid-Atlantic, upland subtropics such as highland Guatemala, and southern England.
climate.poor_climates: Areas with late spring frosts (early blossom) and wet, canker-prone sites. Chill figure is an estimate based on its success in tropical highlands.

health.other: Known to be susceptible to canker; fruit has very short shelf life.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant on well-drained soil to limit canker and choose an early-flowering partner. Pick the moment fruit colours and use it within a few days.

varieties.name: Wagener

origin.place: Penn Yan, Yates County, New York
origin.parentage: Seedling from Dutchess County apple seed; parents unknown
origin.raised_by: George Wheeler; propagated by Abraham Wagener

varieties.history: Grown about 1791 by George Wheeler at Penn Yan from Dutchess County seed and later propagated and sold by Abraham Wagener, after whom it is named. It won a New York State Agricultural Society award in 1847 and an RHS Award of Merit in 1910, became popular in Germany, and is a parent of Idared.

look.description: Medium, flattened and ribbed apple with smooth glossy skin, pale green turning sulphur-yellow, striped to solidly blushed red on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Very crisp, fine-grained, juicy white flesh with a harmonious sweet-sharp, aromatic flavour; German growers liken the aroma to cinnamon and rosemary, others find it honeyed or Northern Spy-like. It turns mealy if left too long or stored too warm.
taste.storage_change: Crisp and juicy when picked, turning mealy at full ripeness and in store (de.wikipedia).
taste.peak: Nov-Feb (de.wikipedia); Oct/Nov to Feb (Apples of New York).

tree.notes: Grows fast and upright at first, then slows as it starts cropping very early and heavily. Without thinning it overcrops, gives small poor fruit and falls into a strong biennial habit even on dwarfing stocks.

pollination.notes: Fairly early flowering with relatively frost-tolerant blossom; Brogdale records full bloom around 6 May (group 2-3).

climate.best_climates: Cool to warm temperate climates of the north-eastern USA, Canada, England and Germany; it is also grown in warmer southern US states, where it ripens about three weeks earlier and keeps less well.
climate.poor_climates: Wet districts, where scab and fruit rots are severe; poor, dry soils give small fruit.

health.other: Very susceptible to scab and fruit rot in wet regions; attractive to codling moth and sawfly. Stored below about 2.5 C the skin and flesh can brown.

varieties.grow_notes: Thin hard every year to keep fruit size and avoid alternate bearing, and give it a fertile, moisture-retentive soil. Pick early in the harvest window if the fruit is to be stored.

varieties.name: Warner's King
varieties.history: Believed to be a Kentish apple, known in the late eighteenth century simply as the King Apple. A Mr Warner sent it to the Rivers nursery, which added his name to distinguish it; it is a parent of Norfolk Beauty and Encore.

look.description: Very large, broad, slightly ribbed fruit, pale green ripening yellow, sometimes with faint brownish streaks.

taste.summary: Juicy, rather soft and coarse greenish flesh with a very sharp acidity. Breaks down quickly into a tart puree when cooked.
taste.storage_change: Keeps 1-2 months (Orange Pippin).

tree.notes: A vigorous, spreading triploid tree; give it room or use a dwarfing rootstock.

pollination.notes: Early flowering (group 2, estimated partly from National Fruit Collection dates); as a triploid it will not pollinate others and needs two early-flowering diploid partners.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist south-eastern and central England, where it was once a popular cooker.
climate.poor_climates: No documented use in hot climates; frost pockets can damage its early blossom.

health.other: Specific disease ratings not well recorded; triploid, so a poor pollinator.

varieties.grow_notes: A big, productive cooker for orchards with space. Plant two diploid pollinators that flower early, and pick in late September for use through the autumn.

varieties.name: Wealthy

origin.parentage: Long said to be a crab-apple seedling; DNA analysis (reported by Montana State University) indicates Duchess of Oldenburg x Jonathan.

varieties.history: Raised by the pioneer fruit-grower Peter Gideon at Excelsior on Lake Minnetonka from seed he sowed in the early 1860s, and named after his wife, Wealthy. It was the first large-fruited apple to survive Minnesota winters reliably and by the early 1900s was among the most planted apples in the US. It is the likely pollen parent of Haralson.

look.description: Smooth, pale yellow-green apple mostly hidden under bright red streaks and flush; the white flesh is sometimes stained pink.

taste.summary: Crisp at first, with tender, very juicy white flesh and a lively, vinous sweet-tart flavour; it is tart unless fully ripe, when growers find it remarkably sweet, and one taster caught a lingering hint of strawberry or banana. It softens and loses its zest within two or three weeks, but makes a pink-tinged sauce and rich apple butter.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct, fresh from the tree or within a few weeks
taste.peak: picked mid September (NFC) to mid October (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: Small-to-medium, early-bearing tree that overcrops and then slips into alternate years unless fruitlets are thinned hard. Fruit ripens unevenly, so pick over two or three passes; overripe fruit drops.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 3 (Orange Pippin). Any diploid flowering in groups 2-4 will pollinate it; in very cold gardens use another hardy apple or a crab.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates with short, warm summers and cool nights: Minnesota, Wisconsin, northern New England, the milder prairies, Scandinavia and Russia.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, humid summers give soft, poorly coloured fruit that drops early, plus heavy cedar-apple rust pressure; mild-winter regions will not meet its chill need.

health.other: Very susceptible to cedar-apple rust; some susceptibility to scab and mildew. Biennial bearing, pre-harvest drop and short keeping are the usual complaints.

varieties.grow_notes: A sound choice for cold, short-season gardens where English dessert apples fail. Thin heavily in a big year to keep it cropping annually, and keep it away from junipers where cedar-apple rust is common.

varieties.name: Westfield Seek-No-Further
varieties.history: Originated near Westfield in western Massachusetts in the late eighteenth century and became a standard New England and New York winter dessert apple, regularly sold in New York markets. Several unrelated apples share the 'Seek-No-Further' name, so the Westfield prefix matters.

look.description: Medium, roundish-conical fruit, dull greenish-yellow splashed with orange-red and carmine stripes, with russet dots and sometimes a thin bluish bloom.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp yet tender, juicy flesh with a rich, distinctive flavour that is aromatic, honeyed and dryly nutty, mostly sweet but finishing with a little tartness. A high-quality dessert and drying apple, not recommended for cooking.
taste.peak: Picked early October / very late; stores 1-2 months (Trees of Antiquity)

tree.notes: Bears on spurs and partly at the tips; little documented on vigour or habit.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not reliably recorded; assume a mid-season pollinator is needed.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter New England-type climates with warm, sunny autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Hot southern lowlands, where late apples of this type tend to drop early and colour poorly.

health.other: Disease profile poorly documented.

varieties.grow_notes: Suited to a sunny garden in a cold-winter area; pick in early autumn and store for winter eating. Prune lightly as some fruit is carried at shoot tips.

varieties.name: Wheeler's Russet

origin.place: England (grown at Brompton Park Nursery, London, by 1717)

varieties.history: An old English russet long credited to James Wheeler, founder of a Gloucester nursery. Robert Hogg doubted this because he found it listed in a Brompton Park Nursery day-book of 1717, when Wheeler would have been a small child, so its true origin is unknown.

look.description: Somewhat irregular, rounded fruit almost entirely coated in pale greyish-yellow russet, with a reddish-brown tinge on the sunny side.
