taste.summary: Greenish-white flesh with a gentle balance of sugar and acid and a light aroma; Victorian writers found it rich and wine-like, especially once the fruit began to shrivel in store. Modern assessments describe it as somewhat soft and only mildly aromatic.

tree.notes: Nineteenth-century accounts describe a healthy, hardy, medium-sized tree that crops well on most soils except wet ones.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering in National Fruit Collection records; plant with a group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Temperate English conditions, particularly the West Country and Gloucestershire where it has long been grown.
climate.poor_climates: Waterlogged soils and very short seasons; no documented performance in hot climates.

health.other: Historically described as healthy; modern disease data are lacking.

varieties.grow_notes: A long-keeping heritage russet for a well-drained site; it dislikes heavy, wet ground. Pick late and keep in a cool, humid store, since the flavour is best when the skin is just starting to wrinkle.

varieties.name: White Jersey
varieties.history: A Somerset 'Jersey', the old local word for a bittersweet apple. It is held in the National Fruit Collection and the Tidnor Wood cider-apple collection, but little else about its origin is recorded.

look.description: Not well recorded; the name suggests a pale-skinned 'Jersey'-type apple.

taste.summary: A medium bittersweet: juice analyses show moderate tannin with low acidity and average sugar, giving a soft, mildly astringent juice for blending.
taste.storage_change: Salt Spring: so-so keeper; best pressed within a couple of weeks of harvest.

tree.notes: Growth habit not documented.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Presumably the mild, moist Somerset cider country where it was grown.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A rare collection variety; treat as a typical Somerset bittersweet and plant alongside other cider apples for pollination.

varieties.name: White Transparent

origin.place: Russian Empire, probably the Baltic provinces (Livonia, now Latvia/Estonia)

varieties.history: An old summer apple of Russia and the Baltic that reached western European nurseries around the middle of the 1800s and was imported to the USA by the Department of Agriculture in 1870, where it is known as Yellow Transparent. Russian pomologists sometimes separate Papirovka from Belyi Naliv, but collections such as Brogdale treat them as one variety. It is a parent of Lodi and Early McIntosh.

look.description: Pale, almost translucent whitish-yellow apple, slightly ribbed, with fine pale dots and a waxy bloom; no red colour.

taste.summary: Brisk and acidic with a little sweetness and coarse, very juicy white flesh; usually picked while still greenish, since once it yellows it turns soft and mealy within days. Opinions on raw fruit range from bland to delightful at its brief peak, but it cooks quickly to a smooth, pale sauce that needs little or no sugar.
taste.best_eaten: Late Jul-Aug, within a few days of picking; cook slightly under-ripe fruit
taste.storage_change: Soon becomes woolly and dry (NFC); keeps about a week (Orange Pippin).
taste.peak: Late July-August, straight from the tree.

tree.notes: Fruits very young and heavily, which pushes it into alternate-year bearing; thin hard in heavy years. Fruit bruises easily and drops when ripe.

pollination.notes: Early flowering (group 2) and partly self-fertile; a poor pollen donor for others.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates: Russia, Scandinavia, the Baltic and the northern USA and Canada, where its extreme hardiness and earliness are prized.
climate.poor_climates: Warm, humid regions where fire blight is common; in heat the fruit softens and goes mealy almost at once.

health.other: Very susceptible to fire blight. Moderate canker and mildew; fairly scab-resistant. Fruit bruises and becomes woolly very quickly.

varieties.grow_notes: A first-of-the-season cooker for cold gardens. Thin fruit each year to reduce biennial cropping, pick slightly early for cooking, and plant another early-flowering apple nearby.

varieties.name: White Winter Pearmain
varieties.history: An old American pearmain of uncertain origin, recorded by 1849 and once a favourite dessert apple of the Midwest from Ohio to Kansas. It travelled west with settlers and is now valued in California and other mild-winter regions; it is the mother of the Japanese variety Indo.

look.description: Medium, oblong-conical, somewhat ribbed pale yellow apple with a slight brownish-red flush and numerous pale or russet dots.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, fine and tender flesh, juicy and mildly subacid with a sweet, honeyed and very pleasant aromatic flavour that improves in store.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Mar, after some weeks in store
taste.storage_change: Flavour matures in storage; keeps up to four months (Werribee Park).
taste.peak: Dec-Mar (Apples of New York via Bard AppleDB).

tree.notes: Little published tree information; an Australian heritage orchard calls it an excellent pollinator for other varieties.

pollination.notes: An Australian heritage orchard describes it as self-fertile and a good pollen donor. Brogdale scores the flowering of its accession as mid-season (taken here as group 3).

climate.best_climates: Warm temperate and mild-winter regions such as California and south-eastern Australia, where it is treated as low-chill; historically also the Midwest.
climate.poor_climates: It did poorly in New York, where it was not recommended; cool short seasons do not ripen this late apple fully.

health.other: No disease information found.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the better old dessert apples for mild-winter gardens. Pick late and store for a few weeks for the honeyed flavour to develop.

varieties.name: Wickson Crab

origin.parentage: Two of Etter's own crab seedlings, recorded by him as 'Spitzenburg crab' x 'Newtown crab'

varieties.history: Bred by the Californian plant breeder Albert Etter at Ettersburg and introduced by the California Nursery Company in 1944, with a plant patent following in 1947. Named after his friend, the pomologist Edward J. Wickson; it has become a prized single-variety cider apple in North America.

look.description: Golf-ball-sized yellow crab apple with a red to orange-red cheek.

taste.summary: Startlingly intense for a tiny fruit: very high sugar matched by high acid gives a clean, concentrated sweet-tart flavour, with a slight tannic grip to some palates. Excellent fresh and prized in cider blends; it needs plenty of summer heat to reach top quality and keeps only two or three weeks.
taste.peak: Salt Spring: late October; keeps about 2 months refrigerated

tree.notes: Vigorous, hardy and productive, cropping annually; fruit hangs well.

pollination.notes: Early flowering; a good pollinator for other early and mid-season apples.

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer climates such as northern California and the Pacific Northwest, where heat builds its exceptional sugar levels.
climate.poor_climates: In cool, dull summers it reaches less sugar and flavour; otherwise widely adaptable and cold-hardy.

health.other: Some susceptibility to scab and cedar-apple rust; generally regarded as a trouble-free tree.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it the sunniest, warmest spot you have to get full sugar. Useful as a cider blending apple and as a pollinator; harvest by taste in UK conditions since timing is not well documented here.

varieties.name: Wijcik McIntosh

origin.parentage: Limb sport of McIntosh
origin.raised_by: Anthony Wijcik (found); evaluated at Summerland Research Station

varieties.history: A columnar branch mutation found in the mid-1960s on a 50-year-old McIntosh tree in Anthony Wijcik's orchard at Kelowna, evaluated at Summerland and patented by Stark Brothers in 1979. Its dominant compact (Co) gene was the source of the columnar 'Ballerina' and later columnar apples. The fruit is ordinary McIntosh.

look.description: As McIntosh: a medium, flattish apple largely covered by a solid red to pinkish-red flush over pale green.

taste.summary: McIntosh fruit: rather soft, very juicy greenish-white flesh with a sweet, pleasant vinous flavour.

tree.notes: Grows as a single upright stem with very short internodes and almost no side branching, fruiting on spurs along the trunk. Mainly of interest for very small spaces, pots and as breeding stock.

pollination.notes: Early: Brogdale records full bloom around 29 April (group 2, as for McIntosh).

climate.best_climates: Inferred from McIntosh: cool continental climates with cold winters and cool autumn nights, such as British Columbia, New England and eastern Canada.
climate.poor_climates: Inferred from McIntosh: hot summers give soft, poorly coloured fruit.

health.other: Expected to share McIntosh's high scab susceptibility (inferred, not separately documented).

varieties.grow_notes: Needs almost no pruning beyond removing the occasional side shoot; plant 60 cm apart or in a large pot. Pair with an early-flowering pollinator.

varieties.name: William Crump

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Worcester Pearmain
origin.raised_by: Mr Carless, foreman at Rowe's Nurseries

varieties.history: Raised by Carless, a foreman at Rowe's Nurseries in Worcester, and introduced by the firm. It received an RHS Award of Merit in 1908 and a First Class Certificate in 1910, and it is named after William Crump, a noted head gardener at Madresfield Court.

look.description: Conical, fairly large dessert apple almost covered with a bright red flush and darker stripes over a pale yellow ground.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-textured and juicy, with plenty of sweetness and an intense, rich aromatic flavour drawn from its Cox parent.

tree.notes: Average vigour with a spreading, flat-topped habit; a regular-bearing spur type.

pollination.notes: Mid-season blossom; pair with another group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate climates like the English Midlands and south, where both parents do well.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to reduce its colour and aroma; untested in warm regions.

health.other: Considered of average disease resistance; no single major weakness is widely reported.

varieties.grow_notes: A rewarding late dessert apple for a sunny garden in southern or central England. Give it a mid-season pollinator, pick in mid-October and let the fruit mature in store until December.

varieties.name: Williams Favourite
varieties.history: The original tree grew around 1750 on Captain Benjamin Williams's farm at Roxbury, Massachusetts, and the apple was first known locally as Queen or Lady's Apple. It came to wider notice about 1830 and later spread south, where it is still kept in heritage orchards as an early red apple.

look.description: Medium apple heavily washed and striped with two shades of dark red over a green-yellow ground.

taste.summary: Tender, greenish-white flesh, sometimes stained red near the core, with a mild subacid and aromatic flavour. It softens quickly and does not keep.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug, straight from the tree
taste.storage_change: Does not store well (NC Historic Sites).

tree.notes: National Fruit Collection records a drooping habit.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates (full bloom around 13 May).

climate.best_climates: Eastern US conditions from New England to the upland South, where it ripens in July-August.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; probably short cool summers where its colour and flavour develop poorly.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A colonial American summer apple for heritage collections. Pick as it colours and eat or cook at once, as it keeps very poorly.

varieties.name: Williams' Pride

origin.place: PRI co-operative breeding programme (Purdue University, Indiana; Rutgers, New Jersey; University of Illinois)
origin.parentage: PRI 1018-101 x NJ 50; complex pedigree including Mollie's Delicious, Julyred, Rome Beauty, Jonathan and Wealthy, plus the Malus floribunda scab-resistance gene (Vf)

varieties.history: Selected as Co-op 23 by the PRI disease-resistance programme and released in 1988. It honours Edwin B. Williams of Purdue, one of the scientists behind the programme. It carries the Vf gene and is immune to the common races of apple scab.

look.description: Handsome slightly conical apple, mostly covered with a dark red to purplish-red flush over yellow-green.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy cream-white flesh with a rich, aromatic, spicy sweet-tart flavour that is unusually full for a midsummer apple; one taster noted butterscotch hints among the fruit flavours, though another found it bland. Ripens unevenly and keeps only a few days, so pick fully ripe fruit and eat it fresh.
taste.best_eaten: Aug, fresh; will keep a few weeks in a fridge
taste.storage_change: keeps quality and crispness 6 weeks or more in refrigerated storage (Purdue)
taste.peak: seven to eight weeks before Delicious; 'fall quality in the middle of the summer' (Purdue)

tree.notes: Fairly vigorous, vase-shaped tree that needs little spraying. Fruit ripens over several weeks, so pick in two or three passes. Some tendency to biennial bearing.

pollination.notes: Early flowering (group 2) with a long bloom period; a good pollinator for other early apples.

climate.best_climates: Humid continental and warm-summer areas of the eastern and midwestern USA, where its disease resistance and July-August ripening are most useful; also fine in mild damp climates.
climate.poor_climates: Very short-season or high-altitude sites may see erratic crops; otherwise widely adaptable.

health.other: Immune to scab (Vf), very resistant to cedar-apple rust, resistant to fire blight and fairly resistant to mildew. Early fruit attracts wasps and birds.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the best early apples for organic or low-spray growing. Plant with another early-flowering variety and harvest in several pickings as fruit colours.

varieties.name: Winesap
varieties.history: An old colonial American apple of unknown origin, probably from New Jersey; it was described in print as 'Wine Sop' in 1804 and illustrated by William Coxe in 1817. Prized for cider and for keeping, it was widely planted across the South and in Washington State until the mid-20th century, and is the parent of Stayman and probably Arkansas Black.

look.description: Small to medium, slightly oblong fruit with a smooth, tough skin almost entirely dark cherry-red, scattered with small pale dots.

taste.summary: Crisp, firm, juicy yellowish flesh with a tangy, spicy and distinctly wine-like flavour, sweet with a sharp finish. Keeps its character for months in store, which is why it was a favourite cider and winter apple.
taste.peak: Picked early to late October; stores well (3 months or more)

tree.notes: Slow to start bearing but then a regular cropper. Ploidy is reported inconsistently (diploid with sterile pollen in some accounts, triploid in others); either way treat it as a non-pollinator.

pollination.notes: Pollen is essentially sterile, so it cannot pollinate other trees and needs a separate pollinator. Flowers are an unusually deep pink-red. US growers describe it as late-blooming; one UK listing gives group 3.

climate.best_climates: Long, hot summers and mild autumns, from Virginia and the Carolinas to irrigated central Washington; historically one of the better apples for the upper South.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, short seasons such as England's rarely ripen it properly, leaving small, sour fruit.

health.other: Fairly resistant to powdery mildew and cedar-apple rust; some susceptibility to fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: Best in warm regions with a long growing season. Plant two good pollen-producing varieties nearby, since its own pollen is useless. Leave fruit on the tree until well coloured, then store to let the flavour develop.

varieties.name: Winston

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Worcester Pearmain

varieties.history: Raised in 1920 by William Pope at Welford Park, Berkshire, from Cox's Orange Pippin crossed with Worcester Pearmain. It was introduced as Winter King in 1935 and renamed Winston in 1944 in honour of Winston Churchill. It gained the RHS Award of Garden Merit in 1993.

look.description: Small-to-medium, conical fruit with a tough skin; greenish-yellow almost covered by an orange-red flush with darker red streaks and grey russet dots.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-textured, crisp and juicy cream flesh. It is noticeably sharp at picking and mellows in store to a sweet, aromatic, Cox-like flavour. It keeps its crispness well into spring.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Apr; improves after several weeks in store
taste.storage_change: A little sharp at first, mellowing in store to sweet and aromatic; keeps to April and improves somewhat after picking.
taste.peak: After some time in store; keeps to April

tree.notes: Its growing habits follow Worcester rather than Cox: easy, fairly trouble-free and reliably productive. Fruit tends to run small, so thin the crop.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 4. Some sources call it self-fertile, but it crops more reliably with a group 3-5 partner.

climate.best_climates: Southern and central England and similar mild temperate climates with a long autumn, where it ripens fully by mid-October.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season northern sites may not ripen this late apple. Hot regions are untested.

health.other: Very resistant to scab and fairly resistant to canker, so it is well suited to low-spray growing. Its main fault is small fruit when overcropped.

varieties.grow_notes: An easy late keeper for an organic garden. Thin the fruitlets for size, pick in mid-October and store cool to eat through late winter and spring.

varieties.name: Winter Banana
varieties.history: Found in 1876 on David Flory's farm in Cass County, Indiana, and introduced to the trade in 1890. Grown for its distinctive aroma and as a free-flowering pollinator, it is also unusually tolerant of mild winters for an old American apple.

look.description: Large, waxy pale-yellow apple with a soft pink to red blush on the sunny side; the skin marks and bruises easily.

taste.summary: Sweet, low-acid fruit with an unusual perfume; the banana note it is named for is subtle, obvious to some tasters and absent for others, and one grower found light pineapple tones. Texture reports differ: older descriptions call the flesh fairly tender and coarse, while growers describe it as dense and crisp, never mealy. The aroma builds as it mellows in store.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Feb, after a few weeks in store

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous, early-bearing spur type with tidy growth that needs little pruning. Its abundant blossom makes it a widely used pollinator.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 4 (Orange Pippin). A generous pollen donor for other mid-to-late flowering apples.

climate.best_climates: Unusually adaptable: grown in temperate regions down to about zone 5 and in mild-winter areas such as coastal California, where most older apples get too little chill (it needs about 300-400 hours).
climate.poor_climates: Humid regions with heavy cedar-apple rust pressure, since it is very susceptible; very cold zones below about zone 5.

health.other: Very susceptible to cedar-apple rust; average resistance otherwise. The pale fruit bruises easily, so handle and store carefully.

varieties.grow_notes: A good pollinator and aromatic keeper for gardens from cool-temperate to mild-winter climates. Handle the fruit gently and keep it away from junipers where cedar-apple rust occurs.

varieties.name: Winter Pearmain
varieties.history: A very old English apple, long grown in the Sussex Weald as Duck's Bill and sold on the London markets as Winter Pearmain or Winter Quoining. Its date of origin is unknown, and the name has often been mixed up with the medieval Pearmain. It is unrelated to the American 'White Winter Pearmain'.

look.description: Tall, conical, noticeably ribbed fruit, greenish ripening to deep yellow, flushed and streaked with red to crimson and freckled with russet dots.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, juicy yellowish flesh, sweet with a brisk, pleasant acidity. Usable for both dessert and the kitchen through the winter.

tree.notes: A hardy, medium-sized tree that crops regularly. Reported as triploid, so it is no use as a pollinator.

pollination.notes: Early flowering (National Fruit Collection records it with Egremont Russet). As a reported triploid it needs two diploid partners in groups 1-3.

climate.best_climates: Mild south-east England, especially the Weald of Sussex and Kent where it was a traditional orchard apple.
climate.poor_climates: Frost-prone sites threaten its early blossom; no evidence of use in hot climates.

health.other: Shows some susceptibility to powdery mildew and fire blight; otherwise not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A good traditional orchard tree for south-east England. Avoid frost pockets because it flowers early, and provide two early-flowering diploid pollinators since it is a triploid.

varieties.name: Wolf River

origin.place: Near the Wolf River, Fremont, Wisconsin
origin.parentage: Seedling of Alexander, pollen parent unknown

varieties.history: Found by W. A. Springer near the Wolf River at Fremont, Wisconsin, and recorded in 1875; believed to be a seedling of the Russian apple Alexander. Famous for huge fruit and great cold-hardiness, it became a farmstead cooking apple across the northern United States.

look.description: Very large, broad, flattish apple heavily striped and flushed red over pale yellow.

taste.summary: Soft, often dry greenish-white flesh with a fairly sweet, mildly tart flavour; many find it bland or spongy raw, though fruit left until after a frost can be juicier and better. It shines in pies and baking, holding its shape and gaining flavour with little added sugar, and stores for three months or more.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Dec, mainly for cooking and drying

climate_flavour.note: Trees of Antiquity: mostly for baking, but in the right climate on sandy soil it becomes a good dessert apple.

tree.notes: Vigorous, wide-spreading and slow to start bearing; branches may need support under the weight of its huge fruit.

pollination.notes: Needs a diploid partner in group 2-4.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental regions such as Wisconsin, Minnesota and the Canadian prairies, where few large apples survive the winter.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, long summers are not its natural range; in mild maritime climates it grows well but its main advantage, hardiness, is wasted.

health.other: Very scab-resistant and generally healthy; some fire blight susceptibility reported.

varieties.grow_notes: An ideal cooking apple for cold, exposed northern gardens. Use a semi-vigorous rootstock, be patient for first crops, and thin to get the giant fruit it is known for.

varieties.name: Woodcock
varieties.history: One of the earliest-described English cider apples, listed by John Evelyn in 1670 among the main Gloucestershire cider fruits. People thought the name came from the bird-like stalk, but Knight suggested it was the raiser's surname. By 1830 it was in decline, and it is now thought lost. In 1932 a writer suggested that the Monmouthshire apple 'Frederick' might be the same or closely related.

look.description: A medium, oval apple, yellow with a soft red flush that is deeper on the sunny side. It hangs on a distinctive fleshy, curved stalk about 2 cm long.

taste.summary: No flavour description survives. It was valued as a cider apple and usually blended with other varieties.

tree.notes: A large, vigorous tree with heavy, pear-like limbs.

pollination.notes: Not recorded.

climate.best_climates: The cider counties of the English West Midlands and the Welsh borders.
climate.poor_climates: No records elsewhere.

health.other: Not recorded; probably extinct.

varieties.grow_notes: Not available; believed lost. 'Frederick' is the nearest suggested survivor for anyone recreating old Gloucestershire cider blends.

varieties.name: Worcester Pearmain

origin.parentage: Seedling, probably of Devonshire Quarrenden
origin.raised_by: Mr Hale of Swan Pool; introduced by Smith of Worcester

varieties.history: Raised by Mr Hale at Swan Pool outside Worcester and put on the market by the Worcester nurseryman Smith in 1874, winning an RHS First Class Certificate the next year. It became the standard English early-season red apple and an important parent, giving rise to Discovery, Lord Lambourne, Tydeman's Early Worcester and many others.

look.description: Bright, almost all-over scarlet flush with a few streaks over pale green-yellow, dotted with fine russet lenticels; flesh white.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp white flesh that is sweet rather than sharp, with the well-known strawberry-like, slightly perfumed flavour, though its intensity varies. Traditional advice is to let it ripen fully on the tree because early-picked fruit is dull, yet some growers prefer it just short of full ripeness since ripe fruit softens fast; either way it keeps only about a week.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-early Oct; leave on the tree until fully coloured
taste.storage_change: Keeps about a week (Wikipedia); flavour benefits from leaving the fruit on the tree as long as possible (Orange Pippin).
taste.peak: Left on the tree as long as possible; mid-September (Orange Pippin).

climate_flavour.note: Orange Pippin: flavour depends heavily on the weather in the short ripening period (which weather is not stated).

tree.notes: Partial tip-bearer: prune lightly and leave some shoot tips. Reliable, heavy cropper of moderate vigour.

pollination.notes: Group 3 and partly self-fertile; frost-resistant blossom and a decent pollinator for others in groups 2-4.

climate.best_climates: The drier, sunnier parts of southern and western England; a classic of the Worcester and Hereford orchards.
climate.poor_climates: Wet western and northern districts encourage scab and canker; in hot climates the fruit softens and loses its delicate flavour.

health.other: Scab is the main problem; some canker. Good mildew resistance. Fruit attracts wasps, birds and codling moth.

varieties.grow_notes: A dependable early apple for most English gardens. Avoid heavy pruning because it fruits partly on tips, and be patient at harvest: the flavour comes only when the fruit is fully red and ripe.

varieties.name: Wyken Pippin

origin.parentage: Seedling of an unidentified Continental apple

varieties.history: According to tradition, Lord Craven saved pips from an apple he ate while travelling between France and Holland and planted them at Wyken near Coventry in the early 1700s. Lindley reported the very old original tree still alive in 1827. Some accounts, and Orange Pippin, treat it as a Dutch import, but Bunyard noted that no Continental variety matches it. It is the seed parent of Laxton's Superb.

look.description: Small to medium, neat, flattened fruit; pale greenish-yellow with a dull orange-brown cheek and scattered russet dots and patches, especially round the stalk.

taste.summary: Tender to moderately firm, fine-grained, very juicy flesh with a sweet, rich, aromatic flavour and a brisk edge. A highly rated old winter dessert apple.
taste.peak: picked mid October (NFC)

tree.notes: A healthy, moderately vigorous tree that is very upright when young and an excellent bearer, according to Hogg and Bunyard.

pollination.notes: No published group found. Estimated as group 3 from National Fruit Collection flowering dates (full bloom about the same time as Bramley). Plant a group 2-4 partner.

climate.best_climates: The English Midlands and other temperate regions with a long enough autumn for a mid-October apple.
climate.poor_climates: Little recorded. Very short seasons may not ripen it, and hot-summer performance is unknown.

health.other: Old writers call it healthy, but there are no modern disease ratings.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage winter dessert apple for a sunny, sheltered garden. Leave it on the tree until mid-October and store it to eat after Christmas.

varieties.name: Xanthous
varieties.history: Keepers Nursery lists this name among its late-season dessert apples, but no independent record of an apple called Xanthous could be found in the UK National Fruit Collection, Orange Pippin or other pomological sources. The name is an English word meaning yellow, but origin and characteristics are unverified.

taste.summary: Not recorded in any independent source available to us.

tree.notes: No growing data found.

pollination.notes: Unknown.

health.other: Unknown.

varieties.grow_notes: No independent growing advice available; ask the supplying nursery for its experience with the tree.

varieties.name: Xuanina
varieties.history: A traditional Asturian cider apple recognised for the 'Sidra de Asturias' protected designation. It is one of the acid-group varieties studied and recommended by Asturian research for new cider orchards.

look.description: Small-to-medium, round to slightly oblong-conical fruit, yellow-green with red and orange-brown colouring and purple-red streaks; cream to greenish flesh.

taste.summary: An acid-group Asturian apple: brisk, clearly sharp juice with fair sugar and low phenolics, used to give freshness to blends.
taste.peak: Ripens late October to early November (es.wikipedia)

tree.notes: Vigorous, comes into bearing early and yields well, with only a low-to-moderate tendency to alternate.

pollination.notes: Late flowering (early May in Asturias); pair with other late-blossoming cider varieties.

climate.best_climates: Mild, humid Atlantic climates such as Asturias and similar maritime regions.
climate.poor_climates: Regions with early autumn frosts or short seasons; cold-hardiness untested.

health.other: Very low susceptibility to scab and brown rot in Asturian trials; moderately prone to powdery mildew.

varieties.grow_notes: A good low-spray choice for humid areas thanks to its scab resistance. Late flowering helps in frost-prone sites; keep an eye on mildew in dry springs.

varieties.name: Yarlington Mill

origin.place: Yarlington, near North Cadbury, Somerset, England
origin.parentage: Unknown; a wilding
origin.raised_by: Mr Bartlett (finder); propagated by Harry Masters

varieties.history: Found about 1898 as a seedling growing out of the wall beside the mill-race at Yarlington in Somerset. Harry Masters took it up and spread it, and it went on to become a mainstay of West Country cider orchards.

look.description: Small to medium, rounded-conical fruit, yellow flushed and streaked with red.

taste.summary: A medium bittersweet: sweet, soft juice with gentle tannin and low acid, giving a rounded, fruity cider that also works as a single variety.
taste.peak: Mill November (picked late October-early November)

tree.notes: Slow to begin bearing, then heavy but strongly biennial.

pollination.notes: Late-mid flowering; needs a partner in bloom at the same time.

climate.best_climates: Mild maritime climates; grown successfully in English, Irish and North American cider orchards.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season areas where the late crop cannot ripen.

health.other: Good canker resistance; some scab and fire blight susceptibility; strong biennial bearing.

varieties.grow_notes: Thin fruit in heavy years to reduce the biennial swing. Suits standard or half-standard trees in a traditional orchard. Pairs well with Dabinett and Harry Masters Jersey.

varieties.name: Yates
varieties.history: Found around 1844 by Matthew Yates in Fayette County, Georgia, and widely grown across the South for its exceptional keeping. Valued as a winter eating apple and as a cider apple, and reported to grow well from the southern mountains down to the coastal plain.

look.description: Small to very small fruit, pale yellow almost hidden under dark red shading and stripes; flesh sometimes tinged red under the skin.

taste.summary: Pleasant, sweetish yellowish-white flesh, usually described as tender, juicy and aromatic, though one modern grower found it crisp and fairly dry with a tangy flavour suggesting blood orange. Holds its quality through the winter and is well regarded for cider as well as fresh eating.
taste.peak: Ripens October and keeps very well until April (Big Horse Creek Farm).

tree.notes: Tree habit not well documented.

pollination.notes: Listed as a group 4 diploid in one database; plant with a compatible pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Hot-summer, mild-winter regions of the American South, from the Georgia piedmont to the coastal plain.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, short-season climates such as Britain may not ripen this very late apple; chill and hardiness are estimates inferred from its Georgia origin.

health.other: Disease profile not documented in sources checked; its long popularity in the humid South suggests reasonable tolerance, but this is unverified.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the best choices for a long-keeping apple in a warm southern garden. Leave the fruit on the tree as late as possible and store it cool for eating through late winter.

varieties.name: Yellow Bellflower

origin.place: Near Crosswicks, Burlington County, New Jersey

varieties.history: An 18th-century chance seedling from Burlington County, New Jersey, that spread west with settlers and became a staple of early California orchards; Bellflower in California and Bellflower in Illinois are named after it.

look.description: Large, elongated, tapering fruit with ribs at the eye end, pale lemon-yellow with a soft pinkish cheek on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Tender, juicy, fine-grained flesh that is tart and aromatic when picked, mellowing in store into a rich, honeyed, highly flavoured apple; one taster likened it to key lime pie. Used for pies early in the season and for eating later.
taste.storage_change: Acidic early in the season; picked tart and mellowed in storage, becoming a good dessert apple later (Trees of Antiquity, Orange Pippin).
taste.peak: Later in the season after storage

tree.notes: Little reliable modern growing data; fruit bruises easily, so handle with care.

pollination.notes: Plant with a compatible pollinator; UK flowering group not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Warm, long-season districts of the eastern US and California, where it was widely planted in the 19th century.
climate.poor_climates: No firm record; probably under-ripens in short, cool seasons.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded; fruit marks and bruises easily.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage choice for warm-summer gardens. Pick carefully to avoid bruising and allow a few weeks in store for the flavour to soften and sweeten.

varieties.name: Yellow Ingestrie

origin.parentage: Orange Pippin x Golden Pippin

varieties.history: One of the first deliberately crossed English apples, raised around 1800 by the horticulturist Thomas Andrew Knight at Wormsley Grange in Herefordshire; Red Ingestrie came from the same cross. The 'Orange Pippin' parent is an old variety, not Cox. It was a well-regarded Victorian dessert apple for September.

look.description: Small, neat, shiny apple that ripens to a clear bright golden yellow, sometimes with faint freckling.

taste.summary: Fine-textured, tender flesh with an intense, rich sweet-sharp and pleasantly aromatic flavour; one taster found a hint of pineapple. Only moderately juicy, and best eaten within two or three weeks of its early-September picking.
taste.peak: Picked early September (NFC).

tree.notes: Weak-growing, spreading, flat-topped tree that crops regularly; well suited to small gardens.

pollination.notes: Group 3; plant with another group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist English and Irish climates where it has been grown for two centuries.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance in hot or very cold regions; values inferred from its English origin.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A pretty, compact heritage tree for a small garden. Leave fruit until it is fully golden for the best flavour, and give it a mid-season pollination partner.

varieties.name: York Imperial
varieties.history: A chance tree on a farm near York, Pennsylvania, propagated around 1820 by Quaker nurseryman Jonathan Jessop. A. J. Downing later praised it as the 'imperial of keepers', and it became the backbone of the Pennsylvania and Virginia processing industry for sauce and pie filling.

look.description: Distinctly lopsided, oblique fruit, flushed and streaked red over greenish-yellow, with pale specks and a greyish bloom.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, moderately juicy flesh that is tart-sweet at picking and needs a month or more in store to develop, becoming sweeter, mellower and honeyed, with a pear-like note some tasters pick up; it keeps until spring under refrigeration. Holds together well in cooking and gives a good sauce.
taste.storage_change: keeps extremely well and sweetens, becoming mellower, for 5-6 months after picking (Wikipedia)
taste.peak: excellent keeper (Orange Pippin)

tree.notes: Strong tendency to crop in alternate years; fruit thinning in a heavy year helps even it out.

pollination.notes: Needs a compatible pollinator; UK flowering group not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer mid-Atlantic orchards of Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia and West Virginia.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons leave it hard and sour; humid regions bring heavy disease pressure.

health.other: Prone to the calcium disorders cork spot ('York spot') and bitter pit, and susceptible to scab, mildew, fire blight and cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: A warm-region processing and storage apple. Keep soil calcium and moisture steady and thin heavy crops to reduce cork spot and biennial bearing. Store for a month or more before judging the flavour.

varieties.name: Young America
varieties.history: A small 19th-century apple from New York State, held at Brogdale since 1954. The National Fruit Collection records it only to the genus Malus rather than Malus domestica, which hints at crab apple ancestry, and its precise origin and date are not documented.

look.description: Small, tall, somewhat ribbed fruit almost entirely streaked bright red over yellow, with a slightly greasy skin.

taste.summary: Sharp and noticeably astringent, more like a large crab than a typical dessert apple; an unusual, intense fruit flavour for those who like tartness.
taste.peak: Picked late August (NFC)

tree.notes: No published growing data.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records it flowering several days before Cox, so roughly group 2.

climate.best_climates: Cool-temperate climates like its native New York and southern England.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance in hot or very cold regions; values inferred from its New York origin and possible crab parentage.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity for collectors: attractive small red fruit with a tart, astringent bite. Plant with an early-flowering partner.

varieties.name: Zabergau Reinette

origin.place: Hausen an der Zaber, Wurttemberg, Germany

varieties.history: A German russet reinette grown from seed sown in 1885 at Hausen on the river Zaber in Wurttemberg. It is triploid, which helps explain why its fruit is much larger than most russets.

look.description: Big, broad, rounded-conical apple largely covered in grey-brown russet over a greenish-yellow skin, sometimes with a streaky orange flush.

taste.summary: Firm, dense and fairly juicy yellowish flesh with a rich, nutty flavour that one grower likened to a tart, spicy russet. Sharp and hard straight from the tree, it becomes noticeably sweeter after a month or so in cool storage and then has a few weeks at its best.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Feb, after a few weeks in store
taste.storage_change: Rather sharp with dense flesh straight from the tree; much sweeter after a month or so in cold store.
taste.peak: After about a month in cold store

tree.notes: A strong-growing triploid; reported as a regular, heavy cropper. Attractive blossom.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering. Triploid and a poor pollen donor, so plant two compatible diploids from groups 2-4 nearby.

climate.best_climates: Central European climates with cold winters and warm summers, like its native Wurttemberg; also does well in southern England.
climate.poor_climates: Very short, cool seasons may leave it too sharp; hot, dry climates are untested.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not well recorded in English-language sources; the cut flesh browns quickly.

varieties.grow_notes: Give this vigorous triploid space or a dwarfing rootstock, and plant two diploid pollinators nearby. Pick in mid-October and store cool for several weeks before eating, so that the sharpness has time to mellow.

varieties.name: Zestar

origin.parentage: State Fair x MN 1691

varieties.history: Released by the University of Minnesota in 1999 (trade name Zestar!, cultivar name Minnewashta) to give cold-climate growers a high-quality early apple. It ripens in late summer, weeks ahead of Honeycrisp.

look.description: Round apple, about three-quarters covered in red flush and streaks over yellow-green.

taste.summary: Very crisp, light and juicy, far crunchier than most early apples, with a lively sweet-tart balance; the advertised hint of brown sugar is something some tasters find and others cannot detect. Keeps its texture much longer than typical summer apples if stored cool, though warm-stored fruit can go mealy.
taste.storage_change: Keeps its taste and crunch about 2 months refrigerated (University of Minnesota); Wikipedia says 2 months with or without refrigeration.
taste.peak: Late August to early September (Minnesota)

tree.notes: Hardy, moderately vigorous tree bred for cold-climate orchards.

pollination.notes: No UK flowering group recorded; needs a compatible pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cold northern regions with short summers, where an early apple of good quality is otherwise hard to find.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers ripen it in the heat, which spoils colour and storage; mild-winter areas lack chill.

health.other: Rated susceptible to apple scab by the University of Minnesota; plan a spray or sanitation routine in wet districts.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant where an early, crunchy apple is wanted in a cold climate. Rake up and remove fallen leaves in autumn to cut scab carry-over.

varieties.name: Zoete Ermgaard
varieties.history: A Dutch sweet apple known since 1864, once the main sweet apple of North and South Holland where it was grown on tall standard trees. It was eaten fresh and used for stewing in the traditional Dutch way.

look.description: Fairly small to medium, narrowly conical yellow apple streaked light red.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp but coarse and rather dry white flesh with a very sweet, low-acid flavour; prized as a sweet stewing apple as well as for eating.
taste.peak: From mid November, keeping to mid April (nl.wikipedia).

tree.notes: Slow to come into bearing, modest and biennial cropper; fruit clings firmly to the tree.

pollination.notes: Late flowering; Dutch sources suggest partners such as Bloemee, Brabantse Bellefleur, Sterappel or Zoete Kroon. Group estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates (full bloom around 20 May).

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist maritime lowlands like the western Netherlands; late bloom helps it escape spring frost.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; hot dry summers would probably dry the flesh further.

health.other: Little troubled by disease according to Dutch sources; red spider mite is the main pest.

varieties.grow_notes: Suited to a large standard tree in a traditional orchard. Expect slow, irregular crops; thin in heavy years. Store until November before eating.

varieties.name: Zuccalmaglio's Renette

origin.parentage: Ananas Reinette x Purpurroter Agatapfel

varieties.history: Raised in 1878 at Grevenbroich on the Lower Rhine by the breeder Diedrich Uhlhorn the younger, from Ananas Reinette crossed with Purpurroter Agatapfel. It is valued in Germany as a winter dessert apple on a small, weak-growing tree.

look.description: Small to medium, rounded to egg-shaped and somewhat ribbed apple, greenish-yellow ripening to lemon-yellow, with a faint orange-red wash on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained yellowish flesh with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavour and plenty of aroma; some tasters find it on the dry side.
taste.peak: Nov-Mar (de.wikipedia: Genussreife November bis März).

tree.notes: Weak-growing, compact tree suited to small gardens, but it needs good, moist, fertile soil plus regular pruning and fruit thinning to keep fruit size up.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records mid-season flowering (about group 3).

climate.best_climates: Mild central European lowlands such as the Lower Rhine, on rich, moisture-retentive soils.
climate.poor_climates: Dry or poor soils, where the weak tree struggles and fruit stays small.

health.other: German sources describe it as little troubled by pests and diseases.

varieties.grow_notes: A good candidate for a small garden tree, provided the soil is rich and kept moist. Thin fruitlets after the June drop, pick in mid October and store for winter eating; plant a group 2-4 partner.

rootstocks.name: B.491

origin.place: Michurinsk College of Horticulture (now Michurinsk State Agrarian University), Tambov region
origin.parentage: B.9 x 13-14 (2023 SSR pedigree study); an earlier Michurinsk account lists B.9 x 'Naliv Aliy'
origin.note: Selection 57-491 (year of cross from the selection number); red leaves and pink wood.

rootstocks.support: Permanent stake or trellis; wood is brittle
rootstocks.soil_notes: needs fertile, well-drained, weed-free soil; keep away from wet ground (Phytophthora)
rootstocks.best_for: very small trees or hardy dwarfing interstems in severe-winter climates
rootstocks.avoid_when: fire-blight areas, wet soils, poor or grassed ground, commercial blocks wanting full-size dwarfs
rootstocks.variety_fit: Only vigorous scions make a useful tree; weak varieties are stunted.
rootstocks.notes: Very dwarfing, very winter-hardy Michurinsk stock in the M.27 class; in the NC-140 1994 Gala trial trees were about a third to a half the size of those on B.9, with slightly lower yield efficiency. Considered too dwarfing for most commercial orchards but useful as a hardy interstem, and it propagates easily in stoolbeds. Brittle, and very susceptible to fire blight and Phytophthora.

rootstocks.name: M.27

origin.note: Cross made 1929 and selected 1934 (trialled as Malling 3431); not released to growers until the mid-1970s.

rootstocks.support: Permanent stake or wires for life
rootstocks.soil_notes: Only for deep, fertile, well-drained soil kept free of grass and weeds; needs regular watering and feeding or trees stall ('runt out').
rootstocks.best_for: very small gardens, stepovers, mini-cordons, dwarf pyramids and large containers
rootstocks.avoid_when: poor, dry, wet or grassed ground; replant sites; weak or spur-type varieties; severe-winter regions
rootstocks.variety_fit: Best with vigorous varieties (including triploids) that would be too big on M.9; weak growers and spur types make tiny, stunted trees.
rootstocks.notes: The most dwarfing of the Malling stocks, giving a tree roughly half the size of one on M.9 that crops in its second or third year. Roots are small and brittle, so the tree needs a stake for life and good growing conditions. Collar rot resistance is good, but it is susceptible to woolly aphid; fire blight ratings vary between sources (Ontario lists it as tolerant, US extension as highly susceptible).

rootstocks.name: P.16

origin.place: Research Institute of Pomology (now Research Institute of Horticulture), Skierniewice
origin.parentage: M.9 x Common Antonovka (Antonowka Zwykla)

rootstocks.support: Permanent stake or trellis; wood is brittle
rootstocks.soil_notes: needs fertile, well-managed, irrigated soil; too weak for light or grassed ground
rootstocks.best_for: very high-density plantings on good soil; small garden trees
rootstocks.avoid_when: poor or dry soils, cold-winter sites, fire-blight areas
rootstocks.variety_fit: Pairs with vigorous scions; fruit was smaller than on M.9 with some varieties.
rootstocks.notes: Dwarfing Polish stock between M.27 and M.9 in vigour (trunk area roughly a third to two-thirds that of M.9) with the highest cropping efficiency in several Polish trials but low yield per tree. Produced no suckers or burr knots in an 11-year Skierniewice trial and was recommended there alongside M.9 T337 for Golden Delicious Reinders. Early Geneva work found it brittle, and Polish pomologists regarded it as less winter-hardy than other P stocks.

rootstocks.name: P.22

origin.place: Research Institute of Pomology (now Research Institute of Horticulture), Skierniewice
origin.parentage: M.9 x Common Antonovka (Antonowka Zwykla)

rootstocks.support: Permanent stake or trellis
rootstocks.soil_notes: needs fertile, weed-free, irrigated soil like M.27
rootstocks.best_for: very small trees, containers and super-dense plantings in cold regions; hardy dwarfing interstem
rootstocks.avoid_when: poor, dry or grassed ground; woolly aphid or fire-blight hot spots; weak scion varieties
rootstocks.variety_fit: Only vigorous varieties make a worthwhile tree; fruit tended to be smaller than on M.9.
rootstocks.notes: Polish super-dwarf in the M.27 size class, very precocious, with few suckers or burr knots and good crown-rot resistance. In a 1971/72 Polish freeze fewer than a quarter of P 22 plants were damaged against over 85% of M.9. Yields per tree are low and fruit tends to be small; it is very susceptible to woolly aphid and moderately to highly susceptible to fire blight.

rootstocks.name: B.10

origin.place: Michurinsk State Agrarian University, Tambov region
origin.parentage: selection 13-14 (M.8 x 'Tayozhnoe') x B.9
origin.note: Michurinsk selection 62-396 (year of cross from the selection number), renamed B.10 for Western trials. One US extension page gives 'M.27 x Robusta 5', which conflicts with Michurinsk records and a 2023 SSR pedigree study.

rootstocks.support: Support advised in intensive plantings; anchorage reported better than M.9
rootstocks.soil_notes: treat like other M.9-class stocks: fertile, well-drained soil, weed control and irrigation
rootstocks.best_for: high-density orchards in cold-winter regions wanting M.9-sized trees with more hardiness
rootstocks.avoid_when: poor, dry or unirrigated sites
rootstocks.notes: Red-leaved Michurinsk selection 62-396, bred for winter hardiness and released in the West as B.10. In Pennsylvania and NC-140 trials it gave M.9-class trees, in one trial slightly smaller than M.9 T337, with yield efficiency at or above M.9 T337 and wide branch angles; in Polish trials (as B 396) trees matched M.9 EMLA in size and out-yielded it. Fire blight tolerance is reported but pest and disease data outside Russia are still thin.

rootstocks.name: B.9

origin.place: Michurinsk College of Horticulture (now Michurinsk State Agrarian University), Tambov region
origin.parentage: M.8 x 'Krasny Standart' (Red Standard), a red-fleshed Michurin apple
origin.note: Bred by V.I. Budagovsky and introduced in the late 1940s; the red leaves and red-tinged wood come from the red-fleshed parent.

rootstocks.support: Permanent stake or trellis for life; roots are brittle
rootstocks.soil_notes: needs fertile, weed-free, well-drained soil and irrigation in dry spells; copes with heavier soils better than M.26 because it resists collar rot
rootstocks.best_for: high-density spindles and trellised trees in cold-winter regions; hardy dwarfing interstem
rootstocks.avoid_when: dry unirrigated sites, poor or grassed ground, places where trees cannot be supported
rootstocks.variety_fit: Best with moderately vigorous scions; weak or spur-type varieties can be over-dwarfed unless soil and irrigation are good.
rootstocks.notes: Very winter-hardy red-leaved dwarfing stock from central Russia, a little smaller than M.9 in most trials and very precocious and yield-efficient. Leaves and young shoots blight readily when inoculated, but Cornell work found the mature rootstock shank highly resistant to rootstock blight in field plantings; it resists collar rot but is susceptible to woolly aphid and mildew. A European (trailing) and a North American (upright) strain circulate, the latter producing more burr knots; stoolbed propagation is difficult and the stock is drought-sensitive.

rootstocks.name: CG.5087

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.note: Unreleased selection; evaluated in the 2010 NC-140 Honeycrisp trial.

rootstocks.support: Trellised in trials; support in high-density systems
rootstocks.soil_notes: no published soil-specific data
rootstocks.best_for: research and trial plantings only
rootstocks.avoid_when: commercial or garden planting - not released
rootstocks.variety_fit: Only Honeycrisp data published; fruit ran smaller than on M.26.
rootstocks.notes: An unreleased Cornell-Geneva selection; in the 2010 NC-140 Honeycrisp trial it grouped with M.26 and M.9 Pajam 2 as a large dwarf after 8 years and was among the most yield-efficient in that class, with higher projected per-hectare yield than M.26. Survival was 91% (100% at the Minnesota and Wisconsin sites) and suckering was similar to M.26, though Honeycrisp fruit averaged smaller. No published disease-resistance ratings were found.

rootstocks.name: G.11

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: M.26 x Robusta 5
origin.note: Released 1999 (US plant patent PP11,070).

rootstocks.support: Stake or trellis for life; crops come early and heavy
rootstocks.soil_notes: fertile, well-drained ground with irrigation in dry spells; copes with replant soils better than M.9/M.26
rootstocks.best_for: high-density spindle or trellis orchards and small gardens wanting an M.9-sized tree with fire-blight insurance
rootstocks.avoid_when: woolly-aphid-prone warm regions without aphid control; dry unirrigated or grassed sites; winters colder than zone 5 until its hardiness is better proven
rootstocks.variety_fit: Cornell suggests it for strong-growing varieties; weak growers such as Honeycrisp can stay too small on it.
rootstocks.notes: Tree size matches M.9 T337 or runs slightly larger, with yield efficiency at or above M.9 and good fruit size; it was among the most efficient moderate dwarfs in the 8-year 2010 NC-140 Honeycrisp trial. Moderately resistant to fire blight (rarely killed through the rootstock, but not immune) and to crown rot, and tolerant of replant soils, but woolly apple aphid colonises its roots. Roots well in stoolbeds, which made it one of the easiest Geneva stocks to obtain.

rootstocks.name: G.16

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Ottawa 3 x Malus floribunda 821
origin.note: US plant patent PP12,443 (2002); now planted far less than G.41 or G.11.

rootstocks.support: Root system anchors well, but a stake or trellis is needed to carry the crop
rootstocks.soil_notes: needs fertile, well-drained, weed-free soil like M.9; irrigate in dry spells
rootstocks.best_for: M.9-sized trees in fire-blight regions when certified virus-free scions are available
rootstocks.avoid_when: scionwood of unknown virus status (e.g. grafting from old heritage trees); woolly-aphid-prone regions
rootstocks.variety_fit: Use only virus-tested budwood; unsuitable for top-working or home grafting from old trees that may carry latent viruses.
rootstocks.notes: A full dwarf about the size of M.9 that crops very early, is nearly immune to fire blight, tolerates collar rot and makes almost no suckers or burr knots. Its serious flaw is hypersensitivity to common latent viruses: trees budded with infected wood can decline or die, so certified virus-free scions are essential. Susceptible to woolly apple aphid; it was among the best survivors of the 2004-05 New York cold snap.

rootstocks.name: G.202

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: M.27 x Robusta 5
origin.note: Released for New Zealand in 2002 and for the US in 2004.

rootstocks.support: Stake or trellis recommended
rootstocks.soil_notes: reasonably fertile, well-drained soil; tolerant of replant ground
rootstocks.best_for: M.26-sized trees where woolly apple aphid and fire blight are both problems (warm temperate regions, replant sites)
rootstocks.avoid_when: unsupported trees on exposed sites; very cold-winter zones where its hardiness is unproven
rootstocks.variety_fit: A good match for weak growers such as Honeycrisp; Cornell pairs it with G.935 for very weak varieties.
rootstocks.notes: About M.26 in size, precocious and productive, with resistance to fire blight, crown rot and woolly apple aphid plus replant tolerance; aphid resistance made it the first Geneva choice for New Zealand. Stoolbed-grown liners gave noticeably larger trees than tissue-culture liners in the 2010 NC-140 trial, and it suckered more than M.26 there. Stoolbed rooting is moderate and its winter hardiness is less documented than that of G.41 or G.935.

rootstocks.name: G.214

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Ottawa 3 x Robusta 5
origin.note: US plant patent PP23,516; trialled as CG.4214 in the 2010 NC-140 trial.

rootstocks.support: Trellis or permanent stake
rootstocks.soil_notes: fertile, well-drained soil with irrigation; dense fibrous roots explore soil well for a dwarf
rootstocks.best_for: high-density trellis orchards wanting M.9 Pajam 2 vigour with full fire blight and woolly aphid resistance
rootstocks.avoid_when: unsupported trees; poor dry ground; severe-winter zones until hardiness is better documented
rootstocks.variety_fit: Performs well with Honeycrisp and Fuji in trials; vigour suits most commercial varieties at close spacing.
rootstocks.notes: A dwarf close to M.9 Pajam 2 in vigour with very high yield efficiency; as CG.4214 it was among the most efficient large dwarfs over 8 years in the 2010 NC-140 Honeycrisp trial. Resistant to fire blight and crown rot, immune to woolly apple aphid, replant tolerant and with a dense, finely branched root system. Propagates easily in stoolbeds; cold hardiness is less documented than for G.41 or G.935.

rootstocks.name: G.222

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: M.27 x Robusta 5
origin.note: US plant patent PP24,834.

rootstocks.support: Trellis or permanent stake
rootstocks.soil_notes: fertile, well-drained soil with irrigation, as for other dwarfs
rootstocks.best_for: high-density orchards needing a dwarf with fire blight, crown rot and woolly aphid resistance
rootstocks.avoid_when: unsupported trees; poor dry ground; cold-winter zones until hardiness data accumulate
rootstocks.variety_fit: Little published scion-specific experience yet.
rootstocks.notes: A newer dwarf from the same M.27 x Robusta 5 family as G.41 and G.202, sized between M.9 Pajam 2 and M.26 (Cornell's 2024 chart groups it with M.26). It bears as early as M.9 and was more yield-efficient than M.9 and M.26 in Cornell trials, resists fire blight, crown rot and woolly apple aphid, and shows some replant tolerance. Its commercial track record is still short.

rootstocks.name: G.41

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: M.27 x Robusta 5
origin.note: Released 2005; sold as stoolbed (N) and tissue-culture (TC) liners.

rootstocks.support: Trellis or permanent stake; brittle union with some varieties
rootstocks.soil_notes: fertile, well-drained soil with irrigation; small root system like M.9, but copes well with replant ground
rootstocks.best_for: high-density trellis orchards, cordons and espaliers, especially on replant sites or where fire blight and woolly aphid are problems
rootstocks.avoid_when: free-standing trees without support; windy exposed sites; dry, poor or grassed ground
rootstocks.variety_fit: Cornell recommends it for weak-growing varieties and replant sites; with brittle-union scions such as Honeycrisp or Envy (Scilate) support the union from planting.
rootstocks.notes: An M.9-sized dwarf with very high yield efficiency and strong resistance to fire blight, crown rot and woolly apple aphid, plus good replant tolerance - the nearest thing to a disease-proof M.9. It is very cold hardy (good survival in the 2004-05 New York freezes) and also does well in warm climates such as Mexico. Drawbacks are poor rooting in stoolbeds (hence tissue-culture liners, which gave slightly smaller trees in NC-140 trials) and a brittle graft union with some cultivars.

rootstocks.name: G.814

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Ottawa 3 x Robusta 5
origin.note: Trialled as CG.4814 (2010 NC-140 trial); US plant patent PP27,643.

rootstocks.support: Trellis or stake; graft-union breaks occurred in trials
rootstocks.soil_notes: fertile, well-drained soil; fine, branched roots and good calcium supply to the fruit
rootstocks.best_for: high-density orchards wanting an M.26-sized, replant-tolerant, fire-blight-resistant stock
rootstocks.avoid_when: scionwood that may carry apple stem grooving virus; woolly-aphid-prone regions; unsupported trees
rootstocks.variety_fit: Use virus-free scions; Honeycrisp fruit on it ran smaller than on M.26 in NC-140.
rootstocks.notes: Roughly M.26-sized (small semi-dwarf after 5 years, large dwarf after 8 in the 2010 NC-140 Honeycrisp trial) with good precocity and yield efficiency, fire blight and crown rot resistance, replant tolerance and good calcium uptake. Weak points are woolly apple aphid susceptibility, sensitivity to apple stem grooving virus, and the second-highest mortality in that trial (24% after 8 years, from graft-union breaks and some fire blight losses in Mexico).

rootstocks.name: G.935

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Ottawa 3 x Robusta 5
origin.note: Released in the mid-2000s; US plant patent PP17,063.

rootstocks.support: Stake or trellis; some graft-union breaks were recorded in trials
rootstocks.soil_notes: reasonably fertile, well-drained soil; good on replant ground
rootstocks.best_for: M.26-sized trees in cold, fire-blight-prone regions; tall spindle orchards and supported garden trees
rootstocks.avoid_when: woolly-aphid-prone warm regions; unsupported trees on exposed sites
rootstocks.variety_fit: A standard choice for weak growers such as Honeycrisp; Cornell recommends it (with G.202) for very weak varieties.
rootstocks.notes: Sits between M.9 Pajam 2 and M.26 in size with very high yield efficiency, and is one of the most widely planted Geneva stocks. Resistant to fire blight and crown rot, replant tolerant and very cold hardy (among the best survivors of the 2004-05 New York freezes), but susceptible to woolly apple aphid. In the 2010 NC-140 trial it suckered more than M.26 and lost some trees to graft-union breaks, so give it support.

rootstocks.name: M.8

origin.parentage: old French paradise stock, recorded before 1696
origin.note: Numbered in the East Malling sorting of paradise stocks; the American 'Clark Dwarf' interstem was later identified as M.8.

rootstocks.support: Permanent stake for life
rootstocks.soil_notes: Weak, brittle-rooted stock needing good, sheltered soil; rarely used on its own roots.
rootstocks.best_for: historical and breeding interest; formerly a dwarfing interstem on hardy seedling roots
rootstocks.avoid_when: any cold or exposed site; commercial or low-maintenance planting
rootstocks.notes: An old dwarfing paradise stock, rated among the least winter-hardy of the original Malling types, with brittle wood and roots. In North America it was sold as the 'Clark Dwarf' interstem between a hardy seedling root and the variety, giving small trees that tended to lean and break at the unions. Its main legacy is as a parent of Budagovsky B.9 (M.8 x 'Red Standard').

rootstocks.name: M.9

origin.parentage: selected from the French 'Jaune de Metz' paradise stock (found c. 1879)
origin.note: One of the old paradise types sorted and numbered at East Malling from 1912; virus-cleaned EMLA and continental clones replaced the original from the 1970s.

rootstocks.support: Permanent stake or trellis for life
rootstocks.soil_notes: Needs fertile, well-drained soil with a weed-free strip; irrigate in dry spells; shallow brittle roots tolerate collar rot but not drought or competition.
rootstocks.best_for: small gardens, cordons, espaliers, spindles and intensive orchards on good soil
rootstocks.avoid_when: poor, dry or grassed ground; fire-blight areas; cold-winter zones 4 and below; exposed sites without support
rootstocks.variety_fit: Pairs well with vigorous, triploid and tip-bearing varieties; weak growers and spur types can end up under-sized.
rootstocks.notes: The world's reference dwarfing stock: very precocious and efficient, with good fruit size, but brittle roots mean the tree must be supported for life. It is very susceptible to fire blight (whole-tree loss through rootstock blight) and woolly aphid, forms burr knots on exposed shank, and roots are injured in severe winters. Clones differ in vigour: Pajam 2 and Nic29 are the strongest, T337 and Fleuren 56 the weakest; virus-free EMLA 9 is a little larger than the original virus-infected M.9.

rootstocks.name: Mark

origin.place: Michigan State University, East Lansing, Michigan
origin.parentage: open-pollinated seedling of M.9
origin.note: Selected and tested as MAC-9 by Robert F. Carlson; introduced 1979-80 and covered by US Plant Patent 4678.

rootstocks.support: Support recommended; early claims of free-standing trees did not hold on many sites
rootstocks.soil_notes: very drought-sensitive: irrigate even where irrigation is normally optional
rootstocks.best_for: historical interest; existing plantings on irrigated, fertile sites
rootstocks.avoid_when: hot, dry or unirrigated sites; new plantings (better dwarfing stocks exist)
rootstocks.notes: Michigan dwarf from an M.9 seedling, very precocious and often more yield-efficient than M.9 T337 in its early years. Older trees commonly develop root mass proliferation, a tumour-like swelling at or below the soil line that stunts them and makes performance highly variable; it is also very drought-sensitive and did poorly in hot, dry western regions. Hardy in early winter but prone to late-winter injury, fire blight and woolly aphid susceptible, fairly crown-rot resistant, and has largely fallen out of commercial use.

rootstocks.name: Ottawa 3

origin.place: Agriculture Canada Research Station (Central Experimental Farm), Ottawa, Ontario
origin.parentage: 'Robin' crab x M.9
origin.note: Described by Spangelo, Fejer and Granger in 1974; later used as a parent of G.935.

rootstocks.support: Stake or trellis; better anchored and much less brittle than M.9
rootstocks.soil_notes: fertile, well-drained soil; collar-rot resistance similar to M.9
rootstocks.best_for: dwarf trees in cold-winter regions; hardy dwarfing interstem
rootstocks.avoid_when: fire-blight areas; scions carrying apple stem grooving virus
rootstocks.variety_fit: Use certified virus-free scionwood, as the stock is sensitive to apple stem grooving virus.
rootstocks.notes: Canadian hardy dwarf between M.9 and M.26 in size, precocious and productive, with yield efficiency usually above M.26 but below M.9; fruit was occasionally a little smaller. In cold-hardiness tests it tolerated about -35 C but not -40 C. It roots poorly in stoolbeds (often micropropagated), rarely suckers, resists collar rot but is susceptible to fire blight and woolly aphid.

rootstocks.name: P.2

origin.place: Research Institute of Pomology (now Research Institute of Horticulture), Skierniewice
origin.parentage: M.9 x Common Antonovka (Antonowka Zwykla)
origin.note: From S.W. Zagaja's winter-hardiness breeding programme.

rootstocks.support: Stake or trellis
rootstocks.soil_notes: M.9-type requirements: fertile, weed-free soil with support and irrigation
rootstocks.best_for: M.9-sized intensive trees where M.9 suffers winter injury
rootstocks.avoid_when: fire-blight areas; tomato ringspot virus areas (Delicious on P.2 reacted like MM.106 in early Geneva tests)
rootstocks.notes: Polish M.9 x Antonovka dwarf giving trees about the size of M.9 (rated slightly smaller in some US sources). In Warsaw trials Elise on P 2 matched M.9 EMLA in size but yielded more; it is hardier in mid-winter than M.9 and fairly resistant to crown and root rots, with very few suckers. Susceptible to fire blight and woolly aphid.

rootstocks.name: Pajam 1

origin.parentage: clonal selection of M.9 ('Paradis Jaune de Metz') from French stoolbeds
origin.note: Selection programme begun in 1974 by CTIFL with INRA and nurseries; US plant patent PP7714 (filed 1989, granted 1991). Sister clone Pajam 2 (Cepiland) is the more vigorous one.

rootstocks.support: Permanent stake or trellis for life
rootstocks.soil_notes: As for M.9: fertile, well-drained, weed-free soil with irrigation in dry spells.
rootstocks.best_for: high-density spindle and super-spindle orchards; trained garden forms on good soil
rootstocks.avoid_when: poor, dry or grassed ground; fire-blight areas; severe-winter regions
rootstocks.variety_fit: Behaves like a mid-vigour M.9; suits moderately vigorous varieties in intensive systems, while weak varieties are better on Pajam 2 or Nic29.
rootstocks.notes: A French virus-free M.9 clone that roots more easily in the stoolbed than older M.9 lines. In trials it sits in the middle of the M.9 clones for vigour: a little stronger than T337 and EMLA 9 in NC-140 work, weaker than Pajam 2 and Nic29, and similar to standard M.9 in some European trials. It keeps all of M.9's weaknesses (brittle roots, fire blight, woolly aphid) and can sucker noticeably.

rootstocks.name: V.1

origin.parentage: open-pollinated seedling from 'Kerr' crabapple and M.9 material
origin.note: Vineland series selected by A. Hutchinson; tested in the 1994 NC-140 dwarf trial; nursery supply from about 2003.

rootstocks.support: Stake for life
rootstocks.soil_notes: few soil-specific data; treat like M.26 (fertile, well-drained)
rootstocks.best_for: M.26-sized trees in cold-winter regions of Canada and the northern US where fire blight is a risk
rootstocks.avoid_when: unsupported trees; regions where it cannot be sourced
rootstocks.variety_fit: No notable scion problems reported in NC-140 trials.
rootstocks.notes: An M.26-class dwarf from Ontario; after 10 years in the 1994 NC-140 trial trees were about the size of M.26 EMLA with similar or better yield efficiency, excellent survival, and few suckers or burr knots. Reported as cold hardy and, unlike M.26, fairly to highly resistant to fire blight. Mostly of interest in Canada and the northern US.

rootstocks.name: B.64-194

origin.place: Michurinsk State Agrarian University, Tambov region
origin.note: Michurinsk selection classed as semi-dwarfing in Russian sources (year of cross from the selection number); licensed for testing in France and the USA as a donor of frost resistance.

rootstocks.best_for: breeding and trial use; cold-climate semi-dwarf trials
rootstocks.notes: Semi-dwarfing selection from the Michurinsk (Budagovsky) programme that was passed to French and US institutions for evaluation and breeding. Unlike B.9, B.10 or B.118 it has little published orchard data in English, so its vigour, disease reactions and hardiness rating are not well established.

rootstocks.name: CG.4013

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.note: Unreleased selection; evaluated in the 2010 NC-140 Honeycrisp and Fuji trials.

rootstocks.support: Trellised in trials; support in high-density systems
rootstocks.soil_notes: no published soil-specific data
rootstocks.best_for: research and trial plantings only
rootstocks.avoid_when: commercial or garden planting - not released
rootstocks.variety_fit: Only Honeycrisp and Fuji data published (NC-140).
rootstocks.notes: An unreleased Cornell-Geneva selection known mainly from the 2010 NC-140 trials. With Honeycrisp it began as a large dwarf but was a small semi-dwarf after 8 years (trunk area about 20% above M.26), suckered about as heavily as M.9 Pajam 2, and its cumulative yield efficiency was only around M.26 level. Survival was 95%, including 100% at the Minnesota and Wisconsin sites; one tree was lost to fire blight in Mexico.

rootstocks.name: G.210

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station (Cornell / USDA-ARS), Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Ottawa 3 x Robusta 5
origin.note: US plant patent PP23,337.

rootstocks.support: Stake or trellis in high-density plantings; early reports questioned its anchorage
rootstocks.soil_notes: adapts to average and lighter soils; vigorous enough for weaker ground and replant sites
rootstocks.best_for: organic orchards, weaker soils and semi-dwarf garden trees that should still crop early
rootstocks.avoid_when: where a small tree is wanted; severe-winter zones until hardiness is better documented
rootstocks.variety_fit: Suits weak-growing varieties that would stall on a dwarf; strong varieties may grow too large for close spacing.
rootstocks.notes: Semi-dwarf in the M.7 class (some trials place it between M.7 and MM.106) but precocious and at least as yield-efficient as M.9. Resistant to fire blight, crown rot and woolly apple aphid, tolerant of replant disease, and roots well in stoolbeds. Cornell positions it mainly for organic production, poorer soils and weak scions.

rootstocks.name: G.257

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Ottawa 3 x Robusta 5
origin.note: Licensed in 2023 alongside G.66 and G.484; US plant patent PP35,016.

rootstocks.support: Support recommended in high-density rows
rootstocks.soil_notes: average to good soils; vigorous enough for replant ground
rootstocks.best_for: high-density orchards wanting bigger fruit and heavy crops from an M.7-class tree
rootstocks.avoid_when: where a small tree is wanted; growers needing long field experience before adopting
rootstocks.variety_fit: Cornell recommends it for SnapDragon and Gala, where it lifts fruit size; patent trials also suggest larger Fuji fruit.
rootstocks.notes: A semi-dwarf in the M.7 vigour class, released in 2023 for high-density plantings where growers want larger fruit and high crop loads. Resistant to fire blight, crown rot and woolly apple aphid, replant tolerant, very low suckering, hardier in winter than M.7, and it tends to raise boron levels in the scion. Experience outside trials is still limited.

rootstocks.name: G.30

origin.place: Cornell University apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Robusta 5 x M.9
origin.note: Released by Cornell in the 1990s; tested in the 1994 NC-140 semi-dwarf trial.

rootstocks.support: Stake or trellis at least for the first years; the union can snap under early crops or wind
rootstocks.soil_notes: broadly adaptable; tolerates heavier, wetter soils better than MM.106 thanks to crown-rot tolerance
rootstocks.best_for: semi-dwarf orchard or garden trees in fire-blight country where an M.7-sized tree should crop much sooner
rootstocks.avoid_when: unsupported trees on windy sites; brittle-union varieties; woolly-aphid-prone regions
rootstocks.variety_fit: Union strength varies widely by scion: in Cornell nursery tests Northern Spy, Fuji and Golden Delicious made strong unions while Wijcik McIntosh, James Grieve and Cox were among the weakest.
rootstocks.notes: A semi-dwarf usually placed near M.7 in size (reports range from M.26 to M.7 depending on site) but far earlier-bearing and more productive than M.7. Highly resistant to fire blight and tolerant of crown rot, with few suckers and rare burr knots, and it came through the 2004-05 New York freezes well. The graft union is brittle with some varieties, so young trees need support, and woolly apple aphid can infest the roots.

rootstocks.name: G.969

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Ottawa 3 x Robusta 5
origin.note: US plant patent PP24,073.

rootstocks.support: Better anchored than the dwarf Geneva stocks; still support in high-density rows
rootstocks.soil_notes: average soils; more forgiving than dwarfs on lighter ground
rootstocks.best_for: semi-dwarf trees that crop early, in cold or fire-blight regions; garden trees needing less support
rootstocks.avoid_when: where a small tree is wanted at close spacing
rootstocks.variety_fit: Cornell rates it excellent for weak scions such as Honeycrisp.
rootstocks.notes: A semi-dwarf between M.26 and M.7 (Cornell's 2024 chart puts it at the M.26 end) that bears far earlier and more efficiently than M.7. Resistant to fire blight, crown rot, powdery mildew and woolly apple aphid, winter hardy, and better anchored than the dwarf Geneva stocks.

rootstocks.name: M.26

origin.note: Cross made 1929; released 1958-59.

rootstocks.support: Stake advised for life on light, exposed or windy sites; may stand alone on deep good soil
rootstocks.soil_notes: Wants well-drained loam; very intolerant of wet feet; plant with the union only 2-5 cm above soil to limit burr knots on the exposed shank.
rootstocks.best_for: small to medium gardens, bush and spindle trees, and large containers on reasonable soil
rootstocks.avoid_when: poorly drained or heavy wet soils; fire-blight regions; very cold zones without hardier alternatives
rootstocks.variety_fit: Graft incompatibility has been reported with some cultivars (e.g. 'Rome Beauty' and 'Stayman'); in the UK Cox on M.26 is noted as prone to collar rot.
rootstocks.notes: A dwarfing-to-semi-dwarf stock between M.9 and M.7 in size, precocious and productive, and stronger rooted than M.9 though still best staked. It is very susceptible to fire blight and burr knots, and its collar rot rating depends on region (resistant in UK trials, susceptible in North America). Older US guides called it the hardiest M/MM stock, but root injury in severe test winters means it is not a substitute for Budagovsky or Geneva stocks in cold zones.

rootstocks.name: P.1

origin.place: Research Institute of Pomology (now Research Institute of Horticulture), Skierniewice
origin.parentage: M.9 x Common Antonovka (Antonowka Zwykla)
origin.note: From S.W. Zagaja's winter-hardiness breeding programme; one of the first P-series introductions.

rootstocks.best_for: hardy semi-dwarf trees in cold continental climates (historical/trial interest)
rootstocks.avoid_when: fire-blight areas
rootstocks.notes: Early Polish M.9 x Antonovka selection that controls tree size roughly like M.7, though in some trials trees were nearer M.26 size. It survived severe Polish test winters and resists collar rot, but is susceptible to fire blight and woolly aphid and is hard to propagate in stoolbeds. Little planted now; P 14 and P 60 are the Polish semi-dwarfs in current use.

rootstocks.name: P.14
