regions.pests_diseases: The brown marmorated stink bug caused severe fruit damage here after it spread in the 2010s, and codling moth is persistent through the long summer. Scab, powdery mildew and fire blight (mainly on pears) also occur.
regions.tips: On the plain, choose heat-tolerant varieties and irrigate; in the hills, Rosa Romana and similar old keepers do well as standard trees. Fine-mesh exclusion netting over small trees helps against both stink bug and codling moth.

regions.name: Mount Etna slopes (Sicily)
regions.summary: A Mediterranean island climate made apple-friendly by altitude: on Etna's slopes above the citrus and vine belt, winters are cold enough for chilling (with snow higher up), and cool nights temper the hot, dry summer. The deep volcanic soils drain freely, so summer drought is the main stress.
regions.apple_culture: Etna has long grown small, fragrant mountain apples on its terraced volcanic slopes; the ancient Etna apples - Cola, Gelato, Gelato Cola and Cirino - were made a Slow Food presidium in 2016, and Gelato Cola is still sold today. Elsewhere in Sicily apples are scarce because the lowlands are too warm.
regions.pests_diseases: Mediterranean fruit fly attacks apples at lower elevations in warm autumns, and codling moth is widespread. Sunburn and drought stress are bigger issues than scab.
regions.tips: Grow apples only at altitude; on the coastal lowland, choose low-chill varieties or other fruit. On the volcano, mulch and water young trees, try the local Etna types for flavour and keeping, and harvest promptly where fruit fly is active.

regions.name: Asturias (Spain, cider country)
regions.summary: Green Atlantic Spain: mild winters, cool cloudy summers and rain in every season, with sea fogs and high humidity. Frost rarely threatens blossom, but the constant damp makes fungal disease the dominant concern.
regions.apple_culture: Asturias is the cider capital of Spain: natural sidra is poured from a height (escanciado) in sidrerías, pressed in family llagares and protected as DOP Sidra de Asturias, which allows only approved local cider varieties. Villaviciosa, home of the SERIDA research centre and its apple collection, is the heart of the apple country, and many farms still keep traditional tall orchards (pomaradas).
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab, European canker and woolly aphid are persistent in the wet climate, and rosy apple aphid and codling moth reduce yields. Traditional orchards also crop in a strong alternate-year rhythm.
regions.tips: Plant robust local cider varieties and mix sweet, bittersweet and sharp types for a balanced cider. Choose well-drained slopes for airflow, prune for an open crown, and thin heavy crops to soften biennial bearing.

regions.name: Lleida (Catalonia)
regions.summary: The inland Ebro depression is semi-arid and continental: hot, very sunny summers, cold winters with long spells of ground fog (boira), and too little rain to grow fruit without irrigation. Spring frost on the flat plain and summer heat are the main constraints, and warm nights limit red colour.
regions.apple_culture: The irrigated plains of the Segrià and Pla d'Urgell, watered by historic canals, form one of Spain's biggest fruit districts; stone fruit and pears dominate, but apples - especially Golden Delicious and Gala - are a major crop. The area is a hub of cooperatives, packhouses and IRTA fruit research.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth runs several generations through the long summer and is the key pest. Sunburn, powdery mildew and occasional fire blight matter, while scab is minor in the dry climate.
regions.tips: Irrigation is non-negotiable - drip plus mulch is ideal for a home tree - and shade netting or a well-leafed canopy protects fruit from sunburn. Choose varieties that do not depend on cool nights for colour (Golden types, Granny Smith) and expect repeated codling moth control.

regions.name: Alcobaca (Portugal)
regions.summary: The Oeste region north of Lisbon has an Atlantic-tempered climate: mild winters with modest chilling, warm summers cooled by sea breezes and frequent morning fog, and rain concentrated in the cool season. The maritime humidity favours fungal disease but slows ripening, giving a fresh sweet-sharp balance.
regions.apple_culture: Apples have been grown here since the Cistercian monks of the Alcobaça monastery developed the surrounding farmland in the Middle Ages, and Maçã de Alcobaça has been a protected geographical indication since the 1990s. The Oeste is Portugal's main apple and pear district (alongside the Rocha pear), and the old local Casa Nova de Alcobaça is still certified under the IGP.
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab and powdery mildew are encouraged by the Atlantic humidity, and codling moth is the main pest. Mediterranean fruit fly can attack ripening fruit in warm autumns, and fire blight has reached Portuguese pome-fruit orchards.
regions.tips: Choose varieties with modest chilling needs that suit mild winters - the local Casa Nova and Reineta, Gala and Granny Smith all perform here. Give trees open, airy crowns against scab, and pick promptly where fruit fly is active.

regions.name: Pelion (Greece)
regions.summary: A steep, forested mountain peninsula on the Aegean that catches unusually high rainfall for Greece; the cool, moist eastern slopes above Zagora give apples the chilling and mild summers they need despite the southern latitude. Snow can fall at altitude in winter, and elevation and sea moisture soften the dry Mediterranean summer.
regions.apple_culture: Apples are a mountain-village crop on the terraces of eastern Pelion, organised around the long-established Zagora cooperative. Two apples hold PDO status: the small, aromatic Firiki of Pelion, grown here since at least the 1700s, and Zagora Starking Delicious, introduced in the mid-20th century.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth and apple scab are the main problems, and the Mediterranean fruit fly can strike lower orchards. Hail and summer drought are the chief weather risks.
regions.tips: Grow apples at altitude on the moist eastern side; on the hot lowland, choose low-chill types. The local Firiki is a good keeper suited to traditional standard trees, and young trees need mulch and water through the dry summer.

regions.name: Moscow (Russia)
regions.summary: Long, hard continental winters with reliable deep chilling and usually a protective snow cover, followed by a short but warm summer. The real dangers are test winters with sudden thaws and deep cold snaps that injure bark and buds, and late spring frosts that catch early bloom.
regions.apple_culture: Apples are the backbone of the Moscow dacha garden: almost every allotment around the city has a few old trees, and autumn markets overflow with homegrown fruit. The old Kolomenskoye estate orchard keeps a living memory of pre-revolutionary Russian varieties, and most local favourites are hardy Russian classics rather than Western supermarket types.
regions.pests_diseases: Scab is the main disease in cool, wet summers, with codling moth and brown fruit rot close behind. Winter sunscald and frost cracks on trunks, plus hares and voles gnawing bark under the snow, kill more young trees than insects do.
regions.tips: Choose proven Russian hardy varieties on vigorous or hardy rootstocks rather than dwarfing M.9, which is often too tender here. Whitewash trunks in autumn and guard them with mesh against rodents, and do not plant in frost-pocket hollows where late frosts settle.

regions.name: Michurinsk (Tambov, Russia)
regions.summary: Black-earth steppe country in central Russia: cold, often harsh winters, warm and fairly dry summers, and fertile chernozem soils. Winter hardiness is the limiting factor, while dry spells in summer and late spring frosts can cost crops in some years.
regions.apple_culture: This is where Ivan Michurin spent his life breeding fruit for Russian winters, crossing tender Western apples with hardy Chinese and Siberian crabs; the town was renamed in his honour and is now an official science city built around fruit research. His descendants in the local breeding institute still release apples for central Russia, and the surrounding Tambov chernozem belt has become a centre of large new intensive orchards.
regions.pests_diseases: Scab and codling moth are the routine problems, with powdery mildew on susceptible types. Winter injury after cold snaps without snow, and occasional drought stress on the open steppe, are the climate-driven risks.
regions.tips: Use regionally bred, scab-tolerant winter-hardy varieties rather than imported Western cultivars, and give the trees shelter from steppe winds. Mulch and water young trees through dry summers so they ripen their wood before winter.

regions.name: St Petersburg (Russia)
regions.summary: Cool, cloudy Baltic climate: winters are long but less brutal than inland Russia, with frequent thaws, while summers are short, mild and often wet. Apples struggle more for warmth and sunshine to ripen wood and fruit than for chilling.
regions.apple_culture: Apples are grown mainly in dacha gardens in the Leningrad oblast, where hardy summer and autumn types do best; late-keeping winter apples often fail to ripen well. The city is home to the Vavilov Institute, one of the world's great plant gene banks, which holds collections of fruit gathered from across the former Soviet Union.
regions.pests_diseases: Scab and fruit rots thrive in the damp summers, and waterlogged, heavy soils cause root and collar problems. Winter damage tends to come from repeated freeze-thaw cycles rather than steady deep cold.
regions.tips: Plant on a raised mound or well-drained slope in the sunniest, most sheltered spot, and stick to early and mid-season hardy varieties that ripen in a short summer. Prune for an open canopy so leaves and fruit dry quickly after rain.

regions.name: Novosibirsk (Siberia)
regions.summary: Severe Siberian continental climate: winters are long and bitterly cold, summers short and surprisingly hot, and the swing between seasons is abrupt. Ordinary European apples rarely survive; tree survival through winter is the whole game.
regions.apple_culture: Siberian gardeners rely on ranetki and semi-cultivated apples (polukulturki), hybrids of the native Siberian crab with European apples, bred for this climate by stations such as the Lisavenko institute in Barnaul and Ural breeders. A distinctive local trick is the stlanets, a tree trained flat along the ground so the snow blankets and protects it through winter.
regions.pests_diseases: Winter injury, sunscald and frost cracking on trunks are the main killers, along with rodents feeding under deep snow. Scab is generally less of a problem than in western Russia because summers are drier.
regions.tips: Grow Siberian-bred ranetki and semi-cultivated varieties, ideally on Siberian crab rootstock, or train standard varieties as a low stlanets that snow can cover. Avoid late-summer feeding and watering so wood hardens off before the first freezes.

regions.name: Kyiv (Ukraine)
regions.summary: Forest-steppe continental climate with cold winters, warm summers and a good balance of rain, which suits apples well. Late spring frosts and occasional very cold winters are the main hazards, and recent summers have brought more heat and drought.
regions.apple_culture: Ukraine is one of Europe's large apple producers and Kyiv sits in the heart of its forest-steppe fruit zone, with the national horticulture institute on the city's edge. Home orchards around village houses are traditional, and the country's best-known native apple, Renet Symyrenka, comes from the Symyrenko family nursery at Mliiv in nearby Cherkasy region.
regions.pests_diseases: Scab and powdery mildew are the dominant diseases, and codling moth is the main insect pest. Fire blight appears in some warm springs, and late frosts during bloom can wipe out a crop.
regions.tips: Scab-resistant varieties save a lot of spraying in a home garden. Plant on gentle slopes rather than in hollows to reduce frost damage at bloom, and mulch and water through dry summer spells.

regions.name: Almaty (Kazakhstan, home of the wild apple)
regions.summary: Foothill climate below the Tian Shan: cold continental winters, hot dry summers, and a strong altitude gradient up the mountain slopes. Irrigation water from mountain streams makes apples possible, and the cooler mid-slope band gives the best fruit.
regions.apple_culture: The wild forests of Malus sieversii on these slopes are recognised as the main ancestor of the domestic apple, and the city's old name, Alma-Ata, is linked in local tradition to apples. The huge red Aport, brought by Russian settlers in the 1800s, became a Soviet-era symbol of the city but declined as orchards gave way to housing; there is now a programme to revive it.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth is the main fruit pest, and ermine moths can strip wild and cultivated trees. Fire blight has spread in the region in recent years, threatening both orchards and the wild apple forests.
regions.tips: Water deeply through the dry summer and pick a site at middle altitude in the foothills if you can, where nights are cooler. Watch closely for fire blight in spring and cut out infected shoots well below the visible damage.

regions.name: Georgia (Tbilisi and Kakheti)
regions.summary: Continental Caucasus climate: hot, fairly dry summers in the lowlands around Tbilisi and in Kakheti, cold but not extreme winters, and cooler, wetter conditions as you climb into the hills. Hailstorms in summer are a well-known hazard for eastern Georgian orchards.
regions.apple_culture: Georgia's forests hold wild Caucasian crab apples and the country has a deep stock of folk varieties, many now rare. Commercial apple growing is centred mainly in Shida Kartli around Gori rather than in wine-focused Kakheti, and a small craft cider scene has grown up recently.
regions.pests_diseases: Scab and powdery mildew are the usual diseases, and codling moth is the main fruit pest. The invasive brown marmorated stink bug arrived in Georgia in the mid-2010s and also damages fruit.
regions.tips: In the hot lowlands, plan on irrigation and choose disease-tolerant varieties; old Georgian varieties are worth seeking out from local collections. Consider hail netting or at least a sheltered site if you are in Kakheti or Shida Kartli.

regions.name: Amasya (Turkey)
regions.summary: A narrow river valley on the Yesilirmak, inland from the Black Sea coast: cold enough in winter for good chilling, hot in summer, with the valley walls giving some shelter. Late spring frosts are the main climatic risk in exposed sites.
regions.apple_culture: Amasya gives its name to one of Turkey's most famous native apples, the small, fragrant, half-red Amasya misket apple, which now has protected geographical indication status. Turkey is one of the world's biggest apple producers, though most volume today comes from Isparta and other provinces planting Delicious and Golden types.
regions.pests_diseases: Scab in wet springs, powdery mildew and codling moth are the routine problems. Fire blight is present in Turkey and can be serious in warm, humid bloom periods.
regions.tips: The local Amasya apple is a good choice for its aroma and keeping quality, but it is a vigorous traditional tree and needs room. Irrigate through the hot summer and keep pruning open to reduce scab and mildew.

regions.name: Urmia (Iran)
regions.summary: High plateau climate west of Lake Urmia: cold winters with reliable chilling, hot dry summers and a large day-night temperature swing that helps fruit colour. Water is the limiting factor; orchards depend on irrigation from rivers and wells, and the shrinking lake has made drought and salinity a growing concern.
regions.apple_culture: West Azerbaijan province around Urmia is Iran's leading apple region, and Iran is one of the world's top apple producers. Orchards are dominated by Red and Golden Delicious, though the country also has prized aromatic native apples such as the Golab group.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth is the key insect pest, and powdery mildew is common in the dry heat. Fire blight is established in Iran and can flare in warm springs.
regions.tips: Drip irrigation and mulch are essential, and avoid salty well water where you can. Try one of the early native Golab-type apples alongside the standard Delicious types for flavour.

regions.name: Golan Heights (Israel)
regions.summary: Highland Mediterranean climate on a basalt plateau: winters are cool and wet with occasional snow at the northern end near Mount Hermon, summers long, hot and dry. Chilling is only just enough for standard apples, and mild winters can leave bloom ragged.
regions.apple_culture: The northern Golan and nearby Upper Galilee are Israel's main apple areas, with large cooperative orchards and cold stores; the Druze villages near Mount Hermon are also known for apples. Israel bred the low-chill apples Anna and Ein Shemer, though in the high Golan growers mostly plant standard varieties such as Pink Lady, Gala and the Delicious types.
regions.pests_diseases: Mediterranean fruit fly can attack ripening apples, especially late varieties, and codling moth is the main orchard pest. Sunburn on fruit in the summer heat and powdery mildew are also common.
regions.tips: At lower, warmer sites choose low-chill varieties such as Anna or Ein Shemer; on the high plateau standard varieties work but need reliable irrigation. Shade netting or careful canopy management helps prevent sunburn, and fruit-fly traps are worth setting in late summer.

regions.name: Mount Lebanon and the Bekaa
regions.summary: Apples grow in Lebanon's mountains and the high Bekaa valley, where altitude brings real winter chill and snow, warm sunny summers and cool nights. The Bekaa side is drier and more continental; the western slopes of Mount Lebanon are wetter.
regions.apple_culture: Mountain villages such as Akoura, Mnaytreh and Qartaba have long been known for their apples, and apples are a major crop in the Lebanese highlands. The industry has suffered repeated crises from low prices and lost export routes through Syria, and most orchards are planted with Delicious and Golden types.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth, scab in wet mountain springs and powdery mildew are the main problems. Mediterranean fruit fly can affect fruit at lower, warmer altitudes.
regions.tips: Higher sites give better colour and keeping quality, but watch for spring frost and hail. In the drier Bekaa, irrigate and mulch; on the wetter mountain slopes, keep trees open-pruned to reduce scab.

regions.name: Kashmir (Srinagar)
regions.summary: A high, enclosed Himalayan valley with cold, snowy winters that give ample chilling, a wet spring and warm but not scorching summers. Spring rain during bloom and leaf-out drives disease, while hail and early snow are the weather shocks growers fear most.
regions.apple_culture: Kashmir is India's largest apple-growing region and apples are central to the rural economy, with fruit markets such as Sopore among the biggest in Asia. Delicious-type apples dominate, but the valley also has its own traditional apples, above all the crisp, aromatic Ambri, and new high-density plantings on dwarfing rootstocks are spreading.
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab has caused severe epidemics in wet springs, and premature leaf fall from Marssonina blotch and Alternaria leaf blotch has become a major problem. San Jose scale and woolly aphid are long-standing insect pests.
regions.tips: A careful scab programme starting at bud break, plus raking or shredding fallen leaves, matters more here than almost anything else. Keep the canopy open, and if you plant an old Kashmiri variety like Ambri, accept that it needs extra disease care.

regions.name: Himachal Pradesh (Shimla)
regions.summary: Steep mid-Himalayan slopes where altitude replaces latitude: cool winters with snow higher up, a monsoon summer, and conditions that change sharply from one ridge to the next. Warming winters have reduced chilling at lower elevations and pushed good apple growing higher up the hills.
regions.apple_culture: Apples arrived on a commercial scale when the American Samuel Stokes planted Delicious trees near Kotgarh in the early twentieth century, and today Himachal is India's second big apple state with mostly small family orchards. Royal Delicious became the signature apple, though newer spur types and Gala are now being planted.
regions.pests_diseases: Marssonina premature leaf fall and scab are the most damaging diseases, especially in wet monsoon years. San Jose scale, woolly aphid and root rots are persistent, and hail can ruin a crop in minutes.
regions.tips: At lower elevations choose lower-chill varieties or accept patchy crops; higher up, standard Delicious types still do well. Plant a pollinator variety and encourage bees, as poor fruit set from weak pollination is a common local complaint.

regions.name: Quetta (Pakistan)
regions.summary: A dry highland basin with cold winters that give good chilling and hot, very dry summers. There is little rain, so orchards depend entirely on groundwater from wells and traditional karez channels, and long droughts are the overriding threat.
regions.apple_culture: Balochistan is one of Pakistan's two main apple regions, with orchards around Quetta, Pishin, Kalat, Ziarat and Killa Saifullah. Local types such as Kala Kulu and Tor Kulu are well known in Pakistani markets, but falling water tables and severe droughts have killed or abandoned many orchards.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth and powdery mildew are the main pest and disease problems in the dry climate. Water stress and sunburn are as damaging as any insect.
regions.tips: Use drip irrigation and heavy mulch to stretch scarce water, and favour well-adapted local varieties. Protect young trunks and fruit from intense summer sun with whitewash and a canopy that is not over-thinned.

regions.name: Shandong (Yantai, China)
regions.summary: Coastal peninsula climate where the sea moderates both seasons: cold, dry winters with good chilling and a warm, humid monsoon summer. Most rain falls in summer, so disease pressure is high during fruit growth, and autumn is usually dry and sunny for ripening.
regions.apple_culture: Yantai is one of the oldest modern apple centres in China, where Western apple varieties were introduced in the late nineteenth century, and Yantai apples are a nationally famous brand. Red Fuji and its many local sports dominate, and almost every fruit is grown inside a paper bag for a flawless skin.
regions.pests_diseases: Valsa canker is the most destructive trunk disease, and ring rot and Marssonina blotch flourish in the wet summer. The peach fruit moth and other borers are why fruit bagging became standard practice.
regions.tips: Prune and sanitise carefully to keep Valsa canker out of large wounds, and protect cuts. Bagging fruit in early summer is worth copying on a small scale if moths and summer rots are a problem.

regions.name: Luochuan (Shaanxi, China)
regions.summary: High loess tableland on the Loess Plateau: deep, well-drained soils, cold dry winters, plenty of sunshine and big day-night temperature swings that build sugar and colour. Rainfall is modest and mostly in summer, and late spring frost and hail are the main weather risks.
regions.apple_culture: Shaanxi is China's largest apple province and Luochuan is its flagship county, with a protected regional brand and apples as the main income of local farms. Fuji dominates, and Northwest A&F University in Shaanxi bred Qinguan and the newer Ruiyang and Ruixue.
regions.pests_diseases: Valsa canker is the biggest disease threat, along with Marssonina blotch in wet summers. Spring frost at bloom and summer hail regularly cost crops, so netting is increasingly used.
regions.tips: Deep loess suits apples well, but keep moisture in with mulch or cover crops since much of the area is rain-fed. Avoid valley bottoms for frost, and keep pruning wounds clean to limit canker.

regions.name: Aksu (Xinjiang, China)
regions.summary: A desert oasis on the edge of the Taklamakan: very dry, sunny, with hot summer days, cold nights and cold winters. Everything depends on irrigation from mountain meltwater, and the huge day-night swing produces very sweet fruit.
regions.apple_culture: Aksu is known across China for its 'ice-sugar heart' Fuji apples, whose sweet watercore is prized rather than seen as a defect. Orchards are irrigated oasis plantings, many established on reclaimed desert land.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth is established in Xinjiang and is a key pest. The low humidity keeps fungal disease light, but sunburn, saline soils, dust and winter freeze injury are real problems.
regions.tips: Irrigate regularly but do not waterlog, and watch for salt build-up in the soil. Protect trunks from winter sunscald and freeze injury, and leave enough leaf cover to shade fruit from the summer sun.

regions.name: Aomori (Japan)
regions.summary: Northern Honshu climate with long, very snowy winters, a cool spring and mild summers that rarely get too hot. Heavy snow can break branches, and late-summer typhoons are the main threat to a hanging crop.
regions.apple_culture: Aomori produces roughly half of Japan's apples, centred on the Tsugaru plain around Hirosaki below Mount Iwaki. Fuji, Mutsu and Sekai Ichi were all bred in the prefecture, and growers are famous for meticulous hand-thinning, fruit bagging and leaf-picking to colour every apple evenly.
regions.pests_diseases: Scab, Alternaria blotch and Valsa canker are long-standing diseases, and Monilinia blossom blight has been a local problem. Typhoon winds and snow-load breakage are major physical risks.
regions.tips: Train trees with strong, wide-angled branches and prop them before heavy snow, and remove snow from young trees. Choose disease-tolerant varieties for a low-spray home garden, as the humid summer favours fungal problems.

regions.name: Nagano (Japan)
regions.summary: An inland, high-elevation basin climate, unusually sunny and dry for Japan, with cold winters, warm summer days and cool nights that help colour and sweetness. Typhoon rain and river flooding are occasional threats, as are hailstorms.
regions.apple_culture: Nagano is Japan's second apple prefecture and promoted compact, closely spaced orchards on dwarfing rootstocks early. Its own breeding produced the 'three apple brothers' Shinano Sweet, Shinano Gold and Akibae, and Fuji and Tsugaru are also widely grown.
regions.pests_diseases: Scab, Alternaria blotch and Marssonina blotch are the main leaf and fruit diseases, and Valsa canker affects older wood. Typhoons and hail cause sudden losses, and 2019's Typhoon Hagibis flooded many riverside orchards.
regions.tips: Dwarfing rootstocks and a compact tree suit small gardens here and make spraying and netting easier. Try the Nagano-bred varieties, which are chosen for local conditions and ripen across the autumn.

regions.name: Daegu (South Korea)
regions.summary: A hot inland basin in south-east Korea: cold, dry winters with adequate chilling, but long, humid and increasingly hot summers that make it hard for red apples to colour. Warming has made the city itself marginal, and good apple growing has moved to cooler uplands to the north.
regions.apple_culture: Daegu was once synonymous with Korean apples, but production has shifted north to upland Gyeongbuk counties such as Cheongsong, Yeongju and Andong and even into Gangwon. Fuji is the main variety, alongside Korean-bred apples such as Hongro, grown for the Chuseok holiday market.
regions.pests_diseases: Bitter rot (anthracnose) and Marssonina blotch flourish in the hot, wet summers, and sunburn is common. Fire blight arrived in Korea in 2015 and is a strictly controlled quarantine disease.
regions.tips: In the hot lowlands, choose early or mid-season varieties that ripen before peak heat or yellow and bicolour apples that do not need cold nights to colour. Provide afternoon shade or netting against sunburn, and keep the canopy airy to limit summer rots.

regions.name: Elgin (Western Cape, South Africa)
regions.summary: A cool, high basin by Western Cape standards, with wet, mild winters and dry summers often softened by cloud and the south-easterly wind. Winters are too mild for full chilling, so trees can leaf out unevenly and growers commonly use rest-breaking sprays.
regions.apple_culture: Elgin and the town of Grabouw form one of South Africa's main apple export areas, built up in the early twentieth century by families such as the Moltenos. The sparkling apple juice Appletiser was created on a farm here in the 1960s, and the cool valley is also known for wine.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth and fruit flies are the main insect pests, and woolly apple aphid and mealybug matter for export fruit. Scab can be an issue in wet springs, and powdery mildew is common.
regions.tips: Choose varieties known to cope with mild winters, and expect patchy bloom after warm winters. Shelter from the summer south-easter helps, and fruit-fly traps or bagging protect backyard crops.

regions.name: Ceres (Western Cape, South Africa)
regions.summary: A high valley ringed by mountains, colder in winter than the coastal Cape, with frost and snow on the surrounding peaks giving better chilling than Elgin. Summers are hot, dry and very sunny, so irrigation and sunburn control are essential.
regions.apple_culture: The Ceres valley and the higher Koue Bokkeveld above it form one of South Africa's largest deciduous fruit areas, with apples, pears and stone fruit packed and processed locally. The town's name is familiar across South Africa from the fruit juice brand that started there.
regions.pests_diseases: Sunburn on fruit is a major loss in the hot, bright summers, and codling moth and fruit flies are the key insect pests. Hail can damage crops, and powdery mildew is common in dry conditions.
regions.tips: Plan for drip irrigation and use shade netting or a fuller canopy to protect fruit from sunburn. The colder winters here allow a wider choice of varieties than coastal Cape gardens.

regions.name: Ifrane (Middle Atlas, Morocco)
regions.summary: High Middle Atlas plateau with cold, often snowy winters that give ample chilling and warm, dry summers. Late spring frosts and summer hailstorms are the main climate risks, and recent years of drought have stressed orchards.
regions.apple_culture: The Middle Atlas is Morocco's apple heartland, with orchards around Ifrane, Azrou and especially Midelt, which hosts an apple festival. Morocco is one of Africa's larger apple producers, mostly growing Golden and Delicious-type apples.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth is the main pest, with scab in wetter springs and powdery mildew in dry spells. Hail and late frost can destroy a crop in one event.
regions.tips: Choose later-flowering varieties and avoid frost-prone low ground. Secure reliable irrigation for summer and consider hail netting if the investment is justified.

regions.name: Nairobi highlands (Kenya)
regions.summary: Equatorial highlands with mild temperatures all year and two rainy seasons, but no cold winter at all. Apples never get natural chilling here, so trees do not go properly dormant and flowering must be managed by hand.
regions.apple_culture: Apple growing in Kenya is small but growing, mainly in higher, cooler counties such as Nyeri, Kiambu and Uasin Gishu. Growers strip leaves and bend branches to force a flush of bloom, which can give more than one crop a year, though results vary and yields are modest.
regions.pests_diseases: Powdery mildew and woolly aphid are common, and fruit flies attack ripening fruit. Because trees grow almost continuously, pests and diseases build up without a winter break.
regions.tips: Use very low-chill varieties such as Anna with a matching pollinator like Golden Dorsett, and time manual defoliation before the rains to trigger bloom. Be wary of exaggerated seedling sales; buy grafted trees from a known nursery.

regions.name: Cape Town (coastal)
regions.summary: Mild Mediterranean coast with wet winters, dry, windy summers and very little winter cold. Chilling is too low for standard apples, and the strong summer south-easter batters trees.
regions.apple_culture: Commercial apples are grown inland in cooler valleys such as Elgin and Ceres, not in Cape Town itself. In city gardens apples are an occasional backyard tree, usually low-chill types.
regions.pests_diseases: Fruit flies and codling moth attack fruit, and woolly aphid and powdery mildew are common. Wind scarring and salt spray near the sea also mark fruit and leaves.
regions.tips: Plant low-chill varieties in pairs for pollination, in the most wind-sheltered spot you have. Water through the dry summer and bag or trap against fruit fly.

regions.name: Hawke's Bay (New Zealand)
regions.summary: Sunny east-coast climate sheltered by the ranges: warm, fairly dry summers, mild winters and free-draining river gravels that make irrigation routine. Spring frost and hail are the usual hazards, and Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023 buried many orchards in silt.
regions.apple_culture: Hawke's Bay is New Zealand's largest apple region, centred on the Heretaunga Plains around Hastings. The national apple breeding programme at Havelock North gave the world Jazz, Envy and Pacific Rose, and the export industry is highly modern and intensive.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth, leafrollers and woolly apple aphid are the main pests, and fire blight is present in New Zealand. Black spot (scab) appears in wet springs, and powdery mildew is common in the warm, dry summers.
regions.tips: Irrigate on the gravels and mulch to hold moisture. Choose scab-resistant or mildew-tolerant varieties for low-spray gardening, and avoid frost-prone low spots near rivers.

regions.name: Nelson (New Zealand)
regions.summary: Sunny but wetter than Hawke's Bay, with mild winters, warm summers and rain spread through the year. The Waimea plains and the Moutere hills are the main orchard areas, and the humid conditions favour fungal diseases.
regions.apple_culture: Nelson is New Zealand's second big apple region with a long export history, and Braeburn was found here as a chance seedling in the Moutere area in the 1950s. Today orchards grow Braeburn alongside Royal Gala and the newer club varieties.
regions.pests_diseases: European canker is a serious problem in the wetter, milder conditions, along with black spot (scab). Codling moth, leafrollers and woolly apple aphid are the main insect pests.
regions.tips: Cut out canker promptly and prune in dry weather, sealing larger wounds. Choose scab-resistant varieties for a home garden, and plant on a well-drained site.

regions.name: Central Otago (New Zealand)
regions.summary: New Zealand's most continental climate: hot, dry summers, cold, frosty winters and a sharp spring frost risk. Low rainfall keeps disease light, but water must come from irrigation and frost protection is essential.
regions.apple_culture: Central Otago fruit growing dates back to the gold-rush era, and old wild apple trees still line roadsides and goldfields. Today apples are grown mainly in the Teviot Valley around Roxburgh and Ettrick, alongside the region's better-known cherries and apricots.
regions.pests_diseases: Frost at bloom and hail are the biggest risks, while the dry climate keeps scab and canker low. Codling moth and powdery mildew are the main ongoing problems.
regions.tips: Plant on slopes so cold air drains away, and choose later-flowering varieties. Irrigate through summer, and enjoy the low disease pressure, which makes low-spray gardening easier.

regions.name: Auckland (New Zealand)
regions.summary: Mild, humid, subtropical-leaning maritime climate with little winter cold and frequent rain. Chilling is low for many standard varieties, and the humidity drives heavy disease pressure.
regions.apple_culture: Apples are a garden tree here rather than a commercial crop, though orchards once dotted the city fringe at places such as Kumeu. Home growers often look to disease-resistant and heritage varieties suited to warm, wet conditions.
regions.pests_diseases: Black spot (scab) and powdery mildew are common in the humid conditions, and woolly aphid and codling moth are widespread. Fire blight is present in New Zealand.
regions.tips: Choose scab-resistant and lower-chill varieties, plant in full sun with good airflow, and avoid heavy, wet clay soils. Clean up fallen leaves to reduce black spot next season.

regions.name: Huon Valley (Tasmania)
regions.summary: Cool, maritime climate in southern Tasmania with reliable rainfall, mild summers and frosty but not severe winters. Long, gentle autumns suit slow ripening and good flavour, while wet springs bring disease.
regions.apple_culture: The Huon Valley is the historic heart of Tasmania's 'Apple Isle', where orchards planted from the 1850s grew into a huge export trade to Britain. Many old varieties survive here, a cider revival centred on Willie Smith's at Grove has taken off, and the valley holds a mid-winter wassail festival.
regions.pests_diseases: Black spot (scab) is the main disease in wet springs, and codling moth, light brown apple moth and woolly aphid are the usual pests. Australia is free of fire blight, and Tasmania's strict quarantine keeps fruit flies out.
regions.tips: Plant scab-resistant varieties or be ready for a spring spray programme in wet years. Heritage Tasmanian and English varieties do well here, and the cool climate suits cider apples too.

regions.name: Goulburn Valley (Victoria)
regions.summary: Hot, dry inland plain on the Goulburn River: summers are long and harsh, winters mild with only moderate chilling. Irrigation from the Murray-Goulburn system makes fruit growing possible, and heat and sunburn are constant concerns.
regions.apple_culture: The Goulburn Valley around Shepparton is the 'Fruit Bowl of Australia', best known for pears and canning fruit but also a big apple producer. Orchards are increasingly netted against hail, birds and sun.
regions.pests_diseases: Queensland fruit fly is established and requires active management, while codling moth and light brown apple moth are long-standing pests. Sunburn on exposed fruit is a major source of loss.
regions.tips: Net trees against fruit fly, birds and sunburn, and water deeply and regularly. Varieties that tolerate heat and mild winters, such as Pink Lady and Granny Smith, do best.

regions.name: Batlow (New South Wales)
regions.summary: Upland foothill country near the Snowy Mountains with cold, frosty winters that give good chilling, and warm sunny summers with cool nights that colour fruit well. Spring frost and hail are the main risks, and bushfire is a real threat in dry years.
regions.apple_culture: Batlow is one of Australia's best-known apple towns, with a long-standing growers' cooperative brand and a local cider maker. The 2019-20 Black Summer bushfires came right to the edge of town and damaged orchards and packing sheds.
regions.pests_diseases: Black spot (scab) in wet springs, codling moth and light brown apple moth are the main problems. Hail and late frost cause sudden crop losses.
regions.tips: Plant on slopes for cold air drainage, and keep a scab spray plan for wet springs. Keep the area around trees clear for fire safety and mulch to hold moisture through dry summers.

regions.name: Orange (New South Wales)
regions.summary: Central Tablelands climate on the slopes of Mount Canobolas, with cold, frosty winters, warm summers and fertile volcanic soils. Elevation gives good chilling and colour, but hailstorms and late frosts are frequent.
regions.apple_culture: Orange is a major New South Wales apple and cherry district with many family orchards. Much of the industry has been reshaped by hail netting and newer high-density plantings.
regions.pests_diseases: Hail is the biggest risk to the crop, and black spot (scab) appears in wet springs. Codling moth and light brown apple moth are the main insect pests.
regions.tips: Netting is worthwhile to protect against hail and birds. Choose later-flowering varieties and avoid frost-prone low spots.

regions.name: Manjimup (Western Australia)
regions.summary: Cool, Mediterranean-type climate in Western Australia's south-west, with wet winters, mild summers and good soils in former karri forest country. Winters are mild, so chilling is moderate, but the region is the coolest major orchard area in the west.
regions.apple_culture: The Manjimup and Donnybrook area is Western Australia's main apple region, and the state has a remarkable breeding record: Pink Lady and Sundowner were bred in WA, and their parent Lady Williams came from a Donnybrook orchard. The newer apple sold as Bravo is another product of the state's breeding programme.
regions.pests_diseases: Western Australia is free of codling moth thanks to strict quarantine, which makes life easier for growers. Mediterranean fruit fly, light brown apple moth and woolly aphid are the main pests, and powdery mildew is common.
regions.tips: Respect WA's quarantine rules on bringing fruit and plants in from other states. Late varieties like Pink Lady suit the long, mild autumns here, but protect them from fruit fly.

regions.name: Granite Belt (Queensland)
regions.summary: A high granite plateau near Stanthorpe that is cold enough in winter for apples despite being in Queensland, with summer rain and storms. Frost is common, and summer hail is the biggest crop risk.
regions.apple_culture: The Granite Belt is Queensland's only real apple district, and the Stanthorpe area is known for apples, stone fruit and wine. Netting against hail has become common in local orchards.
regions.pests_diseases: Queensland fruit fly is a serious problem, and hail and summer storms damage fruit. Codling moth and black spot (scab) in humid spells are also common.
regions.tips: Net trees against hail and fruit fly, and choose late-flowering varieties to dodge spring frost. Good air movement helps reduce disease in the humid summers.

regions.name: Perth (Western Australia)
regions.summary: Hot, dry Mediterranean summers and mild, wet winters with little chilling on the coastal plain. Sandy soils hold little water or nutrient, so watering and feeding make or break backyard apples.
regions.apple_culture: Apples are a backyard tree in Perth itself, but the cooler Perth Hills have long had orchards, and Pink Lady was bred at Stoneville in the hills. Western Australia's quarantine keeps out codling moth, a big advantage for home growers.
regions.pests_diseases: Mediterranean fruit fly is the main pest of backyard fruit, and sunburn and heat stress are common. Codling moth is absent from Western Australia.
regions.tips: Use low-chill varieties on the coastal plain and keep standard varieties for the Hills. Improve sandy soil with compost and mulch, use drip irrigation, and bag fruit or use traps against Medfly.

regions.name: Sydney (New South Wales)
regions.summary: Humid subtropical coast with mild winters, hot humid summers and rain in every season. Chilling is low, so only low-chill varieties crop reliably.
regions.apple_culture: Sydney is the birthplace of the Granny Smith, which arose as a chance seedling in Maria Ann Smith's orchard at Eastwood in the 1860s and is still celebrated by a local festival. Today apples are backyard trees, with low-chill types the usual choice.
regions.pests_diseases: Queensland fruit fly is the main pest, and humid summers favour black spot (scab) and bitter rot. Codling moth and woolly aphid are also common.
regions.tips: Plant low-chill varieties in pairs for cross-pollination, and net or bag fruit against fruit fly. Keep the canopy open and remove fallen leaves to reduce disease.

regions.name: Maule Valley (Chile)
regions.summary: Mediterranean central-Chile valley: wet, mild winters that still give most mainstream varieties enough chilling, then a long, dry, cloudless summer with strong sun. Orchards depend on irrigation from Andean rivers, and the main climate risks are radiation frost in low spots at bloom and sunburned fruit in midsummer.
regions.apple_culture: Maule is the heart of Chile's export apple industry, with large modern orchards shipping counter-season fruit to Europe, Asia and North America. Planting follows the global market closely, so bicolour and red strains of the big club and commodity varieties dominate rather than local types.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth, woolly apple aphid, San Jose scale and mealybugs are the key insects, and export rules make them worth controlling. Sunburn is the most visible fruit defect; fire blight is absent from Chile, and scab is a problem only in rainy springs.
regions.tips: Water deeply and regularly through the dry summer and keep a full leaf canopy over the fruit; shade netting or kaolin clay sprays help against sunburn. Avoid frost-pocket hollows, and band trunks with corrugated cardboard to trap codling moth larvae.

regions.name: Los Lagos (Puerto Montt, Chile)
regions.summary: Cool, very wet temperate-oceanic climate on the Reloncavi Sound: plenty of winter chilling, mild winters, few hard frosts, and short, cool summers with rain in every month. Lack of summer heat and constant leaf wetness, not cold, are what limit apples here.
regions.apple_culture: Apples arrived with Spanish colonists and later German settlers around Lake Llanquihue, and old farmhouse orchards are part of the landscape. Southern Chile, especially neighbouring Chiloe, keeps a living tradition of chicha de manzana (rustic cider) made from dozens of old Spanish-derived and seedling varieties.
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab is severe in the near-constant damp, and European canker (Neonectria ditissima) is one of the main diseases of southern Chilean orchards. Woolly apple aphid is common on older trees.
regions.tips: Choose scab-resistant or old local cider and cooking types rather than dessert apples that need summer heat, and prune for an open, airy crown that dries quickly. Cut out canker lesions in dry weather and avoid pruning wounds during long wet spells.

regions.name: Alto Valle del Rio Negro (Argentina)
regions.summary: Irrigated desert valley in northern Patagonia: dry, sunny and windy, with cold winters that satisfy chilling easily and hot summer days with cool nights that colour fruit well. Spring frost is the defining hazard, along with occasional hail and the strong westerly winds.
regions.apple_culture: The Alto Valle of the Negro and Neuquen rivers is Argentina's main pome-fruit region, created by early twentieth-century irrigation canals and lined with tall poplar windbreaks. Pears are at least as important as apples, and much of the fruit is packed for export or turned into juice concentrate.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth (carpocapsa) is the main pest and the focus of a long-running area-wide control programme; oriental fruit moth, woolly aphid and San Jose scale also need watching. Low humidity keeps fungal diseases relatively light.
regions.tips: Plant behind a windbreak and away from low ground where frost pools, and favour later-flowering varieties. Irrigation is essential, and codling moth must be controlled every year: band trunks, thin fruit, and pick up fallen apples.

regions.name: Mendoza (Argentina)
regions.summary: Arid irrigated oases at the foot of the Andes: cold, dry winters with good chilling, intensely sunny summers, and very little rain. Spring frost and summer hail are the two weather events that wipe out fruit crops here, and high orchards in the Uco Valley see the biggest swings.
regions.apple_culture: Mendoza is wine country first; its apples are concentrated in the Uco Valley (Tunuyan, Tupungato, San Carlos), and the planted area has shrunk sharply as growers switched to vineyards and other crops. Most remaining apples go to the domestic market and processing.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth is the chief insect pest, and the province runs area-wide programmes against it and against Mediterranean fruit fly, so fruit movement can be restricted. Hail damage and sunburn spoil more fruit than disease does in this dry air.
regions.tips: Plan on full irrigation and, if you can, hail netting, which also cuts sunburn. Site trees on slopes rather than valley floors to dodge frost, and pick late-flowering varieties.

regions.name: Sao Joaquim (Brazil)
regions.summary: One of Brazil's coldest highland towns, on the Santa Catarina plateau, with frosty and occasionally snowy winters, but chilling is still marginal for classic varieties and winters vary a lot. Summers are mild, humid and rainy, and hailstorms are frequent.
regions.apple_culture: Brazil built its apple industry from the 1970s with government programmes, and Sao Joaquim, with Fraiburgo and Vacaria, became one of its centres, helped by Japanese-Brazilian growers. Gala and Fuji dominate, and the state research agency Epagri breeds varieties adapted to mild winters and local diseases.
regions.pests_diseases: Glomerella leaf spot (very damaging on Gala), apple scab and bitter rot thrive in the warm, wet summers; South American fruit fly and oriental fruit moth are the main insects. Brazil officially eradicated codling moth in 2014, so fruit movement rules matter.
regions.tips: Prefer varieties bred for mild winters and resistant to scab and Glomerella, such as the Epagri releases, rather than relying on Gala. Commercial growers use dormancy-breaking sprays to even out bloom after weak winters; at home, expect patchy flowering after warm winters and protect fruit from hail where you can.

regions.name: Cuauhtemoc (Chihuahua, Mexico)
regions.summary: High, semi-arid plateau in northern Mexico: cold, dry winters give reliable chilling, and summers are warm with a monsoon rainy season. Late spring frost and violent summer hailstorms are the main threats, and groundwater for irrigation is under heavy pressure.
regions.apple_culture: The Cuauhtemoc and Guerrero district is Mexico's largest apple region, built up through the twentieth century, with Mennonite farmers who settled there in the 1920s playing a big part. Golden and Red Delicious have long dominated, and hail netting now covers many orchards.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth is the main insect pest, and leafrollers have also appeared; fire blight can flare in warm, stormy springs and powdery mildew is common. Hail is the most destructive single risk to the crop.
regions.tips: Irrigate efficiently (drip), use hail netting if possible, and avoid frost-prone low ground. Choose later-flowering varieties and plant a compatible pollinizer, since many of the region's mainstays are not self-fertile.

regions.name: Zacatlan (Puebla, Mexico)
regions.summary: Misty highland town in the Sierra Norte of Puebla, cool all year, with dense fog and a long summer rainy season. Chilling is modest and winters are mild, so traditional varieties adapted to these conditions outperform imported temperate ones.
regions.apple_culture: Known as Zacatlan de las Manzanas, the town has held an apple fair every summer for decades and is famous for artisanal sidra (sweet sparkling cider) and fruit wines. Orchards are small family plots, overwhelmingly of the local striped apple 'Rayada' plus a range of other criollo varieties.
regions.pests_diseases: The persistent fog and summer rain favour scab and other fungal leaf and fruit diseases, and codling moth is present. Old seedling-based trees are often vigorous but carry plenty of disease.
regions.tips: Grow the local criollo types or other low- to moderate-chill varieties rather than northern classics, and prune hard for airflow so leaves dry between fog banks. Clean up fallen leaves and fruit to reduce scab carry-over.

regions.name: Bogota highlands (Colombia)
regions.summary: High Andean savanna almost on the equator: cool and spring-like all year, with no true winter, frequent cloud, and two rainy seasons. Apple trees never get the seasonal cold signal to go dormant, so without intervention they grow and bloom erratically.
regions.apple_culture: Colombia does grow apples, mainly in nearby Boyaca, where low-chill varieties are forced into a cropping cycle by stripping the leaves after harvest and applying bud-break treatments, sometimes giving two crops a year. 'Anna' is the dominant variety; around Bogota itself, apples are a curiosity in gardens.
regions.pests_diseases: Constant mild, humid conditions favour powdery mildew and scab, and fruit flies attack fruit. Uneven, out-of-season flowering also makes pest control harder because some trees are always at a vulnerable stage.
regions.tips: Only very low-chill varieties are worth trying, and you will need to defoliate the tree by hand after harvest to trigger a new flush and bloom. Treat it as an experiment; local deciduous fruits such as plums and pears grown the same way, or highland fruits like tree tomato, are easier.

regions.name: Wenatchee (Washington)
regions.summary: Semi-arid rain-shadow valley on the east side of the Cascades: cold winters with ample chilling, hot, dry, very sunny summers, and almost no summer rain. Irrigation is essential, disease pressure is low, and the main weather risks are spring frost, sunburn, and occasional severe winter freezes.
regions.apple_culture: Wenatchee calls itself the Apple Capital of the World and sits in the middle of Washington's industry, which grows most of the fresh apples sold in the United States. Washington State University runs a tree-fruit research centre here, and its breeding programme produced 'Cosmic Crisp'.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth is the key pest, and fire blight can strike in warm springs; powdery mildew is common on susceptible varieties. Sunburn and bitter pit are major fruit disorders, while scab is rare in the dry air. Apple maggot is kept out of the commercial districts by quarantine.
regions.tips: Water deeply and regularly, keep foliage over the fruit, and consider kaolin sprays or shade cloth against sunburn. Control codling moth every year, because neglected backyard trees threaten commercial neighbours, and do not bring home-grown fruit in from western Washington.

regions.name: Hood River (Oregon)
regions.summary: Valley in the Columbia River Gorge on the transition from wet west-side to dry east-side climate: snowy winters, warm dry summers, and a steep gradient from the lower to the upper valley. Strong Gorge winds, spring frost and occasional damaging winter freezes are the main hazards.
regions.apple_culture: Hood River first won fame for Yellow Newtown and Spitzenburg apples, but a severe 1919 freeze killed many trees and growers replanted largely with pears. Today it is a leading winter-pear district with apples as a secondary crop, and the 'Fruit Loop' farm-stand route draws visitors at harvest.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth is the main insect pest and fire blight is a constant concern in this pear-heavy valley. Powdery mildew is common, and scab appears in wet springs, especially in the upper valley.
regions.tips: Give trees shelter from the Gorge wind and avoid frost-prone low spots. Choose varieties suited to your elevation, since upper-valley sites are cooler and later, and remove fire blight strikes promptly because pears nearby carry it.

regions.name: Puget Sound (Seattle)
regions.summary: Mild maritime climate: wet, cool winters with adequate chilling, long, damp springs, and dry but cool summers. Summer heat is limited, so late-ripening varieties often fail to mature, while the wet season drives disease.
regions.apple_culture: Western Washington is backyard and community-orchard country rather than a commercial belt, with active fruit societies, urban food forests and cider makers. Washington State University's Mount Vernon station trials cider and dessert varieties suited to the cool, wet west side.
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab and anthracnose canker are the signature diseases of the wet west side; powdery mildew and bull's-eye rot also occur. Apple maggot and codling moth are well established in backyard trees.
regions.tips: Plant scab-resistant, early- to mid-season varieties and give them the sunniest, best-drained spot you have. Bag young fruit (nylon footies are a local favourite) to stop apple maggot and codling moth, and cut out anthracnose cankers in dry weather.

regions.name: Sebastopol (Sonoma, California)
regions.summary: Coastal-influenced western Sonoma County: wet, mild winters with moderate chilling, then dry summers cooled by fog drifting in from the Pacific. The cool mornings suit early and mid-season apples, while a fully dry summer means trees need watering in light soils.
regions.apple_culture: Sebastopol is the home of the Gravenstein in California, with a Gravenstein Highway, an apple blossom festival and an apple fair, though many orchards have given way to vineyards. Luther Burbank's experimental farm was here, and a lively cider and heirloom scene keeps old varieties in demand.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth is the main insect, scab appears in rainy springs, and powdery mildew thrives in the foggy, dry-leaf summers. Fire blight is occasional.
regions.tips: Gravenstein ripens in mid-summer and keeps poorly, so pair it with later keepers and use it for sauce and juice. Mulch and water through the dry season, and choose scab- and mildew-resistant varieties if you want to spray little.

regions.name: Pajaro Valley (Watsonville, California)
regions.summary: Cool, foggy coastal valley near Monterey Bay: mild winters with marginal-to-moderate chilling, and long, cool, overcast summers that ripen fruit slowly. Fog-tolerant green and yellow apples historically did better here than varieties needing strong sun to colour.
regions.apple_culture: The Pajaro Valley was once called Apple City, famous for Newtown Pippin and Bellflower apples dried and shipped worldwide, and Martinelli's has made sparkling cider from local Newtown Pippins since the late 1800s. Strawberries and cane berries have replaced most orchards, and the remaining growers depend heavily on juice markets.
regions.pests_diseases: Powdery mildew is favoured by the foggy, mild summers, and codling moth is the main insect pest. Scab can appear in wet springs.
regions.tips: Choose moderate-chill varieties that colour without much sun, and favour mildew-resistant types or prune for airflow. Thin fruit early so it sizes during the long cool season, and leave late varieties on the tree to develop flavour.

regions.name: Los Angeles basin (California)
regions.summary: Mild Mediterranean basin with warm, dry summers and frost-free or nearly frost-free winters, so winter chilling is very low near the coast and only a little better in the inland valleys and foothills. Hot spells and dry Santa Ana winds can sunburn fruit and stress trees.
regions.apple_culture: Apples are a backyard crop here, made possible by low-chill varieties from Israel, Bermuda and California breeding. Southern California is the birthplace of the California Rare Fruit Growers and of the 'backyard orchard culture' style of small, summer-pruned trees.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth is the main fruit pest, and sunburn and heat stress are common. Low-chill trees bloom early and over a long period, which can expose them to fire blight in warm, damp spring weather.
regions.tips: Plant genuinely low-chill varieties and pair them for pollination (Anna with Dorsett Golden is the classic match). Inland valleys and foothills get more chill than the coast; water deeply but infrequently, paint trunks white, and keep trees small with summer pruning.

regions.name: Southern Michigan (Berrien and Van Buren)
regions.summary: Lake Michigan's 'fruit belt': prevailing westerly winds over the lake keep springs cool, delaying bloom past many frosts, and soften autumn freezes. Winters bring lake-effect snow and plenty of chilling, while humid summers create high disease pressure.
regions.apple_culture: Southwest Michigan has grown apples, peaches, cherries and grapes for well over a century, with roadside markets, u-pick farms and Michigan State University research stations in the area. Michigan is one of the top apple states, and this end of it is known for processing apples and a strong cider scene.
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab and fire blight are the big diseases; a severe fire blight epidemic in 2000 killed large numbers of trees here. Plum curculio, codling moth, apple maggot and oriental fruit moth all need managing, and cedar-apple rust is common.
regions.tips: Plant on slopes with cold-air drainage, close to the lake if you can. Choose scab-resistant varieties and fire-blight-resistant rootstocks (such as the Geneva series), and avoid heavy nitrogen that drives soft, blight-prone growth.

regions.name: Traverse City (northern Michigan)
regions.summary: Grand Traverse Bay country, where deep lake water moderates temperatures: cold, snowy winters, late springs that hold bloom back, and pleasant but shorter summers than the south of the state. Lake-moderated hillsides and peninsulas are much safer than inland hollows.
regions.apple_culture: The region is best known for tart cherries, but apples are a major crop on Old Mission and Leelanau peninsulas, much of it for processing such as slices and sauce. It also has a thriving hard-cider and winery trade, and Michigan State runs a horticultural research station nearby.
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab is the main disease in the cool, wet springs, with fire blight in warm bloom periods. Plum curculio, apple maggot and codling moth are the key insects.
regions.tips: Choose hardy varieties that ripen before mid-October; very late ones such as Fuji or Granny Smith rarely mature well. Plant on a slope near the water for frost protection and keep a scab programme or plant resistant varieties.

regions.name: Hudson Valley (New York)
regions.summary: Humid continental river valley: cold winters with ample chilling, warm, humid summers and frequent rain. The river and valley slopes moderate frost somewhat, but late spring frosts and long wet periods are routine, so disease pressure is high.
regions.apple_culture: One of the oldest apple-growing regions in North America, settled by Dutch and English farmers and the birthplace of Esopus Spitzenburg. It remains a major McIntosh district for the New York City market, with Cornell's Hudson Valley lab and a fast-growing craft cider movement.
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab, fire blight and summer diseases such as sooty blotch and flyspeck are constant; cedar-apple rust is common. Plum curculio, apple maggot, codling moth and brown marmorated stink bug are the main insects.
regions.tips: If you want to spray little, start with scab-resistant varieties like Liberty, Enterprise or GoldRush and bag fruit to beat curculio and maggot. Rake leaves in autumn to cut scab, and favour hillside sites over the valley floor.

regions.name: Finger Lakes (New York)
regions.summary: Glacial lakes too deep to freeze moderate the surrounding slopes, delaying spring bloom and extending autumn. Winters are cold and snowy with abundant chilling, and summers are warm and humid, with Lake Ontario's shore to the north as the core commercial apple belt.
regions.apple_culture: Geneva is one of the world's centres of apple science: Cornell AgriTech bred Cortland, Macoun, Empire, Jonagold, Liberty and SnapDragon, the Geneva rootstocks come from here, and the USDA keeps a vast apple germplasm collection nearby. Northern Spy originated near the region, and cider houses now sit alongside the wineries.
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab and fire blight are the major diseases; codling moth, apple maggot, plum curculio and obliquebanded leafroller are the main insects.
regions.tips: Use Geneva rootstocks for fire blight tolerance and plant on slopes near the lakes for frost protection. Local releases like Liberty give you scab resistance without giving up flavour.

regions.name: Champlain Valley (Vermont)
regions.summary: The warmest, driest corner of Vermont, where Lake Champlain softens temperatures on its shores. Winters are still severe, with occasional deep cold that injures tender varieties, and springs are cool and wet; summers are warm enough for a full McIntosh-type season.
regions.apple_culture: Addison County along the lake is Vermont's main commercial apple area, long devoted to McIntosh and its relatives. Orchards here now supply a strong Vermont cider scene, and old varieties such as Snow apple (Fameuse) recall the region's links with Quebec.
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab is the dominant disease, and McIntosh-type apples are very susceptible; fire blight and cedar-apple rust also occur. Apple maggot and plum curculio are the key insects, and voles and deer damage trees in winter.
regions.tips: Pick cold-hardy varieties and rootstocks, and use vole guards and deer fencing. Choose scab-resistant varieties or commit to a scab programme, and avoid varieties that ripen too late for the season.

regions.name: Pioneer Valley (Massachusetts)
regions.summary: Connecticut River valley in western Massachusetts: cold winters with ample chilling, warm, humid summers and regular rain. Low valley floors are notorious frost pockets, while the hill towns on either side drain cold air better but have shorter seasons.
regions.apple_culture: Massachusetts is the cradle of New England apples, home of Roxbury Russet and Baldwin, and the valley has old family orchards, u-pick farms and heirloom collections. UMass Amherst's Cold Spring Orchard in Belchertown carries out apple research for the region.
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab, fire blight and cedar-apple rust (with abundant red cedar nearby) are the major diseases. Plum curculio and apple maggot are the classic New England insect pests.
regions.tips: Plant on a gentle slope rather than the valley bottom so cold air drains away. Scab-resistant varieties such as Liberty, Freedom or Redfree cut spraying, and you should keep ornamental junipers well away from apples.

regions.name: Central Maine
regions.summary: Cold, snowy interior New England: long winters with deep cold snaps, short but warm summers, and plenty of rain. Hardiness and early ripening matter more than chilling, and snow cover brings vole and deer damage.
regions.apple_culture: Central Maine is the heart of the US heritage-apple revival: Fedco Trees and orchardist John Bunker have spent decades rescuing old Maine varieties, and MOFGA's Maine Heritage Orchard in Unity preserves hundreds of them. Old farmhouse trees and wild seedlings are everywhere, and cider making is popular.
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab and apple maggot are the main problems, with plum curculio close behind. Winter moth is an invasive defoliator near the coast, and voles under the snow can girdle young trees.
regions.tips: Use hardy rootstocks such as Antonovka seedling or B.118 and varieties proven in Maine, many of which local nurseries stock. Put hardware-cloth guards around trunks before snowfall and pick early- to mid-season varieties that ripen before hard frost.

regions.name: Adams County (Pennsylvania)
regions.summary: Mid-Atlantic fruit belt along the slopes of South Mountain: cold-enough winters for full chilling, hot and humid summers, and a long season. Ridge and slope sites drain frost well, but the summer heat and humidity bring heavy disease and insect pressure.
regions.apple_culture: Adams County is Pennsylvania's apple county, with a large processing industry built around the Knouse Foods cooperative, the National Apple Museum in Biglerville and Penn State's fruit research centre. York Imperial, a processing favourite from neighbouring York County, has long been grown here.
regions.pests_diseases: Brown marmorated stink bug became a severe pest here after about 2010, alongside codling moth and oriental fruit moth. Fire blight, scab, bitter rot and sooty blotch/flyspeck are the main diseases in the hot, wet summers.
regions.tips: Choose disease-resistant varieties such as GoldRush or Enterprise and fire-blight-tolerant Geneva rootstocks. Bagging fruit helps against stink bugs and summer rots, and good sanitation of mummified fruit reduces bitter rot.

regions.name: Shenandoah Valley (Winchester, Virginia)
regions.summary: Northern Shenandoah Valley between the Blue Ridge and Alleghenies: cold enough in winter for full chilling, but with hot, humid summers and frequent thunderstorms. Erratic spring warm-ups followed by frost are a recurring risk, and the long humid summer favours fruit rots.
regions.apple_culture: Winchester has held the Shenandoah Apple Blossom Festival since the 1920s and was long one of the great apple towns of the East, with processing plants making sauce and juice. Virginia Tech runs a fruit research centre here, and the state's cider revival draws on Virginia apple traditions.
regions.pests_diseases: Summer rots (bitter rot and white rot), fire blight, cedar-apple rust and sooty blotch/flyspeck are the main diseases. Codling moth, oriental fruit moth and brown marmorated stink bug are the key insects.
regions.tips: Remove mummified fruit and dead wood every winter to reduce summer rots, and choose varieties with good disease resistance. Plant on slopes for frost drainage, and favour late-blooming types.

regions.name: Henderson County (North Carolina)
regions.summary: Plateau of the southern Blue Ridge at moderate elevation: mild for the latitude but with enough winter chill, warm, humid summers and frequent rain. Hillside 'thermal belts' stay noticeably warmer on frosty spring nights than the valley bottoms, which is why orchards climb the slopes.
regions.apple_culture: Henderson County grows most of North Carolina's apples, and Hendersonville hosts the NC Apple Festival every Labor Day weekend. The wider southern Appalachians are rich in old 'mountain apples', many rescued by heirloom collectors.
regions.pests_diseases: Bitter rot and Glomerella leaf spot are serious in the warm, wet summers, alongside fire blight, scab and cedar-apple rust. Codling moth, brown marmorated stink bug and Japanese beetles are the main insects.
regions.tips: Plant on a mid-slope thermal belt, not in a frost hollow. Choose varieties that tolerate southern summers and resist rots, and keep a strict winter clean-up of mummies and cankered wood.

regions.name: Ellijay (Georgia)
regions.summary: Low mountains of north Georgia: winters give moderate chilling but swing between warm spells and cold snaps, so early bloom followed by frost is common. Summers are long, hot and humid, making disease the main limit on fruit quality.
regions.apple_culture: Ellijay calls itself Georgia's Apple Capital, with roadside stands and u-pick orchards lining the mountain highways and a big apple festival each October. Southern heritage apples such as Yates, which originated in Georgia, sit alongside commercial varieties.
regions.pests_diseases: Bitter rot, Glomerella leaf spot, fire blight and cedar-apple rust are the main diseases in the humid heat. Plum curculio, codling moth and brown marmorated stink bug need managing.
regions.tips: Choose disease-resistant or southern-adapted varieties (GoldRush, Enterprise or heirlooms like Yates and Arkansas Black) and fire-blight-tolerant rootstocks. Site trees on slopes, and clean up fallen and mummified fruit to reduce rots.

regions.name: Wooster (Ohio)
regions.summary: Humid continental northeast-central Ohio: cold winters with reliable chilling, warm, humid summers and regular rainfall throughout the season. Late frosts after early warm spells and steady disease pressure are the main challenges.
regions.apple_culture: Wooster is home to Ohio State's agricultural research campus (formerly the Ohio Agricultural Experiment Station), where 'Melrose', Ohio's official state apple, was bred. The area is in the heart of Johnny Appleseed country and nearby Amish communities keep up small orchards and cider pressing.
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab, fire blight, cedar-apple rust and sooty blotch/flyspeck are the main diseases. Codling moth, plum curculio and apple maggot are the key insects.
regions.tips: Choose scab-resistant varieties or be ready to spray in wet springs, and use fire-blight-tolerant rootstocks. Rake and remove leaves in autumn and plant away from red cedars.

regions.name: Bayfield (Wisconsin)
regions.summary: Bayfield Peninsula on Lake Superior, one of the most northerly commercial fruit areas in the US: long, cold, snowy winters, cool lake-chilled springs that hold back bloom, and short, mild summers. Orchards sit on the hills above the lake, where cold air drains away.
regions.apple_culture: Bayfield's orchards date to the late 1800s, when fruit shipped by boat, and its Apple Festival each autumn is a regional event. Hardy varieties like Wealthy and McIntosh were the historic staples, now joined by Minnesota-bred apples.
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab is the main disease in the cool, damp springs. Apple maggot and plum curculio are the main insects, and winter injury, voles and deer cause much of the damage.
regions.tips: Grow very hardy varieties, especially Minnesota and Wisconsin releases, on hardy rootstocks. Plant on a slope facing the lake, and protect trunks from voles and sunscald.

regions.name: Twin Cities (Minnesota)
regions.summary: Severe continental climate: very cold winters with occasional deep freezes, short springs, and hot, humid summers. Winter hardiness of both variety and rootstock decides what survives, and late frost and sunscald on trunks are common problems.
regions.apple_culture: The University of Minnesota's breeding programme near the Twin Cities is one of the most influential in the world, producing Haralson, Honeycrisp, Zestar!, SweeTango and many more; Wealthy was raised nearby in the 1860s. Small orchards ring the metro, and Minnesota-bred apples are a point of local pride.
regions.pests_diseases: Apple scab, fire blight and cedar-apple rust are the main diseases; apple maggot and plum curculio are the key insects. Rabbits, voles and deer cause serious winter damage.
regions.tips: Grow Minnesota-bred or similarly hardy varieties on hardy rootstocks, and wrap or paint trunks to prevent southwest winter injury. Fit rabbit and vole guards before snow, and avoid late varieties that cannot ripen before hard frost.

regions.name: Paonia (Colorado)
regions.summary: High-elevation western Colorado valley: cold winters with ample chilling, dry air, strong sun, and warm days with cool nights in summer. Irrigation water comes from mountain snowmelt, and spring frost is the defining risk, with some years losing the whole crop.
regions.apple_culture: Fruit has been grown in the North Fork Valley since the town was founded in the 1880s, and Paonia fruit won prizes at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair. Today it is a hub of small organic farms, u-pick orchards and cideries reviving Colorado's once-large apple trade.
regions.pests_diseases: Codling moth is the main insect pest, and fire blight and powdery mildew are the significant diseases. Iron chlorosis on alkaline soils and frost damage are common, while scab is rare in the dry air.
regions.tips: Plant on mesas or benches above the valley floor where cold air drains away, and choose late-blooming varieties. Use drip irrigation, watch for yellowing leaves on alkaline soils, and keep codling moth in check every year.

regions.name: Texas Hill Country (Medina)
regions.summary: Hot, subtropical-edge climate on the Edwards Plateau: chilling is limited and varies greatly between winters, and warm spells in late winter can trigger early bloom that is then frosted. Summers are long, hot and often dry, with alkaline, rocky soils.
regions.apple_culture: Medina styles itself the Apple Capital of Texas, thanks largely to Love Creek Orchards, which showed from the 1980s that dwarf apple trees could crop here, and an apple festival each summer. Apples remain a niche, high-effort crop in Texas compared with peaches.
regions.pests_diseases: Cotton root rot, a soil fungus common in alkaline Texas soils, can kill apple trees suddenly in summer. Fire blight, codling moth, heat stress and drought are the other major problems, and deer browse young trees.
regions.tips: Check whether cotton root rot is known on your land before planting, and choose low- to moderate-chill varieties suited to central Texas. Irrigate reliably, mulch, and fence out deer.

regions.name: Gainesville (Florida)
regions.summary: Humid subtropical north-central Florida: very little winter chilling, frequent winter warm spells, then long, hot, wet summers. Standard apple varieties never get the cold they need, so they leaf out poorly and do not fruit.
regions.apple_culture: Apples are a hobbyist's challenge here, possible only with low-chill varieties; the University of Florida has trialled them and released 'TropicSweet' for this kind of climate. Fruit ripens in early summer, ahead of the worst heat.
regions.pests_diseases: Fire blight, bitter rot and other summer fruit rots are serious in the heat and humidity. Early bloom is often hit by late frosts, and trees tend to be short-lived.
regions.tips: Grow only true low-chill varieties and plant two that bloom together (Anna with Dorsett Golden). Give full sun and good drainage, pick fruit as soon as it is ripe, and treat apples as a bonus rather than a staple.

regions.name: Phoenix (Arizona)
regions.summary: Low Sonoran Desert: very mild winters with little chilling, and extremely hot, dry summers. Heat, sunburn and alkaline soil are bigger obstacles than cold, and only a few low-chill apples fruit at all.
regions.apple_culture: Apples are a backyard novelty in the Valley, grown by enthusiasts with low-chill varieties that ripen in early summer; commercial apple growing in Arizona happens at higher elevations, not in Phoenix. Citrus and dates are the region's tree crops.
regions.pests_diseases: Sunburn of fruit, bark and leaves is the main damage, along with heat stress. Iron chlorosis is common in alkaline soil, and cotton (Texas) root rot can kill trees. Codling moth is still present on backyard trees.
regions.tips: Plant low-chill varieties in winter, give afternoon shade or shade cloth in summer, and paint trunks white. Water deeply and regularly, mulch heavily, and harvest in late spring to early summer before the peak heat.

regions.name: Anchorage (Alaska)
regions.summary: Subarctic coastal climate: long, cold, snowy winters, late springs, and short, cool summers with very long days. Heat to ripen fruit, not winter chill, is the limiting factor, and hardiness matters as much as earliness.
regions.apple_culture: A dedicated community of growers, led by the Alaska Pioneer Fruit Growers Association, has trialled a long list of varieties and holds annual apple tastings. Very hardy Canadian prairie apples and crab hybrids are the backbone of Anchorage orchards.
regions.pests_diseases: There is little of the classic apple pest list here; the main damage comes from moose browsing, voles under the snow, and winter dieback. Spider mites and aphids are occasional problems.
regions.tips: Choose early, prairie-hardy varieties or apple-crab hybrids on hardy rootstock, and plant against a warm, south-facing wall or slope. Fence against moose and guard trunks against voles; a greenhouse or high tunnel widens the range of what ripens.

regions.name: Okanagan Valley (British Columbia)
regions.summary: Semi-arid interior valley of long, deep lakes: cold winters with ample chilling but occasional damaging arctic outbreaks, and hot, dry, sunny summers.
